en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Guide (Nettippakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā) in the Minor Collection (Khuddakanikāya).
Introduction to the Work:
I pay homage to the Lord of Great Compassion, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of all that is to be known, and who teaches through methods that are skillful, profound, and diverse.
I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, honored by the Fully Enlightened One, endowed with true knowledge and conduct, by which one is led out from the world;
it is perfected in qualities such as virtue and is established in the paths and fruits.
I pay homage to that Noble Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
By the power of whatever merit has been generated through this homage to the Triple Gem,
may I be free from all obstacles everywhere.
Requested by the elder named Dhammarakkhita, who desires the long endurance of the guidance of the True Dhamma,
[this was composed] at the feet of the Lord Padumuttara.
To him who had passed beyond the initial resolve and reached its ultimate peak— to him, the supreme among the Great Disciples,
whom the Neutral One (Tādi) designated as "the foremost" while analyzing what had been briefly stated—
he was established in this position of preeminence.
The Elder Mahākaccāyana, possessed of the six direct knowledges, attained to mastery, and having broken through to the analytical insights, was praised by the Fully Enlightened One.
The Guide Manual (Netti) which was spoken by him was approved by the Teacher.
This commentary on the meaning of the ninefold Teaching of the Dispensation always depends upon that Dispensation itself.
Although the exposition of its meaning is difficult for me to compose— since it must be plunged into by those possessing profound knowledge— [I nevertheless undertake it].
Since it preserves the Teacher’s Dispensation along with its commentary,
and the exposition of the lions among the ancient masters remains intact,
therefore, relying upon that and delving into all five [Piṭakas], [one should study].
Having compared it with the Piṭaka according to the Nikāyas, as far as my ability allowed,
I have produced this precise determination of meaning— utterly pure, unadulterated,
and not contrary to the doctrine of the Mahāvihāravāsins.
Avoiding the errors of negligence and correctly applying the canonical text (pāḷi),
while elucidating the instructions (upadesa), I shall compose this commentary on the meaning.
Thus, for me, the meaning of the *Nettippakaraṇa* remains unconfused.
"Listen attentively as I analyze it, O virtuous ones.

In this context, in what sense is it called *netti* (the guide)? It is called *netti* in the sense of guiding the True Dhamma (*saddhammanayana*). For just as craving (*taṇhā*) is called "the guide to existence" (*bhavanetti*) because it leads beings to existence such as that of sensual desire (*kāma*), so too this [work] is called *netti* in the sense of guiding the True Dhamma because it leads those beings who are to be trained (*veneyyasatta*) to the Noble Dhamma (*ariyadhamma*).
It is called "Netti" (The Guide). Alternatively, it is a "Netti" because they lead by means of it;
for by means of the *Nettippakaraṇa* acting as the instrument, preachers of the Dhamma lead those beings who are ready to be trained to the path of vision, bringing them there.

Or else, it is a "Netti" because those to be trained are led—having been established within this treatise acting as the foundation—to reach Nibbāna. It is not... [the sentence is incomplete in the source].
For indeed, without reliance upon the guidance of the *Netti*, the unerring comprehension of the meaning of the Suttas is not possible. Thus it has been said:
"Therefore, by one desiring to attain Nibbāna," and so forth. For all exegesis of the meaning of the Suttas is dependent upon the guidance of the *Netti*;
the *Netti* itself originates from the Suttas; and the Suttas originate from the Perfectly Enlightened One.
This *Netti* is threefold according to the divisions of its treatise, by way of the *hāra* (modes of conveying), the *naya* (guidelines), and the *paṭṭhāna* (foundations).

For first there is the investigation of the *hāras*, then the investigation of the *nayās*, and finally the investigation of the *paṭṭhānas*. According to the establishment of the text, however, it is twofold, by way of the section on Compendium (*saṅgahavāra*) and the section on Analysis (*vibhāgavāra*).
For the entire *Netti* consists of only these two sections: the Compendium Section and the Analysis Section.

Therein, the section on inclusion (saṅgahavāra) is demarcated by the first five verses. Indeed, there is no purpose of this treatise that is not encompassed by these five verses beginning with “That which the world worships.
[Objection: But is it not the case that the *Paṭṭhāna* (the Book of Causal Relations) is not included here?
[Reply: This should not be viewed in such a way, because the *Paṭṭhāna* is included by virtue of the inclusion of its root-terms.
For it will be said: "Where are the eighteen root-terms to be found? In the *Sāsanappaṭṭhāna*.
Indeed, the root-term *paṭṭhānas* are mutually grouped together, just like the triads of meaning, method, and formations.

Furthermore, the section on analysis (*vibhāgavāra*) is threefold, by way of enumeration (*uddesa*), exposition (*niddesa*), and detailed exposition (*paṭiniddesa*). Among these, "In that regard, which are the sixteen... [and so forth].
The section on the summary begins with “The strings” and extends as far as “there are eighteen terms.

The section on the exposition begins with “In terms of gratification and danger” and extends as far as “the net consists of thirty-three such [terms]. The section on further exposition, however, is fourfold:

the section on the analysis of the strings, the section on the convergence of the strings, the section on the origin of the methods, and the section on the foundation of the Dispensation. Among these, “Therein... [is the beginning of the first sub-section].
Beginning with “What is the Mode of Conveying a Teaching? and extending as far as “This is the coordination by way of abandoning,” this is the section on the Analysis of the Modes (Hāravibhaṅgavāra).

Therein, beginning with “What is the Coordination of the Mode of Conveying a Teaching? and extending as far as “and the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining,” this is the section on the Coordination of the Modes (Hārasampātavāra).
Here it is asked: what is the difference between the sections on the Analysis of the Modes and the Coordination of the Modes?
It is said: Where even by means of many illustrative suttas a single method (hāra) is demonstrated, this is the section on the analysis of methods (hāravibhaṅgavāra).
But where many methods converge within a single sutta, this is the section on the convergence of methods (hārasampātavāra).
For this has been stated in the Peṭaka: “And where all the methods, converging together, lead to the meaning of the sutta...”
"Because of the diversity of the methods of phrasing, that stage is the convergence of the modes of exposition.
The analysis of the sections on the origin of the methods and the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna* (the Foundation of the Dispensation) is indeed evident.

However, the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna* section has not been extracted in its own form from either the sections on the summary or the sections on the enumeration and exposition, as it was in the summary section. Here it is said: "This is the *Nettippakaraṇa*..."
And how is it known that this was spoken by the Great Disciples and approved by the Blessed One? It is known from the Canon (Pāḷi) itself;
for there is no authority greater than the Canon. Whatever text is not contradicted by the four Great Authorities (mahāpadesa) is authoritative.
Thus, like the *Peṭakopadesa*, this *Nettippakaraṇa* has come down through an unblemished succession of teachers.
[It was] brought forth. If this is so, why was its introductory narrative (*nidāna*) not stated?

For is it not the case that for certain discourses spoken by disciples—such as the *Subha-sutta*, the *Anaṅgaṇa-sutta*, and the *Kaccāyana-saṃyutta*—an introductory narrative was indeed spoken? This is not an absolute rule;
for among those spoken by disciples, as well as some spoken by the Buddha, such as the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, the *Niddesa*, and others like the *Dhammapada* and the *Buddhavaṃsa*, [the same applies].
The introduction (nidāna) was not spoken [by the Buddha], yet it does not follow that those [other parts] are not of immeasurable value; this should be understood in the same way here as well.
Furthermore, the introductions to the Suttas and the Vinaya were indeed spoken by great disciples such as the Elder Upāli, the treasurer of the Dhamma, and others;
and since this [present work] is spoken by a great disciple—and because there is no other scope for this investigation apart from the Elder—what is the point of this [objection]?
By investigating the introduction (*nidāna*), it is the meaning alone that should be sought here, provided it is not in conflict with the text (*pāḷi*).

Alternatively, it should be understood that because this work is a commentary on the meaning of the text, there is no need for a separate statement of an introduction, as is the case with the *Paṭisambhidāmagga-niddesa* and other such works.
Now, in order to provide proficiency in various aspects regarding this treatise, this classification should be understood: all of it...
This treatise is of one kind because it consists in the search for the Dispensation (*sāsana*), as well as because it accomplishes the Noble Path and yields the flavor of liberation.

It is of two kinds because it consists in the investigation of both the letter and the meaning; likewise, because it consists in both compendium and analysis; because it provides a commentary on the meaning of both the Dhamma and the Vinaya;

because it encompasses both mundane and supramundane meanings; because it discerns both material and immaterial phenomena; and because it consists in the relationship between the characteristic and that which is characterized.
Because it speaks of the occurrence and cessation [of existence], because of its exposition of the similar and the dissimilar, and because of its analysis of common and uncommon phenomena;

because of its exposition of the three types of persons, because of its analysis of the three kinds of excellence, because of its discussion of the threefold full understanding, because of its instruction on the threefold abandonment, because of its inclusion of the three trainings, because of its purification of the threefold defilements,
and because of the distinctions between the root recitation, the subsequent recitation, and the communal chanting.
It is threefold by way of the commentary on the meaning of the Three Piṭakas, and by way of the divisions of the *Hāra*, the *Naya*, and the *Paṭṭhāna*.

It is fourfold by way of being the object of the four analytical insights (*catuppaṭisambhidā*), by way of the teaching of the four methods (*catunaya*), and by way of its profound nature in the penetration of the teaching of the Dhamma and its meaning.

It is fivefold by way of the classification of phenomena such as those to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*), by way of the exposition of the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandha*), and by way of the delimitation of the five destinies (*pañcagati*).

It is fivefold by way of the exposition of the meaning of the five collections (*nikāya*). It is sixfold by way of the classification of the six objects and the classification of the six internal and external sense bases.
It is sevenfold by way of the delimitation of the seven stations of consciousness. It is ninefold by way of the description of the nine factors beginning with the discourses (*sutta*).
It is fourteenfold by way of the classification of the discourses as their basis. It is sixteenfold and twenty-eightfold by way of the divisions of the *Sāsana-paṭṭhāna*.

The classification of the treatise should be understood according to the method beginning with: "It consists of eighty-four thousandfold divisions, as it comprises the investigation and cultivation of eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma.
In this context, regarding the cultivation of the search for the Dispensation, the entire *Nettippakaraṇa* is comprised within the ninefold collection that subsumes the three trainings.

Because it is a commentary on the meaning of the Teacher’s dispensation (*satthusāsana*). "By way of accomplishing the Noble Path" means by way of accomplishing the stage of vision (*dassanabhūmi*) and the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanābhūmi*).
"From the flavor of liberation" is stated because the dispensation has the Deathless as its ultimate goal (*amatapariyosāna*).

"Because of the nature of investigating the phrasing and the meaning" is said because there is an investigation of the phrasing through the modes of stringing together (*hāra*), phrasing (*byañjana*), words (*pada*), and functions (*kamma*), and an investigation of the meaning through the modes of words (*pada*) and meaning (*attha*).
It has been stated. The nature of the analysis of the categories will be made clear later on.
"As a commentary on the meaning of the Dhamma and Vinaya" is said because the entirety of the scriptural teaching (pariyatti-sāsana) possesses the nature of both Dhamma and Vinaya.

"As having the nature of the characteristic and the characterized" is said because the *Netti* statement functions as the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) and the illustrative suttas function as the characterized (*lakkhiya*). "As a description of the similar and the dissimilar" is said...
Phenomena (dhammas) of the same class are "homogeneous" (sabhāga), while those that are opposites are "heterogeneous" (visabhāga); this is the meaning of "by way of their state of investigation.

By way of the distinction between common and uncommon phenomena: the meaning is that they are twofold by way of distinguishing those phenomena which, through their commonality—such as being abandoned together or arising together—are common to certain other phenomena by way of name, basis, and so forth, and those which, due to being the opposite of that, are uncommon.

"By way of the exposition of the three types of persons" means by way of the exposition of the three types of persons, such as those who understand through a brief summary (*ugghaṭitaññu*), and so forth. "By way of the analysis of the threefold excellence" means by way of the analysis of being excellent in the beginning and so forth.
"By way of the distinction between the root-verse, the subsequent verse, and the formal recitation" means that the first statement is the root-verse (*mūlagīti*);

the summary verses of the very meaning already stated are the subsequent verses (*anugīti*); and [the commentary] is composed by way of connecting the various meanings of the suttas, which had been scattered [in the original].
"Recitation" (*saṅgīti*) refers to the rehearsal of the treatise; it should be understood as having proceeded after the Elder.

The meaning is that it is "threefold" by way of the division of these three [recitations]. The meaning is that it is "fivefold" by way of the exposition of the five aggregates, such as form, and the exposition of the five aggregates of dhammas, such as virtue.
The meaning is that it is "divided according to the basis of the suttas" by way of greed, hatred, and delusion, and non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.

The meaning of "of fourteen kinds" is that it is so called because it explains the classification of the fourteenfold exposition based on the discourses (*sutta*), by way of the bodily, verbal, and mental actions as well as the five faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*).
The remainder is easy to understand and has not been elaborated upon.
1. Commentary on the Section on Compendium (*Saṅgahavāra-vaṇṇanā*)
Thus, regarding this *Nettippakaraṇa* which is analyzed into many divisions, it has been stated that "it is twofold by way of the sections on Compendium (*saṅgaha*) and Analysis (*vibhāga*).
Therein, the Section on Compendium comes first. Of that too, the verse beginning "That which the world worships" (*yaṃ loko pūjayate*) is the first.
Therein, "that" (*yaṃ*) is an indefinite designation of the object; its restriction should be understood by means of the word "its" (*tassā*). "The world" (*loko*) is the designation of the agent.

"Pūjayata" (worship) is a designation of the action (*kiriyāniddesa*). "Salokapālo" (the world-guardian) is a qualification of the agent (*kattuvisesana*). "Sadā" (always) is a designation of time (*kālaniddesa*).

"Namassati ca" (and worships) is a designation of the action by way of accumulation (*upacayena*). "Tassa" (of him) is a designation of the possessor (*sāminiddesa*). "Etaṃ" (this) is a designation of the object itself (*paccattaniddesa*).

"Sāsanavaraṃ" (the excellent teaching) is an indication of the phenomenon (*dhammanidassana*) designated by the designation of the object itself. "Vidūhi" (by the wise) is a designation of the agent by means of an instrumental expression (*karaṇavacanena*).

*Ñeyya* is a designation for the action that expresses the *kamma*. *Naravarassa* (of the Best of Men) is a direct description of the essential nature (*sarūpa*) of him who has been identified by the word "his" (*tassā*).
In this context, *loka* refers to that wherein merit and demerit, as well as their ripening, are found; the meaning is "the world," "the generation," or "the class of beings.
For the word *loka*, by virtue of being a generic term (*jātisadda*), includes all beings without exception through its general sense. Although...

For it should be understood that although the word *loka* is seen to be used even for the "vessels" of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), here it must be taken as referring specifically to the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*) by virtue of its being a fit object for the act of worship. "Pūjayate" means he honors; the sense is that he pays respect.

They protect the world, thus they are the World-Protectors (*lokapālā*); these are the four Great Kings. However, the worldly [deities] Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, and Kuvera are also called World-Protectors.
They say. "Together with the world-protectors" (*salokapālo*) means having the same grammatical core (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) as the word "world" (*loko*).

Alternatively, because they protect and guard their respective worlds of sentient beings through sovereignty and lordship, the Kṣatriyas, the Four Great Kings, Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Sunimmita, Paranimmita-vasavatti, Mahābrahmā, and so forth, are called "world-protectors.
Together with them, each respective group of sentient beings is called a "world with world-protectors. Or else: "Bhikkhus, these two... [and so on].
For, according to the statement, “White (virtuous) phenomena protect the world,” the qualities of moral shame (*hiri*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*) are the guardians of the world.

Possessed of these, the world has its guardians. Indeed, virtuous persons who are endowed with moral shame and dread of blame, being reproachers of evil, become intent on honoring and respecting the Blessed One due to their desire for the Dhamma.
"Always" means at all times, both by night and by day; or alternatively, "always" refers to the period while the Blessed One was still living and thereafter.
Or else, "always" means from the time of the initial resolution (*abhinīhāra*) until the disappearance of the Dispensation, or even beyond that.
For from the time of the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*), the Great Bodhisattvas, being destined for enlightenment, become like sprouts of a Buddha for the world including the devas.
They become worthy of worship and worthy of homage. As the Blessed One, having become Sumedha, said:
“Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World, the recipient of offerings;
having proclaimed my deed, he raised his right foot.”
“Those sons of the Conqueror who were there paid me homage;
having saluted me, the devas, humans, and asuras departed.

And as for the phrase “he pays homage”: even while some are performing acts of worship and honor toward certain others, they offer salutation because the virtues of those [others] are not yet manifest.

They do not act [in that way]; rather, the meaning is that because the Blessed One’s fame and renown have truly arisen, the world together with its devas honors and pays homage to the Blessed One. Some read "sadā naramanusso," but that is not good.
"Tassa" means of him whom the world together with its devas honors and pays homage to. "Etaṃ" [means this].
Now, he shows in general terms that which is revolving within the intellect as it ought to be stated. He shows "the excellent teaching" (*sāsanavara*) by way of its specific nature.
Therein, it is called "teaching" (*sāsana*) because it instructs and guides beings, as appropriate, regarding the truths pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal;
and that very same thing is [called] "excellent" (*vara*) in the sense of being exclusively leading to liberation and in the sense of possessing qualities not shared by others.

It is called the "excellent teaching" (*sāsanavara*) because it is chosen by the wise as the cause for the fulfillment of their respective aspirations, or because it is itself excellent. "By the wise" (*vidūhi*):
those who know actions and their fruits, as well as the phenomena categorized as wholesome and so forth, according to their true nature, are "the wise" (*vidū*);

that is, learned persons. "That which is to be known" (*ñeyya*): it is that which ought to be known, or that which is worthy of being known through wisdom. "Of the best of men" (*naravarassa*): of the most excellent person.
The meaning is "of the Supreme Person.

This is what is meant: the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—who, through his possession of distinguished qualities such as great compassion and omniscience that are not shared by others, is worthy of worship and homage by the world including the devas—of him, in the world...
This teaching, which is now the subject of our analysis regarding the method of classification and the investigation of the *Paṭṭhāna*, belongs to the Supreme Person;

it is excellent, foremost, and supreme due to its perfection of qualities such as being "good in the beginning," and it is to be experienced only by the wise because it is the domain of subtle knowledge.

For even a single verse of the Blessed One’s word is capable of defining the essential nature of phenomena—such as the truths, dependent origination, the aggregates, bases, elements, faculties, and foundations of mindfulness.
Furthermore, it is supremely profound because of its suitability for investigation through the sixteen ways of analysis, the five methods, and the twenty-eight modes of the *Paṭṭhāna*;
in terms of its meaning, it is bottomless and shoreless, being the domain of subtle and refined knowledge alone. For this very reason, it was said: "This Dhamma is for the wise;
this Dhamma is not for the unwise. Alternatively, the Blessed One’s teaching proceeds by way of full understanding (*pariññā*) through the awakening to characteristics and the practice of the path.
Because it must be penetrated by means of the doors of emptiness (*suññatāmukha*) and so forth, it is not an object even in a dream for those who lack wisdom;
thus he said, "to be known by the wise. And so it has been said: "Let a wise man come," and so on.
However, others read "that is his excellent teaching" (*taṃ tassa sāsanavaraṃ*); according to their view, the word *yaṃ* [is connected] with the word *sāsana*.

It should be understood as being in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). This is what is meant: that excellent teaching which the world, together with its guardians, honors and reveres—that excellent teaching is to be known by the wise. And in this interpretation, the Blessed One is also referred to by the term "guardian of the world" (*lokapāla*).
For the Blessed One, being the supreme leader of the world, is literally the guardian of the world; therefore, [the word] "of that" (*tassā*)...

The meaning is "of the Teacher, the World-Protector. Here, although the word *lokapāla* (World-Protector) is subordinate (*guṇībhūta*), because it refers to the Teacher and is dependent upon the word *sāsana* (the Dispensation), it is entitled to a specific designation as a correlate, appearing as if it were the primary term in its relation of ownership (*sāmibhāva*).
But how is it that the Blessed One, who himself is the Master of the Dhamma, honors the Dhamma? This is not a contradiction; for he is one who reveres the Dhamma.
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, always dwell in reverence for the Dhamma. Indeed, this has been said:
"What if I were to dwell honoring, respecting, and relying upon that very Dhamma which has been fully awakened to by me?"
Moreover, the worship of the Blessed One’s Dhamma should be illustrated by his conduct during the seven days following his enlightenment and so forth.

As for the phrase "Lord of the Dhamma," the meaning is that he is the Lord of the world including its devas *by means of* the Dhamma, not that he is the Lord *of* the Dhamma. Thus, the statement "he pays homage even to it" is not untenable.
For it is not the case that the Blessed One pays homage to anyone; this [explanation] is also faultless. It is not that he "pays homage."
"To pay homage to the word" has this very meaning; however, by way of showing respect, the meaning "inclined toward it, leaning toward it, and bent toward it" is also obtained.
And the Blessed One dwells at all times with a nature inclined, leaning, and bent toward the Dhamma due to his reverence for the Dhamma.
This meaning is also found in such Sutta passages as: "By which indeed I always dwell," and so forth.

It should be illuminated. There is also a reading, "to be led by the wise" (*vidūhi neyya*); its meaning is that it is to be led—that is, brought to attainment—by the wise within their own and others' continuums (*santāna*).
In this context, "bringing to attainment" within one's own continuum should be understood as awakening, and "awakening" within the continua of others as causing them to awaken.
Thus, the Blessed One’s state of being worthy of worship and homage by the world including the devas, as well as his status as the Supreme Person (*aggapuggala*), is being described.
It illuminates the excellence of qualities, and that excellence of qualities is to be understood as Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

For omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) has the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*) as its proximate cause, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints has omniscient knowledge as its proximate cause; this is what is called "Great Enlightenment.

It is understood that this [Great Enlightenment] is well-established in the Tathāgata because of his teaching of the Dhamma without error. Indeed, the abandonment of all defilements (*kilesa*) together with their latent tendencies (*savāsana*) without remainder—[is what constitutes it].
Furthermore, such a teaching of the Dhamma is not possible without unobstructed knowledge (*anāvaraṇañāṇa*).

Thus, he possesses the four grounds of self-confidence (*catuvesārajja*). By this, the perfection of all the qualities of omniscience is manifested, including the ten powers (*dasabala*), the six unique knowledges (*cha asādhāraṇañāṇa*), and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*aṭṭhārasāveṇikabuddhadhamma*).
And such a manifestation of these qualities is preceded by the excellence of the initial resolve (*abhinīhārasampatti*) and is led by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Since it is not found apart from the equipment of merit and knowledge known as the thirty perfections (*pāramī*) which he accomplished after having performed [them],
the perfection of causes (*hetusampadā*) is also thus explained by way of its meaning; in this manner, all the Buddha-qualities—
excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, and serving as the cause for the acquisition of absolute welfare for all beings in all three states— are here [described] in their entirety.
It should be understood that this was made clear by means of a verse.

Furthermore, in the second method, it refers to the teaching of the Noble Path together with its fruit— which comprises the three trainings— as well as the Deathless Element which serves as its object,
the teaching on the preliminary practice which is the means for its attainment, and the teaching of the scriptures (pariyatti) which elucidates their meaning.
Realizing [the Dhamma] through the penetration of the truths as appropriate, attending to its specific qualities such as being well-expounded,
and cultivating familiarity through careful listening, retention, interrogation, and so forth— the world together with its devas truly honors him.
And the Lord of the World, for the sake of attaining perfect enlightenment, through his careful teaching of the Dhamma to those capable of being trained, [establishes] the Noble...
“Monks, I shall teach you right concentration”; “The eightfold path is the best among paths”;
“Monks, to whatever extent there are phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared to be the foremost among them”; “Destruction, dispassion, the deathless, the sublime”;
“Monks, this is the one-way path for the purification of beings”; “Monks, the Dhamma to you...”
One honors [the Teaching] by means of praise through such statements as, "I shall teach that which is good in the beginning," and so forth. Therefore,
when the state of being worthy of honor for the sublime Dispensation is spoken of here, it illuminates the qualities of the Dhamma in their entirety— namely, those states of nobility and so forth,

the factors of deliverance and so forth, the destruction, dispassion, and so forth, the crushing of pride and so forth, the unconditioned and so forth, the well-expounded nature and so forth, and the goodness in the beginning and so forth.
It should be understood that many qualities of the Dhamma, which have been proclaimed through numerous passages of the Suttas, are revealed without exception by this verse. Furthermore,
since it is only those who have eradicated delusion through the penetration of the Noble Truths who are wise in the ultimate sense— due to their transcendence of ignorance and so forth—
it is specifically the noble persons (*ariyapuggala*) who have cultivated the supramundane path and realized the fruits of recluseship who are "the knowers" (*vidū*).
They are so called because they are able to know and lead others to know the aforementioned sublime teaching (sāsana) without error within their own and others' mental continuities.
Since the ultimate Saṅgha— the assembly of the eight noble persons— is also included here, it should be understood that the qualities of the Noble Saṅgha,
such as being well-practiced and so forth, which have been extolled by numerous Sutta passages, are also revealed here in their entirety.
Having thus, by means of the first verse, provided an especially excellent exposition of the qualities of the Triple Gem,
he now says: “Refraining from all evil, the cultivation of the wholesome,
and the complete purification of one’s own mind— this is the teaching of the Buddhas.”

In brief, according to its verbal expression, the Dispensation (sāsana) comprises the three trainings (sikkhā). That threefold training, moreover, is of three kinds according to the distinction of the objects of specific types of knowledge and according to the distinction of their stages.
How so? There is that which is the domain of knowledge consisting of hearing (*sutamayañāṇa*), which is called the "True Dhamma of the scriptures" (*pariyatti-saddhamma*).

And there is that which is the domain of knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmayañāṇa*), the mode of which is to be grasped through the investigation of aspects, the contemplation of views, and the acceptance [of those views].
The distinction of the bases of liberation is called the "true Dhamma of practice" (*paṭipatti-saddhamma*).

That which is accompanied by insight-knowledge (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) and so forth, and which is the domain of knowledge consisting in development (*bhāvanāmaya-ñāṇa*), is called the "true Dhamma of penetration" (*paṭivedha-saddhamma*).

Thus, having subsumed this threefold Dispensation under the term "the excellent Dispensation" (*sāsanavara*), that which is first among them is the means for attaining the others; therefore, it is the root of the entire Dispensation.

Briefly analyzing the very teaching of the scriptures (pariyatti-sāsana), which constitutes both the subject matter of his own work and its objective domain, he uttered the verse beginning with "twelve terms.
Therein, "twelve" is the numerical limit; "terms" (padāni) indicates the phenomena so delimited. Among these, the terms of phrasing (byañjana-padāni) are...
They are "words" (*padāni*) because meaning (*attha*) proceeds (*pajjati*) by means of them; alternatively, they are "words" because meanings proceed—that is, are known—by means of them.

Or rather, both [explanations] may be applied to both [types of words], since phonetic words (*byañjanapada*) must be engaged with without error, and semantic words (*atthapada*) serve as the cause for attaining further distinction. Those words will be made clear later in the text itself.
We shall explain that very point here. As for the meaning of the term *sutta*, it is so called because it indicates the meaning (*atthasūcanā*), and so forth.

For this has been stated in the *Saṅgaha*: “Because it indicates meanings, because it is well-spoken, because it is heard, because it flows forth, Because of its instruction, and because it shares the nature of a thread—therefore it is called a ‘discourse’ (*sutta*).”
That [definition] was given there according to the Sutta Piṭaka; here, however, it should be applied according to the three Piṭakas.
It is said that "a discourse (sutta) consists of twelve words," which means the teaching of the scriptures (pariyatti-sāsana).
"All of that" refers to the entirety of the Buddha’s word (buddhavacana) described as "discourse. "Phrasing and meaning" means both the phrasing and its meaning.
And because it is said, "The sutta consists of twelve words. This is what is meant: the *pariyatti*-dhamma is called a "sutta" because it indicates the meaning (*attha*) and so forth;
and all of that, in terms of its meaning, consists of twelve words—namely, six words of phrasing (*byañjana*) and six words of meaning (*attha*).
Alternatively, that which was called the "excellent teaching" (*sāsanavara*) is entirely the sutta, [which is] the teaching of the *pariyatti*.

Because it is intended [as such]. In terms of meaning (*attha*), however, there are twelve words, because of their nature as a collection of words consisting of both phrasing (*byañjana*) and meaning (*attha*).

As it has been said: "The phrasing and the meaning. That "both" is to be understood; that is to say, when there is a connection between the phrasing and the meaning through the relationship of the speaker and the spoken, the designation "sutta" applies.
Both of those must be understood according to their specific characteristics. Among them, what is the phrasing? What is the...
"What is the meaning? To this he said: "What is the meaning, and what is the phrasing?

Thus, having shown that the Sutta spoken of as the "Excellent Teaching" (Sāsanavara) is the Dhamma to be studied (pariyatti), and that it is to be understood through its meaning, phrasing, and constituent words, [the author] now presents the *Nettippakaraṇa*—the means for its investigation—by way of an analysis of the meaning of those words.

To demonstrate this, he recited the verse beginning with “The sixteen modes of conveying (soḷasahārā). In that context, “soḷasahārā” means that which has sixteen modes of conveying. The same method applies here to the phrase “five methods and eighteen root-terms.

Alternatively, “soḷasahārā” means sixteen modes of conveying; the same applies to the other terms as well. For indeed, [the compound] refers to the modes of conveying, the methods, and the root-terms themselves.
"Expounded both in brief and in detail as the *Nettī* (The Guide). "The search for the Dispensation" means the seeking of the meaning of the Dispensation;
the sense is that it is a commentary on the meaning of the Dispensation as the teaching (*pariyatti*), or else the sense is that it is an investigation into the meaning of the entire Dispensation.
For even regarding practice (*paṭipatti*) and realization (*paṭivedha*), people attain them by following the method of the *Nettī*. "By Mahākaccāyana."
*Kacca* was an ancient seer (*isi*); this Great Elder, who became the ornament of his lineage, is called *Kaccāna*.
The term *Mahākaccāna*, however, is a word of honor, just as in the case of *Mahāmoggallāna*; there is also a reading: "indicated by the clan name Kaccāyana.
And it should be understood that this verse was placed by those reciting the *Netti* for the purpose of summarizing the meaning of the treatise. Just as...

And thus, in this section on the analysis of the strings (*hāravibhaṅga*), at the conclusion of the respective explanations of each string, there is the statement beginning with “Therefore the Venerable One said.

In this *Netti*, which consists of a collection of strings and so forth, and in the investigation of the collection of words and meanings within the Sutta—asking what is investigated by what—it says: “The strings are the investigation of the phrasing,” and so on.
In this context, all sixteen modes (hāra) constitute an exposition of the Sutta solely by way of the phrasing (byañjana), without extracting the root-terms;
they do not, like the methods (naya), function by way of extracting the intrinsic nature (sabhāva-dhamma) designated as the root-terms.

Therefore, they are called "the investigation of the phrasing of the Sutta. However, the methods of meaning (attha-naya) bring about the correct comprehension of the Sutta's meaning precisely by way of the aforementioned meaning.
He says, "The methods and the three [types of] Sutta-meaning," for this investigation will also follow later.
Some read "and the method" (*nayo ca*), but that is not good. Both are encompassed;
thus, "the strings and the methods"—both of these are grasped all around by way of determining the meaning of the Sutta, and are applied in every respect to the Sutta.
It is said that he "speaks according to the Sutta" (*yathāsuttaṃ*) and "expounds" (*saṃvaṇṇeti*). How so? "According to the Sutta" means in accordance with the Sutta;
the meaning is that he expounds it in whatever manner a particular Sutta ought to be expounded. Or, "according to the Sutta" means "whatever [portion of] the Sutta," implying the entire Sutta.
For, according to the method of the *Netti*, there is no Sutta whatsoever that cannot be expounded.

Now, regarding what was stated—"the excellent dispensation is to be known by the wise"—in order to demonstrate specifically, by way of another classification, the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma) which constitutes the subject matter of this *Nettippakaraṇa-vaṇṇanā*, the passage beginning with "And that which... was spoken.
In this context, "teaching" (*desanā*) is a sequence of phonemes (*byañjana*) for which a delimitation of meaning has been established; it is what is called the "recitation" (*pāṭha*).

Its "meaning" (*attha*) is that which is taught because it is awakened by that teaching. And both of these [teaching and meaning] are for those who cultivate familiarity under the heading of the "bases of liberation" (*vimuttāyatana*).
Because it is the cause for all attainments culminating in final Nibbāna without clinging, it must be understood exclusively;
and because there is no object of knowledge (*ñeyya*) apart from these two, it shows this meaning—that these two alone are what is to be understood—by the words "both... are to be understood.

In that context, the locative case in "therein" (*tatra*) refers to that act of cognizing which is to be accomplished or brought about. "This is the sequence" (*ayamānupubbī*) means this... *Note: The ellipsis (*pe*) indicates that the full passage beginning with "both the conditioned and the unconditioned" is to be supplied.*
The sequence (*anupubbī*) refers to the order of the methods of analysis (*hāranaya*) that will be explained; the meaning is that the methods of analysis are to be explained in successive order.

"The investigation of the ninefold discourse" (*navavidhasuttantapariyeṭṭhī*) means the search for the teaching consisting of the nine divisions, beginning with the *sutta*, or the examination of their meaning.
Alternatively, this nominative form is used in the sense of the genitive: "the sequence of the investigation of the ninefold discourse. Now...
Or, *anupubbī* (succession) is used in the nominative case in the sense of the instrumental. This is what is meant:

when the aforementioned understanding is to be accomplished, this is the search for the meaning of the ninefold Suttanta by means of the succession of the methods of extraction (*hāra-naya*) that will be explained.
Here it is asked: "But how is it that the Geyya-factor and the others possess the nature of a Sutta? And if they have the nature of a Sutta, how do they [contribute] to the Teaching?"

[There would be] the state of having nine divisions (*navaṅgabhāva*). Furthermore, regarding what is stated in the *Saṅgaha*—that "a discourse with verses is *geyya*, while a discourse without verses is *veyyākaraṇa*"—if that were the case, there would be no such thing as the *sutta* division at all.

Alternatively, if the *sutta* division were to exist separately [from those two], then discourses such as the *Maṅgalasutta* would not be included in the *sutta* division, because they contain verses, just like the *Dhammapada* and other such works; nor would they be included in the *geyya* division.
Or it might be so, because the Sagāthāvagga contains verses, just as the Ubhatovibhaṅga and other sections contain prose passages interspersed with verses. To this it is replied:

"Sutta" is a general designation, while the others are specific designations; they possess their respective characteristics due to conventional usage, being distinct from one another and not otherwise.
For indeed, "Sutta" is the general designation for the entire word of the Buddha.
Thus, from such statements as, "So much of that Blessed One’s teaching has come down as Sutta, is included in the Sutta;

in the Sutta-vibhaṅga of Sāvatthī, there are five hundred suttas in our own tradition," the term "Sutta" is seen to be applied even to specific portions of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma Piṭakas. Within those very parts—

However, the specific types beginning with *geyya* are established by their respective characteristics. For instance, the state of being accompanied by verses (*sagāthakatta*) is the characteristic of *geyya*.
Indeed, even in the world, they call a collection of stanzas together with prose (*sasiloka*) and verses (*sagāthaka*) "geyya.
But when there is an absence of verses, the state of answering after having asked is the characteristic of *veyyākaraṇa*; for it is the act of answering a question.

It is called "byākaraṇa" (exposition). Exposition itself is "veyyākaraṇa" (analytical exposition). If this were the case, would it not follow that even those discourses such as the *Sagāthaka*, which proceed by way of answering questions, would possess the status of *veyyākaraṇa*?

It does not so follow, because there is no occasion for the designations of *geyya* and so forth [to apply], and because it is specifically qualified by the phrase "when there is an absence of verses. For indeed, in the *Dhammapada* and other such works, only...

Just as the designations *gāthā*, *udāna*, *itivuttaka*, and *abbhutadhamma* were established respectively for specific types of discourses— namely, those consisting of verse compositions (*sagāthaka*),
those joined with verses consisting of joy and knowledge (*somanassañāṇamayika*), those connected with statements such as "For it has been said" (*vuttañhetaṃ*),

and those associated with marvelous qualities (*abbhutadhamma*)— likewise, even though they consist of verse compositions, [the designation *jātaka* was established] for those works that reveal the power of the Blessed One’s conduct (*cariyānubhāva*) in his past births.
Because certain discourses (suttantas), despite being in the form of question-and-answer sessions and containing verses, are designated as *veda*, the designation *vedalla* is established for them.

Thus, by means of such respective characteristics as the presence of verses and so forth, the designations *geyya* and the rest are established for those specific discourses; therefore, *geyya* and the others are categories distinct from the *sutta* category.

As for the discourse (*sutta*) here that is devoid of the characteristics of the *geyya* factor and so forth, it is the *sutta* factor because it proceeds by means of a general designation (*sāmañña-saññā*), avoiding specific designations (*visesa-saññā*).
Is it not the case that the objection—"A discourse with verses is *geyya*, while a discourse without verses is *veyyākaraṇa*;
therefore, the *sutta* factor is impossible"—remains in force? It does not remain in force.
Because it has been purified. For it was previously established that when a verse is absent, the nature of question and answer constitutes the defining characteristic of a *veyyākaraṇa*.

As for what was said—that "because they lack the form of verses, the *Maṅgalasutta* and others would not be included within the category of *sutta*"—that too is not correct, because the term is conventional.
Indeed, the status of being a *sutta* is conventionally established in the case of the *Maṅgalasutta* and so forth; for they are not [merely prose].
Like the *Dhammapada*, the *Buddhavaṃsa*, and others, these are renowned as being in the form of verses (*gāthā*), yet they exist precisely as discourses (*sutta*).
For this very reason, the name "called a discourse" (*suttanāmaka*) was applied to it in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).
As for what was said—that "because it contains verses, it might be included within the *geyya* division"—that too is not the case, because it is accompanied by something else.

“Together with verses” (*saha gāthāhi*) means that which possesses verses (*sagāthaka*). Furthermore, co-existence (*sahabhāva*) in a real sense occurs through something other than itself; yet, in the *Maṅgala-sutta* and other such texts, there is no portion of a sutta that exists apart from its verses, such that it could be called "together with verses. Nor is there any such thing as a "collection" (*samudāya*) [that exists independently]. As for what was said—namely, that in the *Ubhatovibhaṅga* and other works, those portions containing verses are included within the *geyya* factor [of the nine-fold division]—that too is incorrect. For even in the *Dhammapada*, there are prose passages that do not contain verses, and these would have to be excluded from the *geyya* factor. Furthermore, the *Sutta-nipāta* is traditionally held to consist of five hundred verses; if it were to include prose, it would exceed that number. Therefore, this [definition of *geyya*] is not tenable. Moreover, the *Geyya-aṅga* is defined by the Blessed One as "whatever is spoken in mixed prose and verse (*gāthā-vītivitta*)"; since there is no such thing in the *Sutta-nipāta*, it cannot be considered *geyya*. Consequently, the *Sutta-nipāta* is a collection of suttas distinct from the nine-fold division. Thus, it is established that the *Sutta-nipāta* consists of fifty-six suttas. 2. Commentary on the Section on Enumeration.

1. Thus, after the modes of conveyance (*hāra*) and so forth have been shown briefly by way of the section on inclusion (*saṅgahavāra*), the teaching beginning with “In this regard, what are the sixteen modes of conveyance? is now commenced in order to show them in detail.
Therein, the phrase “therein” (*tattha*) refers to that statement—“The sixteen modes of conveyance are the guide (*nettī”)”—or to that verse;
it means “among those root-terms of the modes of conveyance and methods (*nayamūlapada*) which have been extracted.”
The meaning [of the word] is this. "What" is the interrogative expression. This interrogation, moreover, is fivefold:

interrogation for the illumination of what is not seen, interrogation for the verification of what is seen, interrogation for the cutting off of doubt, interrogation for assent, and interrogation out of a desire to speak. Among these, this is an interrogation out of a desire to speak.
"Sixteen" is a delimitation by way of number. By that, there is no more than that—neither beyond nor below—which establishes their limit.
[The author] shows this. That ultimate meaning will be made manifest later. "Chains" (*hāra*) refers to the general presentation of those [topics] delimited by way of enumeration.
"Exposition," "investigation," and so forth, are the demonstration of their specific characteristics.

In that regard, in what sense are they "chains"? They are called "chains" because by means of them, or in them, ignorance, doubt, and perversion regarding the objects of the discourses, verses, and so forth, are removed (*harīyanti*).

They are "strings" (*hārā*) because they take away (*haranti*) those [defilements] themselves, or because they are merely the act of taking away; thus, by way of metaphorical designation, they are called "strings.

Alternatively, they are "strings" because they are carried away (*harīyanti*) or discussed (*voharīyanti*) by those who expound the Dhamma and those who receive the Dhamma, in the sense of giving and receiving the Dhamma.

Or else, they are "strings" because they are like strings (*hārā viya*). For just as a collection of many strings of jewels, known as a "necklace," through the contact with the jewels that constitute its own parts...
Just as a mass of water, becoming pleasant through the joy arising from its emergence, allays the bodily heat of those who enjoy it— heat produced by the scorching heat of summer—
in the same way, these various excellent commentaries, which are a succession of jewels of ultimate meaning,

allay the feverish distress in the hearts of those who receive the Dhamma through the attainment of the jewels of ultimate meaning that constitute their own constituent parts, as they produce the bliss of Nibbāna.

They are called *hāras* because they pacify the defilements such as sensual lust. Alternatively, they are *hāras* because they "take away" (*hārayanti*), that is, they effect the removal of ignorance and so forth, or because they "declare" (*ācikkhanti*) it.
Or again, by way of etymology (*niruttinaya*), they are *hāras* because they "carry off" (*haraṇa*) and "delight" (*ramaṇa*) the minds of those who hear them, just as it is said:
"The Blessed One is one who has vomited out existence. This, then, is the general meaning of the *hāras*.

However, it is called *desanā* (teaching) because by means of it the meaning of the sutta is taught (*desīyati*) and explained (*saṃvaṇṇīyati*). Or, it is called *desanā* because of its association with the teaching.
But are not the other *hāras* (modes of conveying meaning) also associated with the teaching, since they too explain the meaning of the sutta which is reckoned as a teaching?
This is true; however, this particular *hāra* is, for the most part, understood through the literal expression itself, and thus [it is distinguished] from the others which accompany the teaching.
He deserves to be called one who "practices," whereas others do not.

For there is no teaching of the Suttas that is devoid of the demonstration of gratification, danger, and escape. And this method (*hāra*) has the characteristic of demonstrating and analyzing gratification and so forth.

By means of this, or in this, the words, questions, and so on, are sifted; or else, these [words, etc. are the sifting itself—thus it is "sifting" (*vicaya*). In the Canon, however, the meaning shown is: "it sifts," thus it is "sifting" (*vicaya*).

*Yutti* (reasoning) means reasoning that establishes through logical proof (*upapatti-sādhanayutti*). However, here it refers to the investigation of reasoning (*yuttivicāraṇā-yutti*), as in the case of "form-existence" (*rūpabhava*) being called simply "form" (*rūpa*)—where the latter member of the compound is elided—or because it is associated with reasoning. Here too, the meaning should be explained in detail according to the method stated under the "Mode of Teaching" (*desanāhāra*).
*Padaṭṭhāna* (proximate cause) means the immediate cause; here too, the "investigation of the proximate cause" and so forth should be understood by the same method already stated.
*Lakkhaṇa* (characteristic) is so called because by means of it, or in it, phenomena possessing a single characteristic are characterized even when not explicitly mentioned, using a single term.

*Byūha* (array): By means of this, things are "arrayed" (*viyūhīyanti*) through division, or they are "gathered together" (*piṇḍīyanti*) therein; thus it is *byūha*. Regarding the fourfold array (*catubyūha*), it is the "array" (*byūha*) of the four—such as etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) and so forth—which are shown in the Sutta; or, it is that wherein the array of the four occurs, hence it is the "fourfold array. *Āvaṭṭa* (turning back):
By means of this, or therein, similar and dissimilar phenomena are "turned back" (*āvaṭṭīyanti*); or, it is the "turning back" of those [phenomena], hence it is *āvaṭṭa*. *Vibhatti* (analysis):

By means of this, or therein, the grounds for both common and uncommon phenomena of defilement and purification are "analyzed" (*vibhajīyanti*); or, it is the "ground" (*bhūmi*) for their analysis, hence it is *vibhatti*. Alternatively, it is the "analysis" (*vibhajana*) itself of these [phenomena] upon their ground, hence it is *vibhatti*.
"Parivattanā" means that by this [method], the factors taught in this sutta are turned around by way of their opposites;

or else, it is "parivattana" because they are turned around. "Vivacana" means that there is various (vi-) expression (vacana) here for the very same meaning; "vevacana" is simply another term for "vivacana," or alternatively, it is "vivacana" because the meaning is expressed (vuccati) in various ways by it. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
"Paññatti" means that by this [method], things are made known (paññāpiyanti) through their modes (pakāra) or distinctions (pabheda); or else, it is "paññatti" because the meaning is found therein.

It is called *otaraṇa* (descent) because by means of it, or in this [sutta], the doctrines found in the discourses—such as dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and so forth—are descended into or entered upon.
It is called *sodhana* (clarification) because by means of it, or in this sutta, the words, word-meanings, and the commencement of questions are purified and brought into harmony.

It is called *adhiṭṭhāna* (determination) because by means of it, or in this [sutta], the doctrines that constitute the general and specific characteristics are determined or made to proceed without conceptual differentiation (*vikappa*).

*Parikkhāra* (requisite) means that which surrounds, constructs, and bears fruit; it is both cause (*hetu*) and condition (*paccaya*). It is called *parikkhāra* because it explains a requisite (*parikkhāram ācikkhati*), or it is a "mode" (*hāra*). It is also called *parikkhāra* because it is the domain of requisites or because it accompanies the requisites.

*Samāropana* (correspondence) is so called because by means of it, or in this [context], phenomena (*dhammā*) are superimposed (*samāropīyanti*) through such means as the "basis" (*padaṭṭhāna*). In all cases, the meaning can also be established by way of the abstract noun (*bhāvasādhana*);

therefore, it should be applied according to that method as well. *Tassa* refers to the aforementioned exposition of the modes (*hāruddesa*). *Anugītī* (recapitulation) is for the purpose of easy grasping of the very same meaning already stated.
The verses at the end [of each section] are the concluding verses; they are "unmixed in meaning" (*atthato asaṃkiṇṇā*), meaning they are free from confusion regarding the sense of the words.
By this, he shows that although some of these strings of gems (*hāra*) appear as if indistinguishable from one another, nevertheless there is no confusion among them in their meaning.
And this lack of confusion among them is clearly evident in the exposition of their characteristics (*lakkhaṇaniddesa*). "And of these very... [etc.]
Regarding these sixteen modes of exposition (*hāra*): it occurs exactly as there is no confusion. What [occurs]?
By way of expansion—that is, by means of detailed elaboration. "Analysis according to method" (*nayavibhatti*) means a classification by way of method, approach, and principle.
By this, he clarifies that very same absence of confusion. Some read "vitthāranayā," but that is not good; moreover, this verse does not exist in some manuscripts.
2. Having thus indicated the *hāra* (modes of conveying), he now states "In this regard, what are they? and so forth, in order to indicate the *naya* (guiding principles).

In that context, they are called *nayas* because they lead (*nayanti*) by making known the divisions of defilement (*saṃkilesa*) and purification (*vodāna*); or else, they are *nayas* because by means of them things are led (*nīyanti*), or because they are led therein; or else, they are *nayas* because they are merely the act of leading (*nayanamatta*);
or else, they are *nayas* because they themselves are led—that is, they are brought forward by the preachers of the Dhamma (*dhammakathika*)—of the Sutta.
The word *nayā* means "modes of discerning the meaning. Alternatively, *nayā* means "like modes," for they are like the modes [of analysis].

Just as the modes such as unity (*ekatta*) and so forth, when correctly penetrated, reveal the intrinsic nature of conventional truth and ultimate truth without confusion—by demonstrating the state of being a cause, an effect, their respective order, their connection, their differentiation, their functional absence, and their corresponding results—thus leading to the penetration of ultimate truth.
In this way, by means of the demonstration of the classification of phenomena into dark, bright, and those corresponding to both,
these [methods] enable those to be trained to understand the meaning of the suttas without error, thereby leading them to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. Alternatively,

they are called "guides" (*naya*) because they guide one toward the meaning of the scriptures through the methods of defilement, purification, and restraint, according to the method of etymological analysis (*niruttinayena*).
Regarding the terms *nandiyāvaṭṭa* and so forth: it is called *nandiyāvaṭṭa* because its turning (*āvaṭṭa*) is like that of a *nandiyāvaṭṭa* (a "joy-turning" diagram).
For just as a *nandiyāvaṭṭa* turns outward by means of its principal part situated within, so too does this method; such is the meaning.

Alternatively, it is called *nandiyāvaṭṭa* because there is a turning toward *nandi*—that is, toward craving or delight. By means of the three factors belonging to the side of defilement, such as greed and the rest...
It is called *tipukkhalo* because it is beautiful (*pukkhalo*) on the side of purification (*vodāna-pakkhe*) due to non-greed (*alobha*) and the other [wholesome roots].

The Blessed One is a lion (*sīho*) by virtue of his possession of such distinctions as fearlessness, speed, and prowess; and considering that his "sport" (*vikkīḷita*) consists of his dwelling in the activity of teaching, it is called *sīhavikkīḷito* because it illustrates the antidotes to the perversions (*vipallāsa*).
Alternatively, it is so called because it resembles the sport of a lion by way of illustrating the possession of specific powers.
The method is the "Lion’s Play" (*sīhavikkīḷita*). Here, the distinction of power refers to the powers of faith and so forth, or indeed the ten powers (*dasabala*) themselves.

The "surveying of directions" (*disālocana*) is the examination of wholesome and other phenomena by way of the threefold method of meaning (*atthanaya*). Because it yokes those phenomena thus examined to the threefold method of meaning and brings them together, it is like a hook;
thus it is called a "hook" (*aṅkusa*). In the verses, it is called a "pointer" (*lañjaka*) because it points out or reveals the meaning of the Sutta; this is the method (*naya*).
And "so lañjako" (and that mark) means "the mark of the method. "Gatā" means known; the sense is "dead," or rather, that is the reading itself.
The remainder should be understood according to the method already stated.
Having thus indicated the methods, he now begins with the words "In this regard, which are... in order to indicate the root terms.

In this context, they are called "root-terms" (*mūlapada*) because those roots are both the bases for the methods (*naya*) and the foundational states of the *Paṭṭhāna* sections, and they are the "terms" (*pada*) because they constitute the means for attainment and the constituent units [of the teaching].
They are called "roots" (*kusala*) in the sense of being produced by skill; or, in the sense of flowing away from, or destroying, base and evil qualities (*pāpadhamma*);
or, in the sense of reaping away the "weeds" (*kusa*) of passion and so forth; or, in the sense of reaping like weeds; or, by means of the "weed" [of wisdom].

The meaning of the terms should be understood as follows: they are "wholesome" (*kusala*) because they are to be acquired or practiced through knowledge, and "unwholesome" (*akusala*) because they are the opposites thereof.

Having thus shown the root terms by way of numerical limit and classification by type, he now presents them according to their own nature, first enumerating the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkha*) with the words beginning "craving" (*taṇhā*).
In that context, "it thirsts" (*tasati*) means it is distressed (*paritasati*).

Craving (*taṇhā*). Ignorance (*avijjā*) is so called because it finds what should not be found and does not find what should be found; or alternatively, ignorance is that which is the opposite of true knowledge (*vijjā*).
Greed (*lobha*) is so called because one is greedy by means of it, or it itself is greedy, or it is merely the state of being greedy. The same method applies to hatred (*dosa*) and delusion (*moha*).

The perception that occurs regarding the unattractive as "attractive" is the perception of beauty (*subhasaññā*). The same [method] applies to the perception of pleasure (*sukhasaññā*) and the others as well.
The meaning should be understood according to the method. *Saṅgaha* means enumeration. *Samosaraṇa* means convergence.
It is called *samatha* because it brings together (*sameti*) opposing states. It is called *vipassanā* because it sees [the object] through various aspects such as impermanence and so forth.
Non-greed and the others are to be understood as the opposites of greed and the others. Perception that occurs regarding the foul as "foul" is the perception of the foul (*asubhasaññā*).

The foundation of mindfulness through contemplation of the body. For the teaching is given by way of the headword "perception" (*saññā*). This same method applies to the perception of suffering and the others as well. "This is the summary" (*uddāna*):
this is the giving upward (*uddha-dāna*)—that is, protection—of the very meaning already stated, so that it does not perish due to being scattered;
the meaning is "a word of compendium. There is also the reading, "the four perversions. "The plane of defilements" (*kilesabhūmi*).
The "ground of defilement" (saṃkilesabhūmi) is so called because it is the place where all unwholesome states converge. Regarding the wholesome states, there are the three roots;
some also read the word as "wholesome ones" (kusalāni). By "foundations of mindfulness" (satipaṭṭhānā), he refers to the perception of foulness and the others.

The "ground of the faculties" (indriyabhūmi) is stated because it is the place where the faculties—faith and the rest—which ripen liberation, converge. "They are joined" (yujjanti) means they are applied (yojīyanti).
*Kho* is a particle used for filling out the meter or for emphasis. By this, he shows: "these indeed. Or [it means] "only eighteen.
*Mūlapadā* means "root-terms," or it is a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*).
The commentary on the section of enumeration is finished.
3. Explanation of the Section on Exposition (Niddesavāravaṇṇanā) 4.

Since the strings of meaning (*hāra*) and so forth have thus been enumerated, the passage beginning with “Therein, in brief” is commenced in order to explain them. Therein, “therein” (*tattha*) refers to that recited enumeration.
“The Guide (*netti*) has been proclaimed in brief” means that the *Nettippakaraṇa* has been expounded in summary.
For the demonstration of the actual form of the root-terms of the methods (hāra) and principles (naya) has been accomplished by means of the recitation of the summary (uddesa).

And herein, the wise should understand the meaning of the terms, their characteristics, their sequence, and [the categories] beginning with "cause" (hetu), for these methods and principles, both generally and specifically, as follows: "The meaning of the terms, the characteristic, the sequence, And likewise 'cause' and so forth— By this much should they be understood by the wise."
In these [sections], the meaning of the *hāras* (modes of conveying) and *nayās* (guiding principles) has been shown both generally and specifically.

Regarding the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth, however, generally speaking, all *hāras* and *nayās* alike have as their characteristic the exposition of the meaning of the ninefold Teaching (*sāsana*) by way of its phrasing (*byañjana*) and its meaning (*attha*), respectively.
Specifically, we shall explain the characteristic of each individual *hāra* and *naya* in the section on definitions (*niddesa*).
And since the "desire" and so forth are to be understood once their characteristics have been known, we shall therefore explain those as well further on in the exposition.
This concludes the summary of the modes of conveying meaning (*hārasaṅkhepa*).
1. As for the explanatory verses beginning with “assādādīnavata,” in them the phrase “assādādīnavata” is analyzed as the words “assādo” (gratification) and “ādīnavata” (from danger).
And “ādīnavata” is simply “ādīnavo” (danger). Some read it as “assādādīnavato,” but that is not good.
In this context, that which is tasted is “assādo,” namely pleasure (*sukha*) and mental joy (*somanassa*). For this has been said: “Bhikkhus, whatever is pleasant and agreeable... [etc.]
“Dependent upon the five aggregates of clinging, pleasure and joy arise; this is the gratification in the five aggregates of clinging.
And just as this pleasure and joy are [the gratification], so too is the desirable object.
For it has been said: “He relishes that, he desires that”; and, “He relishes form, he delights in it; with that as a basis, lust arises.”
“And, monks, those who contemplate gratification in things that fetter. Here, *assāda* (gratification) is so called because one relishes by means of it;
it is craving (*taṇhā*). For through craving acting as the cause, a person relishes even pleasure, as well as the object of pleasure.
And just as with craving, so too with the perversions (*vipallāsa*). For through the influence of the perversions, beings perceive even an undesirable object in an agreeable manner.
They relish them; in this way, the investigation of the relishing of all formations belonging to the three planes—of feeling, craving, and the perversions—should be understood.

But how can painful and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings be objects of relishing? It is because of the presence of perversions and because of the existence of a figurative expression for "pleasure.
For it has been said: "Friend Visākha, pleasant feeling is pleasant in its persistence and painful in its change."
"Painful feeling is suffering in its persistence and pleasant in its change; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is pleasant through knowledge and suffering through ignorance.

In this context, [the exposition] is according to the method of the "Eight Hundred" regarding feeling; according to the "Exposition of the Categories" (*Nikkhepakaṇḍa*) and the "Exposition of Matter" (*Rūpakaṇḍa*) regarding the formations of the three planes;

and according to the description of craving in the "Exposition of the Bases of Defilement" (*Saṃkilesavatthu-vibhaṅga*) and the "Exposition of the Categories" (*Nikkhepakaṇḍa*) regarding craving; and regarding the perversions...
The classification should be understood by way of the sixty-two types of views, beginning with the perception of pleasure (*sukhasaññā*).

The danger (*ādīnava*) consists of painful feeling (*dukkhā vedanā*) or the three types of suffering (*dukkhatā*). Alternatively, all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) of the three planes are the danger.

It is called "danger" (*ādīnava*) because it proceeds as something exceedingly miserable (*ādīnaṃ ativiya kapaṇaṃ*); just as one speaks of a "miserable person" (*kapaṇamanusso*), so too is its nature.
The phenomena belonging to the three planes [of existence] are [contemplated] by way of their impermanence and so forth.
Since the contemplation of danger therein is called the "method of reality" for those who have begun insight meditation, it has been said accordingly:
"Bhikkhus, that the five aggregates of clinging are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in the five aggregates of clinging. Therefore...

The danger (ādīnava) is to be explained by analyzing it according to the forty-two aspects, such as impermanence and so forth, which pertain to birth and the other factors that constitute the description of the truth of suffering.
It is called "escape" (nissaraṇa) because one escapes by means of it; thus, escape is the Noble Path. Alternatively, escape is Nibbāna, because one escapes [to] it. Both of these [are meant].

It is stated as "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) either by way of a general description or by the grammatical rule of *ekasesa* (retaining one from a group). The word "and" (*pi*) has the sense of joining the preceding and the following.

Therein, escape should be demonstrated after analyzing it according to the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment—such as the foundations of mindfulness and so forth—belonging to the side of the Noble Path, as well as the specific divisions included therein, such as the contemplation of the body and so forth.

Regarding the side of Nibbāna, although there is no literal division of the unconditioned element, there is a figurative division by way of the distinction between that with residue remaining and that without residue remaining.
Or else, it is distinguished according to those six doors— the eye and so forth— whose classifications are shown in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*,
and the six objects such as visible forms, from which [Nibbāna] has emerged, and the consciousnesses occurring through those respective doors.

Each and every [instance] of consciousness, contact, feeling, perception, volition, craving, applied thought, and sustained thought; each and every one of the six elements beginning with the earth element;
the ten kasina bases; the foulness [meditations] consisting of the thirty-two aspects beginning with head-hairs;
the five aggregates; the twelve bases; the eighteen elements; and the mundane faculties.

It should be analyzed and demonstrated by way of the state of escape from such conditioned phenomena as the three realms beginning with the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu), the three types of existence beginning with sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), the four meditative absorptions (jhānas), the four immeasurables (appamaññās),
the four formless attainments (āruppas), and the twelve factors of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda).
They bear fruit as the result of the teaching. But what is that? It is that which is produced by the teaching.
Is it not the case that the attainment of Nibbāna is produced by the Blessed One’s teaching? And has Nibbāna not already been described by the term "escape"?

True, this is so; however, that is by way of succession. Here, however, the intended fruit of the teaching is that which is directly perceived. And that is knowledge consisting of what has been heard (sutamaya-ñāṇa).
The six purifications are the preliminary practice for the Noble Path beginning with the knowledge of the meaning and phenomena (*atthadhammavedādi-ariyamagga*).
Furthermore, at that moment, they may serve as the cause for attaining the Path at a later time for one who has not yet reached it, and as the cause for a fortunate rebirth (*sampattibhava*).
For thus he will say: "Having uprooted the view of self, 'thus one may be a crosser of death'—this is the fruit."

“Indeed, Dhamma protects the one who lives according to Dhamma”—this is the fruit. By this method, among both gods and humans, there are the attainments of long life, beauty, strength, happiness, fame, retinue, and sovereignty;
the attainments of the physical basis (upadhi); the glory of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti); the glory of divine kingship; the four wheels of attainment;
the perfection of virtue (sīla); the perfection of concentration (samādhi); the three knowledges (vijjā); and the six [superknowledges].

It should be understood that all perfections—namely, the four direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*), the enlightenment of disciples (*sāvakabodhi*), the enlightenment of solitary buddhas (*paccekabodhi*), and perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*)—bear fruit as results to be accomplished through the Blessed One’s teaching, having the accumulation of merit as their cause.
"Skillful means" (*upāya*) refers to the preliminary practice that serves as the proximate cause for the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). For each preceding stage leads to the subsequent one.
It is the means because it is the state of being the means for attainment in the future, and because it serves as the cause for the successive attainment of the path and Nibbāna.
Furthermore, it is the practice of the means for the attainment of the fruit mentioned previously. However, some say that "the path together with insight (vipassanā) is the means";
according to their opinion, "escape" would have been stated as Nibbāna alone. The Fruit.
It might be said that the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*) is also a means (*upāya*); however, as he will later state: "‘All phenomena...
for the sake of purification’—this is the means," it can be understood that here too, only the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*) is being cited.
For he will later state that the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*) is the state of escape (*nissaraṇa*), saying: "Having abandoned those [fetters], one crosses the flood; this is the escape."
For the Noble Path is the crossing over the flood.

"Instruction" (āṇatti) means the direction given by the Blessed One, who is worthy of being obeyed, to those people to be trained for the sake of accomplishing their welfare, saying, "Practice in this way. For he will say: "Mogharāja, look upon the world as empty;

this is the instruction. "Of yogis" refers to those disciples who are devotedly engaged in the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Truths. "For the benefit" is an elliptical expression [meaning "for the benefit of..."].
"Exposition as nutriment" (desanāhāra) means that a specific kind of commentary characterized by the analysis of the aforementioned gratification and so forth is called "exposition as nutriment.
Here it is asked: Is the exposition of all these—gratification and the rest—without exception what constitutes "exposition as nutriment," or only some of them?
It is indeed those without exception; for in whatever discourse the gratification, the danger, and the escape [are found]...
Where [the texts] have come down in their original form, there is nothing at all that needs to be said.

However, where they have come down only partially or not in their original form, one should determine what has not been stated by way of its meaning and then apply the method (*hāra*). And since this matter will be explained in the "Analysis of the Method of Teaching" (*desanāhāravibhaṅga*), it is not elaborated upon here.

2. *Yaṃ pucchitaṃ* means "that which is asked"; the words *viciyamānā* (being investigated) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. *Vissajjitaṃ anugītī* (the answer is the subsequent recitation)—here too, the method is the same.
In this context, *vissajjitaṃ* means "answering" (*vissajjanā*), which is the fourfold mode of answering, such as categorical answering (*ekamsabyākaraṇa*) and so forth.
The word *ca* has the sense of conjunction; it includes terms such as "verse" (*gāthā*) that were not explicitly mentioned [in the previous rule]. These...
But as for the question "To whom does the answer to the inquiry belong?", he says: "Of the Sutta. By this, he shows that the answer to the inquiry found in the Sutta is to be discerned.

And as for "the subsequent song" (*anugīti*): it is the song (*gīti*) that follows (*anu*), i.e., comes after, the very meaning already stated; it is a summary verse (*saṅgahagāthā*), or a song corresponding to the inquiry.
By this, the preceding and following [context] is grasped. For of the exposition (*byākaraṇa*)...
In this context, "conformity with the question" (pucchānurūpatā) is intended as the sequence of what precedes and follows; it is what is called the "connection of the question" (pucchānusandhi).

The preceding word "of the sutta" is looked back upon [as the subject], and thus it is stated again as "of the sutta. By this, one comprehends the gratification and so forth that serve as the support for the sutta.
To this extent, the domain of the method of investigation (vicaya-hāra) has been demonstrated without remainder.
And so it will be said in the *Vibhaṅga* of the *Vīmaṃsāhāra*: “He investigates the phrase... [and so on] ...he investigates the refrain.
Therein, the investigation of all the phrases in the Sutta, both according to their meaning and according to their phrasing, in successive order, is the “investigation of phrases” (*padavicaya*).

“This is a question for the illumination of what has not been seen, a question for the correlation of what has been seen, a question for the cutting off of doubt, a question for assent, and a question out of a desire to speak.”

The investigation of questions (*pucchāvicaya*) should be understood through such passages as: "based on existence," "based on phenomena," "based on one thing," "based on many things," "within the sphere of conventional designation," "within the sphere of ultimate reality," "within the sphere of the past," "within the sphere of the future," and "within the sphere of the present. Furthermore, this response [to questions] is to be understood as:
