a categorical answer (*ekaṃsabyākaraṇa*), an analytical answer (*vibhajjabyākaraṇa*), an answer by counter-question (*paṭipucchābyākaraṇa*), a setting aside (*ṭhapana*), and an answer with remainder (*sāvasesa*).
Investigation by way of answering is [the analysis] such as: "Is it exhaustive or not? Is it surpassed or unsurpassed? Is it mundane or supramundane?

Investigation by bringing the meaning of the question into alignment is the investigation that determines, "This question accords with this, but does not accord with that," after having brought the intended meaning of the question forward.

And investigation by reconciling what precedes and follows is the investigation that harmonizes earlier and later statements. A verse of summary (*anugīti*) is one that summarizes the meaning already stated and summarizes the meaning not yet stated.

The investigation by way of re-statement (*anugītivinicchaya*) is as follows: "comprising both meanings," "comprising wholesome meanings," "comprising unwholesome meanings," and so forth. Regarding gratification and the rest:
for pleasant feeling, it is stated as "having the characteristic of experiencing a desirable object," and so forth; for craving, as "having the characteristic of grasping an object," and so forth;

for the perversions, as "having the characteristic of distorted grasping," and so forth; and for the remaining phenomena of the three planes, as "having their respective characteristics," and so forth.

The investigation of gratification (*assādavicaya*) is the discernment of the specific distinctions of gratification and purpose found within all twenty-two triads and more than four hundred dyads by way of their respective applicable terms. For example,
[the definition] of painful feeling as "having the characteristic of experiencing the undesirable," and of the truths of suffering as "having the characteristic of rebirth-linking," and so forth.

The investigation of disadvantage (*ādīnavavicaya*) occurs through the extraction of the vowel *o* (in the word *okāra*), by way of the fact that impermanence and so forth have a beginning and an end and are terminable, thus being "impermanent" and so on;
and by way of the occurrence of disadvantage in all mundane phenomena through their being subject to defilement, subject to decline, and so forth.

It occurs by way of extracting the specific distinctions of the preliminary practice, such as the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā*), because the Noble Path arrives at the state of deliverance (*nissaraṇa*).
Investigation of escape (*nissaraṇavicaya*) is thus [to be understood] by way of determining the specific distinctions among the various modes of expression regarding Nibbāna as previously described.

Investigation should be understood as the discernment of the fruits and so forth, achieved through the respective Sutta teachings—namely, the fruit to be accomplished, the means thereto, and the specific injunctions found in the Suttas here and there.
Likewise, [it applies to] the questions and answers regarding words, and the sequence of preceding and following verses.

Furthermore, the "Investigation Mode" (*vicayo hāro*) should be understood as having the characteristic of investigation precisely through the process of distinguishing the specific qualities of gratification (*assāda*) and so forth. 3.

"Of all" refers to the sixteen [modes]. "Ground" (*bhūmi*) is said with reference to the phrasing (*byañjana*). For the phrasing is the ground—that is, the locus of occurrence—for the guiding principles (*naya*) and the modes (*hāra*), just like the root words [are for the meanings], because it serves as the basis for the investigation of those [principles and modes]. Indeed, it has been said: "The modes..."
“Investigation of the phrasing” (*byañjanavicaya*). For it is also stated in the *Peṭaka*:

“Where all the methods (*hāra*) converge, they lead to the meaning of the discourse (*suttattha*), due to the diversity of the rules for the phrasing. “The domain” (*gocara*) refers to the meaning of the discourse; for the application of the methods occurs through the extraction of the word-meanings of the discourse.

“Examination of what is appropriate and inappropriate” (*yuttāyuttaparikkhā*) refers to those [methods] regarding the meanings of the phrasing, as well as to what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.

Investigation (*upaparikkhā*). There is also a reading, “investigation of what is logical and what is illogical,” the meaning of which is the examination of what is consistent and what is inconsistent.
But how is their consistency and inconsistency known? By way of not contradicting the four great authorities (*mahāpadesa*).

In that regard, first, for the phrasing (*byañjana*), its state of being a natural expression and its state of expressing the intended meaning constitute its consistency. For the meaning (*attha*), however, [its consistency is determined] by the discourses (*sutta*), the discipline (*vinaya*), and the nature of things (*dhammatā*).
Non-contradiction. This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, will be made clear further on.

Since it has been defined as "the method (hāra) is the reasoning (yutti)," the method of reasoning should be understood as having the characteristic of discerning the state of being logical or illogical regarding both the phrasing and the meaning within the Sutta.
4. "Dhamma" refers to any wholesome or other dhamma contained in the Sutta. "Of that dhamma" refers to that which has been so described.

Of wholesome and other states (*dhamma*). "That which is the proximate cause" (*padaṭṭhāna*) means that cause—whether mentioned in the Sutta or not—which should be explained by determining it according to what is possible, such as appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) and so forth; this is the intended meaning. "Thus" (*iti*) means in this way, that is, by the method already stated.
"As far as all states" (*yāva sabbadhammā*) means for as many states as have been mentioned in that Sutta, for all of them respectively.
The intention is that [the teaching] should be explained after having determined its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).

Alternatively, the meaning is that an investigation into the proximate causes should be carried out for all phenomena (*sabbadhamma*), as far as possible, by asking: "What is the proximate cause of this phenomenon mentioned in the Sutta, and what, in turn, is the proximate cause of that?
This is the Mode of Conveying Proximate Causes (*padaṭṭhāna-hāra*); thus it applies to the phenomena as they appear in the Sutta.

The meaning is that the "method of footing" (padaṭṭhāna-hāra) is characterized by the selection of those phenomena that serve as the footing for others, and which themselves have other phenomena as their footing, according to their logical occurrence. 5.

Regarding the phrase "when one phenomenon has been stated": this refers to any single phenomenon—whether among the wholesome factors and so forth, or among the aggregates and so forth—that is mentioned in a discourse (sutta).

Or it is stated by way of selection based on similarity of form (*sarūpato niddhāraṇavasena*). "Whatever phenomena have a single characteristic" means whatever phenomena, whether by way of being wholesome and so forth, or by way of being the aggregate of form and so forth, possess a characteristic identical to that phenomenon.

"They are all said to exist" means that all those phenomena—whether they consist of the nature of the wholesome and so forth, or the nature of the aggregates and so forth—even if not explicitly mentioned in the Sutta, [are included] by that [statement].
The intention is that they are stated by way of bringing them forward according to the method of commentary because of their having identical characteristics (*samānalakkhaṇatā*).

And here, "having a single characteristic" (*ekalakkhaṇā*) means having identical characteristics (*samānalakkhaṇā*). By this, even those things not explicitly stated—such as co-existence, identical function, identical cause, identical fruit, and identical object—should be understood as being determined just like those that have been stated.
That mode of conveying is called the "Characteristic" (*lakkhaṇo*) mode of conveyance.

Thus, the method of exposition which determines even those teachings not explicitly present in the Sutta as if they were present in the manner already described—that is the meaning of the "Method of Characteristics" (*lakkhaṇa-hāra*). 6.
*Nerutta* means etymology; the meaning is the grammatical derivation of words. "Intention" (*adhippāya*) refers to that of the Buddhas or their disciples.
The intention of the teachers of that sutta. "By way of the phrasing" (*byañjanena*): this is the nominative case used in the sense of the instrumental, for it is an instrument.

And while all the modes of convergence (*hāra*) consist in the investigation of phrasing, this [mode] is stated as "phrasing" because it specifically seeks the meaning through the door of the phrasing itself.
For he will say: "The etymological derivation and the intention of the sutta are [sought] by way of the phrasing."
"And the introduction (nidāna) and the connection between what precedes and what follows (pubbāparānusandhi) should be investigated. Here, "atha" is merely for the purpose of completing the meter.

"Desanānidāna" means that which gives forth or bears fruit is the *nidāna*, i.e., the cause; the meaning is: that by which the teaching is set in motion is the motive for the occurrence of the teaching.
"Pubbāparānusandhi" means the connection (*anusandhi*) by means of what precedes and what follows. It is also said: "The connection by means of what precedes and what follows."
"Recitation" (pāṭha) means explaining by correlating the latter part of a sutta with its preceding part.
Alternatively, it is the correlation of a sutta being commented upon—by way of a formal recitation—with other suttas that precede or follow it;

and also the connection of one word with the subsequent word—this too is "pubbāparānusandhi" (connection between what precedes and what follows). This method of analysis is the "fourfold array" (catubyūha).
The meaning is that the method called the "Fourfold Array" (catubyūha-hāra) is characterized by the analysis of these four factors:
etymology, intention, and so forth. 7. Regarding the phrase "in one footing" (ekamhi padaṭṭhāne):

when a phenomenon such as the element of exertion (ārambhadhātu), which serves as the footing for phenomena such as the element of striving (parakkamadhātu), has been set forth in the teaching; [the method] seeks the remaining footing by not grasping it because of its dissimilarity.
Or, because they are proximate causes for negligence and so forth, he seeks out and investigates with wisdom other states such as indolence that serve as their proximate bases;
and having sought them out, while connecting them through his commentary, he turns back to the teaching— that is, he adapts it— by explaining,
according to the method already stated, how the discourse commenced by means of the arousal of energy and so forth is presented in terms of negligence and the rest.
It is called "turning back" (*āvaṭṭa*) by way of the opposite of the teaching. "Turning back" is a method (*hāra*);
the meaning is that the method characterized by turning back the phenomena grasped in the teaching by way of similar and dissimilar factors is called the "turning-back method.
8. "Phenomenon" (*dhamma*) means a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature; it is of many kinds, such as wholesome and so forth. "Footing" (*padaṭṭhāna*) refers to that in which...
When one is established [in the path], one attains further specific qualities; that is the cause for the attainment of those specific qualities.

"Ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to grounds such as the ground of the worldling (*puthujjana-bhūmi*), the ground of seeing (*dassana-bhūmi*), and so forth. "By way of analysis" (*vibhajjate*) means he explains by means of differentiation.

"Common" (*sādhāraṇa*) means common, undifferentiated, or equal—either by way of names such as "to be abandoned by seeing" and so on, or by way of the bases such as "worldlings," "stream-enterers," and so forth. By the reverse of what was stated...
They should be understood as uncommon. "Analysis" (vibhatti) means that this method of conveying (hāra), which analyzes the aforementioned phenomena and so forth, should be known as "analysis";

this is the meaning. Therefore, the "method of analysis" (vibhattihāra) should be regarded as having the characteristic of analyzing defiled phenomena and purified phenomena by way of their common and uncommon aspects, their proximate causes (padaṭṭhāna), and their planes (bhūmi).
9. *Niddiṭṭhe* means when it has been stated, recited, or commented upon in the Sutta. *Bhāvite*:

just as things similar to those already arisen are called "arisen," so too the meaning of *bhāvite* is that which is similar to what has been developed (*bhāvita*) is "to be developed" (*bhāvetabba*).
*Pahīne*: here too the same principle applies. *Parivattati*: it turns around by way of the opposites of those factors mentioned as their counterparts.
Meaning (*attha*). The "Method of Reversal" (*parivattana-hāra*) should be understood as having the characteristic of turning back by way of the opposites of the phenomena thus demonstrated.
10. "Synonyms" (*vevacana*): various expressions for one and the same meaning are "vivacanāni"; "vivacanāni" themselves are "vevacanāni," meaning alternative terms (*pariyāya-saddā*).
These are the synonyms. "Many" means numerous. The particle *tu* is used for emphasis; thus, there are indeed many alternative terms.
This should be explained by means of synonyms, etymologies, and applications; it shows that they are not merely a few.

"Stated in the Suttas" means spoken within the word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Pitakas, which is designated as the ninefold Suttanta. Here too, the sense of the particle *tu* must be brought in and applied;
by this it is meant that only those synonyms actually occurring in the Canon (Pāḷi) should be taken. "Of a single phenomenon" means of a single referent (padattha).

"One who knows the suttas" means that just as when it is said, "Know the ghee," the meaning is that one commands, "Investigate with ghee," "Give ghee," or "Give!"—so too, one who is skilled in the suttas, a preacher of the Dhamma, investigates, clarifies, and coordinates many synonymous expressions for a single meaning.
This is the method known as "Synonyms. Regarding its meaning:

The method of synonyms (vevacanahāra) is characterized by the application of various synonymous terms as previously described. Therefore, it should be understood that the "method of synonyms" is characterized by the application of many synonymous terms to a single meaning.

11. "Phenomenon" (dhamma) refers to phenomena such as the aggregates (khandha) and so forth. "By means of designations" (paññattīhi) means by means of modes of making known or ways of informing, [so as to distinguish them] without confusion.
Or by means of establishing [the meaning]. "By various ways" means by many kinds of methods, such as through the modes of presentation (*nikkhepa*), origin (*pabhava*), and so forth.
"That mode" refers to the manner in which a single object is presented by means of numerous designations (*paññatti*)—such as presentation, origin, and description.

It should be understood that "the method known as presentation" means it is to be known as the method of presentation (*paññattihāra*). Therefore, [it is applied] to each individual phenomenon by means of its numerous designations.
The "method of description" (*paññatti-hāra*) should be understood as having the characteristic of elucidating the modes in which things are to be described.
12. "Dependent arising" (*paṭicca-samuppāda*) means dependent origination. "Faculties and aggregates" (*indriya-khandhā*) means both faculties and aggregates.
"Elements and bases" (*dhātu-āyatana*) means both elements and bases. By these [is meant]: that twelvefold mode of conditions and those twenty-two faculties.

The five aggregates, the eighteen elements, and the twelve bases—when these are determined by way of the meaning of the terms as they appear in the Sutta—the "entry" (*otaraṇa*) is that method of commentary which penetrates them; the sense is that it enters into dependent origination and so forth.
That specific mode of commentary thus described is called the "mode of entry" (*otaraṇahāra*).
And here, by the word "ca" (and), the inclusion of the "gateways of emptiness" (*suññatāmukha*) and so forth—though not explicitly mentioned in the verse—should be understood.

Thus, it should be known that the "method of penetration" (*otaraṇahāra*) is characterized by the penetration into the meaning of the Suttas through the gateways of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and so on. 13.
*Vissajjitamhi* means "when explained" by the Buddha and others. *Pañhe* refers to the matter desired to be known. *Gāthāyaṃ* means "in the verse" as it appears in the metrical text.
And it is stated that those asking this question generally do so by way of composing verses. Regarding the phrase "having taken as a basis" (*yamārabbha*):
that verse was asked with reference to, or having made a certain matter its subject; it refers to that matter. As for the classification of "pure and impure":
there is the case where the word is purified but the basis is not; and the case where both the word and the basis are purified. Thus [it concerns] the words and so forth.
The Investigation of Purified and Unpurified States: "The Purifying Mode" means that the aforementioned investigation is called the purifying mode (*sodhana-hāra*).
Thus, it should be understood as the "Purifying Mode," characterized by the purification of the words, word-meanings, questions, and undertakings within the Sutta.
14. Regarding "oneness" (*ekattatā*): the state of being one is "oneness" (*ekatta*); oneness itself is "oneness-ness" (*ekattatā*); [it is] by that oneness-ness. The word *eka*—
And here, *sāmañña* is a synonym for *samāna* (common); therefore, the meaning is "by way of commonality. *Vimattā* means differentiated; *vimattā* itself is *vematta*;
the state of that is *vemattatā*; by that *vemattatā*, the meaning is "by way of distinction.

"Those [factors] should not be conceptualized" refers to those phenomena which, though [already stated] by way of commonality as "suffering, origin," and so forth, are [further specified] as "birth, aging, craving for sense-pleasures, craving for existence," and so forth.

Furthermore, those [terms] taught specifically in the Sutta should not be conceptualized by way of distinguishing between their commonality and their particularity—asking, for instance, "What is the commonality here, or what is the distinction?

Why? Because the conceptualization of commonality and distinction lacks stability due to its being merely conventional usage, and because it is established through mutual dependence, like the distinctions of time, direction, and so forth.
For just as specific times such as "today," "yesterday," or "tomorrow" are spoken of, they lack a fixed intrinsic nature.
Just as specific directions are spoken of when one says, "the eastern direction" or "the western direction," so too are general and specific [qualities].
For instance, that which is called "this is suffering" is a generality in relation to birth and so forth, yet it is a particularity in relation to the Truths.
This same method applies to the Origin and the other [Truths] as well. This mode of analysis is called the "Basis" (*adhiṭṭhāna*); thus [should one analyze] the teachings contained in the Suttas.
The meaning is that the "mode of determination" (adhiṭṭhāna-hāra) is so called because its characteristic is the determination of generalities and particularities by way of non-repudiation.

15. "Those states" (ye dhammā) refers to those causal states such as ignorance (avijjā) and so forth. "That state" (yaṃ dhammaṃ) refers to that causally arisen state such as volitional formations (saṅkhāra) and so forth.

"They produce" (janayanti) means they bring about. "By way of conditions" (paccayā) means by way of being co-nascent conditions (sahajāta-paccaya). "Successively" (paramparato) means by way of being successive conditions (parampara-paccaya).
The meaning is: "having become a condition by way of connecting with a corresponding continuity.
For it is the pinnacle of decisive support (*upanissaya-koṭi*) that is intended here. As for the phrase "having drawn down the cause":

having drawn down—that is, having extracted from the Sutta—that cause which consists of the aforementioned conditions and is divided into types such as the producer (*janaka*), etc., [this refers to] that which is called the commentary.

"This is the string, this is the accessory"—thus, having determined the causes and conditions designated as "accessories" for those phenomena mentioned in the Sutta, the meaning is that the string is the accessory characterized by such a description. 16.

"Those phenomena" refers to those phenomena such as virtue (sīla) and so forth. "Whose roots" means those things, such as concentration (samādhi) and so forth, of which [virtue and the rest] are the roots; they [are the roots] of those [phenomena].
The connection is that [the terms] are to be applied by way of being the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for concentration and so forth.

And as for those words shown by the Sage to have a single meaning— namely, the terms "fading away of lust," "mind-liberation," "fruit of the trainee," and "transcending the sense-sphere" (*kāmadhātu*),

which the Buddha-Muni has explained as having a single meaning in terms of the state of the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*)— the connection is that these are to be applied by way of being synonyms for one another.

In this context, "ascription" (*samāropana*) refers to the explanation of the fulfillment of development by way of elucidating another aspect of the three aggregates of virtue and so forth—comprised within the three trainings—which are grasped either according to the literal sense or by way of selection from the Sutta.

Furthermore, since the fulfillment of development occurs through the abandoning of what is to be abandoned, the ascription of abandonment is also effectively shown by implication. This is the ascription.

The term *hāra* (mode of conveying) means that which has the characteristic of coordinating—by way of the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*), synonyms (*vevacana*), development (*bhāvanā*), abandoning (*pahāna*), and investigation (*vicāraṇa*)—the teachings found in the Suttas;
this is called the mode of conveying.
This is the summary of the methods (*naya*).

17. Having thus demonstrated all sixteen modes (*hāra*) by way of verse composition, the passage beginning with “craving and ignorance” (*taṇhañca*) is now stated in order to demonstrate them by way of method (*naya*).

Therein, the connection is: “he who leads both craving and ignorance”—that is, craving and ignorance as they appear in the Sutta, or as they are taken by way of analytical determination according to their meaning.
That specific excellence of commentary which leads [them] leads them to the side of defilement (*saṃkilesa-pakkha*).
The intention is that one "brings [them] to" by way of defilement, and thus applies them to the meaning of the sutta. "By means of calm" (samathena) means by means of concentration (samādhi).

"By means of insight" (vipassanāya) means by means of wisdom (paññā); the intention is that one who leads [them] brings them to the side of purification, and likewise applies them to the meaning of the sutta.

"Having joined them with the truths" means that craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and ignorance (avijjā) constitute the truth of origination (samudayasacca) because they are rooted in existence (bhava); as for the remainder...
Phenomena belonging to the three planes are the truth of suffering; serenity and insight are the truth of the path; and the unconditioned element attainable through them is the truth of cessation.

Having thus applied these four truths, this method is called the "Joyous Turn" (*nandiyāvaṭṭa*), because it applies the meaning of the Sutta concerning the side of defilement—consisting of craving and ignorance—to the side of purification—consisting of serenity and insight—by way of the application of the four truths.
The meaning is that this specific method of exposition characterized by the "guiding eye" (nayanalakkhaṇa) is called the *Nandiyāvaṭṭa* method.

Here, the "ground" (*bhūmi*) of the method is referred to as "method" (*naya*) in the verse; therefore, it is described as a "specific method of exposition. For the "method of the meaning" (*atthanaya*) is not the exposition itself;

rather, the "method of guidance" (*anugāhaṇanaya*) in the preliminary stage, which is conducive to the penetration of the Four Truths, is the method of the meaning. Now, regarding that [method], for those who understand through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*), etc.—
The arrangement of the system-ground by way of craving and so forth is the terminology for that system. 18.
"Unwholesome" refers to all unwholesome phenomena comprised within the twelve types of consciousness-arising.

"With their roots" means with their own roots; the meaning is: with greed, hatred, and delusion. "Wholesome" refers to all wholesome phenomena belonging to the four planes. "With wholesome roots" means...
He leads by means of wholesome [states] rooted in non-greed and so forth. While leading, he leads that which is wholesome and unwholesome;
it is "real" (*bhūta*) because it does not exist as something unreal like an illusion or a mirage. It is "suchness" (*tatha*) because it is not a mere conventional truth like a cloth or a jar.

Since there is no occurrence of desirable ripening for the unwholesome and no occurrence of undesirable ripering for the wholesome, it is "not otherwise" (*avitatha*) because it is non-deceptive when there is ripening. Thus, of these...

The three terms should be understood as qualifying both the wholesome and the unwholesome. Alternatively, this method leads the unwholesome by means of the unwholesome roots and the wholesome by means of the wholesome roots;
thus, it "leads what has come to be" (bhūta) as it truly is (tatha), not otherwise. The meaning is that, having determined the four truths, it applies them.
For suffering and the rest, because they possess the nature of being oppressive and so forth, lack any state of being other than that.
The elements (*bhūtāni*) are "thus" (*tathā*) because they possess the nature of reality; they are "not otherwise" (*avitathā*) because they are non-deceptive. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, these four are thus, not otherwise, and not different.

They call that method *Tipukkhala*, which [deals with] the side of defilement through the roots of unwholesomeness, and the side of purification through the roots of wholesomeness, according to the meaning of the Sutta.

The specific distinction of the commentary is characterized by guidance through the application of the Four Noble Truths; the meaning is that they lead [the disciples] to that "three-peaked" (tipukkhalam) [method].
19. "By means of the perversions" (vipallāsehi): this refers to the four perversions (vipallāsas) that proceed according to the method of perceiving the beautiful in the unattractive, and so forth.

"Defilements" (kilesa): they are called defilements because they defile and afflict; they are defiled phenomena, meaning the side of defilement (saṃkilesapakkha). Some also read "in defilement" (saṃkilese).

They recite [this], meaning "together with the defilements. "By means of the faculties" means by means of the faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*). "In the true Dhamma" means in the true Dhamma of practice and penetration;

the meaning is "on the side of purification. That which leads this [Dhamma] is a specific mode of exposition characterized by leading—by means of the faculties of faith and so forth—the entire side of defilement through the perversions such as the perception of beauty (*subhasaññā*), and [leading] the side of purification through the application of the Four Truths.

The meaning is: those who know the methods, who are skilled in the method of the true Dhamma, and who are indeed proficient in the method of the goal, lead [the teaching] according to this method; they "lead" it by way of the "lion's sport" (*sīhavikkīḷita*), so it is said. "In the expositions" (*veyyākaraṇesu*) means:
in the explanations of the meaning of the Sutta composed for the purpose of applying each respective method of meaning;
such is the meaning. For that very reason he says, "here and there. "Wholesome and unwholesome" refers to those things that are purifying and those that are defiling, respectively.
The phenomena that have become the directions of this method (*naya*). "Stated" means explained by extracting them from the discourses (*sutta*).

"One should survey with the mind" means one examines and investigates those aforementioned phenomena with the mind alone, in the manner of "this is the first direction, this is the second direction," and so forth, as being the directional aspects of each respective method; such is the meaning. There is also a reading: "He surveys them not externally."
In that context, "those" (*te*) refers to the phenomena (*dhammā*) as previously described. "Not outside" (*abahī*) means "within"; the meaning is "in the mind itself.

Regarding the phrase "they call that the surveying of directions" (*taṃ khu disālocanaṃ āhu*), it means: "surveying" (*olokana*) is what they call the method known as "surveying of directions" (*disālocana*).
The particle *khu* is a particle used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). By this, he shows that this method is indeed the act of surveying itself, and not some distinct entity.
21. "Having looked" means having examined by way of the first and subsequent directions.
"By means of the surveying of directions" means by means of the method of surveying directions acting as the instrument.

Or rather, the meaning here should be understood thus: that method by which the directions are surveyed through the application of the principles of various meanings is called "the surveying of directions. "Having lifted up" means having extracted [them] from the phenomena that constitute the directions.
The meaning is: "having extracted from the Sutta. They also read: "He who, having picked up [the parts], brings them together"; the meaning of that is:
"he who performs the bringing together of those phenomena which have become the directions. Or, *yaṃ* is a reference back to the action (*kriyā*).

"Brings together" (*samāneti*) means he brings them equally (*samaṃ*) or correctly (*sammā*) by way of applying each respective method (*naya*). But what does he bring together? All wholesome and unwholesome [phenomena].
"Bringing together those things that have become the respective directions of method":

here, the meaning is that this "hook" (*aṅkusa*)—which brings together those phenomena that have become the respective directions of method—is called the "method" (*naya*). And these two are also called the "method of conventional usage" (*vohāranaya*) and the "method of action" (*kammanaya*).
Having thus demonstrated the modes (*hāra*) and the methods (*naya*), he now states, beginning with "The sixteen modes first," in order to show the sequence of their application.

In this context, the first sixteen modes of conveyance (*hāra*) are to be "joined"—this is the ellipsis. The intention is that the commentary on the modes of conveyance should be composed first, because it constitutes the search for the phrasing (*byañjana*).
"From the perspective of surveying the directions" means by means of surveying the directions; or rather, this is the very reading itself.
In the phrase "with the hook," the word *hi* is a mere particle. The rest is self-evident.
23. Twelve Phrases.
Now, in order to point out those phrases—both phonetic and semantic—by virtue of which it is said that a sutta consists of twelve phrases, he says:
"A syllable, a phrase," and so forth. Therein, a phoneme (*vaṇṇa*) within an incomplete phrase is a syllable (*akkhara*).
Because it does not shift or move by way of transition (*pariyāya*). For there is no transition of a phoneme (*vaṇṇa*);
in what sense, then, is it called a "phoneme"? It is in the sense of describing meaning (*atthasaṃvaṇṇana*).

Indeed, it is the phoneme itself—which, due to its momentary nature, proceeds through successive states and is grasped as words and so forth—that expresses this or that meaning according to its connection. A single phoneme...
Or it is a word (*pada*) or a syllable (*akkhara*). Some, however, say that a "syllable" is so called because it is articulated by means of the mind through the speech of instruction.

A "word" (*pada*) is that by which a meaning is reached (*pajjati*); it is fourfold: the noun-word (*nāmapada*), the verb-word (*ākhyātapada*), the prepositional-word (*upasaggapada*), and the particle-word (*nipātapada*).
Among these, a noun-word is one whose primary focus is a sentient being, such as "contact," "feeling," or "consciousness."
“Touches, feels, cognizes”—such terms as these are verbal nouns (*ākhyātapada*) that primarily denote action (*kiriyā*).

“*Pa-*” and so forth are prepositional particles (*upasaggapada*), serving as the means for grasping the specific distinctions of the action. “*Eva*” and so forth are indeclinable particles (*nipātapada*), acting as the cause for manifesting the specific qualities of both the action and the agent that possess the same form.
"Phrasing" (*byañjana*) is stated briefly as that which "manifests" (*byañjayati*) the meaning expressed by a word;
thus, it is a sentence (*vākya*). That, however, should be understood in terms of its actual substance as a collection of words.

For even when hearing only a single word, the comprehension of the meaning occurs only after connecting it with other words obtained through the context and so forth; therefore, it is indeed the sentence [that constitutes the phrasing].
It clarifies the meaning. *Nirutti* means etymological derivation (*nibbacana*) expressed through its formal structure (*ākāra*).

*Niddesa* means detailed exposition; it is called *niddesa* because it is a teaching that leaves nothing unexplained. The *ākāra* (formal structure) is the analysis of a sentence into its constituent words (*pada*).
If this is so, what is the distinction between a word and a formal structure? It is [the distinction] when a sentence is not yet concluded or when it is not being analyzed.
A word (*pada*) is a constituent part of that [sentence]. Alternatively, when a sentence is analyzed after its pronunciation has been completed, a vowel such as *ā* is a constituent part of it;
this is the distinction between them. "The sixth case" means the genitive case (*chaṭṭhavacana*).

That which has the vowel *ā* as its sixth case is "that which has the vowel *ā* as its sixth case," namely, a consonant-word (*byañjanapada*). And here, immediately following this word "consonant" (*byañjana*)—
By one stating the phrase containing the mode (*ākāra*) immediately after the explanatory phrase (*niddesapada*), it is said to be the "sixth case of the mode.
However, for those who desire a sequential order of the phrases, that [phrase] should be placed immediately after the word for the phoneme (*byañjanapada*). For he will say:
"The phonemes are immeasurable and the modes are immeasurable; one clarifies by means of the phonemes and analyzes by means of the modes."
Some, however, read: "The modes, words, phonemes, and terminology are the exposition.
"All phonemes are just this much" means that all these phonemes and so forth which have been specified constitute the entirety of phonemes;
there is no such thing as a phoneme not included among them.
24. *Saṅkāsanā* means concise exposition. *Pakāsanā* means detailed exposition; it is so called because it is first expounded (*kāsīyati*), that is, it is illuminated (*dīpīyati*).
By these two terms, the aspect of the meaning is grasped as it is being analyzed through the syllables and words.
Since the specific determination is made for those who hear when the syllables are being heard, there is the comprehension of the word-meaning at the conclusion of each word.

It exists. For it will be said: "Therein, the Blessed One makes known by means of syllables (*akkhara*) and reveals by means of phrases (*pada*)," and also, "He discloses by means of syllables and phrases.
"Vivaraṇā" means expansion. "Vibhajanā," "uttānīkamma," and "paññatti" together constitute "vibhajanuttānīkammapaññatti."
In this context, "analyzing" (*vibhajana*) means making a division; by both [terms], he expresses "indicating" (*niddisana*).

Here, it should be understood that while the mode of meaning (*atthākāra*) is being indicated through the modes of phrasing (*byañjanākāra*) according to the previous method, the mode of meaning itself is thereby shown. "Making plain" (*uttānīkamma*) means making manifest. "Designation" (*paññatti*) is making known through various modes.
By both [terms], he speaks of "counter-indication" (*paṭiniddisana*). Here too, by those [terms] reckoned as "etymological analysis" (*nirutti*) and "indication" (*niddesa*)...

The aspect of the meaning (*atthākāra*) being pointed out by means of the phrasing and words is said to be that which is "re-pointed out" (*paṭiniddisīyati*). "By these" (*etehehi*) refers to these very [phrasings], because there is no purpose of teaching (*desanāttha*) apart from the making known (*saṅkāsanādi*) and so forth.
"Meaning" (*attha*) is the meaning of the discourse (*suttattha*). "Function" (*kamma*) is the function of causing comprehension (*ugghaṭanādi-kamma*) and so forth;

for when the teaching proceeds by way of the meaning of the discourse, it [performs] the function for those to be converted who are "to be enlightened by a brief statement" (*ugghaṭitaññu*) and the rest.

The production of an activity that awakens the continuum of consciousness (cittasantāna). And that meaning of the sutta consists of the modes of "making known" (saṅkāsanā) and so forth. Therefore it was said: "The meaning and the function have been demonstrated.
25. "Three" is stated with a change of gender; it means "three" (tayo). "By nine phrases" means by nine sections (koṭṭhāsa).
"Meaning is properly connected" means that the meaning is correctly joined and does not occur without it. For since the entire word of the Buddha reveals the Four Noble Truths,

and since the methods of meaning proceed by way of connecting them to the Four Noble Truths, the entire meaning of the Pāḷi is comprised within the three methods of meaning and functions through the specific modes of manifestation such as "making known" (saṅkāsanā) and so forth.

26. Now, in order to facilitate the easy grasping of the meaning of the terms in the *Nettippakaraṇa*—namely, the modes of exposition (*desanāhāra*) and so forth as they have been explained—he says, beginning with "of the meaning" (*atthassā*), demonstrating them by way of enumeration.

Therein, "twenty-four" refers to sixteen modes of exposition, six phrases of phrasing (*byañjanapada*), and two methods of action (*kammanaya*); thus, twenty-four. "Both" refers to the six phrases of meaning (*atthapada*).
“Three ways of meaning”: this refers to both the ninefold [ways] as already stated and the twenty-fourfold [ways].
“Having combined” means having condensed them. There is also the reading “saṅkhepato,” which means “for one who makes them into one. “Ettikā” means of such a measure;
the meaning is that there is no object of the guide’s categories (nettipadattha) apart from these.

Thus, regarding the investigation of the meaning of the *Sutta* of the Guide (*Netti*) consisting of thirty-three topics, it was shown by way of the "Guides" (*Nayas*) that the "Modes of Conveying" (*Hāras*) should first be commented upon—according to the statement, "The sixteen Modes of Conveying come first. This sequence for the commentary on the Modes of Conveying and the Guides is established precisely by the order of their teaching.
Since this is established in this way, the present undertaking illuminates the following point:
All these modes (hāras) and methods (nayas) should be applied to the discourses by way of commentary according to this very sequence shown here, and not out of order.
What, then, is the reason that these modes and methods are taught in this specific sequence?

Although this inquiry does not find a fixed place in any particular [textual] order, nevertheless, regarding the teaching of the Dhamma—which consists of its basis, its fruit, its means, and its body—...
Because it has the nature of analyzing [the factors] such as gratification (*assāda*), it is naturally in accordance with all the Suttas; because it is easy to understand;
and because it serves as the foundation for other specific commentaries such as the method of investigation (*vicayahāra*) and so forth, the "mode of teaching" (*desanāhāra*) was shown first.

This is because, together with the questioning of words, their resolution, and the sequence of what precedes and follows, the mode of teaching has the nature of investigating the meaning of the words.
Immediately after that comes Investigation (*vicaya*). For it will say: "He investigates the words... [and so on] ...he investigates the injunction, he investigates the subsequent verse.

Since the investigation of what is appropriate and inappropriate regarding meanings already sifted by the method of Investigation is "proper" (*yuttā*), the method of Coordination (*yutti-hāra*) is stated immediately after Investigation, because its nature consists in the investigation of what is coordinated.
For it will say: "Having sifted by means of the method of Investigation, one should coordinate by means of the method of Coordination."

The "Investigation of Footings" (padaṭṭhānahāra) is shown immediately after the "Conveying of Reason" (yuttihāra), because one must perform an investigation of footings characterized by determining, through a series of causes, meanings that are either appropriate or inappropriate in accordance with their arising.
For it will be said: "Whatever is a decisive support (upanissaya) and whatever is a condition (paccaya), all that is a footing."

The Mode of Conveying Characteristics (lakkhaṇa-hāra) is stated immediately after the Mode of Footings (padaṭṭhāna) in order to show that even those phenomena not explicitly mentioned must be grasped as having a single characteristic, provided their individual natures have been determined through a series of causes— both appropriate and inappropriate.
For instance, in the *Lakkhaṇahāravibhaṅga*, dependent origination is presented by such statements as, "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," and so forth.
Having shown this, it was said: "In this way, those phenomena that have a single characteristic," and so forth.

After the characteristics, the fourfold analysis (catubyūha) is stated in order to show that the etymologies and other details of even those phenomena already determined by their meaning must be explained, and not only of those that have come down in the Suttas in their specific forms. For in this way, there is a complete understanding of the meaning without exception.

And having done so, he will speak of the exhaustive inclusion [of all factors] in the passage: “For when a bhikkhu knows the name of the goal (attha) and knows the name of the Dhamma, he applies it accordingly.
Likewise, regarding the phrase “he enters the womb again and again,” [the commentary will explain]:
“Those who wish to be repelled by aging and death will, O friends, be [restrained] regarding nutriment...”
By such passages as "knowing the measure [of food] and guarding the doors of the sense faculties," he will explain right practice (sammāpaṭipatti) as the intended meaning (adhippāya).
When the word-meanings (padattha) in a sutta have been shown along with its etymology (nibbacana), intended meaning (adhippāya), and causal origin (nidāna)— that is,

in the investigation of the preceding and following sections known as the correlation with other suttas— it is possible to easily demonstrate how those meanings turn toward other similar and dissimilar phenomena.
Immediately after the Fourfold Array (cattubyūha), the Conversion (āvaṭṭa) is taught. For it is by that very means—in the verse beginning "Exert yourselves!

Strive!"—that the faculties of energy, concentration, and wisdom are extracted through exertion, striving, and application to the Buddha’s teaching; and then, having shown in another sutta that "negligence" (pamāda) is the root of non-application to that [teaching], negligence is converted.

Since the classification of defiled and purified phenomena according to their common and uncommon aspects—both in terms of their proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) and their plane (*bhūmi*)—can be easily applied once they have been directed toward the turning back [of the mind] from similar and dissimilar phenomena, the Mode of Conveying Analysis (*vibhattihāra*) is stated immediately after the Mode of Turning Back (*āvaṭṭahāra*). Thus, in the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Analysis, it is asked:
"Which phenomena are common? Two phenomena are common..."
Having begun with the words, "those common in name and those common in substance," he will analyze the phenomena according to their similar and dissimilar aspects, stating:

"The defilements to be abandoned by vision are common to beings fixed in wrongness and to beings not so fixed; lust for sensual pleasure and ill-will are common to the worldling and the stream-enterer," and so forth.

Because there is no lack of counterparts for phenomena that are blameworthy and blameless, once their distinction has been made, it is possible to easily reverse the factors mentioned in the sutta by means of their opposites;
thus, immediately after the analysis, the Mode of Reversal (parivattana-hāra) is stated.
For instance, in the case of the individual person with right view, whose wrong view has been worn away, the nature of the factors is analyzed in this way.
He will provide examples in the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Reversal (*parivattanā-hāra*).

The Mode of Synonyms (*vevacana-hāra*) is stated immediately after the Mode of Reversal for the purpose of showing that phenomena which have been reversed by way of their opposites must also be understood through synonymous expressions, and are not limited to those appearing in the Suttas alone.
Thus, those phenomena are made manifest even through synonymous terms; therefore, [the following concerns] phenomena manifested by way of synonyms.

The Mode of Conveying Designation (paññatti-hāra) is stated immediately after the Mode of Synonyms (vevacana-hāra), because it is possible to easily understand the classification by way of designation according to its divisions.

For he will explain in the analysis of the Mode of Designation both the classification of the designations used as synonyms for the teachings found in the Suttas and the means of making them easy to understand.

When the classification of phenomena such as dependent origination and the Truths has been made by way of the classification of designations such as the full understanding of manifestation (pabhāva-pariññā), etc., [the Mode of Conveying Designation follows].
Since it is possible to demonstrate the determination of the teachings contained in the Suttas by way of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) and so forth,
the Mode of Conveying the Entry (*otaraṇahāra*) is stated immediately after the Mode of Description (*paññatti*). For instance,

having cited the verse beginning with "above and below," one will determine the knowledge of the Adept (*asekkha-vijjā*) by means of the word "emancipated" (*vippamutta*), and then illustrate dependent origination through such passages as "With the arising of knowledge comes the cessation of ignorance."

Since it is possible to easily accomplish the purification of the commencement of the inquiry into the meaning of the words for those who have been introduced to the *Dhātu-āyatana* and other sections of the Sutta, the "Mode of Purification" (*sodhana-hāra*) is stated immediately after the "Mode of Introduction. For he will say:
"Wherever the commencement is thus purified, that question is answered," and so forth.

In order to show that once the words and their meanings in the suttas have been purified, it is easy to discern the state of general and specific characteristics found therein, the Mode of Conveying the Foundation (adhiṭṭhāna-hāra) is presented immediately after the Mode of Purification (sodhana). For purification is of great assistance to the foundation;
for this very reason, he will later say: "In whatever way the question is asked, in that same way it should be answered."

When the qualities that constitute the specific and general characteristics of asceticism have been proclaimed—both those common and those uncommon—the classification of the "requisites" (*parikkhāra*), which consist of both common and uncommon forms and serve as the cause for conditions (*paccaya-hetu*), is easy to understand;
thus, the requisites are mentioned immediately after the foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*). For it will be said: "The cause has an uncommon characteristic; the condition has a common characteristic."
"How so? Just as, for instance, in the production of a sprout, the seed is the specific cause, while the earth and water are the common causes," and so forth.
When both the specific and the common causes have been shown, one should determine the causal mode of that [cause] toward its own effects;
the manner of teaching through the classification of those causes and effects; and the cultivation and abandonment of the phenomena to be cultivated and abandoned.

Since the meanings of the Sutta being correctly explained lead to the realization of suchness (*tathattāvabodha*), the "Method of Coordination" (*samāropano hāro*) is shown immediately after the "Requisites" (*parikkhāra*).
This is the reason for the sequence of the methods (*hāra*).

As for the "Guiding Principles" (*naya*), because they are applied to the three types of those to be trained (*veneyya*), the teaching of the three guiding principles of meaning follows that same sequence, namely the "Joyful Cycle" (*nandiyāvaṭṭa*) and the others.

The sequence of the three methods of meaning (atthanaya) should be understood. For the three types of those to be trained—namely, those who understand through a condensed statement (ugghaṭitaññu) and so forth—employ the Nandiyāvaṭṭa and other methods.
Therefore, like the summary (uddesa), the exposition (niddesa), and the detailed exposition (paṭiniddesa), these [methods] function in their respective order for the benefit of those [trainees].
For indeed, four, six, and eight root-terms have been expounded for them. But as for the other two methods...

The sequence of the summary (uddesa) should be understood by this reason: first, the examination of the ground of the threefold meaning and method, and second, the bringing together of that [meaning] therein.
For it is not possible to bring them together without having first examined them.
And the extraction of meanings (hāra) is limited to this extent; for by these many specific modes, accompanied by the threefold meaning and method, the meaning of the Sutta is [fully revealed].
It should be understood that when [the text] is extracted, it is sufficient for those to be trained (veneyya) to attain the first stage of the unsurpassed [path].
For the teaching of the *Nettippakaraṇa* has as its purpose the attainment of the stage of vision (*dassanabhūmi*).

Alternatively, because all the specific commentaries on the Sutta are included within this, the "modes" (*hāra*) should be seen as complete at this point; for whatever [modes] there are of the Sutta...
It has already been stated that all these specific methods of commentary depend upon the instructions of the *Netti*;
for indeed, whatever modes of commenting upon a discourse (*sutta*) are pointed out, they are as follows:

the origin of the discourse must be stated, its underlying intention (*adhippāya*) must be clarified, the meaning of the words must be commented upon in various ways, and there must be injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*).
Furthermore, one must understand the connection [between sections], resolve contradictions, and provide a conclusion appropriate to the sequence.
Likewise, when explaining the meaning, one must state the purpose of the sutta, the summarized meaning, the word-by-word meaning, the sequence, the objection, and the resolution.
Similarly, the introductory remarks, the grammatical analysis of the words, the word-meanings, the interrogation, and the presentation [of the answer] must be stated.

Likewise, there are three types of discourse: the single-reed, the four-cornered, and the seated-circle. Among these, the exposition that consists of reciting the text and explaining the meaning of each individual word is called the "single-reed.

The exposition that demonstrates the opposing side, provides an illustration for the opposing side, demonstrates one's own position, and provides an illustration for one's own position is called the "four-cornered.
The exposition that proceeds to its conclusion by way of dissimilar factors alone, and then again proceeds to its conclusion by way of similar factors alone, is called the "seated-circle."

"A discourse should be commented upon by means of analysis, by discourse on the true nature, and by figurative expressions"— these and others are included right here, because they are comprised within a few of the methods (hāra) mentioned herein.
As for the guiding principles (naya), since only the three types of those to be trained— namely, those who understand through a brief summary and so forth— are capable of realizing the Truths,

and the teaching of the method of meaning (atthanaya) is intended for their sake, therefore, even though the phenomena of defilement and purification exist, [they are not treated separately] from the aforementioned divisions of the root-terms.

Having expanded them, they should be analyzed according to their various modes; likewise, the root terms are not expanded, but are stated as having this maximum number solely by way of the three types of those to be trained.
For since all phenomena of defilement and purification are included within these nine sets of nine root terms, they should not be increased;
and because the three types of those to be trained are the subject matter, they should not be diminished. Thus, this should be understood as the maximum limit of the methods.

As for the "method of action" (*kammanaya*), its limit is this alone, because there is no other way of presentation possible apart from the processes of examination (*ālocana*) and coordination (*samānayana*).

Regarding the phrase "the cause and so forth" (*hetvādi*): here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the result (*phala*), plane (*bhūmi*), proximate cause (*upanisā*), the similar (*sabhāga*), the dissimilar (*visabhāga*), characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*), method (*naya*), and others are included.
Among these, "cause" (*hetu*) means a reason (*kāraṇa*); it is also called a "dharma," and it is of one kind insofar as it functions as a condition (*paccaya*). It is the agent (*kāraka*).
It is twofold as "that which brings about" (sampāpaka). Furthermore, it is threefold as the "doer," the "informer," and the "bringer about.
It is fourfold as the "cause-cause," the "condition-cause," the "supreme cause," and the "common cause. It is fivefold as a condition-dhamma that is wholesome, unwholesome, sound, or the Noble Path.
Likewise, there are the homogeneous cause, the non-homogeneous cause, the internal cause, the external cause, the productive cause, and the appropriating cause.

It should be understood that [the cause] is of many kinds, such as the common cause (*sādhāraṇa-hetu*), the uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*), the immediately preceding cause (*samanantara-hetu*), the successive cause (*parampara-hetu*), the co-nascent cause (*sahajāta-hetu*), the non-co-nascent cause (*asahajāta-hetu*), the cause with taints (*sāsava-hetu*), and the cause without taints (*anāsava-hetu*).

The fruit (*phala*) is likewise of one kind by virtue of its being arisen through conditions. Furthermore, the designation "fruit" is applied by way of the cause that brings about what is to be attained.
It should be understood that "is obtained" (*labbhati*) is twofold by way of being something to be produced and something to be attained.

It is threefold by way of being something to be made known, something to be produced, and something to be reached. It is fivefold by way of being a conditionally arisen phenomenon, a result, a functional state, a designation, and Nibbāna.

Furthermore, it is manifold, such as being produced by a similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) or produced by a dissimilar cause (*asabhāga-hetu*), and so forth. Likewise, it is mundane (*lokiya*) or supramundane (*lokuttara*).
In this context, the supramundane consists of the four fruits of recluseship. Mundane fruit is twofold: bodily and mental.

Therein, the bodily is that which pertains to the five sense-doors; the remainder is mental. Furthermore, whatever is to be accomplished through each respective teaching of the Suttas is also considered fruit.
As for "planes" (bhūmi): there is the plane with taints, the untainted plane, the conditioned plane, the unconditioned plane, the plane of seeing, and the plane of development.

The levels are manifold: the level of the worldling (*puthujjana-bhūmi*), the level of the trainee (*sekkha-bhūmi*), the level of the one beyond training (*asekkha-bhūmi*), the level of the disciple (*sāvaka-bhūmi*), the level of the solitary Buddha (*paccekabuddha-bhūmi*), the level of the perfectly enlightened Buddha (*sammāsambuddha-bhūmi*);

the level of meditative absorption (*jhāna-bhūmi*), the level of non-concentration (*asamāhita-bhūmi*); the level of one practicing (*paṭipajjamāna-bhūmi*), the level of one who has entered the path (*paṭipanna-bhūmi*);

the first level up to the fourth level; the sense-sphere level (*kāmāvacara-bhūmi*) up to the supramundane level (*lokuttara-bhūmi*). Among these, the level associated with taints (*sāsavabhūmi*) is either limited (*paritta*) or sublime (*mahaggata*).

States. The ground of the taintless (*anāsava*) consists of immeasurable states (*appamāṇa-dhamma*). The ground of the conditioned (*saṅkhata*) consists of all states possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), with the exception of Nibbāna.
The ground of the unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*) consists of states that are without conditions (*apaccaya*). The ground of vision (*dassana*) consists of the states of the first path and its fruit.

The ground of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) consists of the remaining states of the paths and fruits. The ground of the worldling (*puthujjana*) consists of inferior and intermediate states. The ground of those in training (*sekkha*) consists of the four [paths and fruits].
The noble path states and the three lower fruit states belong to the stage of the learner (*sekha*). The stage of the adept (*asekha*) consists of the supreme fruit state.

The stages of the disciple, the solitary buddha, and the fully enlightened buddha consist of the states belonging to the disciples and so forth. The stage of meditation (*jhāna*) consists of the meditative states. The stage of non-concentration consists of states excluding the meditations.

The stage of one practicing the way consists of the path states. The stage of one who has practiced the way consists of the fruit states. The four paths together with their fruits constitute the first and subsequent stages.
The "unincluded states" (apariyāpannā dhammā) are so called because of such statements as, "for the attainment of the first plane" (paṭhamāya bhūmiyā pattiyā).

The planes of the sense sphere and so forth are the states belonging to the sense sphere and so forth. Furthermore, those states which are extracted in the Suttas by way of being the foundation for various methods of exposition (hāranaya) should also be understood as "planes."
*Upanisā* is a powerful cause, which is called the *upanissaya-paccaya*. It is with reference to this that it is said in the Sutta:
"Faith has suffering as its *upanisā*; virtue has faith as its *upanisā*, and so on, up to: the knowledge and vision of liberation has liberation as its *upanisā*.
Furthermore, *upanisā* is said to be the internal core, the very heart of the doctrine established at each respective time.

Here too, there is a "guiding heart" (nettihṛdaya), by correctly grasping which Dharma-preachers become capable of applying all the methods of interpretation (*hāra-naya*) through the various doctrinal themes (*dhammamukha*) presented in each respective Sutta. What, then, is this guiding heart?
It is this very [work] consisting of thirty-three types of treatise-terms (*pakaraṇapada*), sixteen topics (*vatthu*), and twenty-eightfold analytical matrices (*paṭṭhāna-vibhaṅga*).
The object is established without confusion along with its analysis of characteristics (*nimitta*).

That is to say: the gratification (*assāda*) and so forth are the objects of the "nutriment of teaching" (*desanāhāra*), because that [teaching] has the characteristic of making manifest the gratification and so forth. Its analysis is as follows:
"the gratification is pleasure, mental joy," and so on; its characteristic is a desirable object (*iṭṭhārammaṇa*) and so forth; and this—
The meaning has already been explained in detail in the commentary on the Exposition of the Modes of Conveying (Hāraniddesa).

The Mode of Conversion (Āvaṭṭahāra) has as its domain the application of similar and dissimilar phenomena to the teaching found in the Discourse (Sutta), because it is characterized by the conversion of both of these.
The Mode of Reversal (Parivattanahāra) has as its domain the phenomena that are opposites to those found in the Discourse, because it is characterized by the reversal of opposing phenomena.

Among the proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*) and the requisites (*parikkhāra*), the proximate cause is the immediate condition and the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-kāraṇa*), while the requisite is the root cause (*hetu*);
this is the distinction between them. Furthermore, similar and dissimilar states should be understood respectively as those states that are favorable or unfavorable to each respective state.
For example: right intention is similar to right view, whereas wrong intention is dissimilar.
In this manner, everything should be understood according to its similarity and dissimilarity.
"Characteristic" (lakkhaṇa) means intrinsic nature (sabhāva). That has already been explained in the exposition of the Modes of Conveying (hāranaya).
However, that which serves as the basis for the application of the Modes of Conveying, being free from specific distinctions such as cause (hetu) and so forth, is the "Method" (naya). As it is said:

In the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇahāra*), there is the passage beginning: “Thus those phenomena which have a single characteristic, both by way of function, characteristic, and commonality,” and so forth.

Likewise, having investigated by means of the Mode of Investigation (*vicayahāra*), one should apply them by means of the Mode of Logical Reasoning (*yuttihāra*). Similarly, in the Modes of Purification (*sodhanahāra*) and the rest, the undertaking becomes purified;
that question is thereby answered, and so on. Furthermore, the methods such as Unity (*ekatta*) and the others should also be understood here as "methods" (*naya*).

Having thus examined cause, fruit, and so forth, these strings (hāras) and methods (nayas) should be applied according to their respective characteristics by way of determining the meaning of the terms found here and there in the Suttas.
Specifically, however, the "basis" (padaṭṭhāna) and "equipment" (parikkhāra) [methods] are by way of cause;

the "analysis of the teaching" (desanāvicaya), "fourfold array" (catubyūha), and "application" (samāropana) are by way of cause and fruit; likewise, the "synonyms" (vevacana), "description" (paññatti), "crossing over" (otaraṇa), and "purification" (sodhana).
"By way of the fruit alone," say some. "Analysis" is by way of the plane of the cause. "Reversal" is by way of the dissimilar.
"Turning back" is by way of both the similar and the dissimilar. The application of characteristics, reasoning, and the foundation should be joined by way of the method (*naya*).
And to this extent, that which was stated—“The general meaning, the particular, the word-meaning, the characteristic, and the sequence; —[is explained].
"And to this extent, the wise person should understand the reasons and so forth.
This verse has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the section of the detailed exposition is finished.
4. Explanation of the Section on Detailed Exposition (Paṭiniddesavāravaṇṇanā) 1. Explanation of the Analysis of the Modes of Conveying (Desanāhāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) 5.
Having thus pointed out the modes of conveying (hāra), etc., by way of verse composition for the sake of easy comprehension, [the author] now, regarding those...
In order to analyze [the factors] by way of counter-explanation (*paṭiniddesa*), the passage beginning with "Therein, what is the sustenance of teaching (*desanāhāra*)?
is commenced. Therein, "what" (*katamo*) is a question expressing the desire to explain. "Sustenance of teaching" (*desanāhāra*) is an indication of the dhamma to be questioned.

Although the sustenance of teaching is shown in its own form during the section on exposition (*niddesa*), in order to show the domain of the counter-explanation, [it is stated]: "The state of gratification (*assāda*) and disadvantage (*ādinava*)," and so forth.
It refers back to the verse by means of a single portion. This "nutriment of teaching" (desanāhāra) depends on what precedes and what follows it.

In that regard, when it depends on what precedes, after asking "What is the nutriment of teaching?", there is a conclusion for that which was shown in its own form as "the state of gratification and danger" (assādādīnavatā).
However, when it depends on what follows, it is a designation of the agent of the act of teaching, [expressed as] "What does this nutriment of teaching teach? (ayaṃ desanāhāro kiṃ desayati).
It exists. By this, he shows that the "conveying of the teaching" (desanāhāra) is designated according to its meaning. "He teaches" means he praises; the sense is that he elaborates.

Now, showing the phenomena to be taught by this [teaching] in their own form, he says "the gratification" (*assāda*) and so forth; since that follows the method already stated previously, it is self-evident.
Therefore, we shall explain even what is not explicitly stated hereafter. But in which [text] are the gratification and the rest included?
Having reflected on the inquiry, "This string [of teachings] provides the commentary," he shows the dhamma that is to be commented upon by means of the "string of teaching" (*desanāhāra*),

thereby presenting— in part— the Blessed One’s sixfold set of teachings (*chachakkadesanā*) which encompasses all the dhamma of the scriptures, beginning with: "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma."

In this context, regarding the word *dhamma*: this term *dhamma* is seen to be employed in many senses, such as the scriptures (*pariyatti*), the truths (*sacca*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*paññā*), nature (*pakati*), merit (*puñña*), attainment (*āpatti*), and the knowable (*ñeyya*).
For instance, in passages such as "Here, bhikkhu, one masters the Dhamma," it is seen in the sense of the scriptures.
In passages such as "one who has seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma," it refers to the truth. In [passages] such as "they are of such a nature... [it refers to nature].
In such passages as "the Blessed Ones were," it refers to concentration (*samādhi*). In such passages as "truth, the Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity," it refers to wisdom (*paññā*).

In such passages as "Bhikkhus, of beings subject to birth," it refers to nature (*pakati*). In such passages as "The Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by the Dhamma," it refers to merit (*puñña*).
In such passages as "the four offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*)," it refers to an offense (*āpatti*). [And] "wholesome..."
In such passages as “dhammā akusalādhammā,” it refers to objects of knowledge (*ñeyya*). However, here it should be understood as referring to the scriptural tradition (*pariyatti*).
As for the word *vo*, this particle *vo* occurs in the sense of the accusative case in the passage, “Handa dāni, bhikkhave, pavāremi vo”;
in the sense of the instrumental case in passages such as, “Sannipatitānaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dvayaṃ karaṇīyan”ti; and [in the sense of the genitive] in passages such as, “Ye hi...”.

In such passages as "You noble ones are pure in bodily action," it serves to complete the meter (*padapūraṇe*). In such passages as "I announce to you, O monks" (*ārocayāmi vo, bhikkhave*), it has the sense of the dative (*sampadānatthe*).
Here too, it should be understood as having the sense of the dative.

They are called *bhikkhus* because they possess qualities such as the habit of begging (*bhikkhana-sīlatā*), or because they possess qualities such as having destroyed the defilements (*bhinna-kilesatā*). Alternatively, in *saṃsāre*...
"Bhikkhus" means those who see fear; "bhikkhave" is an address to them. By that, while enjoining them to listen to the Dhamma, he turns them toward his own face.

"I shall teach" means I shall speak. By this, it is not because of my status as a master of the Dhamma that I would command you to do anything else, but rather because, through unobstructed knowledge, I have made all knowable phenomena directly manifest before me.
"But I shall teach the Dhamma"—with these words, he promises the teaching of the Dhamma as it is currently being delivered.

Regarding the phrase "good in the beginning" (*ādikalyāṇa*) and so forth: that which is good at the beginning is "good in the beginning"; or, that which has what is good at its beginning is "good in the beginning.

The same method applies to the other two phrases as well. In this context, it is good in the beginning by way of virtue (*sīla*); good in the middle by way of concentration (*samādhi*); and good in the end by way of wisdom (*paññā*).
It is "good in the beginning" because of the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment; "good in the middle" because of the Dhamma’s perfect nature;
and "good in the end" because of the Saṅgha’s perfect practice. Alternatively, it is good in the beginning through the training of those who understand by a condensed statement;

good in the middle through the training of those who understand by detailed exposition; and good in the end through the training of individuals who must be led. This is precisely the meaning intended here.
It is "possessing the meaning" (sāttha) because of the perfection of its meaning; it is "possessing the phrasing" (sabyañjana) because of the perfection of its phrasing.

Alternatively, it is "possessing the meaning" through its association with the eight types of words beginning with "making known" (saṅkāsanādi); it is "possessing the phrasing" through its association with the six types of words beginning with "syllables" (akkharādi).
This very meaning is intended here. It is "absolutely complete" (kevalaparipuṇṇa) because there is nothing further to be added; it is "pure" (parisuddha) because there is nothing to be removed.
It is "complete" because it fulfills the five aggregates of dhamma beginning with virtue (*sīla*).
It is "pure" because it functions for the crossing over of the four floods and because it is independent of worldly gain.

The meaning is: "I shall proclaim and illuminate the *brahmacariya*—the teaching comprised of the three trainings, which is the conduct of the *brahmans*, that is, the supreme and highest among the noble ones (*ariya*)."
Thus, the Dhamma of the Dispensation taught and elucidated by the Blessed One proceeds by way of showing the gratification and so forth;
those gratifications and other factors which constitute the objective domain of the "nutriment of the teaching" have been stated in various specific passages here and there.

Having extracted them from those respective locations and brought them here by way of illustration, the passage beginning with "In this context, what is gratification? is commenced in order to demonstrate them.
In this context, "desire" (*kāma*) refers to sense-pleasures consisting of agreeable forms and so forth, which are comprised of the phenomena of the three realms;
that is, objective desire (*vatthukāma*). "Of one who desires" means of one who wishes.
"If this succeeds for him" means if that objective basis, termed desire, succeeds for that being who desires—it is said, "if he obtains it. "He will certainly be joyful" means with certainty.
He is glad at heart. "Having obtained" means having acquired. "A mortal" means a living being. "Whatever he desires" means whatever he wishes for.
This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the Niddesa.
"This is the gratification" means that this success of one's purpose—the joy and mental happiness resulting from obtaining what was desired—is the gratification because it is to be relished.
"Tassa ce kāmayānassa" means of that person who desires sensual pleasures, or who is striving through sensual desire. "Chandajātassa" means one in whom craving has arisen.
"Jantuno" means of a living being. "Te kāmā parihāyanti" means if those sensual objects (vatthukāmā) are destroyed by some obstacle.
"Sallaviddhova ruppati" means then he is afflicted like one pierced by an arrow made of iron or other such materials.

The meaning is that he is oppressed as if pierced. "This is the danger" means that this distress and the arising of mental grief—which result from the transformation and alteration of sensual pleasures for a being who desires them—is the danger.
"He who avoids sensual pleasures" refers to that bhikkhu who, by means of suppressing desire and lust for the aforementioned sensual pleasures, [avoids them].
He avoids it either by cutting it off completely or by avoiding it in every respect. How so? "Like the foot of a man avoiding the head of a snake.
Just as a certain person desiring to live, upon seeing a black snake on the path, avoids its head with his own foot;
so too... he overcomes it. That bhikkhu, because he stands having transcended the entire world, [overcomes] what is called "clinging to the world" (visattikā).
"Being mindful, one transcends this craving"—this is the escape.
This means that the transcendence of craving, which is termed "clinging," by means of the Noble Path having Nibbāna as its object, is the escape.
"Field" refers to fields such as rice paddies and the like. "Site" refers to sites such as house-sites and the like. "Or gold" refers to what is known as the *kahāpaṇa* coin.
And gold, which is reckoned as wealth. The word *vā* has the sense of an alternative; it should be applied to all the following terms.
"Cattle and horses" (*gavāssaṃ*) means both cattle (*gāvo*) and horses (*asse*). "Slaves and laborers" (*dāsaporisaṃ*) means both slaves (*dāse*) and laborers (*porise*).

"Women" (*thiyoti*) means female beings. "Relatives" (*bandhūti*) means kinsmen and relatives. "Various desires" (*puthū kāme*) means other numerous strands of sensual pleasure, such as agreeable forms and so forth.
"Whatever person is covetous" means whatever being longs for and yearns after [objects] one by one; this is the meaning.

"This is gratification" means that this very coveting of fields and so forth is the gratification (*assāda*); it is called gratification because one enjoys sense-pleasures (*vatthukāma*) by means of it.
"The weak overpower him" means that because that person who covets various sense-pleasures such as fields is to be abandoned by those skilled in the wholesome, the weak [defilements] overpower him.

The defilements, termed "weak," become powerful and overcome [him]; or, because he lacks the powers such as faith (*saddhābala*), those weak defilements become powerful over that weak person—the meaning is that they overcome him due to his weakness.

"Crushing these dangers" means crushing this one who is greedy for sense pleasures, who seeks after sense pleasures, and who guards them; [these include] lions and other such manifest dangers, as well as bodily misconduct and so forth.
And manifest dangers crush him. Then... [as before] ...water.

The meaning is that when that person is overcome by those manifest and unmanifest dangers, the suffering of birth and so forth follows and pursues him, just as water follows a ship wrecked in the ocean.
"This is the danger" means that this continuous succession of suffering, such as birth and so forth, which has its cause in the defilement of craving and misconduct—this is the danger.
Therefore, because for one who is greedy for sensual pleasures there exists a succession of suffering in the manner described, for that reason: *jantu* means a living being.
*Sadā sato* means being mindful by devoting oneself to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night.

*Kāmāni parivajjaye* means that by way of suppression and by way of eradication, one should avoid all forms of defilement-desire (*kilesa-kāma*) regarding the object-desires (*vatthu-kāma*) such as visible forms and so forth.

Not giving rise to them, one should avoid and abandon sensual pleasures. Having abandoned them, "one may cross the flood"—the meaning is that by abandoning those sensual pleasures through the Noble Path which effects such abandonment, one may cross, or be able to cross, even the fourfold flood.
"Having baled out the boat, one reaches the further shore": just as a person, having removed the heavy burden of water taken in, bails out the water from the boat...
Just as one might cross over to the further shore with little difficulty by means of a light boat, so too,
having sprinkled the boat of one's own person with the water of the defilements so that it becomes heavy, one would cross over to the further shore by means of a light person—
meaning one would go to the further shore, which is Nibbāna, by attaining Arahantship through Parinibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue. This is "escape."
Having crossed the four floods by means of the abandonment of sensual desire, one attains Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue;
this is called "escape" because it is the escape from all that is conditioned.
"Dhamma" refers to the wholesome dhamma of giving and so forth. "Hava" is merely an expletive. "He protects the practice of Dhamma" refers to one who [practices] that Dhamma.
The heedful one lives; it protects and guards that practitioner of the Dhamma from harm, which is twofold, distinguished by the present life and the future life.
