Just as a large umbrella—just as when it rains during the rainy season, a large umbrella held by a skillful person protects one from the falling rain—so it is there. In this regard:

Just as that umbrella, when one is heedful, protects and covers oneself from the rain and so forth, even so the Dhamma, being heedful through right self-application, likewise protects one who protects oneself by practicing the Dhamma;
this is the intended meaning. By the phrase "this... practice," he makes the very same point already stated even more clear. That—

This is indeed easy to understand. "This is the fruit" refers to the protection of the Dhamma from both present and future misfortunes, as well as the accomplishment of prosperity culminating in that protection;
it is called the "fruit" because it is to be produced through the teaching, without having touched upon the final escape (nibbāna).

"All phenomena" (*sabbe dhammā*) means all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*). "Non-self" (*anattā*) means that they have no self (*attā*)—that is, no intrinsic nature of an agent or an experiencer—or that they themselves are not a self;

thus they are "non-self. "Thus" (*iti*) means in this way. "When one sees with wisdom" (*yadā paññāya passati*) means at whatever time, while exerting oneself in insight (*vipassanā*), one sees with the wisdom known as the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*).
"Then one becomes disenchanted with suffering" (*atha nibbindati dukkhe*)...
Then, because impermanence and suffering have already been clearly seen through the contemplation of non-self,
one becomes disenchanted with and attains disenchantment toward the suffering of the five aggregates, which are the objective domain of insight by way of the contemplation of disenchantment.
"This is the path to purification" refers to the contemplation of disenchantment, characterized as previously stated, which is called "purification" because it purifies all defilements.
The Noble Path is the means for ultimate purification or for the deathless element.

This is called the "means" because that which was described as "disenchantment with the entire round of existence by way of the contemplation of non-self" is the means, since it serves as the cause for the attainment of purification.
The summary meaning of this verse—“A man with eyes... [should] avoid”—is as follows: just as a man with eyes...

Just as when walking on uneven ground, an elephant or other beast avoids them out of its own wildness and caution, so too should a wise person in the world, knowing what is beneficial and harmful through their wisdom, avoid evil and base misconduct. This is the injunction:
that which is the command of the Dhamma-King, the Blessed One, saying "Evil deeds are to be avoided"—this is the injunction.

Having thus shown by way of examples the injunctions regarding the fruits and the means as they appear individually in the various suttas, he now spoke the verse beginning with "suññato" in order to show them together.
Therein, the injunction "Mogharāja, look upon the world as empty" means:

"O Mogharāja, perceive the entire world of conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāraloka) as empty, either by way of its characteristic of being subject to lack of mastery, or by way of contemplating its state of hollowness."
This word of the Dhamma King is an injunction by virtue of its prescriptive nature. Because the vision of that emptiness is accomplished through the constant practice of mindfulness, it is said:
"‘Always mindful’ is the means. “Having torn up the view of self” means having uprooted and utterly severed the twenty-based view of individuality (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
“Thus one may be a crosser of death”—this is the fruit. What [is this fruit]?

The meaning is this: by the method thus stated, "crossing over death" refers to the transcending of the domain of death; the practice of its preliminary path is what constitutes the fruit of the teaching.

However, whereas gratification and so forth are shown in some suttas in their own form, in some as things to be extracted, in some individually, and in some collectively, it is not so with the fruit and the other factors.
However, since fruits and the rest should be shown together in both the Suttas and the Gāthās,
it should be understood that although they were cited individually to illustrate this method, they are cited again together by way of the passage beginning with “The world as empty,” and so forth.

Having thus shown the gratification and the rest in their own form by way of examples, the passage beginning with “Therein the Blessed One” was stated in order to show the classification of the teaching according to the classification of individuals therein.

In this context, one who knows that which is "condensed" (*ugghaṭita*)—that is, merely condensed, merely indicated, for which neither a detailed exposition (*niddesa*) nor a sub-exposition (*paṭiniddesa*) has been made—is called "one who gains knowledge through what is condensed" (*ugghaṭitaññū*).

The meaning is that by means of a mere indication, he penetrates the meaning along with its classifications and its details; or, "condensed" (*ugghaṭita*) means "lifted up" (*uccalita*) or "set forth" (*uṭṭhapita*); one who knows that is "one who gains knowledge through what is condensed. [The same applies to] the Dhamma.

For when it is being taught, the teaching—as it were—passes over to the recipient of the teaching who has been made ready; the meaning is that he knows it as having already moved, or rather, as having moved and become manifest.

For the unique teaching of the Buddhas, directed toward the inclinations of those to be trained regarding modes such as eternalism and so forth, serves to cause movement at the very moment it is encountered;
thereafter, through successive transmission, this [teaching] occurs therein.
One who knows and understands the Dhamma as soon as it is briefly stated, while the mind is merely stirred in its own disposition, is called *ugghaṭitaññū*.
The Teacher teaches the escape for such a person of quick understanding, because his purpose is accomplished by that much alone.
One who knows the Dhamma when it is elaborated, expanded, and demonstrated is called *vipañcitaññū*; or alternatively, one who [understands] the Dhamma slowly and gradually is a *vipañcitaññū*.

One who understands through detailed exposition is called *vipañcitaññū*; for such a person, he teaches both the danger (*ādīnava*) and the escape (*nissaraṇa*), because the goal is accomplished through a teaching that is neither too concise nor too prolix.
One who is to be led to the meaning by means of a further explanation of the Dhamma is called *neyya*;
or, because of dull faculties or because of grasping [the teaching] in reverse order, one who must be led or guided is called *neyya*. For such a *neyya*...
He teaches the gratification, the danger, and the escape, because the purpose of his teaching is accomplished by teaching them without omission.

Here is the text on this point: “And what kind of person is one who understands through a brief indication? It is the person for whom there is a breakthrough to the Dhamma at the very moment it is uttered.

This is called the person who understands through a brief indication. “And what kind of person is one who understands through detailed exposition? It is the person for whom there is a breakthrough to the Dhamma when the meaning of what was spoken in brief is being analyzed in detail. This is called the person who understands through detailed exposition.”
“And what kind of person is one who is to be led (neyya)?

It is that person for whom, through the brief instruction, through questioning, through wise attention, and by serving, associating with, and attending upon spiritual friends, there comes about the gradual realization of the Dhamma.
This is called the person who is to be led.”

Furthermore, it should be understood that the "word-perfect" (padaparama) person is not included here in the *Netti* because they are not a fit vessel for penetration (*paṭivedha*). And herein, there are these seven methods of the *Paṭṭhāna*:

the gratification (*assāda*), the danger (*ādīnava*), the escape (*nissaraṇa*); the gratification and the danger; the gratification and the escape; the danger and the escape; and the gratification, the danger, and the escape.
Among those, the third, sixth, and seventh are included because they possess the capacity to discipline the three types of those to be trained; the other four are not included.

For the disciplining of those to be trained is not possible by means of a discourse on gratification alone, on danger alone, or on both together, because such discourses do not mention the abandoning of the defilements.
Furthermore, the fifth [discourse] is not included because it mentions neither danger nor the means of escape.
Indeed, the Blessed One’s teaching, which has the flavor of liberation, does not proceed without touching upon liberation and its means.

Therefore, these four methods have not been extracted [separately]. However, if one considers the teaching that proceeds according to an individual who takes words as the ultimate—whether it pertains to defilement, to purification, or stands at the junction of both—one may take a portion of a sutta or a verse.
Or, he extracts such [examples] as illustrations for these methods; if that were the case, there would be an inclusion of all seven methods.
However, the "taming of those to be tamed" (veneyyavinayana) is the arising of the Noble Path within their mental continuums.
That occurs through the methods exactly as stated above, and not by the remaining ones; thus, the others are not mentioned here. For it is said in the *Peṭaka*:
“In this regard, what is the gratification and what is the danger?
Whatever a person does, they see that within themselves:
one who performs good sees what is good, and one who performs evil sees what is evil.”
In this regard, that which a doer of good experiences as good is the gratification (*assāda*). That which a doer of evil experiences as evil is the danger (*ādīnava*).

"Monks, there are these eight worldly conditions (*lokadhammā*). Which eight? Gain, etc. In this context, gain, fame, happiness, and praise—this is the gratification. Loss, ill-fame, suffering, and blame—this is the danger.
In this regard, what is the gratification and the escape?
“The ripening of meritorious deeds is pleasant, one’s intention succeeds,
and one quickly attains the supreme peace,
Nibbāna. This is the gratification and the escape.
“Bhikkhus, there are these thirty-two marks of a Great Man possessed by which a Great Man has only two destinations and no other...
[as in the full Lakkhaṇa Sutta] ...he is one whose veil is rent.
This is both the gratification and the escape.
In this regard, what is the danger and the escape?
"The five aggregates are indeed a burden, and the person is the bearer of the burden;
the taking up of the burden is suffering in the world, while the laying down of the burden is happiness."
“Having laid down the heavy burden, without taking up another burden,
having uprooted craving, he is hungerless and has attained final Nibbāna.
This is the danger and the escape.
In this regard, what are the gratification, the danger, and the escape?
“Sensual pleasures are indeed variegated, sweet, and delightful; they agitate the mind in manifold forms.
Therefore, O King, I have gone forth, for the unerring state of a recluse alone is better.”
"It has been said: 'This is the gratification, the danger, and the escape. Therefore, those same methods should be extracted and understood here as well.
This method is indeed applicable to the fruits and so forth as well. For in the *Peṭaka* it is said: "In this regard, what is the fruit and the means?
'A wise man, established in virtue'—this is both the fruit and the means."
In this regard, what is the fruit and the injunction?
"If you fear suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you,
do not perform an evil deed, whether in public or in private."
This is the fruit and the instruction.
In that regard, what is the means and the instruction?
“Having understood this body as like a jar, and having established this mind as like a city;”
“Fight Māra with the weapon of wisdom; guard what has been won, and be one who dwells nowhere.
This is both the means and the instruction. In this way, the examples for the fruit and so forth should also be understood by way of pairs.

Furthermore, herein, the classification of individuals is established according to the divisions of the teaching—such as the “one who understands through a condensed statement” (ugghaṭitaññū)—for those who are to be guided by the teaching on escape.

"Thus, for one who gains knowledge through a condensed statement, the Blessed One teaches the escape"— by such means, a classification of the teaching according to the classification of individuals is possible,
and thus it has been shown accordingly.
Having thus shown the classification of the teaching by way of those individuals, [the text now proceeds] to show those individuals by way of the classification of their practice.
In order to show [them] by way of analysis, it was said: “Four modes of practice,” and so forth.

Therein, since the classification according to the modes of practice (*paṭipadā*) is based on the distinction between the mode of practice and direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), he said: “Four modes of practice.

Furthermore, these are twofold by way of the practice of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). How so? First, regarding the side of serenity: starting from the initial application of attention up until its—
The development of serenity (*samathabhāvanā*) that occurs as long as the access (*upacāra*) to that jhāna arises is called the "way" (*paṭipadā*).
However, the wisdom (*paññā*) that occurs from the point of access until absorption (*appanā*) is called "direct knowledge" (*abhiññā*).
Moreover, this way is painful for some, because of the difficulty in overcoming the occurrence of opposing states such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
The meaning is that it is difficult and involves the practice of what is unpleasant; for some, however, it is pleasant due to the absence of those qualities.
Even direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) is sluggish, dull, and slow in its occurrence for some, while for others it is swift, not dull, and rapid in its occurrence.

Therefore, for one who suppresses the defilements from the outset with difficulty, with volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāra*), and with exertion (*sappayoga*), becoming weary in the process of suppressing them—[for such a person...]

The practice is painful. However, for one whose defilements have been suppressed and who dwells in the preliminary stage of absorption (*appanā-parivāsa*), but only after a long time attains the manifestation of the factors [of jhāna], his higher knowledge is called "slow" (*dandhābhiññā*).
For one who quickly attains the manifestation of the factors, his higher knowledge is called "swift" (*khippābhiññā*).
For one who suppresses the defilements easily and without fatigue while suppressing them, [his practice is pleasant].
For him, there is what is called the "pleasant way of practice.

On the side of insight (vipassanā), however, one who applies himself to insight by way of both the material and the immaterial—having discerned the four great elements, discerns derived matter and discerns the immaterial; and while discerning both the material and the immaterial...
If one is able to comprehend [the aggregates] only with difficulty, through pain and exertion, for such a person there is what is called the "painful way" (*dukkhā paṭipadā*).

However, for one who has comprehended both the material and immaterial [aggregates], but whose penetration of the path is sluggish due to a long period of preparatory development in insight (*vipassanā-parivāsa*), there is what is called "slow direct knowledge" (*dandhābhiññā*).
Furthermore, even for one who, having comprehended the material and immaterial, is defining name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) with difficulty and exertion...

If he defines [the aggregates] while fatigued, and having defined name-and-form, dwells in the preparatory stage of insight (*vipassanā-parivāsa*), he is only able to arouse the Path after a long time.
For him, too, there is the "painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge" (*dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā*).
Another, having defined name-and-form and then grasping the conditions, does so with pain, difficulty, and fatigue.
He grasps at the requisites, and while dwelling in the retreat of insight having thus grasped the requisites, he arouses the Path only after a long time.
In this way, it is called the painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge.
Another person, having grasped even the requisites, penetrates the characteristics while experiencing pain, difficulty, and exhaustion.
He penetrates [the characteristics], and while dwelling in the preparatory stage of insight (*vipassanā-parivāsa*) characterized by that penetration, he arouses the path only after a long time.
In this way, it is called the "painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge" (*dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā*).
Another person, having also penetrated the characteristics, while the knowledge of insight is sharp, keen, very clear, and flowing, arouses [the path]...
While consuming his attachment to insight, he consumes it with pain, difficulty, and exhaustion;
and having consumed that attachment, while dwelling in the probationary period of insight, he arouses the path only after a long time.

In this way, there is what is called the painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge. By this same method, the other three practices are also to be understood. This pertains to the side of insight (*vipassanāpakkhikā*).
In this context, four modes of practice (paṭipadā) are to be understood.

"Four types of persons" refers to the four individuals who are practicing according to the aforementioned classification of modes of practice. To show that classification of practice together with its causes, methods, and fruits, it is said:

"one whose temperament is dominated by craving," and so forth. In this regard, "temperament" (carita) means conduct (cariyā), which is to say, behavior (vutti). One whose temperament is produced by craving is "one whose temperament is dominated by craving" (taṇhācarito).

One who has proceeded by way of craving is "one of craving-temperament" (*taṇhācarita*); the meaning is that he has a disposition toward greed (*lobha*). The same method applies here for "one of view-temperament" (*diṭṭhicarita*).
"Dull-witted" (*manda*): dullness (*mandiya*) is said to be ignorance (*avijjā*); one possessed of that is "dull-witted," meaning one in whom delusion (*moha*) predominates.
"By the faculty of mindfulness" (*satindriyena*): by means of mindfulness exercising its sovereignty. For it is the faculty of mindfulness itself that becomes clear for him. Because...
Due to being of a craving temperament (*taṇhācarita*), in the prior stage, energy (*vīriya*) is not strong because it is overwhelmed by indolence;
due to a predominance of delusion (*moha*), wisdom (*paññā*) is not powerful. Because of both of these, concentration (*samādhi*) is also not strong;

therefore, it is said: "For him, the faculty of mindfulness (*satindriya*) alone is clear. For this very reason, he said: "By means of the foundations of mindfulness as supports. Due to being of a craving temperament...
The path of practice is painful because the suppression of defilements is not easy for him; and it is slow in direct knowledge due to his lack of lucid wisdom.
This should be applied by bringing in the method explained previously. "It leads out" means that one goes forth from the suffering of the round of existence by means of the Noble Path.
"Udattha" is a contraction of "uda-attha," meaning one of exalted wisdom. And through the acquisition of the companion of wisdom, his concentration becomes sharp.
It exercises sovereignty over the associated states; therefore it is said, "by the faculty of concentration.

Because of the clarity of his knowledge, it is called "swift direct knowledge" (*khippābhiññā*). Because concentration is the primary factor among the jhānas, the distinction is made "by means of the jhānas as their support.
The rest is exactly as before. One of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*), perceiving even a path that does not lead to liberation as one that does, therein—
Because of his abundance of enthusiasm, he is superior in energy (*vīriya*). Due to this very superiority in energy, the suppression of the defilements (*kilesa*) is easy for him;

thus, it is a "pleasant way of practice" (*sukhā paṭipadā*). However, because of his lack of clarity in knowledge (*avisada-ñāṇatā*), his direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) are slow; this point is shown by the passage beginning with "one of speculative temperament is dull," and so forth.
The remainder is exactly as previously explained.

"By the truths" means by the noble truths (*ariyasacca*). For the noble truths serve as the support for mundane knowledge by way of being the basis for comprehension (*sammasana*) during the preliminary stage, and they serve as the support for supramundane knowledge by way of resolute confidence (*adhimuccanatā*) and by way of being the basis for the breakthrough (*abhisamaya*) of path-knowledge.

The rest is exactly as stated in the method already explained. And herein, one of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*) is keen and one who gains knowledge by a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*); one of craving-temperament (*taṇhācarita*) is dull.

*neyya*. The other two are *vipañcitaññū*. Thus, it should be understood that the three types of those to be trained (*veneyya*), by which the classification of the teaching was previously shown, are here shown by this classification of the practice (*paṭipadā*).

Now, taking that classification of individuals to be trained as the subject matter for an application of the method of meaning (*atthanayayojanā*), [the text] says: "Both are of craving-temperament" (*ubho taṇhācaritā*), and so forth.
It has been said. Because craving is the direct opposite of concentration, one whose temperament is dominated by craving becomes purified through the gateway of concentration;

thus it was said: "preceded by serenity. Furthermore, because of the statement, "He develops serenity and insight coupled together," deliverance occurs through right concentration accompanied by right view, and not through right concentration alone; thus it was said:

“Insight preceded by serenity. Regarding the phrase “the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust,” it is stated in the *Saṅgaha* that this refers to the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship;
however, here he will say it is the concentration of the fruit of Non-returning, for that [concentration] brings the state of concentration to fulfillment.

In this context, “lust” (*rāga*) is so called in the sense of coloring. It is “through the fading away of lust” (*rāgavirāgā*) because lust fades away by means of this; thus, “by that which is the fading away of lust” means by that which abandons lust.

Regarding "deliverance of mind" (*cetovimutti*): "mind" (*ceto*) refers to consciousness (*citta*); and here, by way of metonymy, concentration (*samādhi*) is meant, as in the expression, "develop both mind and wisdom.
It is called "deliverance" (*vimutti*) because it is liberated from its opposite by way of subsiding;
or it is that by which one is liberated; or it is the act of being liberated from that—thus, deliverance is simply concentration itself. For just as in worldly parlance, perception...

And the mind is the objective for the teaching. As it is said: "Diverse in body, diverse in perception," and "What is your state of mind, monk?"—thus, in discourse on the supramundane, there are both wisdom and concentration. As it is said:
"Right concentration possesses five kinds of knowledge," and "He develops serenity and insight coupled together. Among these, here [it refers to] that which is the direct antidote to lust.

Because it is stated that serenity (samatha) is the precursor, concentration (samādhi) is expressed by the inclusion of "mind" (ceto). Likewise, it is expressed by the term "liberation" (vimutti). Therefore, it is said: "concentration itself.
It is "liberation of mind" (cetovimutti) because it is both the mind and liberation. Alternatively, liberation (vimokkho) is the release from the opposites of the very kind of mind already described;
thus it is "liberation of mind. Or else, it is the very same kind [of liberation] within the mind, that is, within the resultant consciousness (phalaviññāṇa).

"Deliverance" (*vimutti*) means deliverance of mind (*cetovimutti*). Alternatively, it is "deliverance" or liberation from that which is opposed to the mind—that is, to the resultant consciousness—within this [state];

thus it is "deliverance of mind," which is simply concentration (*samādhi*). This same method should be applied here as well for "deliverance through wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*), according to what is possible.
Since the activity of view within its own domain is similar to that of wisdom, one whose temperament is dominated by views is purified by way of wisdom when being purified.

He said: “Both insight and [tranquility] are for those of speculative temperament,” and so forth. “Liberation through wisdom by the fading away of ignorance” refers to the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship.
Having identified craving as the opposite of tranquility and ignorance as the opposite of insight, he said:
“Those which... should be abandoned,” in order to easily show the ground of the first method.
In this context, the "practice preceded by serenity" (samatha-pubbaṅgamā paṭipadā) refers to the first two practices;
the other should be understood as "preceded by insight" (vipassanā-pubbaṅgamā). "To be abandoned" (hātabbā) means to be traversed or led away—that is the meaning.

Because of the presence of the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, and non-self within insight, and because the perception of foulness is accompanied by the perception of suffering, these four perceptions are shown. By way of their opposites...
And since it is possible to easily demonstrate the ground for the entire method of the lion’s play by means of the four perversions, he said:
“Those [defilements] which are to be abandoned by insight... etc. 7.
Having thus shown the classification of persons to be trained by way of the classification of the path of practice, he now [shows it] by way of the classification of that knowledge.
Since the Blessed One’s teaching is solely for the purpose of training those who are to be trained,

and that training consists in the gradual production of the three types of wisdom— beginning with that consisting of what has been heard— and since the function of the "modes of interpretation" (*hāranaya*) is to clarify the state of the activity of the Blessed One’s teaching,
[the author] first asks about the manner in which this mode of interpretation arises, and then, by means of showing the classification of individuals...

Having analyzed the vessel for the teaching, and wishing to apply the "nutriment of the teaching" within that teaching, he said, "Where does this mode of conveyance (hāra) arise? and so forth, in order to demonstrate it.
Therein, "of whom" means of one who is liberated from the eight inopportune moments (akhaṇa) and possesses the accomplishments ending with the application of the ear (sotāvadhāna).

"Endowed with which": he is endowed with that [quality]. "Teacher" (*satthā*): he is a teacher because he instructs appropriately according to the ultimate meanings pertaining to this present life and the future life.
"Dhamma": it is called *dhamma* because it supports (*dhāreti*) those who practice as instructed from falling into the states of misery;
that *dhamma*. "Teaches" (*desayati*): he speaks and explains by way of both concise and detailed methods. "A certain one" (*aññataro*): [referring to] the Blessed One’s...

One among the disciples. "Worthy of honor" means one who is to be respected due to being endowed with specific qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), learning (*suta*), and so forth. "Fellow-practitioner of the holy life" (*sabrahmacārī*):
"Holy" (*brahma*) refers to the entire teaching of the Teacher in the sense of being supreme.

One who practices or engages in that holy life together with or equally [with others] is a fellow-practitioner of the holy life. "He gains faith" means: "Truly, that Blessed One is a perfectly awakened Buddha (*sammāsambuddho*)."

The meaning is that one gains and arouses faith in the Tathāgata by thinking, "He is the teacher of such a Dhamma," and in the Dhamma by thinking, "Truly well-expounded is this Dhamma, which is thus entirely complete and entirely pure," and so forth.
"Therein" means in that Dhamma as it has been heard and mastered. "Investigation" refers to [the investigation] of the text and the meaning of the text.
It is the wisdom of investigation (*vīmaṃsanapaññā*). The remainder [of the terms] are its synonyms.

For that [wisdom], not falling into contraction regarding the aforementioned investigation, is called "endeavor" (*ussāhanā*) by way of exertion, "weighing" (*tulanā*) by way of weighing, and "examination" (*upaparikkhā*) by way of scrutinizing.
Alternatively, it is "investigation" (*vīmaṃsā*) because it investigates; it is the wisdom that discriminates words and their meanings. It is "endeavor" (*ussāhanā*) by way of energy (*vīriya*).
Wisdom that is supported by the retention and mastery of the Dhamma.
"Weighing" (*tulanā*) is the wisdom of grasping after having weighed and compared one word with another, or one teaching with another.

"Investigation" (*upaparikkhā*) is the wisdom of investigating both the text and the meaning of the text by applying it to the Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*). By those who desire their own welfare and the welfare of others...
It is called "heard" (*suta*) because it is heard; this is due to the absence of a desire for a specific time, just as in the case of the word "milked" (*duddha*).

But what is that [which is heard]? From the context or by implication, it is understood to be the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*). Alternatively, "hearing" (*savana*) is "the heard" (*suta*);

the meaning is the retention of the Dhamma of the scriptures following the path of the ear-door. That which is produced by means of hearing as its cause is "consisting of what is heard" (*sutamayī*). In detail...
"Paññā" means that which knows. That which is investigation (*vīmaṃsā*) should also be applied individually as "wisdom consisting of what has been heard" (*sutamayī paññā*).

"In the same way" means that just as wisdom consisting of what has been heard possesses synonyms such as investigation and possesses divisions such as investigation, so too does wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*);
this is the meaning. Or else, it shows that just as wisdom consisting of what has been heard is limited and unstable, so too is wisdom consisting of reflection.

"By means of what has been heard as a support" (*sutena nissayena*): by means of the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*) or by means of the hearing of the Dhamma of the scriptures as a decisive support (*upanissaya*).

The instrumental case is used in the sense of a characteristic of being thus accomplished; the meaning is "having relied upon the aforementioned hearing. Regarding "investigation" (*vīmaṃsā*) and so forth:
[it refers to] those various phenomena such as "this is virtue," "this is concentration," "these are form and formless phenomena," and "these are the five aggregates."
Wisdom that consists in the investigation of intrinsic nature is *vīmaṃsā*.
Wisdom that grasps those same phenomena by setting aside their conventional verbal designations and as if weighing their intrinsic essence, flavor, and characteristic is *tulanā*.

Wisdom that scrutinizes those same phenomena without abandoning their specific characteristics, by conjecturing and reflecting upon their modes such as impermanence and their conditions such as arising, is *upaparikkhā*; and when phenomena have been thus scrutinized...
When things appear as if they were being grasped, the successive examination of them with the mind after having made them acceptable through reflection is "mental scrutiny" (*manasānupekkhaṇā*).

And here, just as wisdom consisting of what has been heard (*sutamayī paññā*) deserves to be called "endeavoring" (*ussāhanā*) because it proceeds by way of retaining and familiarizing oneself with the Dhamma as it was heard—thus giving rise to effort—it is not so with wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*); therefore, [the latter] is not treated in this way here.
The word “ussāhanā” (exertion) is not mentioned. *Cintā* means thinking; the meaning is reflection (*nijjhāna*). The rest is exactly as stated by the previous method.
“By these two kinds of wisdom” means by the two kinds of wisdom already described, acting as causes.

For one who is established in the knowledge consisting of what is heard and what is thought begins insight meditation (*vipassanā*). They also read: “In these two kinds of wisdom. “Born from those... [etc.]

Or rather, the phrase “when they have arisen” (*uppannāsu*) should be construed as an ellipsis. “Associated with attention” (*manasikārasampayuttassa*) means being engaged and intent upon the attention directed toward the discernment of the material and immaterial, and so forth.

“The knowledge that arises” refers to the noble path-knowledge known as purification of vision (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*), which arises for one who has exerted themselves in insight by means of the application of attention according to the method described—namely, through the attainment of purification of view, purification by overcoming doubt, purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, and purification by knowledge and vision of the way.
The connection is: "this is wisdom consisting in development (*bhāvanāmayī paññā*) that arises. Furthermore, since that vision (*dassana*) is twofold—as development—he said:
"either on the plane of seeing (*dassanabhūmi*) or on the plane of development (*bhāvanābhūmi*).
If it is called "seeing," how can wisdom therein be "consisting in development"? For that knowledge is indeed consisting in development; it is so called because of its first seeing of Nibbāna.

However, since it is said to be "seeing" (*dassana*), the first path, being fruitful, is the plane of seeing (*dassanabhūmi*). The remaining states of those in training (*sekkha*) and those beyond training (*asekkha*) are the plane of cultivation (*bhāvanābhūmi*).
Now, in order to show these three types of wisdom through a different method of exposition, the passage beginning with "from the voice of another" (*paratoghosā*) was stated.
Therein, "from another" (*parato*) means not from oneself, but from another—namely, from the Teacher or a disciple. "Voice" (*ghosa*) refers to the sound of their teaching.

The meaning is "conditioned by teaching. Alternatively, it is "paratoghosā" because its source is the voice of another; that wisdom which is thus conditioned should be understood as "consisting of what has been heard" (*sutamayī*).
"Arisen within oneself" means arisen individually within each person's own self.
"Proper attention" (*yonisomanasikāra*) refers to the mental engagement occurring by way of the aforementioned method, such as the discernment of the specific nature (*sabhāva*) of various phenomena.
"And by the voice of another" means by the voice of another acting as a cause. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Now, in order to show the classification of the persons to be trained (*vineya-puggala*) for whose sake these types of wisdom have been set forth, the passage beginning with "Of one who...
was spoken. Therein, having first mentioned "these two" by way of enumeration, he then specifies them as that consisting of hearing (*sutamayī*) and that consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*).
...and thus he shows them by way of their common form. "This one is one who understands through a condensed statement" (*ugghaṭitaññū*):

because the awakening of his disposition and application has been accomplished through wisdom consisting of what is heard and wisdom consisting of reflection, he understands by means of a mere summary; therefore, he is called "one who understands through a condensed statement.

"This one is one who understands through an elaboration" (*vipañcitaññū*): because his disposition has not been fully refined by wisdom consisting of reflection, he understands through both summaries and detailed explanations; therefore, he is "one who understands through an elaboration. This one...

"One who is to be led" (*neyya*) means that because he lacks even the knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*), he must be led by means of a teaching given in its entirety and in detail;

thus he is "one who is to be led. Having thus analyzed the three types of those to be trained—the recipients of the teaching—by way of the divisions of the teaching, the methods of practice, and knowledge, [the author] now seeks to connect this by determining the "nutriment of the teaching" within the Blessed One’s Dhamma-teaching as it proceeds therein: "This..."
The passage beginning with “the teaching of the Dhamma” (*dhammadesanā*) is commenced.

Therein, “she tastes” means “this [teaching]. This very text—which was previously set forth as the object of the mode of conveying the teaching at the beginning of the section of specific reference, starting with “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma”—is here applied to the mode of conveying the teaching itself.
He refers back [to the phrase] “the evening Dhamma teaching.

To the question “What does he teach?”—having asked for the summarized meaning of the teaching by way of his desire to speak, and having delimited it by way of enumeration—he shows it generally as “the four truths.
For there is no teaching of the Blessed One that is devoid of the truths; and the summarized meaning of that [teaching] is the four truths.

Because there is no object to be known (neyya) that is exempt from the process of occurrence, its causes, and its cessation, it should be understood that the four truths are "truths" by virtue of their non-erroneous nature.
He shows them in their essential form as "suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.

Among these, suffering is so called because it is loathsome due to being the basis for manifold calamities, and because it is devoid of the permanence, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood imagined by foolish people.
And because of its emptiness, it is suffering (*dukkha*). Because it is the cause for the arising of suffering when the remaining conditions come together, it is the origin (*samudaya*).

Because all realms of existence (*gati*) are empty, there is no obstruction to suffering here—namely, what is called the prison of *saṃsāra*—or, when this [emptiness] is attained, there is the absence of that obstruction to suffering called the prison of *saṃsāra*; thus it is cessation (*nirodha*), because it is the condition for the cessation of non-arising.
Or: it is a path (*magga*) because one goes by means of it, or because it is sought after by those seeking *nibbāna*.

In that context, gratification (*assāda*) is through origination (*samudaya*), danger (*ādīnava*) is through suffering (*dukkha*), and escape (*nissaraṇa*) is through the path (*magga*) and cessation (*nirodha*). Thus, in whatever sutta the four truths appear in their own form, there [the analysis] is according to the literal expression.
However, in whatever sutta the four truths do not appear in their own form, [the analysis is according to the underlying meaning].
In this context, having extracted the four truths from the perspective of their meaning, the gratification and so forth should be determined by way of those truths.
Where the gratification and so forth have come down explicitly in their own form, there is nothing further to be said.
But where they have not come down explicitly, there, having extracted them from the perspective of their meaning, the four truths should be determined by way of them. And here, however—

The gratification and so forth have been shown by way of illustration according to their specific forms; therefore, in order to define the Truths by means of them, the passage beginning with “the danger (ādīnavo) and so forth” was stated.
Therein, because of the statement, “In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering,” the phenomena of the three planes, excluding craving, constitute the Truth of Suffering.
And since these possess the intrinsic nature of impermanence and so forth, they are the danger; furthermore, the result must be established through the teaching. Therein—
With reference to that which is mundane (*lokiya*), it is said: "The fruit and suffering. "Gratification" (*assāda*) refers to craving and the perversions (*vipallāsa*) because they are desired;

with reference to these, it is said: "Gratification is the origin. Because the noble path together with insight (*vipassanā*) and the teaching are the means for attaining the fruit of the teaching, it is said:
"The means and the instruction are the path. In the section on escape (*nissaraṇa*):
Furthermore, the Noble Eightfold Path must also be extracted [from this], and it should not be seen that this analysis of the truths (sacca-vibhāga) is confused.

For instance, in the *Saccavibhaṅga*, it is explained according to various methods that "the remaining craving, the remaining defilements (kilesa), the remaining unwholesome states (akusala-dhamma), the wholesome roots with taints (sāsava-kusala-mūla),
and the wholesome states with taints are analyzed as being the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca)"— thus, in each respective method, those specific remaining factors [are so classified].
The phenomena belonging to the three planes have been analyzed by way of their nature as the truth of suffering; it should be understood in the same way here as well.
"These are the four truths" is the conclusion. "This is the Wheel of Dhamma": this sublime teaching of the Dhamma by the Blessed One, according to the four truths, is the Wheel of Dhamma.
Now, in order to show how that teaching of the Dhamma constitutes the Wheel of the Dhamma (*dhammacakka*) by means of the *Saccavibhaṅga Sutta*, it was said:
"As the Blessed One said," and so forth. Therein, "this is suffering" refers to that which is comprised of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandha*), divided into birth and so on;

it is the mass of phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence, accompanied by craving, which—by virtue of being the basis for suffering and by way of the various forms of suffering such as the suffering of suffering—is called "suffering."
And the meaning is: "the noble truth of suffering. "Me" (meti), the Blessed One refers to himself.
"At Bārāṇasī" means in the vicinity of the city named Bārāṇasī. It is called Isipatana because it was the place where the seers of the paccekabuddhas descended from the sky.
And it is called Migadāya because fearlessness was granted to the deer there; it was a hermitage bearing that name. "Uttarati" means he transcends.
It is "supreme" (*uttara*) because it overcomes [all else], or it is "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) because there is nothing superior to it; that is, it is without further excellence or peer.

Although the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma has been delivered hundreds of times in various assemblies of gods and humans for the purpose of bringing about their penetration of the Noble Truths, nevertheless, it was first [delivered] to the assembly headed by Aññā Koṇḍañña.

The teaching of the Dhamma, which reveals the penetration of the Four Noble Truths for a retinue numbering eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, is designated as the "Wheel of the Dhamma" (Dhammacakka) because it is preeminent;

thus it is said, "the Wheel of the Dhamma was set in motion. In that context, the very Dhamma consisting of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth is called the "Wheel" (cakra) in the sense of its setting in motion, hence it is the "Wheel of the Dhamma" (Dhammacakka); or alternatively, "wheel" (cakra) [refers to...]

It is an *ājñā* (command). Because it does not deviate from the Dhamma, it is the "Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*)—that which is both the Dhamma and the wheel. It is also the "Wheel of Dhamma" because it is a wheel by means of the Dhamma, that is, by way of the principle (*ñāya*).
As it has been said: "It sets in motion the Dhamma and it is a wheel, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma; it sets in motion the wheel and it is the Dhamma, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma;
it sets it in motion by means of the Dhamma, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma," and so forth. It is "irreversible" (*appaṭivattiya*).
Because the Blessed One is the Lord of Dhamma and the Perfectly Enlightened One, and because the Wheel of Dhamma is unsurpassed, it is not to be contested.
To the question "By whom is it not to be turned back? he says: "By a recluse," and so forth. Therein, "by a recluse" means one who has entered the homeless life;
"by a brahmin" means by one who is a brahmin by birth. For as for those who are recluses and brahmins in the ultimate sense, their very minds are directed toward the opposite [of worldly ways].
There is none. "By a deva" means by a deva of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). "By anyone" means by any remaining member of the assembly.
By this much, the inclusion of all eight assemblies without exception should be understood. "In the world" means in the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*).
"Therein" refers to that teaching of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Immeasurable words, immeasurable syllables" is a statement in reverse order.

This is for the purpose of showing that syllables are, for the most part, comprised within words (*pada*). It should be understood that the change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*) has been made [in the text] such that "words" (*padā*), "syllables" (*akkharā*), and "phonemes" (*byañjanā*) are used interchangeably.

"Of the meaning" (*atthassa*) refers to the meaning comprised of the Four Noble Truths. "Manifestation" (*saṅkāsanā*) means the manner in which it is to be manifested. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
Furthermore, in the phrase "of the meaning," the genitive case (*sāmivacana*) is used in the sense of a relationship. In the expression *itipi idam*, the word *iti* signifies a mode or manner.
The word *pi* has the sense of inclusion; the meaning is: "In this way and also in that way, this Noble Truth of Suffering is to be understood.

By means of that [word], it establishes the manifold variety of the aforementioned Truth of Suffering through its divisions such as birth, and the immeasurability of the letters, phrases, and so forth that illustrate it, according to the manner described.
"This is the origin of suffering": this refers to craving, which is divided into sensual craving and so forth;

it is the "origin of suffering" because, as the root of the aforementioned cycle of craving, it serves as the cause for the production of that aforementioned suffering. "This is the cessation of suffering":

this refers to the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu), which is detached from all conditioned things; it is the "cessation of suffering" because it is the condition for the non-arising and cessation of the aforementioned suffering. This...

"The way leading to the cessation of suffering" (*dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā*): this collection of eight factors beginning with right view is called the "way leading to the cessation of suffering" because it goes toward Nibbāna—which is designated as the cessation of suffering—by way of its object, since it is directed toward that;

and because it is the means for attaining the cessation of suffering, it is the "way. Regarding the phrase "itipidaṃ," [it refers] to the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*) by way of the eight hundred types of craving-investigations (*taṇhāvicarita*).

The meaning of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasacca*) should be understood by analyzing it through the methods such as "the intoxication of pride" (*madanimmadana*), and the meaning of the truth of the path (*maggasacca*) by means of the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*). The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Thus, regarding the verse beginning with "The twelve terms are the Sutta," the entire teaching consists of six bases of meaning (*atthapada*) and six...

Having pointed out, by way of a partial indication, the sixfold set of sixes (*cha-chakka-pariyāya*)— which was described as a state of twelve phrases by way of the phrasing and words in the passage beginning “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma”—

through the method of showing the objective domain of the "conveyance of the teaching" (*desanā-hāra*), [the author] demonstrates, by way of showing how its meaning is subsumed within the *Dhammacakkappavattana-sutta*,
that all the word of the Blessed One possesses the nature of a teaching on the Four Noble Truths.

Having shown the Saccavibhaṅga Sutta in brief by explaining how that meaning possesses the nature of the Four Noble Truths through the passage beginning, "Bhikkhus, at Bārāṇasī, 'this is suffering'...",
and having elucidated its twelvefold nature by analyzing the words for the phrasing and the meaning through the passage beginning, "Therein, there are immeasurable phrases...",
[the author now] demonstrates their state of connection through the relationship of mutual object and subject.
To demonstrate this, it was said: "In that regard, the Blessed One makes it clear by means of syllables," and so forth.

Therein, the grasping of the word occurs by way of grasping the components of the word; and once the word has been grasped, the comprehension of the word-meaning occurs for one who has previously acquired the linguistic convention.

And in that process, just as there is the grasping of the word through the grasping of its components, so too [is there the grasping of the meaning] through the grasping of the components of the word-meaning.
He says, "He makes it known by means of syllables," because the specific application of the grasping of the meaning arises [thereby].

However, since the meaning being indicated in brief by means of syllables is not yet completed as a sentence until the conclusion of the phrase, it is therefore said, "He makes it manifest by means of phrases. But at the conclusion of the sentence, that meaning...
It is said, "he opens it up by means of phonemes," because it has been stated that "it is made open and disclosed.
And because when distinctions are made through modes [of expression], the meaning of that [text] becomes analyzed (*vibhatto*), it is therefore said, "he analyzes it by means of modes.
Likewise, because when the etymological analysis of each component of the sentence is performed, that meaning becomes manifest, it is said, "he makes it clear by means of etymologies (*niruttīhi*)."
He says, "He makes known by means of expositions," because by teaching through detailed explanations consisting of analyzed word-components,
the satisfaction of the minds of those to be trained and the sharpening of their intelligence are accomplished. And here,
one should understand the restriction not as "he makes known only by means of syllables," but rather as "he indeed makes known by means of syllables."
For this being so, it is established that the eight thematic points (*atthapada*) have various sentences as their domain.

Consequently, in a sutta with a single sequence of thought, there are exactly six thematic points; however, in a sutta with multiple sequences of thought, six thematic points must be extracted for each individual sequence.
By the phrase, "He summarizes by means of syllables and words," etc., he demonstrates the accomplishment of the function of the phrasing of the literal expression (*byañjanapada*).

For their function consists solely in the disciplining of those who are to be disciplined (*veneyya*). However, because it is not the occasion for the penetration of truth, the "mere letter" (*padaparama*) is not mentioned here.

Alternatively, it should be understood that by the mention of the "one to be led" (*neyya*), the "one who has reached the letter" is also included here, just as by the mention of "those in training" (*sekkha*), the "virtuous worldling" (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) is included.

In the phrases beginning with "by means of letters" (*akkharehi*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*), not in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). [The words] "letters," etc.,...

For [the word] has the sense of "expounding" (*ugghaṭana*) and so forth, not the sense of the letters of "expounding" and so forth. And that for whose sake an action is performed is the cause, as in the expression, "he dwells by means of food.

"Expounds" (*ugghaṭeti*) means: having established attentive listening, by way of proclaiming [the Dhamma] to those to be trained who possess concentrated minds, he imparts a distinction through the letters such that, at the conclusion of the phrases, there is an awakening of their underlying disposition (*āsaya*).
"In that way" means he states or recites the intended meaning in brief. "Expounds" means he points out the meaning as it was recited.
"Expands" means he makes it extensive, or having made it extensive, he declares it; the meaning is that he re-explains it.
And because here "concurs" (ugghaṭeti) is intended to mean reciting, and recitation is the beginning of teaching, therefore—
It is said: “The summary is the beginning. Likewise, the exposition (*vipañcana*) is the indication (*niddisana*), and the expansion (*vittharaṇa*) is the re-indication (*paṭiniddisana*);
thus, the indication and the re-indication constitute the middle and the conclusion of the teaching. Therefore it is said: “The exposition is the middle;
the expansion is the conclusion.”

Thus, having shown the function of the six types of phrasing (byañjanapada) through the passage beginning with “he makes known by means of syllables,” he now says “This is the Dhamma and Vinaya,” etc., in order to show the function of the types of meaning (atthapada).

Therein, the Dhamma consisting of virtue and so forth—namely, the meaning of the scriptures—is called “Dhamma-Vinaya” because it disciplines those who are to be trained. “Ugghaṭīyanto” means being pointed out or recited.

"Ten" refers to the training of those who understand through a brief summary (*ugghaṭitaññū*). "Being elaborated" means being demonstrated in detail. "Being expanded" means being further demonstrated.

Having thus shown the threefold excellence (*tividhakalyāṇatā*) of the text (*pāḷi*) announced by the words, "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma," [the Buddha] now said, "Six phrases are the meaning," etc., in order to show the perfection of both the meaning (*attha*) and the phrasing (*byañjana*). That...
It is easy to understand. By the words “Therefore the Blessed One said,” etc., he shows the Pāḷi cited as the object of the exposition by way of its conclusion.
The passage beginning with “supramundane” is an explanation of the meaning of the phrases “entirely complete and pure.
Therein, “established in all distinctions” refers to all those things comprised under the term *uttarimanussadhamma* (superhuman states).
It is the place where the distinctions—namely, the specific trainings such as the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā)—are established.
Its grammatical derivation (*saddasiddhi*) should be understood in the same way as in expressions such as "this is their *padakkanta*.

In passages such as "This is called the footprint of the Tathāgata," this refers to the holy life of the Dispensation (*sāsana-brahmacariya*), which comprises the three trainings, [established] through the practice, the teaching, and the arrival of the Tathāgata, that elephant among scent-elephants.

It is also called "the path gone by after having covered over the thicket of defilements. By that [path], it is also said to be "frequented" and "resorted to" through the cultivation and practice of the range of its activity.
Its meaning is: it is called "the place where the phenomena of the three planes are scorched" because it has been scorched by the teeth of the Great Vajira-knowledge and the Knowledge of Omniscience.
"Therefore it is called" means: because it is called by such names as "the footprint of the Tathāgata," for this very reason.
Of the Blessed One, the Brahmā who is the supreme among all beings, it is known that his conduct is "brahmic" (sublime) because it is most excellent;

this is understood precisely because it has been well-proclaimed by humans in the manner already described. Therefore, he says "the Blessed One," showing the aforementioned meaning as a conclusion to the text.

In order to show that the purpose of the Blessed One’s teaching—due to its being for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging—is precisely the attainment of the Noble Path, he asked, “For whom is this teaching of the Dhamma? and replied, “For yogīs.

Those who are devotedly engaged in the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Truths are yogīs; for they employ this nutriment of teaching. This statement belongs to the *Vibhaṅga* of the nutriment of teaching.
It should be understood that the treatise was established by those who were reciting it in order to show that its state had been correctly arranged according to the sequence [of the sūtras].

For it is said: "Therefore the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said. The term *niyutta* means that it has been joined by extracting the meanings of the words, such as the "delight" (*assāda*) and so forth, from the canonical text (*pāḷi*).
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Teaching is finished.
2. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Investigation (Vicaya-hāra-vibhaṅga). 11.

Regarding the passage beginning "What is the mode of conveying investigation?", this is the analysis of the mode of conveying investigation. Herein, this is the commentary on the previously unstated terms.
Regarding the phrase "what does he investigate": here, by the term "investigates" (*vicinati*), it is shown that the word *vicaya* (investigation) functions as a designation for the agent.

But since it was asked, "What is the object of this method of analysis (*atthahāra*)?", the passage beginning with "he investigates the word" (*padaṃ vicinati*) was stated in order to show its object.
In that context, "he investigates the word" means the entire word of the sutta from the beginning up to the conclusion.
One investigates. This investigation is twofold: by way of sound and by way of meaning. Among these, [one discerns]:
"This is a noun, this is a verb, this is a prefix, this is a particle; this is feminine gender, this is masculine gender, this is neuter gender;
this is past tense, this is future tense, this is present tense; this is an agentive derivation, this is..."
"This is an instrumentive derivation, this is an objective derivation, this is a locative derivation;
this is the nominative case, this is the accusative case, up to this is the locative case;

this is the singular number, this is the plural number"—such is the statement of classification regarding words. Furthermore, this analysis of words occurs precisely through the observation of the unerring nature of linguistic expression.

It should be understood that [the word] *sampajjati* means "it succeeds. In terms of its meaning (*atthato*), however, it is an investigation (*vicayo*) consisting of a commentary on the meaning expressed by each respective term.
Furthermore, if a term occurs as a question and so forth, one must investigate whether that term and its meaning possess the nature of a question and so on;
showing this point, he said: "He investigates the question," and so forth.
And because the entire category of teaching (desanāhāra) is the domain of the category of investigation (vicayahāra), since the discourse (sutta) consists of investigation, it is therefore said:

"He investigates the gratification," and so forth. Furthermore, since the meaning of *anugītī* here is intended as "a song that is in accordance" (*anurūpā gīti*), it follows that other words from different discourses are also included by way of extracting the meaning, in accordance with the words of the discourse being investigated.

Showing that [the meanings] should be investigated by bringing them together either through the sequence of the words or through the sequence of the phrases, he said: "He investigates all nine types of suttas.
"In the nine types of suttas" means in the nine suttas beginning with the Sutta and Geyya; the intention is "according to what is possible.
This is the explanation of the term for the Mode of Conveying Investigation (vicaya-hāra).
Thus, since the method of investigation (vicayahāra) has been briefly explained in the section on exposition (niddesavāra), he now explains it by way of detailed classification.

Then, analyzing it according to the mode of re-exposition (paṭiniddesa), he says, "In what way could it be? and so forth, without touching upon the analysis of words (padavicaya)—because that would be too burdensome due to the necessity of proceeding word-for-word through the Sutta—and instead first demonstrates the analysis of the questions and answers (pañhavissajjanavicaya).
In this context, "in what way" (*yathā*) means "by what manner" that investigation (*vicaya*) should be carried out;
"what might it be? (*kiṃ bhave*) means "of what kind might it be? There is also a reading, *yathā kiṃ bhaveyyā*. Furthermore, *yathā* is merely a particle.
"Venerable sir" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment. "Ajita" refers to one of the sixteen attendants of the brahmin Bāvari.
Regarding the term *Pārāyana*: "the further shore" (*pāra*) is said to be Nibbāna. Since it teaches the means for attaining that, every word of the Blessed One deserves to be called *Pārāyana*.

Nevertheless, because the compilers [of the Canon] gave this name specifically to the sixteen discourses beginning with the Ajita Sutta—along with their introductory verses (*vatthugāthā*) and subsequent verses (*anugītigāthā*)—only those [sixteen discourses] bear the designation *Pārāyana*.
He said, "In the *Pārāyana*. Some read it as "*Pārāyanika*. It is said that before he went forth as an ascetic, they wandered about studying the *Pārāyana*.
Therefore, because he also practices the *Pārāyana*, he is called a "*Pārāyanika*.

Why is it said that he "asks"? Is it not the case that [the Buddha] is past [in time] because the questioning has already been produced? True, this is so; however, [it refers to the Buddha] in the mode of asking.
However, having turned it over in his mind, he spoke thus. Now, this question is indeed one of the following types:

a question for the illumination of what has not been seen, a question for the corroboration of what has been seen, a question for the cutting off of doubt, a question for assent, a question out of a desire to speak, a question to be answered categorically, a question to be answered analytically, and a question to be answered with a counter-question.

The questions to be set aside (*ṭhapanīya*) are of many kinds, such as those based on phenomena (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*) or those based on beings (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*). Therefore, one should examine the question according to its possibility, starting with:

"Is this question one that reveals what was not seen? Just as there is this classification of questions, so too the classification of answers should be stated according to their possibility in the investigation of answers; for the answer conforms to the nature of the question. Herein—

However, having cited the question that cuts through doubt and is based on the person (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*), he said, "By what, indeed, is the world enveloped? and so forth, in order to show the manner of investigation therein.
In this context, "by what" (*kena*) is an instrumental case used for the agent; "su" is a mere particle, or "su" is a particle expressing doubt (*saṃsaya*); by means of that...

This shows that the question is one intended to cut through doubt regarding the matter. "Enveloped" (*nivuta*) means covered. "The world" (*loka*) refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattaloka*).
"Thus said the Venerable Ajita" is the statement of the compiler of the collection. "It does not shine forth" (*nappakāsati*) means it is not made manifest. "What do you say is its defilement?
(*kissābhilepanaṃ brūsī*)—what do you declare to be the defilement of this world? There is also a reading, "What indeed is its defilement? (*kiṃ svābhilepanaṃ*), and of that...
"What is the analysis of the phrase *kiṃ su abhilepanaṃ*?
Regarding "phrases" (*padāni*): they are called "phrases" because meaning is attained through them; that is, they are sentences. Regarding "asked" (*pucchitāni*):
the meaning is that they were spoken by way of being questions. As for "one question": although four phrases were spoken by way of questioning, what was intended to be known [was one].
"Since the meaning is one and the same, it is said 'one question. Regarding this, he states the reason: 'because they are comprised within a single subject-matter.

This is what is meant: although these four meanings—obstruction, non-illumination, defilement, and great fear—are included in the inquiry, they are subordinate to the single world (loka), and since the world is taken as the primary factor, [the question is called 'one'] by virtue of that."
"This is indeed a single question. For this very reason, he says, "The world as a basis," and so forth. But what is that world? He says, "The world is threefold," and so forth.

In that regard, beings of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) constitute the world of defilements (kilesaloka) due to their abundance of defilements such as lust. Beings of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) constitute the world of existence (bhavaloka) due to the development of meditative absorptions and direct knowledges.
Beings of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara) [constitute the world of peace] due to their abundance of imperturbable concentration and the clarity of their faculties.
The world of faculties (*indriyaloka*). Alternatively, defilement (*kilesa*) means that which is afflicted; the meaning is "the suffering of result.

Therefore, because of the abundance of suffering, beings in the states of deprivation are the world of defilements (*kilesaloka*). Other beings, by virtue of their existence in the realm of fortunate rebirths, are the world of becoming (*bhavaloka*).

Among these, those beings who are endowed with faculties that bring liberation to maturity should be understood as the world of faculties. This is by way of the phenomena included [within the three worlds].
“Worldly conventions” (lokasamaññā) here does not include noble persons (ariyapuggala).

“The world is shrouded by ignorance” (avijjāya nivuto loko): the world is shrouded, that is, covered, by ignorance characterized by the concealment of the true nature of phenomena—such as chariots, carts, and so forth—just as by a darkness endowed with four factors.
“Because of doubt” (vivicchā): this refers to the cause of doubt; for it is said, “Doubt is stinginess.”
This is stated in the *Saṅgaha*. "Through negligence" (*pamādā*) means by way of negligence as a cause. "Lusting is the smear" (*jappābhilepanaṃ*): lusting is craving;
it is like the monkey's smear, for this world, which I call its sticky gum. "Suffering" (*dukkhaṃ*): birth and so forth, namely the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*);
such is the meaning of the words. The rest is understood from the text itself. These four phrases are stated in the verse of the question.
“By these”: this refers to the answers given by means of these four words mentioned in the verse of response. To explain how, he says “the first,” and so forth.
By this, he shows that the questions and their respective answers should be understood according to their sequence.
Now, in order to show that sequence of question and answer according to their specific forms, and to clarify the meaning of the verse:
“‘By what [are they obstructed]? and so forth was said. Therein, in order to make the meaning expressed by the term ‘by the hindrances’ (nīvaraṇehi) clear, it was said:

‘For all beings are hindered by ignorance,’ and so on. And here, by showing another sutta with the words ‘As it has been said,’ etc., it should be understood that he demonstrates the investigation of the *anugīti* within this analytical investigation of the answer to the question. Therein, ‘by way of a method’ (*pariyāyato*)...”

By way of cause: because they serve as the cause for sensual desire and the other hindrances—which are themselves designated as "hindrances"—and because they possess the nature of concealment, I speak of ignorance as the one and only hindrance;
the meaning is not that there is an absence of other things whose intrinsic nature is that of a hindrance.
And just as the existence of the hindrances occurs when ignorance exists, so too, when ignorance is absent, the hindrances do not exist.
The phrase beginning with "in every way" (*sabbaso*) was stated in order to show this.
"By that" means by the phrase "the world is shrouded by ignorance. "Of the first phrase" refers to the phrase "by what, indeed, is the world shrouded?
"Appropriate" (*yuttā*) means joined together, or its meaning is "congruent. By this, it is shown that the answer is in accordance with the question.

It should be understood that the investigation of what precedes and what follows has been stated. By the passage beginning, "The person who is shrouded by the hindrances," etc., he shows that doubt (*vivicchā*) and negligence (*pamāda*) are conditions for ignorance (*avijjā*). For it is precisely one who is shrouded who does not shine forth.

"Vivicchā" means doubt (*vicikicchā*). Therefore he said: "What is called 'vivicchā' is said to be doubt. Herein, this is the etymological derivation of the term: just as with wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*) and right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*), [so too with doubt].
“Permanent” and “impermanent,” etc., occur by way of grasping at one side; this [doubt] does not do so.
Rather, because it does not grasp at one side, it desires or seeks various contradictory positions such as, “Is it permanent? Or is it impermanent?”—thus it is called *vivicchā*.
By the phrase “He, being doubtful,” etc., [the author] reveals that lack of clarity is the cause for taking up *vivicchā* (hesitation).
"Does not produce bright qualities" means that one does not practice by undertaking them.
"They do not shine forth" means that those wholesome qualities, not being produced within one's own continuum, do not make that person renowned and famous in the world.
"It smears" means that, like the gum of the *makkaṭa* tree, it causes a person to cling to the objects of form and so forth, just as the *makkaṭa* gum sticks to wood, stone, and the like.
Meaning: "Of one who is full of attachment" means of one who is full of clinging. "Thus making it an obsession" means by reason of its remaining as an active defilement (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
"Therein" means by means of that craving. The world is "besmeared," meaning it is as if smeared with slime.
It is called "fear" because one fears it; "great fear" is a great terror. For this very reason he said: "Suffering is its great fear."
“Suffering and mental grief” means that suffering itself is analyzed; thus, having analyzed all suffering, it is said, “three types of suffering,” and so forth.

“By way of occasion” (*odhaso*) means, by way of such distinctions as sometimes rooted in one’s own effort and sometimes rooted in the effort of another, those [beings] in the fine-material sphere who are liberated from the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*). “Likewise” (*tathā*) means sometimes or occasionally.

Thus it drags [them] along. Beings in the formless realm (arūpāvacara) are especially abundant in the attainment of equanimity (upekkhāsamāpatti), which brings liberation from the suffering of change (vipariṇāmadukkhatā).

The term "free from affliction" (appābādha) is a statement regarding the cause for liberation from the suffering of pain (dukkhadukkhatā). "Long-lived" refers to liberation from the suffering of change;
for in the world, the formless deities (arūpadeva) are preeminently long-lived. And this liberation is absolute, because [they are free] from suffering.
Feeling (vedanā) as well, because it is conditioned, has the very nature of suffering consisting in the formations such as impermanence;
therefore, in order to show—by way of including everything without exception—that from which liberation is absolute, he said: "But by way of the suffering of formations," and so forth.

In that context, "upādi" means that which is grasped (*upādiyati*): the resultant aggregates and the matter produced by kamma (*kaṭattā-rūpa*). The remainder of what is grasped is "with residue" (*sopādisesa*).

"Anupādisesā" means that for her there is no [residue] (*upādi*); it refers to the element of nibbāna (*nibbānadhātu*). By means of that element of nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*), this is an instrumental designation used in the sense of a characteristic of a state attained (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇa*). Furthermore, "the element of nibbāna" (*nibbānadhātu*) signifies merely the state of extinguishing (*nibbāyana*).

"Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because the suffering inherent in conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*) pervades the entire world and encompasses everything; "of the world" (*lokassa*) is used in the sense of a relationship.
This is a word expressing possession (*sāmivacana*). By it, he demonstrates the meaning of the phrase "it has suffering.

Thus, in this context, because it must be answered with absolute certainty by one who either does not know the world's hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth, or who has fallen into doubt therein due to familiarity with other systems, the question was posed with reference to a sentient being (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*);
and that [question] pertains to the state of ignorance or doubt regarding the object of the hindrances and so forth.

It is fourfold. However, in the Pāḷi, it is shown that there is one question [to be considered] because the world of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth is stated in the verse as the supporting basis (*ādhāra*).

This is the investigation of the question (*pucchāvicaya*) here. The investigation of the answer (*vissajjanavicaya*) should also be understood according to the method explained in the investigation of the question, starting with:
"The answer that illuminates what was not seen" and "the answer that cuts off doubt," and so on.
Having thus shown the stream with a single basis, he now says "They flow everywhere," etc., in order to show that which has multiple bases.
Therein, "they flow" means they run. "Everywhere" means in all the sense-bases (āyatana), such as form and so forth.

"Streams" refers to the streams of craving and the like. "What is the obstruction? means what is the hindrance or what is the protection for them? "Speak of restraint" means speak of that [restraint] for them.
"Speak of the restraint known as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). By what are the streams closed?"—the meaning of the words here is:
by what phenomenon are the streams of craving and so forth closed and cut off? The rest will be made clear through the text itself.
"Those two questions"—although this verse proceeds by way of four questions, there are four [phrases].
These are the statements. However, because the meaning desired to be known is twofold, there are two questions. Why is that? He says:
"Because these have been asked by means of words occurring with reference to many [factors]. Herein, this is the summarized meaning:
since these meanings taken up in this verse have been asked by means of words occurring with reference to many factors, therefore they constitute two questions. Together—

Indeed, there are many technical expressions in the Dispensation (*sāsana*); therefore, in order to clarify that very [expression] as having a twofold objective regarding the question, the words beginning with "thus" (*evaṃ*) were spoken.

Its meaning is as follows: by whatever calamities—namely, those consisting of the loss of kinsmen and so forth, or indeed the killing of living beings and so forth—which are causes for an unhappy rebirth, this world is simultaneously (*samaṃ*) or together (*saha*) afflicted (*āpanno*), overwhelmed; [this is said] because of those ten [causes].
It is defiled by the bases of defilement; having brought to mind both the manner in which he has fallen into that offense and the manner of its defilement, he says:
"of one who has thus fallen into it, who is thus defiled. That by which one is cleansed or purified is *vodāna*, namely serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
That by which one emerges from the sign and from the occurrence [of the defilement] is *vuṭṭhāna*, namely the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).

"Of one who is unconcentrated" means of one whose mind is distracted among various objects. "Flow" means they proceed. The passage beginning with "covetousness" shows the causes for the lack of concentration.
For this very reason he says: "Thus, of one who is unconcentrated. With the words "As the Blessed One said," etc., he shows here too the investigation of the verses that follow.
He says that the hearing of these streams occurs mostly through the influence of attachment.

—“It flows toward agreeable forms. And here, the eye and so forth, while functioning as the doors for the streams [of consciousness], are described as if they themselves were flowing by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).
“Thus” (*iti*) means in this manner. “From all” (*sabbā*) means from everything. “In every way” (*sabbathā*) means in every mode.
“This purification” (*idam vodānam*) refers to this purification, which is the abandoning of the obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*), as it was stated: “the destruction of the obsessions.”

"Mindfulness, when present, is the warding off of those [unwholesome states]" means that mindfulness associated with insight, while investigating the courses of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, is the warding off of those streams.
"I call it the restraint of the streams" means that I call that very mindfulness the restraint of the streams.
"By wisdom these are closed up" refers to the wisdom that accomplishes the penetration of impermanence and so forth regarding forms and other objects.
By means of path-wisdom (*maggapaññā*), these streams are completely closed off; the meaning is that they are cut off by way of not providing an opportunity for them to arise.
"He does not pull [them] in" means he does not draw the mental continuum or the person toward himself by way of being a door for the occurrence of covetousness and so forth.
Here, the intended sense of "closing off" is the abandoning of the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*); thus it is said: "by wisdom, the underlying tendencies are abandoned. Because...
