He says, "In the underlying tendencies," and so forth, because the obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) that has the underlying tendencies as its cause does not exist in the absence of those underlying tendencies.
Now, illustrating this very point by means of a simile, he says, "Just as for one who possesses timber," and so forth.

Here too, it is because [the person] either does not know the restraint—which is to say, the closing—that constitutes the blocking of the streams, or is in doubt regarding it, that [the result] is not of a single certainty.

The question was formulated with reference to the Dhamma; thus, here the investigation of the question is to be understood according to the method already stated, and the investigation of the answer is likewise to be understood.

Furthermore, regarding the intention by which it was said that in the verse "By what is the world shut in?", although there are four things to be asked about—namely, the shutting in and so forth—it is nevertheless stated as a single question:
by that [intention], the restraint and the closing of the sense-faculties alone were asked about.
If the streams were taken as having a single referent, then because the question has a single basis, it might be called "one question.
Alternatively, because of the multiplicity of the streams, they are "many"—as many as there are streams, so many are the questions.

However, by which intention [this was said], in the verse "The streams flow everywhere," without referring to the streams themselves, but rather by way of the two types of coverings (saṃvara) that serve as lids, [it is said]: "Two..."

Thus it is said: “questions. By this it should be understood that although the first verse mentions the world as the support for the obstructions and so forth, one could also speak of four questions by distinguishing the obstructions and so forth without explicitly mentioning the world; this method is thus shown.
Now, the one who asks does not ask solely according to the order previously composed by himself, but rather—

Even though he asks while grasping the connection (*anusandhi*) of the Dhamma spoken at the time of the teaching, the Teacher, in order to show the manner in which that connection must be discerned through his question, spoke the verse beginning with "Wisdom and mindfulness" immediately after the verse beginning with "Those which are streams.
This is its summary meaning: that wisdom which was spoken by the Blessed One, and that mindfulness, and...
"Where does all that remaining name-and-form cease? Being asked this by me, please explain.
Now, in the verse of the reply, because the fifty [types of] consciousness are included under the very name "consciousness," they are not mentioned separately.
And here is the summary of the meaning: O Ajita, as for this question which you asked me—
—“Where does this cease? In the immediately following verse, I shall tell you where it ceases without remainder.
For with the cessation of each respective consciousness, this [craving] ceases here simultaneously, neither before nor after;
it ceases precisely through the cessation of consciousness. This cessation of craving does not transcend the cessation of that consciousness.
"It has been said" means: in this question, he asks for the connection [to the following].

In the immediately preceding verse, mindfulness and wisdom were mentioned together with the function of abandoning the outbursts (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) and underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). Having heard that, while wisdom and mindfulness stand for the purpose of abandoning those [tendencies], there must be name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as their support;
and when that is the case, it is indeed appropriate. Where, then, is the support for these two?
He said, "This question was asked with the intention that it is the complete cessation of wisdom and mindfulness," as in the passage: "This question...
the element. In this context, *anusandhi* means that by means of it the teaching is connected (*anusandhīyati*).
That path by which they attain the Nibbāna-element without residue is what is designated as the cultivation of the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths.
In order to show the practice together with its object, it is said: “And the three truths,” and so forth.
Therein, “conditioned” (*saṅkhata*) means made by conditions having come together and combined; they are thus conditioned. “Subject to cessation” (*nirodhadhamma*) means having the nature of ceasing.
“Suffering, origin, and path”—this is the demonstration of their specific characteristics. But how is cessation? To this he says: “Cessation...”
“Unconditioned” (*asaṅkhata*): for it is unconditioned because it is not conditioned by any cause.

In order to show the classification of what is to be abandoned by way of the classification of that which abandons—among the Noble Truths, whose nature consists of both the object and that which abandons—it is said, “Therein, origination,” and so forth.

Therein, “the remainder of ignorance” means ignorance remaining after it has been abandoned by the path of seeing. And this word *sesa* (remainder)— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.*
Sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), ill will (*byāpāda*), conceit (*māna*), and restlessness (*uddhacca*)—these too should be applied here [to the phrase "without remainder"].

For just as ignorance (*avijjā*), so too these states have the nature of leading to the states of deprivation (*apāya*) and are abandoned by the first path. There is also a reading: “ignorance without remainder” (*avijjā-niravaśeṣā*);
here too, the word “without remainder” (*niravaśeṣa*) should be applied to the aforementioned terms beginning with sensual desire. For [if it were] with remainder...
By the first two paths, sensual desire and the other fetters are abandoned; by the others, however, they are abandoned without remainder.
Regarding the phrase "these ten fetters in the three realms," the term "in the three realms" indicates the objective sphere of the fetters, for it is therein that they function as fetters.
"12. Having resolved upon the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (anaññātaññassāmītindriya)" means having reached that which abandons [the defilements].

As for the phrase "but what": here, *yaṃ* is a particle used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). "This is the knowledge of destruction" (khaye ñāṇa) refers to that knowledge acting as a cause by which one knows the state of the exhaustion of one's own birth, thinking, "Birth is exhausted for me. This is the knowledge of the fruit of Arhatship, which serves as the basis for such reflection.

"Knowledge of destruction" (khaye ñāṇaṃ) means this. Regarding the phrase "he understands: 'there is nothing further of this nature,'" the word "which" (yaṃ) should also be supplied here, so that it reads:

"which he understands: 'there is nothing further of this nature. This is "knowledge of non-arising" (anuppāde ñāṇaṃ). Here too, the meaning should be construed according to the method previously stated, by way of the knowledge of the fruit of Arahatship.
However, in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*, it is said: "Knowledge of destruction is knowledge of the Noble Path which effects the destruction of the defilements."

It has been said: "Knowledge of non-arising is the knowledge of the noble fruit that arises at the conclusion of the non-arising of those various defilements to be abandoned by the respective paths, which have reached the state of non-arising by way of rebirth-linking.
However, here both are analyzed specifically by way of the knowledge of the fruit of arahantship. For this very reason it was said:
"These two knowledges are the faculty of one who has already known," and "the two [are distinguished] by way of the designation of their objects."
And it is said: "They receive their names.

Although the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*) arises repeatedly during the arising of the three lower fruits and the three higher paths, it does not—like the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*)—receive its name at the arising of the first fruit or the highest fruit.
He says, "And the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown,'" and so forth, because [the faculties] cease through non-arising cessation (*anuppādanirodha*).

By this he shows that, just like the states to be abandoned, the remaining resultant states (*phaladhamma*) also cease through non-arising cessation at the arising of the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*) via vision and cultivation;
what need is there to mention the states belonging to the three planes? For a single wisdom becomes the faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*).

If it is one, how is it said to be twofold? To this he says, "Moreover," and so forth. "By way of the designation for the object" means by this conventional term for the object: "one brings about non-arising in destruction.

"That is wisdom in the sense of understanding" means that the wisdom previously described as having the function of closing the doors of the senses is wisdom by virtue of its nature as understanding (*pajānana*).
The other, however, [is wisdom] regarding the object exactly as it has been seen and exactly as it has been grasped.
“Mindfulness (sati) is so called in the sense of not-floating-away and in the sense of plunging-in.
Having thus explained the meaning of the phrase “both wisdom and mindfulness,” he now explains the meaning of the phrase “name-and-form” (nāmarūpa), saying:
“In that regard, those which are the five aggregates of clinging—this is name-and-form. And as for name-and-form...

Showing it by way of analysis, and in order that it may be easily grasped, he says "therein, those which... and so forth, specifically to clarify name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as it is commonly understood.
For by the mention of that [consciousness] alone, the other mental states—citta and cetasika—as well as material phenomena (rūpadhamma), are included through their association and so on.
And here, by the term "name" (nāma), only the triad of aggregates is meant; thus, "name-and-form is associated with consciousness."
It was stated [thus]. But is that form associated [with consciousness]? This was not stated by way of the condition of association (*sampayutta-paccaya*).
Rather, it should be understood as having been stated with reference to the nature of being grasped without distinction by ordinary people.

In the verse, the Nibbāna-element without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*) is asked about; therefore, by means of the four bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), through the attainment of the Noble Path—

Showing that these are what must be attained, he said, "In this context, mindfulness and wisdom are the four faculties," in order to distinguish the faculties—which are the roots for the development of the bases of psychic power—by means of mindfulness and wisdom.

Mindfulness, which investigates the courses of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, is perfected and invariably brings about concentration. And by the inclusion of mindfulness here, the abandoning of the obsessions is intended.
Regarding this, he said: "Mindfulness consists of two faculties: the faculty of mindfulness and the faculty of concentration.
Likewise, since wisdom that effects the eradication of the underlying tendencies cannot be accomplished without the energy of the fourfold right exertion, it was stated:
"Wisdom consists of two faculties: the faculty of wisdom and the faculty of energy."

"Regarding 'that which [is faith] in these four faculties'": in these four faculties, beginning with mindfulness, which serve as the foundation by way of being a support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*), there is a state of believing that arises simultaneously with them.
There is also a scriptural reading, "by means of these four faculties";
for that, the ellipsis to be supplied is "associated with these four faculties. Faith has the characteristic of intense clarity toward the object, and its intrinsic nature is the desire to act.
He says, "It is a specific condition for desire," thus: "That one-pointedness of mind dominated by faith is concentration through desire.
"When the mind is concentrated" means when the mind is concentrated by means of insight-concentration (*vipassanā-samādhi*).

"This is abandoning" refers to concentration that accomplishes suppression-abandoning (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*); it is called "abandoning" because one abandons by means of it. There is also the reading "exertion" (*padhāna*), which has the meaning of "supreme."
For it is said that "concentration is one-pointed.

By the phrase "inhalation and exhalation," etc., it is precisely the formations of energy (vīriya-saṅkhāra) that originate it which are grasped under the heading of the bodily, verbal, and mental formations.
For as long as their development is not yet perfected, they are called "with flavor and intention" because they are remembered with a single flavor and because they are to be intended.
It is said that it occurs "in such a way as my development may be," because it serves as the cause for proceeding according to one's wish.

"Both of these" refers to both that which is called desire-concentration (*chanda-samādhi*) and that which is called the volitional formation of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*), namely energy (*vīriya*).

Indeed, by way of figurative usage (*upacāra*), these two are treated as if they were distinct and thus termed "the basis of psychic power endowed with desire-concentration and the volitional formation of striving."
It has been said. For even that which is not distinct is spoken of as if it were distinct by way of conventional usage (*upacāra*), just as one says, "the body of a stone statue.

In this context, it is called *iddhi* because it succeeds (*ijjhati*); the meaning is that it is accomplished or brought to completion. Alternatively, it is called *iddhi* because by means of it beings succeed (*ijjhanti*), become prosperous, and reach excellence.
It is called *pāda* because one goes (*pajjati*) by means of it; according to the first meaning, it is simply *iddhi*.

*Pāda* means the basis of success (*iddhipāda*), in the sense of a constituent part of success. According to the second sense, it is the basis, the foundation, and the means of attainment for success;
thus it is called the "basis of success. For by means of it, one goes to and reaches success, which consists of successive distinctions.

"Dependent on seclusion" refers to the basis of success dependent on seclusion as a factor of that state (*tadaṅga-viveka*), dependent on seclusion through eradication (*samuccheda-viveka*), and dependent on seclusion as escape (*nissaraṇa-viveka*).

The meaning is "he develops. For thus, when this yogi devoted to the development of the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) is at the moment of insight (vipassanā), he develops the basis of psychic power based on seclusion by way of its function (*kicca*) and based on seclusion as escape (*nissaraṇa-viveka*) by way of his aspiration (*ajjhāsaya*).

But at the moment of the Path (*magga*), he develops the basis of psychic power based on seclusion through eradication (*samuccheda-viveka*) by way of its function, and based on seclusion as escape by way of its object (*ārammaṇa*).
This same method applies to the phrases "dependent on fading away" (*virāga-nissita*) and so forth.

For fading away and the rest are simply synonyms for seclusion (*viveka*); however, in this context, relinquishment (*vossagga*) is twofold: relinquishment as giving up (*pariccāga-vossagga*) and relinquishment as leaping forward (*pakkhandana-vossagga*).
Therein, relinquishment as giving up occurs by way of the factor-of-moment (*tadaṅga*) at the moment of insight (*vipassanā*).
The abandoning of defilements occurs by way of their total eradication at the moment of the Path. "Leaping forward" (*pakkhandana*) and "relinquishing" (*vossagga*):
leaping forward toward Nibbāna occurs by way of being inclined toward it during the moment of insight (*vipassanā*), and by way of making it the object during the moment of the Path.
Both of these are appropriate within this method of explaining the meaning, which is a mixture of mundane and supramundane. For thus is this first basis of power (*iddhipāda*).
In the manner described, one abandons the defilements and leaps into Nibbāna.
By the expression "tending toward relinquishment" (*vossaggapariṇāmī*), the meaning is that it tends toward, has tended toward, is maturing toward, and has matured toward relinquishment.

For this yogi devoted to the development of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) acts so that the first base of psychic power serves the purpose of relinquishing the defilements and attaining relinquishment.
It ripens for the sake of leaping forward toward Nibbāna and for relinquishment; and he develops it in such a way that it becomes fully matured.
This same method applies to the remaining bases of accomplishment (siddhipāda). However, this is the distinction:

just as concentration that proceeds by making zeal (chanda) predominant is called "concentration through zeal" (chandasamādhi), so too [it is when] energy (vīriya), mind (citta), or investigation (vīmaṃsā) is made predominant.
"Concentration that has been set in motion is called 'concentration through investigation' (vīmaṃsāsamādhi).
To show that not only the fourth basis for psychic power (iddhipāda) is rooted in knowledge of concentration, but rather that all [four] are so, it is said:
"All concentration is rooted in knowledge, preceded by knowledge, and follows after knowledge. If this is so, why...
Is it said that this very thing is "concentration through investigation"? This meaning is indeed stated as being so because it has proceeded by making investigation the predominant factor.
In that regard, with wisdom belonging to the prior stage, it is rooted in knowledge; with wisdom of attainment, it is preceded by knowledge; and with wisdom of review, it follows after knowledge.
Alternatively, with wisdom belonging to the prior stage, it is rooted in knowledge; with wisdom of access, it is preceded by knowledge.

It should be understood that with insight-wisdom of absorption (appanā-paññā), it follows after knowledge; with insight-wisdom of access (upacāra-paññā), it is rooted in knowledge; with insight-wisdom of absorption, it is preceded by knowledge; and with insight-wisdom of direct knowledge (abhiññā-paññā), it follows after knowledge.
"As before" means as previously, by way of its following after the knowledge of recollection of past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa) within concentration.

In the past births— even throughout incalculable aeons of world-dissolution and evolution— there is nothing regarding one's own aggregates or those connected to the aggregates of others that is difficult to penetrate.
Likewise, subsequently, through the power of the knowledge of future states accompanying concentration,

there is nothing regarding one's own aggregates or those connected to the aggregates of others in the future births— even throughout incalculable aeons of world-dissolution and evolution— that is difficult to penetrate.
The meaning is that there is nothing difficult to penetrate.
Just as "afterwards"— meaning that because it follows upon the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa) within concentration,
there is nothing difficult to penetrate regarding the minds of other beings during the seven future days— so too, "beforehand" regarding the seven past [days].
The meaning is that during the days, there is no such thing as a mind of another being that is difficult to penetrate.

"As by day" means that just as during the daytime, because darkness has been dispelled by the light of the sun, a form that has come within the range of sight is easily discernible for beings possessing eyes;
"so at night" means likewise during the nighttime, even when [the sky] is endowed with the four factors...
When darkness prevails, there is no form-object (*rūpāyatana*) that is difficult to penetrate because of its following upon the divine eye-knowledge of concentration.

Just as at night, so too by day; and just as at night, so too by day, there is no form whatsoever—whether exceedingly subtle, concealed by something, or situated at an extreme distance—that is called "difficult to penetrate. And as it has been stated regarding the form-object, so it is here.
In the same way, this should also be applied to the sense-sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*) through the divine ear-knowledge (*dibbasotañāṇa*) accompanying concentration. For this very reason, it says:
"Thus with a mind that is open," and so forth. Therein, "unobstructed" means not shrouded by the defilements that act as obstacles to direct knowledge (*abhiññāñāṇa*);
precisely because it is unobstructed, the mind is luminous (*sappabhāsa*). By this very [explanation], the supernormal power-knowledge (*iddhividhañāṇa*) accompanying concentration is also [implied].

It should be understood that they are indeed mentioned [in the text]. Regarding the phrase "the five faculties," he says "wholesome" because it is the five faculties of one in training (sekha) associated with the bases of psychic power (iddhipāda) that are intended.
The passage beginning with "co-existent with consciousness" is undertaken for the purpose of showing their cessation through the cessation of consciousness.
The same applies to the passage beginning with "name-and-form. By this, he demonstrates: "It is not only the five faculties alone [that cease]."
“Then indeed, name-and-form has consciousness as its cause, and with the cessation of consciousness, it ceases.
“Of that” means of consciousness. “Cause” refers to craving, ignorance, and so forth. This is an explanation of the meaning of the term “without nutriment.
“Not rejoiced in” means not craved for, precisely because craving—which constitutes rejoicing—has been abandoned. For that very reason, consciousness is without rebirth-linking (*appaṭisandhika*).
That [consciousness] ceases. And just as with consciousness, so too with name-and-form:

due to the absence of the cause and condition designated as "consciousness," and due to the absence of the formations and other factors that are its conditions, it is without cause and without condition. The rest is self-evident.
The analysis of the questions and answers should also be understood according to the method already stated.

Having thus shown the question concerning the connection (*anusandhipuccha*), and since the questions based on the person (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*) and those based on the phenomenon (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*) were previously presented separately, the passage beginning with "Those who have discerned the Dhamma" (*ye ca saṅkhātadhammāse*) is now commenced in order to show them together.

Herein, this is the word-meaning: "those who have discerned the Dhamma" (*saṅkhātadhammā*) means those who have investigated the phenomena by way of impermanence and so forth; [this refers to] the Arahants.
This is the designation. "Learners" (*sekkhā*) refers to the remaining noble persons who are training in virtue and so forth. "Many" (*puthū*) means numerous beings and people.
Regarding the phrase "Tell me their conduct, being asked, O wise one": "of them," meaning of those learners and non-learners; "wise" (*nipaka*) means clever;
"O Blessed One, being asked by me, tell me their practice. The rest is understood from the text itself.

15. *Kissā* means "for what reason" or "by what cause. *Sekhāsekhavipassanāpubbaṅgamappahānayogena* means by way of the method of inquiry regarding the abandonment preceded by insight for both those in training (*sekha*) and those beyond training (*asekha*), that is, by the manner of questioning.
In the verse of the answer, *kāmesu nābhigijjheyya* means one should not covet sense-objects (*vatthukāma*) with the defilement of sensual desire (*kilesakāma*).

*Manasānāvilo siyā* means that one should not be turbid in mind; [this refers to] ill-will thoughts (*byāpādavitakka*) and so forth, as well as bodily misconduct (*kāyaduccarita*) and so forth, which cause turbidity of the mind.

While abandoning phenomena, he should remain undisturbed in mind. Because, however, the one beyond training (asekha) has scrutinized all phenomena by way of impermanence and so forth, and is thus skilled in all phenomena;

and because, being mindful through the foundations of mindfulness such as the contemplation of the body and so on, he has reached the state of a supreme bhikkhu due to having shattered all defilements, he conducts himself in all postures. Therefore: “Skilled... [and so forth].”
"Go forth," he said—this is the summary of the meaning.
In that regard, the word "discerning" (*nipaka*) mentioned in the verse of inquiry was spoken with reference to the Blessed One;

and since the Blessed One’s discernment has reached the pinnacle of perfection, it should be illustrated by his unobstructed knowledge and vision (*anāvaraṇañāṇadassana*). Thus, [it refers to] unobstructed knowledge.

Having thus analyzed [the path] by way of the various doors of action, the passage beginning with "The entire bodily action of the Blessed One" was stated in order to show the practice of those in training (*sekha*) and those beyond training (*asekha*).

By this, he clarifies the Tathāgata’s skill in teaching the practice of those in training and those beyond training through his unimpeded knowledge and vision in all respects. In that context, "wherein" (*ko ca*) means "in what" or "in which object. He shows that object [with the words]: "That which..."
"Impermanent, suffering, and non-self. This is what is meant: when the vision of knowledge arises, it arises as "all that is conditioned is impermanent, suffering; all phenomena are non-self.
However, the non-occurrence of that [vision] regarding its object is "resistance. By this, the difficulty of penetrating the three characteristics is shown.

And it shows its uniqueness, not shared by others. For by means of the elucidation of the three characteristics, the wise acknowledge the Blessed One’s penetration of the Four Noble Truths and his Perfect Enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
Ignorance is non-seeing; it shows that [non-seeing] as a specific entity, which conceals the intrinsic nature of the six objects.

For delusion is an obstruction to knowledge and vision. Since knowledge and vision are capable of arising with respect to a particular object, it must be that very object which constitutes their obstruction;
thus he says: "That which [is perceived] in what is impermanent, suffering, and non-self...

Here, the passage beginning with "Just as a man" and so forth is an illustration by way of a simile. The correlation of this simile is as follows: the entire world is like the man, and the stars are...

Just as there are six kinds of objects, so too for that man, the perception of the forms of stars by means of his visual consciousness and the rest is like the world’s cognition of the six kinds of objects according to their respective spheres; yet, just as that man, while seeing the star-forms,
does not know them through the convention of counting such as "so many hundreds" or "so many thousands," so it is with the world regarding the objects of form and the rest.
"Even for one who knows in some way, there is a lack of realization regarding the three characteristics, such as impermanence. The rest is self-evident.
Now, in order to analyze the meaning of those words by which the Blessed One described the practice of the trainee (*sekha*) and the non-trainee (*asekha*) to the Venerable Ajita, he said:
"In that regard, by the trainee," and so forth. Therein, "in that regard" (*tattha*) is merely a particle; in that—
Or in the context of answering. "By one in training" (*sekha*) means: one whose virtue is that of training (*sikkhā*); thus, by that one in training. "In two things" means:
the intended sense is "in two kinds of things. "Subject to obsession" (*pariyuṭṭhānīya*) means: those objects of resentment (*āghātavatthu*) where one who is obsessed by hatred must turn about;
this is the meaning. There is also a reading, "subject to repulsion" (*paṭighaṭṭhānīya*), which has the same meaning.
And here, in this exhortation to prohibit greed, it is stated that because the fault caused by greed arises when greed exists, the mind must therefore be guarded even from that;
for since the Blessed One said, "One should not covet sensual pleasures," the description was made by way of greed in the passage beginning, "whatever longing there is for them.
Alternatively, [it is stated] regarding the mind's [need for protection] from the fault...
It should be understood that the state of being guarded is indeed expressed by the second line of the verse. For by the second line, the remaining defilements and purification-phenomena are shown.

Thus, having analyzed all defiled and purified phenomena into four categories according to their distinction as arisen or unarisen, and by way of their status as objects of right effort, [the author] has demonstrated the path of training for those in training (sekha) by bringing it to its ultimate conclusion through the gateway of the right exertions (sammappadhāna).

The passage beginning with “the trainee, not coveting” has been stated. Therein, “one whose intention is undisturbed” means one whose intention is undisturbed due to the absence of turbid intentions such as those of sensual desire.
Precisely because of that, he exerts himself without coveting; he puts forth energy. To the question “How does he exert himself? it is said:
“He [exerts himself] for the non-arising of unarisen [unwholesome states],” and so forth.
In this context, "he" refers to a trainee (*sekha*) who is practicing for the sake of further distinction.
"Of those not yet arisen" means of those that have not been produced. "Evil" means base. "Unwholesome states" means states born of lack of skill.
"For their non-arising" means for the purpose of not producing them. "He generates desire" means he arouses wholesome desire, which is characterized by the wish to act.
"Exerts effort" means he performs application and striving. "Arouses energy" means he exercises physical and mental energy.
"Uplifts the mind" means he raises the mind by means of that very co-nascent energy. "Strives" means he performs the energy of exertion (*padhāna-vīriya*).
Furthermore, these four terms beginning with "exerts effort" refer to cultivation through repetition, frequent practice, constancy, and performance.
They are to be applied as follows: "Of evil states that have arisen" refers to unwholesome phenomena that have reached the state of having already arisen.

"For their abandoning" means for the purpose of relinquishing them. "Of wholesome states that have not yet arisen" refers to phenomena produced through skill (*kosalla*) that have not yet come into being.

"For their arising" means for the purpose of bringing them into existence. "Of those that have arisen" refers to those that have already been produced. "For their stability" means for the purpose of maintaining their persistence.
"Non-confusion" means for the purpose of non-decline. "For increase" means for repeated occurrence. "For expansion" means for a state of abundance. "For development" means for growth.
"For fulfillment" means for the purpose of complete perfection—this, first of all, is the meaning of the words.
16. "Which are those that have not arisen," and so forth, refers to unwholesome and wholesome states according to how they have not arisen and according to how they [should arise].
And having begun [the exposition] to show those that have arisen, it is said therein:

"These are unarisen. These—namely, sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*) and the rest—are called "unarisen" either by way of not being currently active or by way of their objects not having been experienced.

For otherwise, throughout the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there are no unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*) that could be called unarisen. Furthermore, the mention of the three types of thought here should be regarded as merely illustrative.
"The unwholesome roots" refers specifically to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), because they constitute the root of all unwholesome states; it does not refer merely to greed and the rest.

These arisen underlying tendencies are called "arisen by way of name" because of the presence of various modes of arising such as "arisen by having gained a footing," "arisen without being eradicated," and so forth;
the meaning is that they are not so called by virtue of being currently active. "These wholesome states have not yet arisen."

These qualities, beginning with faith, belonging to one who has entered the stream and is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, are called "wholesome states that have not yet arisen";

what need is there to mention those of ordinary worldlings? This is what is being shown. Furthermore, in this context, the word *kusala* should be understood as synonymous with "blameless" (*anavajja*), as in the *Bāhitika Sutta*.
"These wholesome states have arisen" refers to these factors, beginning with faith, which have arisen in the first path.
The wholesome states that have arisen in one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry are what is meant [here].
Because sensual thought is well-restrained by the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness, it is said: "That by which one wards off sensual thought is the faculty of mindfulness.
By means of non-distraction, which has the state of blameless happiness as its proximate cause, the condition for distraction—which is based upon mental suffering—is removed.
It is said that "the thought of ill will is well-restrained" because "that by which one wards off the thought of ill will is the faculty of concentration.
One who has initiated energy regarding wholesome states easily endures the offenses of others;

thus, it is said that "the thought of cruelty is well-restrained by energy," for "that by which one wards off the thought of cruelty is the faculty of energy. This also applies to concentration and the other [faculties].
Showing that the abandonment of each respective opposite succeeds only for one possessed of wisdom, he said:
“By which, when they have arisen,” and so forth.
To demonstrate the preeminence of these five faculties as previously defined within their own respective domains, he said: “The faculty of faith...”
The passage beginning with "Where is it to be seen? has already been stated; that is indeed easy to understand.

And showing that through the production of these faculties of the trainee (sekha)—faith and the rest—all qualities of the trainee reach their ultimate perfection, he concludes the path of the trainee with the words "Thus the trainee," and so forth.

17. Having thus analyzed the practice of the trainee (*sekha*), he now speaks the passage beginning with “skilled in all phenomena” (*kusalo sabbadhammānaṃ*) in order to analyze the practice of the one beyond training (*asekha*).

Therein, having first analyzed the phenomena mentioned by the term “all phenomena,” he says “the world, so-called” (*loko nāma*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate the skill of the one beyond training regarding them.
That has already been explained. [The world consists of] the world of defilements (*kilesaloka*) and the world of existence (*bhavaloka*).
"Accumulates" means that, depending upon a dhamma of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), one brings about the arising of dhammas of the fine-material and immaterial spheres (*rūpārūpāvacara*).
"He" refers to one who stands within the sublime states (*mahaggata-dhamma*), or within both limited and sublime states.

"Produces the faculties" means that, having established virtue and concentration as partaking of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), one generates the faculties of faith and the rest which bring liberation to maturity (*vimuttiparipācanīya*).

"When the faculties are being developed" means that when the aforementioned faculties are being increased, there comes to be the full understanding (*pariññā*) of the knowable by way of the discernment of form and the formless, and so forth.

"Full understanding through seeing" is full understanding through knowing (*ñātapariññā*). "Full understanding through development" is both full understanding through investigating (*tīraṇapariññā*) and full understanding through abandoning (*pahānapariññā*). "That..."
The meaning stated briefly by the passage beginning with "In two ways" is explained in detail by the passage beginning with "For when a trainee.
Therein, by the phrase "with perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by disenchantment," he shows powerful insight (*vipassanā*).

And here, regarding the phrase "for when a trainee" (*yadā hi sekho*), since even a virtuous worldling (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) is included under the term "trainee" (*sekha*) due to their habit of training, [the text says] "two things... [End of excerpt]
“...they proceed toward skill, and toward skill in seeing,” and so forth. This is the intended meaning here:

when a noble worldling (kalyāṇaputhujjana), training in the preliminary training, thoroughly understands the knowable through perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by disenchantment, then those factors of insight proceed toward and reach skill in seeing, which is the knowledge of the first path.

They coincide with that. But when one who is still in training, such as a stream-enterer, thoroughly understands the object of knowledge (*neyya*) in the manner described, then those factors of insight (*vipassanā-dhamma*) in him reach proficiency in cultivation (*bhāvanā-kosalla*).
"That knowledge" refers to the thorough understanding of the object of knowledge mentioned previously; it is the knowledge of thoroughly understanding the object of knowledge. [This is] fivefold.

"It should be understood" indicates its differentiation according to the distinction of its objects. "Knowledge of the specific characteristics of phenomena" (dhamma) means knowledge of the specific characteristics of material and immaterial phenomena, such as hardness, contact, and so forth.

Since all that is to be known (neyya) is twofold—namely, by way of the distinction between cause and fruit—it is therefore specified as "the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-patisambhidā) and the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-patisambhidā)."
"Full understanding" (pariññā) here is intended as "full understanding by scrutinization" (tīraṇapariññā).

Since, after having directly known material and immaterial phenomena according to their specific characteristics and conditions, and having encompassed them through their divisions such as the wholesome and so forth, there arises knowledge of them by way of impermanence and so on, it is therefore said:
"Having thus directly known, that which is the full understanding—'this is wholesome,' etc. In this context, "thus grasped" means...
"Taken by way of comprehension of groups (*kalāpa-sammasana*) as impermanent and so forth" means they have been comprehended.
"Producing this fruit" means they produce in succession this fruit beginning with the knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*);

this is said because the sign (*nimitta*) is figuratively treated as the agent, just as the Truths that bring about the state of an Arahant are called the "Noble Truths" (*ariyasacca*). "Of these" refers to the knowledge of rise and fall and so forth. "Thus taken" means...
"Of those that have thus proceeded": this is the meaning. This "meaning" refers to the awakening to and penetration of the truths.

For just as the wisdom of full understanding (*pariññā-paññā*) fully understands the mode of comprehension within the phenomena to be comprehended—that is, the phenomena of comprehension—it likewise fully understands the fruit of that comprehension;
it is with this in mind that this method has been shown.
"Those that are unwholesome" refers to the truth of the origin (samudayasacca), for all unwholesome states belong to the side of the origin.

"Those that are wholesome" refers to the factors of the Path, beginning with right view (sammā-diṭṭhi). Although the fruits of the path (phala-dhammā) are also to be realized, because the intended meaning here is the penetration of the Four Truths, it is said:
"Which phenomena are to be realized? That which is unconditioned (asaṅkhata). One who is skilled in the meaning (attha-kusala)...

"Skilled in things arisen through conditions" means skilled in the phenomena that serve as conditions (*paccaya-dhamma*). Alternatively, "meaning and phenomenon" (*attha-dhamma*) refers to the meaning of the text and the phenomena of the text. "Skilled in excellence" (*kalyāṇatā-kusala*) means skilled in logical consistency (*yuttatā-kusala*);

the sense is "proficient in the four methods" (*catu-naya-kovida*), or "skilled in the consistency of the teaching. "Skilled in the fruit" (*phalatā-kusala*) means skilled in the fruit of one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava-phala*).
Regarding "skilled in acquisition" (*āya-kusala*) and so forth: "acquisition" (*āya*) is growth; it [arises] from the abandoning of what is unbeneficial.
It is twofold by way of occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*). "Disadvantage" (*apāya*) means non-prosperity (*avaḍḍhi*). That too is twofold: by way of the loss of benefit and by way of the arising of harm.
"Expedient" (*upāya*) refers to a cause that arises immediately upon the occasion (*ṭhānuppattika-kāraṇa*) and is capable of remedying a sudden task or fear that has arisen for beings;
therein, "skilled" (*kusala*) is the meaning. For one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), because ignorance has been entirely abandoned, has attained the fullness of wisdom (*paññā-vepulla*).

“He is skilled in these matters, such as income and so forth. Having thus explained the skill of the one beyond training (asekha) by way of a single aspect, he spoke again of it “without remainder,” saying: “He is endowed with great skill.

Since there is no other purpose for the one beyond training who has completed the training than his state of constant mindfulness (satokāritā), it is said: “for the sake of dwelling happily in this very life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra).”
Now, concluding the path of the trainee and the non-trainee as it has been explained, he said, "These two modes of conduct," and so forth.
Therein, *bojjhaṃ* means that which is to be awakened to. "That is fourfold" means that this object of awakening (*bojjhaṃ*) is fourfold, by virtue of being the four truths.
"One who knows thus" refers to one who knows by way of full understanding, clear realization, and so on. "This is called" refers to the non-trainee (*asekha*).
One who has attained the fullness of mindfulness is, in the direct sense, said to be "mindful as he walks forward," and so forth. The rest is of plain meaning.
Here too, the analysis of the questions and the answers should be understood according to the method explained previously.
To this extent, the Great Elder, analyzing the mode of analysis, has treated the analysis of the questions and the analysis of the answers by way of the *Ajita-sutta*.

Having thus shown [the method], he now says, "It should be asked in this way; it should be answered in this way," demonstrating the method for the analysis of questions and answers even in other discourses (*suttanta*).

In that context, "in this way" (*evam*) means by this method. "Should be asked" (*pucchitabbam*) means a question should be made, or it should be stated, or it should be investigated—that is the meaning.
"Should be answered in this way" (*evam vissajjitam*): here too, the method is exactly the same. Of the discourse...
The phrase "cāti-ādi" (and so forth) is an illustration of the investigation of the *anugīti*. The *anugīti* must be made identical in both meaning (*attha*) and phrasing (*byañjana*).
This means that the *anugīti*, which consists of the teaching from another Sutta, should be made identical or similar in meaning and phrasing to the Sutta being commented upon;

or alternatively, it should be properly brought into harmony with that Sutta. The term "atthāpagataṃ" means "departed from the meaning," or a statement whose meaning is disconnected, such as the verse beginning with "ten pomegranates" (*dasadāḷima*).
Thus it is said: "There is idle chatter. By this, he states the reason for the need to reconcile the meaning.
"Ill-placed" means spoken incorrectly. "Difficult to lead" means that which must be led with difficulty, or that which is impossible to lead.
"Endowed with phrasing" means endowed with natural, proper expression.

Having thus shown the investigation of the *anugīti*, in the section on exposition (*niddesa*), in order to analyze the meaning stated briefly as "the investigation of the discourse" (*suttassa yo pavicayo*), he says, "And the discourse is to be investigated.
Then, showing the manner of that investigation, he says, "Is this discourse a direct statement (*āhaccavacana*)? and so forth.
Therein, "direct statement" refers to [a teaching] delivered by the Blessed One directly through his vocal organs (*ṭhānakaraṇāni*).
"Spoken by [the Buddha] himself" (abhihantvā pavattavacanaṃ) means a discourse taught directly by the Perfectly Enlightened One himself.
"Connected speech" (anusandhivacanaṃ) refers to that spoken by disciples; for it is called "connected speech" because it proceeds by connecting itself to the word of the Blessed One.

"Of direct meaning" (nītatthaṃ) means having a meaning that is to be understood according to the literal expression. "Of indirect meaning" (neyyatthaṃ) means having a meaning that must be grasped after further analysis.
The meaning of the terms beginning with "conducive to defilement" (saṃkilesabhāgiya) will be clarified in the commentary on the section of the *Paṭṭhāna*.
However, since there is no part of the Blessed One’s teaching that does not find its place within the sixteenfold *Sāsana-paṭṭhāna*,
this method has also been included here as something to be investigated.
"Wherein of this sutta? means: in which part—beginning, middle, or end—is this sutta?
"All truths are to be seen" means: having determined and investigated wherein, in which part, or in which word the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca) is to be seen;
and wherein the truth of origin (samudayasacca), the truth of cessation (nirodhasacca), and the truth of the path (maggasacca) are to be seen.
"Having extracted what is to be seen, one should investigate"—the intention is that all the truths should be extracted and investigated in this way.
Regarding the phrase "at the beginning, middle, and end": the meaning is that the discourse (*sutta*) should be investigated in this manner;

that is, from the beginning, the middle, and the end, the discourse should be investigated by means of this method of investigating questions and so forth. And here, [there is] the investigation of the questions, the answers, the sequence, and the subsequent verses.
[The analysis of the truths] is shown explicitly in the Pāḷi itself. However, the investigation of gratification and so forth is shown by way of method through the determination of the truths;
it should be understood according to the method stated in the section on the exposition (niddesa). And by that very investigation, the analysis of words (padavicaya) is established.
The commentary on the analysis of the investigative mode (vicayahāravibhaṅga) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Logical Reasoning (Yuttihāra-vibhaṅga) 18.

Regarding the passage beginning "What is the mode of conveying logical reasoning?", this is the analysis of the mode of conveying logical reasoning (*yuttihāra*). Therein, the question "What does it join together?

asks about the domain of the mode of conveying logical reasoning. What, then, is its domain? Its domain consists of the meanings of the discourses (*sutta*) when they are being grasped in a manner that is not [as they actually are]. These...
Indeed, by means of that [method], it should be applied through the discernment of reasoning exactly as it is. This method is certainly intended for the other [sections] as well;

however, in those cases, it is merely a statement of facts. Since this so-called "searching for reasoning" cannot occur without the Great Authorities (mahāpadesa), therefore, in analyzing the method of reasoning, he first pointed out its characteristic by saying, "The four Great Authorities," and so forth.

In this context, "great authorities" (*mahāpadesā*) means great points of reference; the meaning is that they are great reasons spoken by referring to great [authorities] such as the Buddha and others.
Alternatively, "great authorities" means great bases; what is meant is that they are great foundations for the Dhamma. Herein, this is the etymological analysis:
it is "referred to" (*apadissati*), thus it is an "authority" (*apadeso*); that which has the Buddha as its authority is "one whose authority is the Buddha" (*buddhāpadeso*).

This same method applies to the rest as well. When someone brings forward a text, saying, "I have heard this directly from the Blessed One," the criterion for determining whether it is Dhamma or non-Dhamma is as follows:
What is that criterion? It is precisely the testing of that brought-forward text against the Suttas and so forth.
If this is so, why are there said to be four criteria? Because they are distinguished according to what is cited. For regarding the Dhamma—
There are two kinds of accomplishments: those of the Blessed One and those of his disciples. Among these, the disciples are threefold according to the Sangha, the group, and the individual.

There are four types based on the distinctions of those who can be cited with the words, "In this way, this Dhamma was received by me from such-and-such a person. Therefore he said: "The citation of a Buddha...
[and so on] ...the citation of a single elder. "Those words and phrases" refers to the words and phrases of a Sutta brought forward by someone.

And the meaning is: both the words of the sense and the words of the phrasing. Alternatively, it refers to the words and phrases being brought forward by a commentator according to the method of commentary.
"They should be introduced into the Sutta" means they should be inserted into the Sutta. "They should be shown" means they should be compared.
"They should be set down alongside" means they should be placed within it.
In order to show the Suttas and so forth, the passage beginning with “In which? was stated.
Therein, because there is not even a single verse of the Blessed One’s word that is devoid of the Truths, the phrase “in the four Noble Truths” was stated to show the meaning of the term “Sutta.
However, in the Commentary, it is said that the three Piṭakas are the Sutta; this [is explained] by the following statement from the *Netti*:
It should be understood that [the teaching] indeed converges and accords with this. The Blessed One’s teaching is solely for the purpose of final nibbāna through non-clinging;
since it unilaterally speaks of the subsiding of defilements such as lust, he said "in the subduing of lust" and so forth, demonstrating the meaning of the word *vinaya*.
For here, *vinaya* is intended in the sense of the cause, the means for the subsiding of lust and other defilements. As it has been said:
“Gotamī, those qualities that you might know as leading to passion and not to dispassion,
to bondage and not to liberation, to accumulation and not to diminution, to great desire and not to fewness of wishes,
to lack of contentment and not to contentment, and to social entanglement— ”
They lead not to seclusion, they lead to indolence, not to the arousal of energy; they lead to being difficult to support, not to being easy to support.

You should categorically understand, Gotamī, that "this is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher’s instruction. But those teachings which you should know, Gotamī, as leading to dispassion—
They lead away from lust, they lead to disengagement rather than bondage, they lead to diminution rather than accumulation,
they lead to fewness of wishes rather than great desire, they lead to contentment rather than discontent,
they lead to seclusion rather than socializing, and they lead to the arousal of energy rather than [its neglect].

"O Gotamī, you should hold it with absolute certainty: 'This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s instruction,' [for these things] lead to laziness and to being easy to support, not to being difficult to support.
To show the meaning of the phrase "the nature of things" (dhammatā), it is said: "dependent origination" (paṭiccasamuppāda). Dependent origination...
For that element is indeed established; it is called the "established nature of phenomena" (dhammaṭṭhitatā) and the "fixed law of phenomena" (dhammaniyāmatā).

As for the phrase "these should be set aside as the natural order" (dhammatāyaṃ upanikkhipitabbāni), this does not exist in the canonical text (pāḷi); rather, it should be understood as stated here by way of demonstrating the meaning.

And herein, when one elucidates the occurrence, the cessation, and the means thereto as being fixed in their state of obstruction and so forth, it is said to "enter into the Sutta. This is absolutely certain.
Speaking of the subduing of the defilements such as lust, one is said to be "visible in the Vinaya.

Likewise, by avoiding both eternalism and annihilationism and by elucidating the principles of unity and so forth, one reveals the state of phenomena as conditions and conditionally arisen; thus, one does not contradict the nature of things (*dhammatā*).
And such a person does not give rise to the taints (*āsava*) such as the taint of sensual desire; showing this point, [the text says]: "If, in the four..."

He said, “In the Noble Truths,” and so forth. Now, one might ask: since dependent origination in its forward order is the process of occurrence (*pavatti*) and in its reverse order is the cessation (*nivatti*), and thus it is already included within the Four Noble Truths, why is it mentioned separately here? This is true.

However, the reason for its separate mention here is to demonstrate, by showing how phenomena exist in dependence upon conditions, that their characteristic is impermanence and that their characteristic is the inability [of those phenomena] to act as conditions [for themselves].

And having clarified the characteristic of conditions as being devoid of volition, it is for the purpose of showing that from that very fact their state of possessing arising follows, and from that same fact their state of possessing passing away;

that through both of these there is impermanence; and that through the oppression of arising and passing away there is suffering and non-self—thus demonstrating the conjunction of the three characteristics, destroying the deluded views of all speculative opinions, and revealing the unique excellence of the Dispensation.
And here, this fourfold set should be understood: the Sutta, that which is in conformity with the Sutta (suttānuloma), the teacher’s tradition (ācariyavāda), and one’s own opinion (attanomatī).

Therein, "Sutta" refers to the Three Baskets (Tipiṭaka) as recorded in the three councils. "That which is in conformity with the Sutta" refers to the Great Authorities (mahāpadesa), which is called "that which is conformable and allowable.
"The teacher’s tradition" refers to the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā). "One’s own opinion" refers to [judgment] by means of grasping the underlying method (nayaggāha).
One’s own inspired thought (*paṭibhāna*) is based on subsequent realization (*anubuddhi*). In this regard, a Sutta is not to be contradicted; one who contradicts it contradicts the Teacher himself.
However, a rule of conformity (*anulomakappiya*) must be accepted only if it accords with the Sutta, and not otherwise.

Likewise, the opinion of a teacher (*ācariyavāda*) must be accepted only if it accords with the Sutta, and not otherwise. The same applies to one’s own judgment (*attanomati*), though that is the weakest of all.
Now, in order to show the purpose for which the four great authorities (*mahāpadesa*) have been brought forward here, it is said: "By means of the four great authorities," and so forth.
In this context, "whatever" (*yaṃ yaṃ*) refers to whatever category of meaning (*atthajāta*) and category of Dhamma (*dhammajāta*).

"Is consistent" (*yujjati*) means it is consistent with the four great authorities as they have been stated. "By whichever" (*yena yena*) means by whichever reason. "In whichever way" (*yathā yathā*) means in whichever manner.

"By way of that and that": the meaning is that it should be grasped by way of the reason, the context, and the manner presented in the sutta being commented upon, having been extracted from the sutta itself according to the method of commentary.

By this, he shows that one should effect the application of the method of reasoning (*yuttihāra*) by determining the meaning from the sutta through a logic (*yutti*) that does not contradict the four great authorities (*catumahāpadesa*).
19. Now, in order to demonstrate that determination of the reasoning, the passage beginning with "by one who has asked the question" is commenced.
Therein, "how many words" means how many words in number. To show the meaning of the word *pariyogāhitabba*, it is stated as "to be discerned.
As many words as express the intended meaning, so many words [are required] for that single meaning.
Because it is desired to be known, it is called "a single question. By the words "if all [the phrases]" and so forth, he shows this meaning:
that if all the phrases in a single verse, or even if only one phrase, expresses a single meaning, then that is indeed one question.
"That" (taṃ) refers to that question. "To be known" (aññātabbaṃ) means to be understood. "What are these phenomena? and so forth...
The vision of the mode of understanding. In this context, "dhammas" refers to the dhammas of the scriptures.

"Nānatthā" means various meanings. In the verse of inquiry, the meaning of the words is as follows: "By whom is this world struck?"—the meaning is: by whom is this world of beings struck down and slain, like a thief by a thief-killer?
"By whom is it surrounded?"—like a tree supported by a *māluva* creeper.
By what is the world overwhelmed? By what dart is it pierced? It means by what dart, like an arrow whose tip is smeared with poison, has it entered and become submerged within the body.
For what reason is the world smoldering? For what cause is the world heated and tormented?
The word *sada* (always) should be applied to every instance. *Te* refers to the four phrases; they are expressed in the masculine gender because they refer to the word *pañha* (questions).
“*Vissajjeti* (he answers)” shows that by means of this [term], it is understood that there are three questions because they are answered.
20. *Tattha* (therein): in the second line of the verse of answer, aging (*jarā*) is mentioned, and in the first line, death (*maraṇa*).
These two are the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇāni*), because by these two, the five aggregates of the conditioned are characterized as “conditioned.”
For this was said by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, there are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned.
Which three? Arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and the alteration of that which stands is discerned. Therefore it was said: “In aging is the alteration of that which stands;
death is passing away. And here, “the alteration of that which stands” refers to—
By this, it is shown that here "aging" refers to the distinction between the prior and subsequent states of the continuity of the aggregates (*khandhappabandha*),
and not to their momentary duration. And by the phrase "death is passing away," it shows the conventional death spoken of in the world as in "Tissa has died,
Phussa has died," and not momentary death or death as total annihilation.
Now, in order to demonstrate by way of reasoning the meaning already stated—that "those three questions"—the passage beginning with "And by aging" was spoken.

Therein, because death is generally seen in one who is aged, [the author], for the sake of showing the difference between aging and death to those who do not accept their distinctness, said: "For even those in the womb die. This is what is meant:
—Because death is seen as being devoid of the aging intended [by the questioner], aging is one thing and death is another. For this very reason he said, "And they do not become old.
Furthermore, because only death has been seen, aging is indeed distinct from death; he demonstrates this point with the words, "But there is [death] for the gods," and so forth.
It can indeed be possible to provide a remedy for aging through the unsurpassed human dhamma and medical treatment, but it is not so for death;
thus, in order to show that the distinction between aging and death must be accepted in terms of their meaning, the passage beginning with “it can indeed be possible” was stated.
In this context, *sakkate* means *sakyate*, which has the sense of “it is possible. *Paṭikammaṃ* means *paṭikaraṇaṃ* (remedy). But is it not the case that...?
Reflecting on the objection that it might be possible to counteract even death by attaining mastery through the development of the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*), he said:
“Except for those possessing psychic power, within the range of their psychic power. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Ānanda, whoever has developed and cultivated the four bases of psychic power—having made them a vehicle, a foundation, established, consolidated, and well-undertaken—if he so desires, he could remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.”
What, then, is meant here by a *kappa* (eon), and what is meant by the remainder of a *kappa*? A *kappa* refers to a life-span (*āyukappa*).
For, completing whatever measure of human lifespan exists at any given time, one is said to "remain for a *kappa*.
As for the phrase "or more," this means that one who remains for more than a hundred years and so forth is said to remain for the "remainder of a *kappa*. If this is so, [then...]
Why do those possessed of supernormal power, who have attained mastery over their minds and whose taints are exhausted, not remain thus for the sake of the world’s welfare?
Because they have fully understood the burden of suffering known as the aggregates and because they are free from longing. For these supreme persons have all longing completely stilled.
Indeed, this was said by the General of the Dhamma:
“I do not rejoice in death, nor do I long for life;
I await my time as a servant awaits his wages.

Just as there is a difference in meaning between aging and death, so too, when the difference between those two and craving has been shown, this [statement] “three questions” is established; therefore, he said “But that which... and so forth, in order to demonstrate that.

In this context, because aging and death are found even in the continuum of one whose taints are exhausted despite the absence of craving, he said, "Those free from lust are seen growing old and dying," in order to show that aging and death are one thing and craving is another.
But is it not the case that craving also has the nature of aging and dissolution? True; however, this [specific] aging and death is not what is intended here.
This very point has already been stated. By the words "And if," etc., he demonstrates the fault in [the claim that] craving is not different from aging-and-death.

The intended meaning is: even those in the prime of youth would be devoid of craving; this is not logical. The intended meaning is also that aging-and-death itself would be the origin of suffering, given that it is not different from craving. And craving would not be the origin of suffering [if it were distinct] from aging-and-death.
"If there were non-difference" means "in the case of identity. For aging-and-death is not the origin of suffering; craving is the origin of suffering.
Therefore, the intention is that one must understand their difference in meaning.
Furthermore, just as craving is to be abandoned by the Path, so too would aging-and-death be to be abandoned by the Path if it were non-different from craving. And just as aging-and-death...
It should be understood that this principle has also been stated thus: "Just as [the defilements] are not excluded from the path, so too might craving be.
By this reasoning means: by this aforementioned justification. "By way of mutual [differences]" means:
if there is a difference in meaning through various other reasons and justifications, then the difference in phrasing should also be sought; such is the sense.
The phrase "the identity of these phenomena in meaning" explains this very point through the words "for it is not tenable," and so forth.
"When the intention of craving is not fulfilled" refers to the non-attainment of what is desired; by this, the identity of desire (*icchā*) and craving (*taṇhā*) in meaning is stated.
By this [statement], it is shown that it is not tenable for desire and craving to be different in meaning. Just as...

This statement is a justification; likewise, this is also a justification for the fact that aversion and resentment arise toward the bases of malice when there is a perversion regarding desire. However, it is not so with the perversion regarding aging-and-death.
Thus, by the phrase "by this reasoning," etc., he demonstrates that the distinctness of the objects of craving from aging-and-death has also been established in meaning.
If desire (*icchā*) and craving (*taṇhā*) are not different in meaning, then why were they stated in two ways by the Blessed One in this verse?
To that, he provides the answer with the words beginning "But that which... (*yaṃ panidaṃ*). Therein, "that which" (*yaṃ*) is a reference to the action.
"That which is spoken of" (*abhilapitaṃ*) refers to this speaking (*abhilapanaṃ*) by way of the objects of external bases such as visible forms (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Or it should be applied by way of making an object. "By two states" means by two natures. What, then, are those natures?
*Icchā* (desire) is the seeking after an object not yet attained; *taṇhā* (craving) is the wish to manifest an object already attained or one not yet attained.
This is the distinction between them. Even so, all craving swallows up and brings to completion the objects such as form and the rest.
Showing that, by way of their grasping, they are indeed of a single nature, he said: "For all craving has a single characteristic, namely the characteristic of attachment.
Now, illustrating this point through a simile, he said: "All fire," and so forth; this is easy to understand.

Furthermore, it was stated that craving is not only called by two names according to its specific modes of activity toward an object, but also by many other synonyms; to demonstrate this, he said: "It is also desire," and so forth.
In this context, it is called *icchā* because they desire objects by means of it. It is *taṇhā* in the sense of craving (*taṇhāyana*).
It is a *salla* (dart) because it produces affliction and is difficult to extract, like a poisoned arrow. It is *dhūpāyanā* in the sense of causing distress (*santāpana*).

It is a *saritā* (stream) in the sense of dragging along, like a swift-flowing river; or it is a *saritā* in the sense of being moist (*alla*), as in the phrase: "The streams and the endearments, the joys..."
For it is said: "They become for living beings. Here, the meaning is that they are both moist and sticky. "Visattikā" (clinging): it is *visattikā* because it is spread out (*visata*);

it is *visattikā* because it is extended (*visaṭa*); it is *visattikā* because it is uneven (*visama*); it is *visattikā* because it is wide (*visāla*); it is *visattikā* because it sticks fast (*visakkati*); it is *visattikā* because it is deceptive (*visaṃvādikā*);
it is *visattikā* because it carries away (*visamharati*); it is *visattikā* because its root is poison (*visamūla*).
It is called *visattikā* because it is the fruit of poison (*visa-phala*). It is called *visattikā* because it is the enjoyment of poison (*visa-paribhoga*).
Alternatively, that craving is called *visattikā* because it is spread (*visata*) and extended over forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, mental objects, families, and groups.

It is "affection" (*sineha*) by way of its nature as affection. It is "exhaustion" (*kilamatha*) by way of producing weariness in various states of existence. It is [called clinging] in the sense of enveloping (*paliveṭhana*).
It is called a *latā* because it creeps (*viyāti*). For it is said: “The *latā* arises and stands. It is a conceiving (*maññanā*) by way of the conceiving “mine.

It is a bond (*bandha*) in the sense of binding, having drawn back even that which has gone far away. It is hope (*āsā*) in the sense of wishing. It is thirst (*pipāsā*) in the sense of desiring to manifest the flavor of the object.
It is delighting (*abhinandanā*) in the sense of taking pleasure. Thus, in this way, through various modes of activity toward objects, by means of many...
He concludes the aforementioned point by showing that all craving, even when grasped by various names, has a single characteristic, namely the characteristic of attachment (*ajjhosāna*).
Furthermore, he demonstrates through an elaboration beginning with “And just as” how craving is indeed grasped by many names.

Therein, the term “synonym” (*vevacana*) refers to the analysis of the Synonym Section (*Vevacanahāra-vibhaṅga*). We shall explain the meaning of the verse beginning with “Hope and longing” in that very same place.

In the passage beginning with "of one who has not abandoned lust," it is craving itself that is spoken of: as "lust" in the sense of coloring, as "desire" in the sense of wishing, as "affection" in the sense of endearing, and as "fever" in the sense of burning. For this very reason it is said: "This is a synonym for craving.
Thus it is appropriate: since desire and craving are not different in meaning, what was stated—that there are "three questions"—is appropriate.
The meaning is that it accords with reason (*yutti*).
Having thus demonstrated the reasoning regarding the existence of "three questions" for the verse beginning "By what is the world struck?
(*Kenassu bhāhato loko*), he now states "All is the range of suffering" (*Sabbo dukkhūpacāro*) and so forth, showing the search for reasoning through other modes. Therein:

"Proceeding with suffering" (*dukkhūpacāra*) means the occurrence of suffering. "Rooted in the formative forces conditioned by craving for sensual pleasures" (*kāmataṇhāsaṅkhāramūlaka*) intends to mean that it has as its cause the formative forces whose condition is craving for sensual pleasures; this is the intended meaning. "Proceeding with disenchantment" (*nibbidūpacāra*) means the occurrence of disenchantment.

This arises from the transformation and alteration of sensual pleasures, consisting of both dissatisfaction and the knowledge of disenchantment. "Rooted in the requisites of craving for sensual pleasures" (*kāmataṇhāparikkhāramūlaka*) means having as its cause the objects of desire which serve as the requisites for craving for sensual pleasures.

In this context, it is stated that dissatisfaction (*nibbidā*)—which is characterized as "discontent"—is rooted in the equipment of sensual craving (*kāmataṇhā*), and not in the dissatisfaction born of knowledge (*ñāṇanibbidā*);
thus, it is said that the entire conventional usage of the term "dissatisfaction" cannot be logically justified [if applied otherwise].

By this reasoning, he demonstrates the underlying method (*naya*). This is what is meant: just as the justification was stated regarding the absence of the threefold personality (*pañhattaya*), and as it was stated regarding the metaphorical application of "suffering" and "dissatisfaction."

Thus, by this reasoning, by this method, and by this approach, one should seek the logical consistency (*yutti*) through various causes appropriate to each respective passage of the Pāḷi, using different reasons as the case may require.
Now, in order to show that demonstration of the method—which has been presented in brief—by analyzing it in detail, [the author] says: "Just as the Blessed One," and so forth.

This has been undertaken. Herein, this is the summary of the meaning: for those of greedy, hateful, and deluded temperaments, the discourses on foulness, loving-kindness, and the analysis of conditions are, respectively, suitable for the subduing of greed and the other defilements;

this is the logic of the Dispensation (*sāsanayutti*). Such being the case, if one were to teach the liberation of mind through loving-kindness to one of greedy temperament, that teaching would not be appropriate because it is unsuitable.
The same applies to the "pleasant path" and so forth. But is it not true that...
Is it not the case that the "pleasant course of practice" and so forth apply to the practice itself, and not to the teaching? This is true;
however, here the term "one of lustful temperament" (rāgacarita) refers to one whose defilements are intense. For such a person, the cultivation of the painful course of practice succeeds.
And for whomsoever the cultivation of the painful course of practice succeeds, for them the more extensive teaching on the foul (asubha) is suitable.
Showing this point—that for one for whom a more intense teaching on the foul (asubha) is suitable, a less intense one is not suitable as it would be for one with weak defilements—it is said:
"To teach an easy practice... [etc. ...it is not fitting to teach.

In this manner, the meaning should be stated for the remaining phrases as well, according to what is applicable. And here, the attainment of the logical consistency is achieved by way of the avoidance of what is inappropriate.
It is said that even what is illogical should be investigated through logical analysis: "For if... [etc. ...the teaching would not be tenable. This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
Thus, the passage beginning with "whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*) is merely a demonstration of the method for applying the modes of reasoning.
In this context, "thus" (*evaṃ*) means by this method. "Whatever" (*yaṃ kiñci*) refers to anything else whatsoever. "Conformity and abandoning" (*anulomappahāna*) refers to the abandoning...
"Suitable" means capable of abandoning. In the Sutta, "investigation" (*vicaya*) as a method of exposition (*hāra*) is the word-by-word analysis of all the terms.
Since it is easy to seek out the logical connections among the meanings determined by the commentary on the method of investigation, he said:
"Having investigated all that by means of the method of investigation, one should apply it by means of the method of logical connection. To the extent that there is knowledge...

The meaning is this: for a teacher who is expounding the "planes" (bhūmi), whatever knowledge and whatever inspired eloquence he possesses, to that extent is the scope of his application of the "mode of reasoning" (yuttihāra) and his investigation.
Why is that? Because the True Dhamma is infinite in its methods, universally auspicious, capable of withstanding scrutiny, and possesses manifold teachings.

Thus, since the application of the method of reasoning has been shown by way of the demonstration of the guiding principle (*nayadassana*) alone, the passage beginning with "For one who dwells in loving-kindness" (*mettāvihārissa sato*) is commenced in order to demonstrate it by analyzing it through the mastery of the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*), the attainment of their fruits, and the nine successive attainments (*anupubbavihārasamāpatti*).
Therein, "for one who dwells in loving-kindness" means for one who has obtained the dwelling in loving-kindness.
"Being mindful" (*sato*) means being composed; the sense is "being such as that. "Ill will" (*byāpāda*) means malice. "The mind" (*cittaṃ*)...

"Will stand having taken hold" means it will overcome the mind. However, since there is no such thing as the simultaneous occurrence of wholesome and unwholesome states—neither before nor after—it is said "will stand" in order to show that this occurs at a time subsequent to emerging from the attainment.
The teaching is not inconsistent because loving-kindness (*mettā*) is the direct antidote to ill-will (*byāpāda*).
The meaning is that such a statement is not appropriate. However, the teaching that "ill-will is abandoned and passes away" is appropriate;
for this very reason already stated, this discourse is indeed fitting. The meaning in the remaining sections should also be understood by this same method.
We shall explain only those points that have not yet been clarified.
"Of one who dwells in the signless" means: of one who dwells in the attainment of fruition obtained by way of the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*).

"One who follows signs" means: one who follows the signs of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*). "By this or that very [sign]" means: by whichever sign among those such as permanence and so forth has been abandoned. "'I am' has vanished" means:
whatever conceiving as "I am" occurred with respect to the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*) by way of views and conceit.
That has vanished. He explains that same point: "I do not regard [anything] as 'this I am.
The phrase "the dart of doubt and perplexity" is qualified by the term "doubt" because it exists in the form of "discourse" (kathaṃ kathanti) even in the case of remorse regarding the Vinaya.
"The teaching is not appropriate" means that this discourse is not fitting, because it is something to be abandoned along with doubt.
"For one who has attained the first jhāna" means for one possessing the first jhāna. "Sensual desire and ill will lead to distinction" is not tenable;

because when the hindrances are not abandoned, even the access (upacāra) to the first jhāna is not achieved, let alone the jhāna itself, therefore it is not logical that sensual desire and ill will lead to distinction—that is, to the second jhāna.

Regarding the discourse: it is appropriate that the teaching is logical because for one who has attained the first jhāna, sensual lust and ill will—when they reach the stage of obsession—lead to its decline;
thus it should be applied in all instances.
"Perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by non-thinking" refers to the factors of the second jhāna together with access concentration; for here, the purpose is the making of an object.
The word "accompanied" (*sahagata*). "For decline" (*hānāya*) means for falling away from the first jhāna. "For distinction" (*visesāya*) means for the second jhāna.
By this method, the states described as "decline" and "distinction" in various places are to be understood accordingly.

"Accompanied by applied and sustained thought" (*vitakkavicārasahagatā*) refers to the states of the first jhāna, or indeed to sense-sphere states (*kāmāvacara-dhamma*) themselves. "Accompanied by equanimity and pleasure" (*upekkhāsukhasahagatā*) [refers to states] together with access concentration (*upacāra*).
