The phenomena of the second jhāna; for here, "equanimity" (upekkhā) is intended as the specific neutrality (tatramajjhattupekkhā).

"Accompanied by rapture and pleasure" refers to the phenomena of the third jhāna together with its access (upacāra). "Accompanied by purity of mindfulness and equanimity" refers to the phenomena of the fourth jhāna.
"With perception as their access" means any mental states whatsoever that perform the function of clear perception; they are also called "the phenomena of the base of nothingness."

They say: "Accompanied by the cessation of perception and feeling" refers to those states that occur by way of preparation for him [who thinks], "I shall dwell having attained the cessation of perception and feeling.

For it is only by one established in the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception that it is possible to dwell having attained the cessation of perception and feeling, not by one who has fallen away from it.
Therefore, the statement that [these factors] lead to the decline of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is not a logical discourse;
rather, the statement that they lead to its distinction is logical. Thus he said: "The teaching... for the sake of decline... etc.
"Familiarized through proficiency" means familiarized by way of capability; the meaning is that one is familiarized through mastery over the aforementioned attainments. For this very reason he said:
—“The resolution is acceptable. The rest is all plain and clear.

Furthermore, it is logical that sensual desire deceives by means of the perception of the non-repulsive; it is logical that ill will deceives by way of its resemblance to the perception of the repulsive;
it is logical that sloth and torpor deceive by means of concentration; and [it is logical that restlessness and remorse deceive] by means of the arousal of energy.
It is appropriate to say that restlessness deceives by means of the desire for training. It is appropriate to say that remorse deceives by means of the desire for training.
It is appropriate to say that doubt deceives by means of investigating both sides. It is appropriate to say that delusion deceives by means of equanimity toward the desirable and the undesirable.

It is appropriate to say that conceit deceives by means of self-knowledge through not disparaging oneself. [And it is appropriate to say that] by means of inquiry, [it deceives] through the grasping of fallacious reasons.
It is appropriate to say that wrong view deceives. It is appropriate to say that a lack of compassion toward beings, under the guise of dispassion, deceives.
It is appropriate to say that devotion to sensual pleasure, under the guise of practicing what is permitted, deceives.

It is appropriate to say that a lack of the habit of sharing, under the guise of purity of livelihood, deceives. It is appropriate to say that wrong livelihood, under the guise of the habit of sharing, deceives.
It is logical. It is logical that one deceives by means of a character of non-attachment, which is a counterfeit for dwelling in non-association.

It is logical that one deceives by means of association, which is a counterfeit for a character of attachment. It is logical that one deceives by means of malicious speech, which is a counterfeit for speaking truthfully.

It is logical that one deceives by means of a desire for what is harmful, which is a counterfeit for speaking without malice. [It is logical] by means of a character of pleasant speech, which is a counterfeit for...

It is appropriate to say that flattery deceives because it is a counterfeit of measured speech. It is appropriate to say that a lack of sociability deceives because it is a counterfeit of a sociable disposition.
It is appropriate to say that deceit and craftiness deceive because they are counterfeits of a sociable disposition.

It is appropriate to say that harshness of speech deceives because it is a counterfeit of speaking with restraint. It is appropriate to say that looking for the faults of others deceives because it is a counterfeit of censuring evil.
It is appropriate. It is appropriate that family stinginess deceives by way of its resemblance to the non-uprooting of families.

It is appropriate that dwelling-place stinginess deceives by way of the desire for the long-term stability of the dwelling-place. It is appropriate that doctrine stinginess deceives by way of the avoidance of obstacles to the Dhamma.

It is appropriate that delight in talk deceives by way of delight in teaching the Dhamma. [And it is appropriate that] lack of gentleness in speech deceives by way of failing to provide assistance to the community.
It is appropriate to say that delighting in company deceives; it is appropriate to say that delighting in action deceives by way of its resemblance to a desire for merit;
it is appropriate to say that mental distress deceives by way of its resemblance to spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*);

it is appropriate to say that lack of circumspection deceives by way of its resemblance to faithfulness; and it is appropriate to say that lack of faith deceives by way of its resemblance to investigation.
It is appropriate to say that under the guise of self-reliance, one deceives by being obstinate toward the instructions of one’s teachers.
It is appropriate to say that under the guise of reliance on the Dhamma, one deceives by showing disrespect toward one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life.

It is appropriate to say that under the guise of reliance on the world, one deceives by showing contempt for oneself and for the Dhamma. It is appropriate to say that under the guise of loving-kindness, lust deceives.
It is logical that grief deceives by way of appearing like compassion; it is logical that laughter deceives by way of appearing like the dwelling in sympathetic joy;
and it is logical that the lack of desire for wholesome states deceives by way of appearing like the dwelling in equanimity.
Thus, the nature of deception through what merely resembles the scriptures, what merely resembles realization, and so forth, is established by reasoning.
It is to be understood. Thus, the investigation of reasoning (yutti) should be carried out in accordance with the scriptures (āgama).
The commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Reasoning (Yuttihāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) is finished.
4. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Footings (Padaṭṭhānahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā).
22. Therein, what is the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Footings (*padaṭṭhāna-hāra*)? It begins with the words, "Therein, what is the Mode of Conveying Footings?

and so forth. In this context, because it has the characteristic of revealing those things that serve as the footings for various phenomena—by way of [showing] "this is the footing for this" and "this is the footing for that"—it is called the Mode of Conveying Footings.
Therefore, beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*), which is the root of the process of existence (*pavatti*), it presents the footings of all phenomena according to their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
Distinguishing the proximate cause, he defines the intrinsic nature of ignorance (avijjā) thus: “Ignorance has the characteristic of non-penetration of the true nature of all phenomena.
Its meaning is as follows: it is called “non-penetration of the true nature of all phenomena” because by means of this, the unerring intrinsic nature of all phenomena is not penetrated.
That which has this as its characteristic is described in that way. By this, [it is shown that ignorance] has the characteristic of concealing the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
What is meant is "ignorance" (*avijjā*). Alternatively, "right penetration" (*sampaṭivedha*) means thorough comprehension. Its opposite is "non-penetration.
To the question, "In what respect is it the opposite of right penetration? he says: "All... [down to] characteristics.
Furthermore, because when there are perversions such as "beauty in the foul," delusion regarding those objects arises further and further and does not diminish, therefore—
"Its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is the perversions," it is said.
"The agreeable form and the pleasant form" refers to the category of things that are dear and the category of things that are desirable as its proximate cause;

for it is said: "In the world, wherever there is an agreeable form and a pleasant form, it is there that this craving arises when it arises. "Taking what is not given" means the volition of taking what is not given.
For even though it has arisen only once, because one does not see its danger, it becomes a cause for the arising of greed;

thus it is called the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) of greed. Killing living beings is the proximate cause of hatred, and wrong practice is the proximate cause of delusion—the meaning here should also be understood by this same method.
"Characterized by the grasping of color, shape, and marks" means characterized by the grasping of signs (*nimitta*) and secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*).

The characteristic of contact as the approaching [of consciousness] through the perception of pleasure is stated simply as its conditionality by contact; for it is said: "One perceives what has been touched.
"Taste" (*assāda*) refers to craving. The conditioned characteristics (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*) are arising, passing away, and change.

Since the grasping of permanence is for the most part dependent upon consciousness, the state of being the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) of the perception of permanence is stated [to be] consciousness. For it is thus that the bhikkhu [perceives] that very...
"Consciousness runs on and wanders about," he said, thus proclaiming his own grasping at a self within the very domain of consciousness.

He stated, "The perception of a self is characterized by the non-contemplation of the perceptions of impermanence and suffering," because if the impermanence and suffering of the five aggregates are clearly seen, there is no room for the perception of a self or the perception of pleasure. "That which is impermanent is suffering."
For it has been said: "That which is suffering is non-self.
Since the adherence to a self mostly occurs in relation to immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma), he said: "Its proximate cause is the mental body (nāmakāya).
"All that is to be known" refers to the four truths, because there is no object of knowledge (ñeyya) apart from the four truths. The withdrawal of the mind’s distraction—
The suppression of restlessness. "Foulness" (asubha) refers to the contemplation of foulness, or foulness itself as the counterpart sign;
it is said that foulness is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of serenity because it is the antidote to craving.

Abstention from taking what is not given is said to be the proximate cause of non-greed because it attenuates covetousness. Likewise, abstention from killing living beings [is the proximate cause of non-hatred] because it attenuates ill will.
It is said that the footing for non-hatred is the non-deviation from the basis and the penetration of the true nature of the object.
Right practice consists in the perfection of virtue and concentration, or it occurs as the knowledge of disenchantment, or simply as the knowledge of dissatisfaction.
Since all feeling is suffering by virtue of its state of suffering-as-suffering and so forth, it is said: "The footing for the perception of suffering is feeling."
“Perception of phenomena” (dhammasaññā) means the perception that there is merely a phenomenon.
Because beings are not free from lust for the body by way of the five internal sense bases, it is said:

“The five material faculties are the proximate cause for lust for form. For here, “body” (kāya) is intended in the sense of “form” (rūpa). Specifically, regarding that which serves as the support for jhāna...
And because there is attachment to the mind-base (*manāyatana*), it is said: “The sixth base is the proximate cause for craving for existence (*bhavarāga*).
Such delight in form and so forth—as occurring in the thought, “May such form not be produced; may such feeling not be produced”—is the contemplation of the existence that has been produced.

“Of knowledge and vision” means of the knowledge and vision of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakata*). For one who possesses wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), there is the recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati*).
It is the cause for the knowledge that one is the owner of one’s own kamma, not for one who emerges through improper attention (*ayoniso*).
To illustrate this point, the *Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka* and the doctrine of partial eternalism (*ekaccasassatavāda*) in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* should be cited.

By the phrase "having the characteristic of conviction" (*okappanalakkhaṇā*), etc., he shows the distinction between faith (*saddhā*) and serene confidence (*pasāda*). That, however, should be understood as a specific state of faith itself. Therein:
*Okappanā* is the plunging into the object by way of conviction; it is a decision.

*Anāvilatā* is the absence of turbidity in the mind due to the departure of lack of faith. *Abhipatthiyanā* is simply conviction itself. *Aveccapasāda* is the profound confidence accompanied by wisdom that has entered its proper sphere.
*Apilāpana* is non-forgetfulness, or the plunging into the object as if having submerged oneself; and herein—

When it is said that "the factors of clarity, right exertion, the foundations of mindfulness, and the jhāna-factors are, respectively, the proximate causes (*padatthāna*) for faith and the others," it should be understood that the status of being a proximate cause is stated by way of specific states (*avatthāvisesa*).
Alternatively, the body and so forth are the foundations of mindfulness for mindfulness and concentration, while applied thought and so forth are the jhānas; thus they are stated as proximate causes.
Attention to gratification is the contemplation of gratification in phenomena that lead to fettering. "The sprouting of renewed existence" means the sprouting for the sake of renewed existence;

the meaning is the state of being fit for the production of renewed existence, the nature of being a result. "Characterized by arising through conditions for rebirth" means having the inherent nature of producing existence by way of rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
"Characterized by the integration of the mental body and the material body" refers to the immaterial and material bodies.
The state of being accumulated. "The determination of the faculties" means the established nature of the six faculties, beginning with the eye.
"Born of rebirth" means that which produces the aggregates of rebirth. "Bases" (upadhī) refers to the personal existence (attabhāva).
It is said that death is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of sorrow because, for the most part, sorrow arises in a fool who contemplates the death of someone dear to himself.
*Ussukka* is the fevering of the mind. *Odahanaṃ* means applying oneself.

To show what kind of existence (*bhava*) it refers to—namely, that which results in the burning of one’s own basis—the phrase beginning with “these” was stated. In this context, the factors of existence are the *bhava-aṅgāni*, and those factors comprised within existence are the *bhavaṅgāni*.
Among these, the defilements (*kilesā*) are the factors of existence; the cycle of karma and its result (*kamma-vipāka-vaṭṭaṃ*) are what is designated as existence.
“Limbs”: all of them. “Samsara” is the wandering through the successive arising of the aggregates, bases, and so forth.
Its cause is the cycle of defilements and so on produced in each preceding birth; thus it is said: “Becoming is the proximate cause of samsara.
With reference to its state as the cause that brings about [the goal], it is said: “The path is the proximate cause of cessation.”
One who enters upon a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is called "learned" (bahussuta) because of being a point of entry; his proper attendance upon that is "skill in the ford.
Delight connected with the Dhamma is called "drinking"; having produced that by hearing the suitable Dhamma, the cultivation of the meditation subject is "skill in drinking.
Even with regard to the slight occurrence of sinking or over-excitement in meditation, [one must be skilled].
Knowing is *pattaññutā* (knowledge of what has been attained). Knowing oneself as being endowed with one's own five factors of striving is *attaññutā*.
It is very easy to understand that among these, each preceding factor serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for each succeeding one.

Dwelling in a suitable locality occurs only for one who has performed merit in the past, not for another; thus, "having performed merit in the past" is the proximate cause for dwelling in a suitable locality.
It is said, "The proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*). Insight that is still tender, together with its resolution, is the knowledge and vision of things as they really are (*yathābhūtañāṇadassana*).
Disenchantment (*nibbidā*) is powerful insight. Dispassion (*virāga*) is the path. Liberation (*vimutti*) is the fruit.
Thus, by this method, even though the proximate causes of ignorance and the rest have been shown in the passage beginning, "Its proximate cause is the perversions," etc., furthermore—
Whatever is a decisive support (*upanissaya*) is a strong condition; all remaining conditions should be understood as proximate bases (*padaṭṭhāna*) and causes (*kāraṇa*).
Some also read: "Thus, whatever supports there may be, by way of application (*yoga*) and by way of condition (*paccaya*).

In that context, "support" (*upanisā*) means cause; "by way of application" (*yogato*) means by way of connection; and "by way of condition" (*paccayato*) should be understood as the mere state of being a condition. That which...
Herein, it has not been analyzed according to its meaning, as that is indeed easy to understand.
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Footings is finished.
5. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*Lakkhaṇahāra*).
23. Therein, what is the "Mode of Conveying Characteristics" (*lakkhaṇa-hāra*)? This is the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics.
Therein, the question "What does it characterize? asks about the domain of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics.

Having briefly shown the Mode of Conveying Characteristics with the words "Those phenomena," etc., the passage beginning with "The eye," etc., is undertaken in order to analyze it through examples. Therein, [it is said]: "They have a single characteristic in the sense of being murderous."
It should be understood that by this [statement] regarding their lack of stability and so forth, their single characteristic has indeed been stated.

Having thus shown the single characteristic by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*), the Sutta beginning with "Rādha, one is indifferent toward past forms" is cited now to show it by way of the aggregates (*khandha*) and so on.
In the *Yamaka-vāda-sutta*, they are of a single characteristic in the sense of being murderers.
“Stated” means it is stated because it has come down in that Sutta in such passages as: “One does not understand, as it really is, murderous form as ‘murderous form,’ and so forth.

“Thus” means in this way: when mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatā sati) is stated in this verse, mindfulness directed to feelings, mindfulness directed to the mind, and mindfulness directed to phenomena are also stated, because they share the single characteristic of being foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). We shall explain the meaning of "seen" (*diṭṭha*) and so forth later on.
Regarding the instruction, "Dwell contemplating the body in the body" (*kāye kāyānupassī viharāhi*): here, "body" (*kāya*) refers to the material body (*rūpakāya*).

For here, the material body is intended as "body" in the sense of being a collection of limbs, members, and [hair] of the head, etc. And just as it is in the sense of a collection, so too in the sense of being loathsome...
In the sense of a source (*āya*). For that which is the source (*āya*) of things that are vile and most loathsome is called the "body" (*kāya*);

*āya* means a place of origin. Here is the etymological derivation: they arise (*āyanti*) from there, thus it is a source (*āya*). What arises? Vile things such as hair and so forth; thus, the body is the source of what is vile.
"Contemplating the body" (*kāyānupassī*) means one whose nature is to contemplate the body, or one who is contemplating the body. And having said "in the body," again...
“Contemplating the body” (*kāyānupassī*): the second mention of “body” is for the purpose of showing the defining, the breaking up of the compact, and so forth, in terms of non-confusion.
By this, it is shown that one is not contemplating feelings in the body, nor contemplating mind or mental objects; rather, one is specifically contemplating the body.
Thus, by demonstrating the mode of contemplation of the body upon the basis known as the body, the defining in terms of non-confusion is shown.

Likewise, he does not contemplate a single phenomenon as being distinct from the limbs and members of the body, nor does he contemplate a woman or a man as being distinct from the hair of the head, body hair, and so forth.

Furthermore, even regarding that body which is designated as a collection of primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya*), he does not contemplate a single phenomenon as being distinct from those elements and derived matter;
rather, like one who contemplates the parts of a chariot, he contemplates the collection of limbs and members, or like one who contemplates the components of a city.

Thus, by viewing the body— designated as a "mass"— in various ways through its constituent groups, such as observing it as a collection of hair, body-hair, and so forth, like one who separates the sheaths from the trunk and leaves of a plantain tree, or like one who unbinds an empty fist,
the dismantling of the compact mass is demonstrated. For herein, there is nothing apart from the aforementioned groups.

Neither the body nor any other phenomenon is perceived; rather, beings merely form various false attachments toward what is actually nothing more than a collection of the aforementioned phenomena. Thus said the ancients:
"What one sees is not seen; what is seen, one does not see."
“Not seeing, the deluded one is bound; being bound, he is not released.

By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*), this meaning should be understood as referring to the discernment of the compact mass (*ghana-vinibbhoga*) and so forth. For in this body, one is a contemplator of the body alone, and not a contemplator of other phenomena.
This is what is meant: just as people contemplate water even in a mirage that is devoid of water, it is not so [here].
The meaning is: while this body is actually characterized by impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness, he contemplates it as having the nature of permanence, pleasure, self, and beauty;
rather, as one who contemplates the body (*kāyānupassī*), he contemplates it as a collection of modes consisting of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness.

Alternatively, [it refers to] that body which was described in the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta*—beginning with inhalation and exhalation and ending with the analysis down to the minute particles and the bones—and also that which [is described in the passage]: "Here, someone..."
In the *Paṭisambhidā*, "body" (*kāya*) is defined as: "one contemplates the earth-element as impermanent, the water-element, the fire-element, the air-element, the hair-of-the-head element...
[and so on] ...the marrow element. Since one contemplates all of that within this very body, the meaning here should be understood as "contemplating the body in the body" (*kāye kāyānupassī*).

Alternatively, the meaning should be understood as follows: because one does not perceive anything in the body as "I" or "mine," but rather perceives that collection of various phenomena consisting of head-hairs, body-hairs, and so forth, one is called "contemplating the body" (*kāyānupassī*)—that is, contemplating what is designated as the collection of phenomena such as head-hairs within the body.
Furthermore, it is said: "In this body, one contemplates it as impermanent, not as permanent," and so on.

The meaning of "contemplating the body in the body" (*kāye kāyānupassī*) is: because one contemplates the entire collection of modes—consisting of the characteristic of impermanence and so forth—as they have come down in the method of the *Paṭisambhidā*, that is, the body;
thus it means "one who contemplates the body in the body.

"Dwell" (*viharāhi*) is the imperative form. "Ardent" (*ātāpī*): he is called "ardent" (*ātāpa*) because he burns away (*ātāpeti*) the defilements within the three realms of existence; since he possesses that, he is "ardent."
"Ardent. "Clearly comprehending" means endowed with the knowledge designated as clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). "Mindful" means endowed with mindfulness that encompasses the body.
Now, because one contemplates by means of wisdom after having encompassed the object by means of mindfulness—for there is no contemplation devoid of mindfulness—it was said:
"And mindfulness, monks, I declare to be beneficial in all circumstances."
“I say. Now, for one who is not ardent, internal contraction becomes an obstacle, and the meditation subject does not succeed.
Therefore, in order to show by the power of which qualities that success is achieved, it is said: “ardent,” and so forth.
Therein, “having removed” means having removed either by removal as a factor (*tadaṅgavinaya*) or by suppression (*vikkhambhanavinaya*). “In the world” refers to that very same [world].
Regarding the body: here, the body is intended as the "world" (*loka*) in the sense of breaking up and falling apart.
Furthermore, by the mention of covetousness (*abhijjhā*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is included; and by the mention of ill-will (*domanassa*), ill-will (*byāpāda*) is included.

Thus, by showing the abandoning of these two powerful factors among the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the abandoning of the hindrances is stated, thereby demonstrating the factor of abandoning for the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body. By the phrase beginning with “ardent” (*ātāpī*), etc.,...
In order to show that the factor of association has been demonstrated, the passage beginning with “ātāpī” was stated.
Therein, since the subsiding of covetousness and dejection is the direct opposite [of those states], it is said that the removal of covetousness and dejection indicates the faculty of concentration;
thus he says: “Having removed covetousness and dejection for the world—this is the faculty of concentration. This is because the four [faculties] share a single characteristic.

Regarding "the faculties": just as the foundation of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of the body succeeds through the faculties of energy, wisdom, and concentration, so too do the foundations of mindfulness consisting in the contemplation of feelings, mind, and phenomena succeed by means of them.

Thus, because these faculties lack any difference in their intrinsic nature when it comes to accomplishing the four foundations of mindfulness, they possess identical characteristics; therefore, the other foundations of mindfulness [are also included].
The meaning is that they are indeed already included.
24. Now, in order to show that when the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) are taken up, all the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) are thereby included, it is said:

"In the four foundations of mindfulness," and so forth. Therein, "factors of enlightenment" (bodhaṅgama) means those which go toward enlightenment, that is, the noble path-knowledge (ariyamagga-ñāṇa).
The factors of enlightenment (*bodhaṅgama*). They are called "factors conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiya*) because they exist on the side of the aforementioned enlightenment.
Regarding the phrase "by way of the characteristic of leading out" (*neyyānika-lakkhaṇena*): here, *niyyāna* means emergence from both the sign (*nimitta*) and from occurrence (*pavatta*).

Those who are engaged in this leading out (*niyyāna*) are "those who lead out" (*neyyānikā*), just as one says "gatekeeper" (*dovārika*). Alternatively, they are "those who lead out" because they deserve the fruit known as leading out. Or, they are so called because leading out is their purpose (*payojana*).

Or they are "leading out" (*neyyānika*). There is also the reading “leading out” (*niyyānika*); in that case, the meaning is "those which have leading out (*niyyāna*) as their quality" are "leading out.

There is also the reading “to be led out” (*niyyāniya*); its meaning should be understood as "those which lead out" are "to be led out. "By the characteristic of leading out" means by the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of leading out.
Thus, unwholesome states (*akusala-dhamma*) also—just as wholesome states were determined by virtue of having a single characteristic, so too are the unwholesome.
Phenomena (dhammā) are to be determined by way of their single characteristic. How so? Showing that it is by way of having abandonment as their sole function, he said:
"They go to disappearance. Now, in order to demonstrate that abandonment, he said:

"In the four foundations of mindfulness," and so forth. Therein, while the four foundations of mindfulness—beginning with contemplation of the body—are being cultivated, [the perceptions] such as "beauty in the ugly" and so on...
The four perversions are abandoned, and the four nutriments, beginning with physical food, come to be fully understood by him;
the meaning is that the sensual lust and other defilements which act as obstacles to such full understanding are brought to an end. Why?
Because they share the same characteristic in being things to be abandoned by that [knowledge]. In this way, the meaning should be applied in all instances. Therefore he said: "Thus..."
“Even unwholesome states, because they possess a single characteristic, reach abandonment and disappearance.
Now, in order to show examples of the method of characteristics by another way as well, the passage beginning with “Or where” was spoken.
Therein, “where” (*yattha*) means in which teaching. The word “or” (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative. “Panā” (*pana*) is a particle used for the purpose of completing the meter.
The "material faculty" (*rūpindriya*) refers to the eightfold faculty whose intrinsic nature is to be subject to change (*ruppana*).

"Therein" (*tattha*) means in that teaching. The "material element" (*rūpadhātu*) refers to the ten elements whose intrinsic nature is to be subject to change. The "material base" (*rūpāyatana*) refers to the ten bases whose intrinsic nature is to be subject to change; the meaning is that there are ten material bases.
The intention is that these are taught because they share a single characteristic by virtue of the characteristic of being subject to change. Thus it is taught therein.

The intended meaning is that the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) and the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*) have a single characteristic by virtue of being pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*).
As for the phrase "the noble truth of the origin of suffering," this is stated with reference to unwholesome mental joy;

however, it is also entirely applicable with reference to wholesome [states] associated with taints (*sāsavakusala*). The connection is: "And the entire dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) has been taught. Because of being underlain by ignorance (*avijjānusayitattā*).
Regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. For this has been said: "The underlying tendency to ignorance underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
And likewise it is said: "For ignorance underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
By this mention of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he shows that ignorance is thereby included. And when ignorance is included, everything [is included].
In order to show that dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) has been taught, it was stated: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," and so forth.

In the phrase "And that," the word "and" (ca) has a distributive sense; by it, he illuminates this distinction about to be explained, namely, that this dependent origination is twofold, by way of forward and reverse order.
Among these, dependent origination in forward order is as it has been shown, from the side of defilement (saṃkilesapakkha) characterized by lust, hatred, and delusion.

When it is said that [something] "is to be abandoned" (*hātabbo*), with reference to dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) as stated in the Pāli in the reverse order—beginning with "From the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance alone," etc.—it is said:
"It is to be abandoned by means of the noble qualities of being free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion.

Now, in order to show the method for applying the mode of abandoning according to characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-hāra-yojanā*) by way of elucidating their single characteristic (*ekalakkhaṇatā*), he says: "Thus, those phenomena... and so forth.
It has been stated. Therein, "by way of function" means by way of the functions of supporting, impinging, and so forth, belonging to material and immaterial phenomena such as earth and contact;
or else, by way of the function consisting in the state of being a condition for a phenomenon arisen from that particular condition, belonging to those respective conditioning phenomena.

"By way of characteristic" means by way of their intrinsic natures, such as hardness, touching, and so forth. "By way of commonality" means by way of being subject to transformation, being subject to bending, and so forth, or by way of impermanence and so forth.

[The term "by way of" (*-ādi*) refers to] aggregates (*khandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth. "By way of death and rebirth" (*cutūpapāta*) means by way of the dissolution and arising of conditioned phenomena;
that is to say, by way of simultaneous cessation and simultaneous arising.

Herein, it should be understood that "concomitance," "having a common cause," "having a common fruit," "belonging to a common plane," "having a common object," "having a common focal point," and so forth, are also included by the word "and" (*ca*). The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (Lakkhaṇahāra) is finished.
6. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying the Fourfold Array (Catubyūhahāra) 25.
Therein, what is the Mode of Conveying the Fourfold Array? This is the analysis of the Mode of Conveying the Fourfold Array. Therein, [it begins with] "By means of the phrasing of the Sutta..."
“Etymology, intention, cause, and the connection between what precedes and what follows should be investigated”—this briefly shows the fourfold array (*catubyūha*).

By the phrase “by the phrasing,” he shows that since these modes of conveying meaning (*hāra*) constitute an investigation of the phrasing of the discourse (*sutta*), these word-meanings of the fourfold array must be determined precisely through the medium of the phrasing.
“Etymology” (*nerutta*) means derivation (*nirutta*), that is, grammatical analysis.
Meaning (*attha*). *Nerutta* is simply *nirutti*. For this very reason it was said: "That which is the connection of words in their etymological derivation" (*niruttipadasaṃhitā*).
Its meaning is as follows: that which is *nirutti*, this is *nerutta*. But what is that *nirutti*? It is "the connection of words" (*padasaṃhitā*), meaning connected or joined within words;

the sense is that it is the *nirutti* whose intrinsic nature functions in whatever way a particular meaning is to be expressed through the application of distinctions such as gender, number, tense, grammatical function, and person. Likewise...
For it is said: "The knowledge of phenomena by way of their names.

In this context, *yaṃ* is a particle used in the sense of a reason; the meaning is "by which," that is, by which [knowledge] acting as the cause. *Dhammānaṃ* refers to knowable phenomena (*ñeyyadhammānaṃ*).
*Nāmaso* means that knowledge proceeds by way of specific names such as "earth," "contact," "aggregates," "elements," "three," "tangible," and so forth.
This is what is called "conventional terminology" (*sabhāvanirutti*).

For, having grasped sounds such as "earth" and so forth, the subsequent comprehension of their meaning occurs solely by way of grasping various indefinite designations (*nāmapaññatti*) through the medium of convention (*saṅketa*). Alternatively, "connected with words" (*padasaṃhitā*) means connected by means of words;
for the understanding of the meaning of a word arises from the word itself. And that [understanding] is due to [the word] being the cause for the occurrence of its meaning.

It occurs precisely when the designation (*paññatti*) has been grasped; furthermore, since that designation, conjoined with a word termed "etymology" (*nirutti*), makes known the meaning of the word, it is called "the conjunction of words" (*padasaṃhitā*).
With the passage beginning "When, O monks," he explains the meaning of the phrase "knowledge of phenomena by way of their names."
In this context, "of the meaning" (*atthassa*) refers to the meaning denoted by the word.
"He knows the name" means he knows it as "this is the name" by way of designation (*paññatti*). "Of the phenomenon" (*dhammassa*) refers to a phenomenon possessing intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
"He applies it accordingly" means that whatever meaning or phenomenon is to be expressed in whatever manner, he applies the name—that is, the conventional usage—to it in that very same way.

The meaning is "he teaches. Up to this point, it should be understood that this monk is said to be "skilled in meaning" (*atthakusala*) up to "skilled in many synonyms" (*anekādhivacanakuśala*). In this context, "skilled in meaning" means skilled in the meaning of the *pāḷi*;
"skilled in the Dhamma" means skilled in the *pāḷi* itself; and "skilled in the phrasing" (*byañjanakuśala*)...
"Skilled in syllables and sentences": skilled in etymological derivation (*nirukti*). "Skilled in what precedes and follows": skilled in the sequence of the teaching.
"Skilled in teaching": skilled in the teaching of the Dhamma. "Skilled in the designation of the past": skilled in the conceptualization of the past.
This same method applies to the others as well. Thus all [terms] should be treated accordingly; these are the "etymologies of the local dialects" (*janapada-nirutti*).

The meaning is that as many terms as there are for the conventional expression of beings (*sattavohārapada*), all of them should be provided and explained according to their derivation (*nibbacana*) as they occur in the Suttas.
Furthermore, "all local dialects" (*janapadanirutti*) means that all worldly designations (*lokasamaññā*) should be employed as appropriate;
for it has been said: "One should not overstep common usage. For it is precisely by way of conventional truth (*sammutisacca*) that the realization of ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*) occurs.
26. In the *Adhippāyakaṇḍa*, there is nothing that is not explained. 27.

In the *Nidānakaṇḍa*, "by this instance" (*iminā vatthunā*) means by this cause consisting of the mention of children, cattle, and so forth. Here, it is stated that the cause (*kāraṇa*) is the instance (*vatthu*) and the source (*nidāna*). By this method, the determination of the source should be understood everywhere.

"Blinded by desire" (*kāmandhā*) means blinded by the defilement of craving (*kilesakāma*). "Enveloped by a net" (*jālasañchannā*) means shrouded by the net of craving (*taṇhājāla*). "Covered by the veil of craving" (*taṇhāchadanachāditā*)...
“Shrouded by the darkness called craving. “Bound by bonds” means bound by the bond known as the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
There is also the reading “bound by negligence,” which means “by way of heedlessness. “By what precedes and follows” intends the meaning of “by a preceding or subsequent teaching.
“It is joined” means it enters into conjunction; the sense is that it accords. By these words—
"By obsessions" means by these aforementioned lines of verse which illustrate the obsession of craving (*taṇhā-pariyuṭṭhāna*).
"That very same craving" refers to that same craving mentioned in the preceding verse. By the phrase "And whatever...
and so forth, he clarifies the sequence [of the teaching] through a synthesis of the meaning of both verses. "By application" means by active manifestation. "Therefore" refers to where oneself...
Having arisen, it does not allow that continuum to escape; enticing with various objects, it remains having seized the mind through the defilements (*kilesa*).
Therefore, craving is called a "bond" both by way of the defilements and by way of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).

They are called "proliferations" (*papañca*) because they cause one to proliferate, meaning they cause one to remain long in *saṃsāra*. They are called "stabilities" (*ṭhiti*) because one stands by means of them; in the sense of being a bond.
It is called a "sandāna" because it binds; it is called a "paligha" because it acts like a crossbar, obstructing entry into the city of Nibbāna.

One is "free from craving" (nittaṇha) through the abandonment of craving without remainder. One is a "muni" because of being wise (munana) regarding one's own welfare and the welfare of others, as well as this world and the world beyond.
Thus should the meaning of the words in the verse be understood. As for the meanings of "papañca" and so forth, they have already been analyzed in the Pāḷi.
In this context, for one in whom these conceptual proliferations (*papañca*) and so forth have come to an end, not even a trace of craving (*taṇhā*) remains.
Therefore it is said: “He who has completely transcended all this is called ‘one free from craving’.
(28) “Obsession” (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) refers to the discursive tendencies of craving (*taṇhā-vicarita*) as they are described. “Formations” (*saṅkhārā*)...
“Volitional formations conditioned by that” refers to volitional formations caused by craving, views, and conceit.
Among those, since there are seven impulsion-moments of consciousness, the first volition yields its fruit within this very same personal existence when the necessary conditions are assembled;
the last volition yields its fruit in the immediately following personal existence; and the volitions in between yield their fruit wherever it may be.
It gives its fruit; therefore, in order to show it by classifying it according to the occasion of its ripening, it was said:

“Or [kamma] to be experienced in the present life,” and so forth. Since craving associated with each respective volition is also threefold—according to whether it is to be experienced in the present life and so on—just like the volition itself, it was said:
“Thus craving gives a threefold fruit. This is consistent with what precedes and follows.
That which was previously stated regarding the description of formations as being experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) and so forth,

is consistent with this subsequent description of karma as being experienced in the present life and so forth; the meaning is that they flow together and coincide, just as the waters of the Gaṅgā do with the waters of the Yamunā.

"Formations [are abandoned] by the power of vision": this refers to the formations in the five types of consciousness-arising—namely, the four associated with views and that associated with doubt—which are abandoned by the wisdom-power of the first path.
"The thirty-six modes of craving's wandering [are abandoned] by the power of cultivation":
this is stated with reference to those remaining after what was already abandoned by the first path, and not with reference to all of them.
“Consequence” (*anubandha*) means the occurrence through the continuous succession of craving and so forth.

This also accords with the *Rādhasutta*, which speaks of “one who proliferates” (*papañceti*) and so on, beginning with the phrase “And what is proliferation. For this very reason, he says: “This is one in meaning.
Although they are identical in meaning, he says “Moreover,” etc., to show that there is a distinction in the teaching. “In this way” means by the manner just described.
"By the sutta" means by the sutta that is being commented upon. "Sutta" refers to another sutta.

"Having compared" means having mixed them together and made them non-different in meaning. "Having joined it with what precedes and what follows" means having joined it with a connection in meaning either with a preceding sutta or with a subsequent sutta. By this, he makes the very meaning stated in that sutta clear.
It has been indicated and explained in detail by showing its connection with other suttas.

To show that the "connection between what precedes and what follows" (pubbāparasandhi) is not merely the correlation with other suttas, but that there is another kind as well, the passage beginning with "And this...
was stated. In that context, "connection of meaning" (atthasandhi) refers to the relationship of meaning by way of action, agent, and so forth.

However, since that [connection] occurs only with respect to the six thematic categories beginning with "proclamation" (saṅkhāsanā), because all meanings of words are subsumed within them, and since there is no such thing as a meaning called "connection," it was said:
"The connection of meaning consists of the six categories. "Connection of phrasing" (byañjanasandhi) refers to the connection of one word with another word;
for every word, whether a noun or otherwise, is connected by means of the six types of phrasing-words.
There is nothing that is not included [in this]; therefore it was said: "The connection of the phrasing consists of six steps," and so forth.

"Connection of the teaching" (*desanāsandhi*) means the linking together of the teaching by means of the preceding teaching already mentioned. "And not depending on earth" (*na ca pathaviṃ nissāya*) means making earth—reckoned as an object—a support;
the meaning is "having taken earth as an objective support. "A meditator" (*jhāyī*) means one who meditates by means of the jhāna of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
"He is a meditator. For he meditates by way of attaining absorption having taken Nibbāna—which is free from all conditioned phenomena—as his object;
it is not said that he meditates supported by earth. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

And here, because their existence is bound up with material form through the four great elements, the entire sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*) are included. But immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*) is included by its very nature.
"Seized" means having encompassed the entire world; then, in order to show that by another way as well, he said, "And not this world," and so forth.
For the whole world consists of only two divisions: this world and the other world.
However, since "this world" specifically refers to the continuum of sentient beings existing in the present life, while "the other world" refers to...
The continuum of beings that has passed through the compression of successive existences is distinct from both of those [the mental and material continua], being unbound by the faculties;
it is the continuum of form. Therefore, it was said with reference to that:
"That which is between these two," and so forth. As for those who, taking the expression "between the two," assert the existence of an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), their view is incorrect.
For the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is rejected in the Abhidhamma. "Seen" refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). "Hear" refers to the sense-sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*).
"Sensed" refers to the sense-spheres of odor, taste, and the tangible, because they are to be grasped by reaching them.
"Cognized" refers to the remaining matter included within the objective sphere of mental objects (*dhammārammaṇa*). "Attained" means having sought it out, or not having sought it out.
"Attained": whether it has been reached or not yet reached, it has been sought after. "Thought about and reflected upon":
it has been taken as an object by way of initial application (*vitakka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*). "Mentally pondered": it has been thought over again and again by the mind.

"This one, in this world with its devas... [etc. ...by means of a mind independent, does not know while meditating": this one whose taints are destroyed [does not know] by means of the meditative attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti-jhāna*).

Because he has thoroughly abandoned the dependence on craving and views even before meditating, he indeed meditates with a mind that is independent of anything whatsoever in the world including the devas... and humans. For that very reason, no one in the world knows:
"This person is meditating by depending on this or that. For it has been said:
“Homage to you, O noble among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!
We do not understand what it is that you rely upon as you meditate.
Now, the state of being independent of anything whatsoever in one whose taints are exhausted is explained by means of the *Godhika Sutta* and the *Vakkali Sutta*.

In order to clarify this, it was said, “Just as Māra,” and so forth. “Seeking consciousness” means searching for consciousness beyond final Nibbāna. By the words “Beyond conceptual proliferation,” etc., he states the reason for its invisibility.

“Those whose minds are unattached are not known while they are meditating” means that the course of the mind of one whose taints are destroyed is not known not only in the Nibbāna-element without residue, but [also while living].
Māra and the others do not know; moreover, even regarding the element of Nirvana with a residue remaining (*saupādisesa*), they do not know that [attainment] of his—this is the meaning.
"Connection of the teaching" (*desanāsandhi*) means the mutual correlation of the meanings of discourses (*suttanta*), such as the *Godhika-sutta* and the *Vakkali-sutta*.
"Connection of the exposition" (*niddesasandhi*) means the connection of the exposition (*niddesa*), or the connection by means of the exposition.
The meaning is: "the connection of the latter exposition with that very former exposition, or of the former with the latter.

To demonstrate this, it is said: "Because for the most part the Blessed One first shows the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and afterwards shows the turning away from it (*vivaṭṭa*), therefore [the passage] beginning with 'with minds dependent' was spoken. Therein, "dependent mind" (*nissita-citta*)...
The intention is that these persons whose minds are dependent are to be pointed out by way of a teaching based on persons (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*).

However, by way of a teaching based on phenomena (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*), "those whose minds are dependent" means those whose minds are dependent here; thus, they are those possessing a dependent mind—sutta passages that proceed by way of dependence on craving and views.
Everything else here is already evident.
The commentary on the analysis of the Catubyūha-hāra is finished.
7. Commentary on the Analysis of the Āvaṭṭa-hāra. 29.
Therein, what is the "turning-back" (āvaṭṭa) method? This is the analysis of the Āvaṭṭa-hāra. Therein, "begin! refers to that which is designated as the element of initiative (ārambhadhātu).
"Exert energy. "Strive forth" means: because it has emerged from the side of indolence, exert that further energy known as the root-element of striving (*nikkama-dhātu*).

"Apply yourselves to the Buddha's teaching" means: for those established in these qualities—namely, restraint by virtue, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, and mindfulness and clear comprehension—it is by means of devotion to wakefulness (*jāgariyānuyoga*) [that one should apply oneself].
The elements of exertion and initiative succeed; therefore, apply yourselves with diligence to the Blessed One’s teaching, which consists of such serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).

"Shake off the army of Death as an elephant shakes down a reed-hut"—practicing thus, [you will overcome] that which is called his "army," for it is weak and powerless, since it leads beings under the sway of Māra, the King of Death, who is the Lord of the Three Realms.
Just as a powerful elephant, endowed with strength, destroys a hut made of reeds in an instant, even so, "shake off, scatter, and utterly destroy the multitude of defilements"—this is the meaning.
Now, in order to show the purpose for which this verse was set forth, [the text says]: "Exert yourselves! Strive! and so on.
"...the footing of energy," and so forth, is said. In this context, the words "Exert yourselves! Strive!

constitute the footing of energy and the cause for the application of energy, because they enjoin the undertaking of energy. According to the statement, "From application (yoga), indeed, much is born," yoga is cultivation (bhāvanā).
Since the cultivation of insight (vipassanā) will be explained later, it is the cultivation of concentration (samādhi) that is intended here.
It is said: “‘Exert yourselves in the Buddha’s teaching’ is the proximate cause for concentration.
Since the thorough shaking off of the army of defilements—described as “the army of Death”—occurs through wisdom alone, he says: “Shake off... [etc.

...is the proximate cause. Furthermore, among those factors associated with the aforementioned energy, concentration, and wisdom, it is capable of abandoning conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) by virtue of its sovereign function.

The passage beginning with “‘Exert yourselves! Strive! is the footing for the faculty of energy” was stated in order to show that they cause one to reach the non-occurrence [of suffering] by cutting off the root of the round. These are the footings;
as for the teaching, the footings of energy and so forth were stated in the passage beginning with “These are the footings of energy,” namely, “Exert yourselves! Strive! and so on.
The meaning is that it is the primary teaching, not the factors for the arousal of energy and so forth. It has been commented upon in exactly that way.
Having thus determined the meaning of the teaching as it was set forth by way of its proximate cause (*padatthāna*), he now wishes to apply (*āvaṭṭeti*) it by way of similar and dissimilar phenomena;
and in order to show its plane, he says: "Whether for beings who are not applying themselves to yoga, or for those who are applying themselves..."

He said, beginning with “The undertaking,” etc. Its meaning is as follows: this commencement of the teaching is for the purpose of future discernment, either for those beings who do not apply themselves to yoga—that is, to meditation—or for those whose knowledge is immature, by means of a portion of their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*);

or [it is for] those who do apply themselves and whose knowledge is mature. That negligence is twofold: that negligence by which they do not apply themselves to meditation is [distinguished] by the difference in its own causes.
It is twofold. "By ignorance" means by delusion that conceals both the specific and general characteristics of the five aggregates.
"Enveloped" means covered. "The sphere of the knowable" (ñeyyaṭṭhāna) means that it is both the object to be known and the sphere where knowledge proceeds, such as:
"Such is form, such is the origin of form," and so forth. Because evil states (pāpadhammā) have many divisions...

Accordingly, although negligence (*pamāda*) has many subdivisions, it is said to be "of one kind through ignorance" because it is, by its very nature, identical with its root, which is ignorance (*avijjā*).
Gain, decision-making, acquisition, and stinginess are included within seeking, guarding, and enjoyment.
Since desire, lust, and attachment are themselves craving (*taṇhā*), the factors rooted in craving are also subsumed under this very heading; thus it is said: "craving is of three kinds."
“In the realms of form” (*rūpīsu bhavesu*) means among material phenomena (*rūpadhammesu*). “Clinging” (*ajjhosāna*) is the adherence of craving (*taṇhābhiniveso*).

By this, he explains the meaning of the phrase: “The physical body is the proximate cause for craving. For in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), men and women delight in each other’s forms;

this point should be illustrated by the *Cittapariyādāna Sutta*. “Delusion regarding the formless” (*arūpīsu sammoho*) is due to the extremely subtle nature of contact (*phassa*) and the other factors.
And because it is difficult to effect the analytical resolution of the dense mass of continuity, collection, function, and object, there is delusion regarding immaterial phenomena;

"among beings" is the ellipsis for the word *patiṭṭhito* (established). When the five aggregates of clinging—designated as the material body and the mental body—have been thus determined, craving and ignorance, which operate by taking them as objects, are stated without distinction by way of the four types of clinging.
Having analyzed them, he shows by means of the passage beginning with “Therein, the material body,” etc., that those aggregates and acquisitions are both to be fully understood and to be abandoned,
insofar as they constitute the origin of suffering. Thus, having established the first two Truths by way of negligence, he establishes the other two Truths likewise by way of negligence.
To determine this, the passage beginning with “therein, that which... was stated. Therein, “of that” means of that negligence (*pamāda*).

“Through penetration” means through thorough comprehension, that is, through knowing [the faults] such as gratification (*assāda*) and so forth. “Guarding and withdrawing” refers to the withdrawal of negligence, which consists in guarding one’s own mind;
it is its contraction by means of its opposite, namely, through application to diligence (*appamāda*).
"Whatever is the casting aside"—this shows concentration by way of its function as "tranquility" (*samatha*).

This is the "turning back" (*āvattanā*) by way of factors discordant with the side of purification. By the passage, "When he knows the gratification... [and] the danger... and the escape from sensual pleasures," it shows the means for the attainment of tranquility.

Therein, "sensual pleasures" (*kāmānam*) refers to both material objects of pleasure (*vatthu-kāma*) and defilements of pleasure (*kilesa-kāma*). And "the gratification as gratification" refers to [the gratification] dependent upon sensual pleasures.
The "gratification" (*assāda*) is the pleasure and joy that arises, considered as gratification merely because of its quality of being gratifying.
The "disadvantage" (*ādīnava*) is the fault or danger described in such passages as, "Sensual pleasures have little gratification and much suffering. The "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) is the first jhāna;
for it has been said: "This is the escape from sensual pleasures, namely, renunciation. The term "lowly" (*okāra*) refers to the state of being inferior.
“Defilement” (*saṃkilesa*) means the state of being defiled. For it is because of sensual desire that beings become defiled. “Purification” (*vodāna*) means cleansing.

“The benefit in renunciation” (*nekkhamme ānisaṃsa*) refers to the possession of specific qualities such as the abandoning of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). “In that case” (*tattha*) means when the aforementioned tranquility (*samatha*) is present.
“That which is inquiry” (*yā vīmaṃsā*) refers to wisdom (*paññā*). As it is said: “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is concentrated understands things as they truly are.”
For it has been said: just as ignorance accompanied by craving is the condition for volitional formations, so too craving accompanied by ignorance is the condition for clinging.

When these [two] have ceased, there is simply the non-existence of clinging and the rest; thus, demonstrating the cessation of the entire cycle of existence and suffering through the abandoning of craving and ignorance, he said:
"When these two states have been abandoned," and so forth. These...
The intention is that the four truths have been determined by way of turning toward [them] through both dissimilar and similar phenomena.
Thus, having set forth the side of purification (*vodāna*) and shown the turning toward it by way of both dissimilar and similar phenomena,
he now sets forth the side of defilement (*saṃkilesa*) and, by way of its dissimilar phenomena...
And in order to show the turning [of the mind] by way of the nature of the common lot (*sabhāgadhamma*), he spoke the verse beginning with "Just as at the root. Its meaning is as follows:

Just as, for instance, when the part of a tree rooted in the earth—which is designated by the conventional term "root" because it serves as the cause of its establishment—is free from injury due to the absence of obstacles such as being cut with an axe, and is therefore firm and stable, the *assattha* or other such tree continues to grow even if its trunk is severed; even so...

As long as the root of the tree of individual existence—consisting of the underlying tendency of craving—is not severed by the axe of path-knowledge, this suffering arises again and again in successive states and does not cease. To exclude craving for sensual pleasures and the like, the term "craving for existence" (*bhavataṇhā*) is used.
It is the condition for this phenomenon, namely, that which is designated as craving for existence.
It is a condition for the grasping of gratification by way of concealing the danger in states of existence within the Dhamma. For this has been said:
"Bhikkhus, craving increases in one who contemplates gratification in things that fetter. Therefore it was said:
"With ignorance as condition, there is craving for existence. Herein, serenity and insight are the concentration of the path and the wisdom of the path.
And because it is intended [to show this], he said: "By which one eradicates the underlying tendency to craving," and so forth.
These four truths are determined by way of the turning toward (āvattanā) both dissimilar and similar phenomena. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Now, the turning toward occurs not only by means of the dissimilar and similar phenomena already determined, but also by those found in the actual text (pāḷi).

He spoke the verse beginning with "The non-doing of all evil" in order to demonstrate the turning back by means of those [three] turnings. Therein, "of all evil" (*sabbapāpassa*) means of all that is unwholesome (*akusala*).
"Non-doing" (*akaraṇa*) means non-arising. "Of the wholesome" (*kusalassa*) refers to the wholesomeness of the four planes. "Accomplishment" (*upasampadā*) means acquisition.
"The purification of one’s own mind" (*sacittapariyodāpana*) refers to the cleansing of one's own mind; however, that [purification] is [achieved] through Arhatship.

Thus, having abandoned all evil through the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*), and having accomplished the wholesome by means of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), the mind should be purified by the fruit of arahantship;
this is the teaching, the exhortation, and the instruction of the Buddhas—this is the meaning in brief.
However, the detailed meaning is to be understood from the canonical text (*pāḷi*) itself.
In that context, regarding the phrase "all evil" and so forth: "originating from hatred" (*dosasamuṭṭhāna*) means that hatred is its very origin;
it does not mean that hatred alone is the origin, because malicious speech can also arise originating from greed.

The term "bodily misconduct" (*kāyaduccarita*) is expressed in the neuter gender because it refers back to the word [“evil”]. [The same applies to] "originating from greed" (*lobhasamuṭṭhāna*) and "originating from delusion" (*mohasamuṭṭhāna*).
The same principle applies here as well. With the intention that idle chatter proceeds from a mind of restlessness, its origination from delusion (*moha*) has been stated.
Having thus analyzed "all evil" mentioned here by way of the classification of misconduct, unwholesome courses of action, and kamma:
Now, in order to show the classification of going to a wrong course by way of the unwholesome roots (*akusalamūla*), the passage beginning with “the unwholesome root” is stated.
Therein, “the unwholesome roots go toward the application” means that the unwholesome states such as greed (*lobha*) and so forth go toward the application of body and speech;
the sense is that they originate the application of body and speech. “Through desire” means by reason of desire. That which goes to a wrong course through desire—
"This arises from greed" means that one goes to a wrong course through desire; thus, this going to a wrong course arises from greed.
In the same way, the meaning should be understood for the remaining cases as well.

Having thus shown what evil is in the phrase "the non-doing of all evil," he now shows its non-doing by means of the three roots of wholesome action (*kusalamūla*) in the passage beginning with "greed... [through] wisdom," which [counteract] the three unwholesome roots (*akusalamūla*).
By way of abandoning, he speaks of the non-doing of all evil as its non-arising. Likewise, [he speaks] of greed through equanimity and so forth by means of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).

In that context, it is said—taking into account that sympathetic joy (*muditā*) pacifies aversion and abandons the delusion (*moha*) that is its root—that "delusion reaches abandonment and disappearance through sympathetic joy."

31. Now, having shown evil and its non-performance by another method as well, and in order to show the application of similar and dissimilar phenomena by way of explaining the meaning of the remaining phrases, it was said:
"All evil indeed consists of the eight wrongnesses," and so forth.
By all three terms—non-doing (*akiriyā*), non-performance (*akaraṇa*), and non-transgression (*anajjhācāra*)—only the non-arising of the wrongnesses is intended.
It says "speaks. Likewise, by the three terms *kiriya* (action), *karaṇa* (doing), and *ajjhācāra* (transgression), it speaks only of the act of producing [the unwholesome state].
*Ajjhācāra* means acting after having made a resolve. *Atītassa* means of that which is old, by way of having occurred for a long time.
*Maggassa* means of the Noble Path. For this has been said: "The 'ancient path,' the 'ancient straightway'—this is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path."
“Designation”: this is said with reference to the state of having been taught as it was realized by the Blessed One Vipassī in the past;
for this is the Pātimokkha-chapter verse of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
“By the penetration of which” means by the clear comprehension (*pariññā*) and realization (*abhisamaya*) of which. “That which has been purified is cessation (*nirodha*): even though...
The unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*) is not defiled by any defilement; however, it is spoken of in this way by way of the person who attains it.
For as long as his defilements have not vanished, so long is the unconditioned element said to be "not purified.
This is because, through the attainment of Nibbāna, those aggregates which ought to be stilled remain in a residual state.

And just as [the term] is spoken of both as "with a residue remaining" (*saupādisesa*) and "without a residue remaining" (*anupādisesa*) by way of its being non-absolute, so too should this [present case] be understood.
These Four Truths, which have been determined by way of the application of similar and dissimilar states to the phenomena appearing in the Canon,
are now presented once more to demonstrate the method of application (*āvaṭṭahāra*) through the application of similar and dissimilar states to those very same phenomena appearing in the Canon.
He spoke the verse: “Dhamma indeed protects. The meaning of its words has already been explained previously. Here, "dhamma" refers specifically to the dhamma of merit (puñña-dhamma).
Analyzing that further, he said: “Dhamma is twofold: restraint of the sense faculties and the Path.
It should be understood that by way of the heading "restraint of the sense faculties," all moral discipline (sīla) is included here. All rebirths...
The destinies are called "suffering" because they are associated with the suffering of pain (dukkhadukkhatā) and the other types of suffering, and thus constitute miserable states.

Regarding the two kinds of phenomena mentioned above, in order to show everything concerning how the first type of phenomenon is well-practiced, from what it protects, and where it establishes one, it was said:
"In that regard, the state of practicing the virtue of restraint without breach," and so forth. Now, of that phenomenon...
In order to clarify the absolute nature of protection from the states of misery (apāya), the Asibandhakaputtasutta from the Gāmaṇisaṃyutta is cited.
Therein, "evaṃ" means "in this manner. The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of conjunction; the intention is that by this manner as well, this meaning is to be understood.
"Asibandhakaputto" means the son of one named Asibandhaka. He was a "gāmaṇī" because of his seniority in the village.
"Those of the western lands" means those who dwell in the western lands. "Carrying water-pots" means those who possess their own water-pots.

"Wearing water-moss garlands" means those who, having taken water-moss as well as blue lotuses and other flowers from the water early in the morning, fashion and wear garlands for the purpose of demonstrating their state of purity through water.
"Descending into the water" means those who descend into the water every evening and morning. "They cause to rise up" means they cause [the water] to flow upwards.
"Saññāpentī" means they sustain [him] rightly. "They lead him to heaven" means that while standing around him, saying, "Go, sir, to the Brahma-world!
Go, sir, to the Brahma-world!", they cause him to enter heaven.
"Anuparisakkeyya" means he would go all around. "Ummujja" means emerge. "Uplava" means float upon the water.
"From dry land it flows onto dry land": having ascended the dry land, whatever might be there, whatever should be there—whether gravel or pebbles—that [water] would go downward;
it would go below, it would flow downwards. "Of the path" means of the Noble Path. "Sharpness" means keenness.
And this is not like the sharpening of a blade with a whetstone; rather, it is said to be "excessiveness" (*adhimattatā*) in order to show that it is the keenness of the faculties.
But is it not the case that the Noble Path cuts off the defilements to be abandoned by itself without remainder, so that there is nothing called "extremely sharp"?
True, this is so; nevertheless, it is not so, because of the statement: "as in the case of one who has attained through vision."

It can be said that there is some slight distinction between those liberated by faith (*saddhāvimutta*) and those who have attained vision (*diṭṭhippatta*) regarding the abandonment of defilements (*kilesappahāna*).
However, this distinction is not intended here, because what is intended is the transcendence of all rebirths.
Furthermore, since the defilements are abandoned specifically by means of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), and that abandonment of them occurs within the factors of the Path (*maggadhammesu*):

It arises by way of the faculties being dull, moderately sharp, or very sharp; thus, it is the state of extreme acuity of the supreme path-phenomena which have reached their culmination among phenomena that are like diamonds.
This is what is intended here as the "sharpness" (tikkhatā) of the path. For this very reason it was said:
“This Dhamma, when well-practiced, protects one from all rebirths. And [it is said] by the passage beginning, “Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded,” and so forth.
By means of another sutta, it establishes that even those rebirths designated as "good destinations" (sugati) possess the nature of an "unhappy destination" (duggati).

Now, in order to demonstrate the application of the "turning-back" method (*āvaṭṭahāra*) by way of distinguishing between the factors discordant with the aforementioned Dhamma—namely craving, ignorance, and so forth—and the factors concordant with it—namely serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), and so forth—it says: "In that regard, of the unhappy destinations..."
He said, “The cause is craving and ignorance,” and so forth. Since this follows the method already explained previously, it is indeed easy to understand.
“This is called the holy life (brahmacariya)” means that this noble path, consisting of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), is called the holy life.
“That which protects” refers to cessation (nirodha), which serves as the object for the noble path that protects one from all miserable destinies.
It is said as if he were "guarding," because the state of being the agent is figuratively attributed to the sign.
The intention is that these four truths have been determined by way of turning toward states that are both dissimilar and similar.
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Turning is finished.
8. Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Analysis (Vibhattihāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) 33.

Therein, what is the "mode of conveying analysis"? It is the analysis of the mode of conveying analysis. Therein, analysis is threefold: analysis of phenomena (*dhamma-vibhatti*), analysis of planes (*bhūmi-vibhatti*), and analysis of the basis of words (*padaṭṭhāna-vibhatti*). Among these, since when phenomena have been demonstrated through their divisions, the division of planes obtainable therein [is explained].

Furthermore, the analysis of the proximate causes (*padaṭṭhāna*) is easy to understand when it is being demonstrated; therefore, while demonstrating the classification of the factors (*dhammavibhatti*), [the author] stated, "There are two types of sutta:

that partaking of purification through cultivation (*vāsanābhāgiya*) and that partaking of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*)," in order to show those suttas by means of which the sixteenfold *Paṭṭhāna* is to be specifically analyzed.
In this context, "cultivation" (*vāsanā*) refers to the cultivation of merit (*puññabhāvanā*).

Its "portion" (*bhāga*) or "division" (*koṭṭhāsa*) is the portion of purification (*vāsanā-bhāga*); that which is beneficial for it is "pertaining to the portion of purification" (*vāsanābhāgiya*), [referring to] a discourse (*sutta*).
Penetration (*nibbijjhana*) is the breaking through of the mass of greed and so forth; its "portion" is the remainder, which is exactly like the previous [explanation].

That discourse in which the three bases of meritorious action are taught is a discourse pertaining to the portion of purification. However, in that [discourse] in which those in training (*sekkha*) and those beyond training (*asekkha*)...

That which has been taught is that which pertains to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*). This meaning will also appear in the Pāḷi itself. "Pertaining to merit" (*puññabhāgiya*) means existing in the portion of merit.
Likewise, those pertaining to the fruit (*phalabhāgiya*) should be understood. "Fruit," however, refers to the fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*).
"Restraint-virtue" (*saṃvarasīla*) consists of the restraint of the Pātimokkha, the restraint of mindfulness, the restraint of knowledge, the restraint of patience, and the restraint of energy.
The fivefold restraint is the virtue of restraint (*saṃvara-sīla*). As for "virtue of abandoning" (*pahāna-sīla*), there are five kinds of abandoning:

abandoning by way of its own factor (*tadaṅga-pahāna*), abandoning by suppression (*vikkhambhana-pahāna*), abandoning by eradication (*samuccheda-pahāna*), abandoning by subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-pahāna*), and abandoning by escape (*nissaraṇa-pahāna*).

Among these, virtue of abandoning should be understood by way of the abandonings excluding the abandoning by escape. "He" refers to one who receives the discourses conducive to the removal of latent tendencies (*vāsanā-bhāgiya-sutta*).
"By that holy life": by means of that supreme conduct, termed the virtue of restraint, acting as the cause, one becomes a practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārī*).
And here, there is no negation of the holy life consisting of the eight attainments;
however, some read "by that very holy life," and according to their view, there might be a negation of it.
"Established in the virtue of abandoning" means established in the virtue of abandoning by way of both its eradication (*samuccheda*) and its subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi*).
"By that holy life" (*tena brahmacariyena*) means by that distinguished holy life of the Path (*maggabrahmacariya*), which consists of that virtue of abandoning.

However, for those who read "by that very holy life" (*teneva brahmacariyena*), their reading refers to the discourse on giving (*dānakathā*), which is called a "discourse pertaining to the stage of purification by habituation" (*vāsanābhāgiya-sutta*).
“Discourse on virtue, discourse on heaven, and discourse on the ripening of merit. However, for those who read “by that holy life,” their reading is as follows:
“The discourse known as ‘conducive to perfuming’ consists of discourse on giving, discourse on virtue, discourse on heaven, the danger in sensual pleasures, and the benefit in renunciation.
Of these two readings, which is more appropriate? The latter reading.

One must reach the conclusion. For the Elder will say, "A discourse pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) is that which reveals the Four Truths," and it is not as if the Great Elder taught the Dhamma leaving anything remaining.
By the words "There is no understanding" and so forth, he shows the preeminent reason for the non-confusion of these two discourses. Therein:
"Understanding" refers to the wisdom of insight leading to emergence, which serves as the proximate cause for the Noble Path.

"These four suttas" means that there are four suttas by way of these suttas—namely, those dealing with the partaking of the habitual and the partaking of penetration—which will be discussed here, as well as those dealing with the partaking of defilement and the partaking of the Adept.
"By way of teaching" means by way of the method of teaching. "Having investigated by means of the method of investigation in every respect" means...
Having included [the factors] in all their aspects within the eleven places, and having investigated them by means of the method of investigation;
by the phrase “they should be joined by means of the method of joining,” he shows that the methods of investigation and joining are the preliminary stage for the method of analysis.
By the phrase “as far as the range of knowledge extends,” he shows the vast scope of the method of analysis.
