34. Having thus analyzed the states by way of their being conducive to the habitual (vāsanābhāgiya) and conducive to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), [the text] now begins with the words, "In this regard, which states are common?

in order to analyze them by way of their being shared or unshared through their being conducive to defilement (kilesabhāgiya) and conducive to the state of one beyond training (asekkhabhāgiya). Therein, "which states" means which states possessing intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma). "Common" means...
“Undistinguished” means “identical. “Two states” means two natures;

for this word *dhamma* has the sense of “nature,” as in such expressions as “beings subject to birth” (*jātidhammānaṃ sattānaṃ*). “Common in name” means common by way of name; the meaning is that they share the same name, namely, “wholesome” and “unwholesome.
“Common in basis” means common by way of the physical basis or support, because they both fall within the same continuum (*ekasantatipatitatāya*).

The meaning is "having a common basis" (*samānavatthuka*). Specifically, on the side of defilement, those that are to be abandoned by the same [path] are "common in name," while those to be abandoned simultaneously are "common in basis.
The phrase "and whatever else of this kind" includes other things that are similar in terms of function, condition, opposition, and so forth.
The terms "those fixed in wrongness" and "those not fixed" are a characterization of worldlings (*puthujjana*). Therefore, the eternalists...
The entire classification of worldlings (*puthujjana*), beginning with those who hold the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*), should be cited and discussed.

The ten defilements to be abandoned by vision (*dasanappahātabba-kilesā*) are common to both those fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata*) and those not so fixed (*aniyata*), because they can occur in them, whereas they cannot occur in those fixed in truth (*sammattaniyata*).
The meaning should be understood in this same manner for the remaining terms as well.
"Ariya disciple" refers here to one in training (sekkha).

"All that is common to those not free from lust" means it is shared by way of such synonyms as mundane attainments, the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, the divine abodes, the sublime abodes, and the attainment of the first jhāna.
However, by this same method, wholesome attainment may be uncommon; this—
However, some who perceive a fault read it thus: “Whatever... [etc. ...all that is common to those who are not free from lust.
How is it that these are taken specifically (odhiso), and how should they be taken specifically;
and how are they common? Having considered this inquiry, he spoke in order to clarify it: “For phenomena that are common are thus mutually... and so forth. Its meaning is as follows: just as...
It has been stated that these are common to those fixed in falsehood and those who are unfixed. Thus, these "common" phenomena are not called "common" because they are shared by all sentient beings.
Why? Because each does not overstep its own respective domain in relation to the other.
For their sphere of occurrence is strictly determined; otherwise, such conventional designation would not even exist.
This is the intended meaning. And because these very phenomena have such fixed objects, he said: "Even one who is endowed with these phenomena does not transcend that state.

For it is not the case that those defilements to be abandoned by vision do not exist for those fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyata*) and those undetermined (*aniyata*), nor that they exist for others; the same should be stated for the remaining cases as well.

The so-called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) dhamma is to be sought as that which is individually determined for each person—by way of the *sekha* and *asekha* dhammas among the noble ones (*ariya*), and by way of the total abandonment of all incapacity among the ignoble (*anariya*). This is because such a state of being demonstrable does not exist for others [in the same way].
Furthermore, this is due to the non-deficiency of what is shared; it is according to the teaching spoken in that manner with reference to this or that [person]. Such is the meaning.

This is shown by the passage: "Which phenomena are uncommon? They are to be sought up to the point of the teaching regarding those in training (sekha), those beyond training (asekha), those capable, and those incapable.

"Of the eighth person" means of one who has entered upon the practice for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). "The nature of things" (dhammatā) refers to the intrinsic nature of phenomena:

the state of being on the path for the first [fruit], and the state of being established in the fruit for the second; or alternatively, the state of having defilements currently being abandoned for the first, and [the state of having them already abandoned] for the second.

The state of having abandoned the defilements (*pahīnakilesatā*). Again, "of the eighth" (*aṭṭhamakassa*) refers to one who stands on the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*). "Name" (*nāma*) means the name "trainee" (*sekkha*).

"State of things" (*dhammatā*) means the state of standing on that respective path and the state of standing in the lower fruit. "Of those practicing" (*paṭipannakānaṃ*) refers to those possessing the path (*maggasamaṅgīnaṃ*).
"Name" (*nāma*) means the name "those practicing" (*paṭipannaka*). Thus, by [the phrases] beginning with "of the eighth," the uncommon quality among noble persons (*ariyapuggala*) is [shown].
Having shown this, the passage beginning with "Thus, for one who perceives the distinction" was stated in order to demonstrate the other methods.

For the states of being inferior and so forth exist only among mundane phenomena (*lokiya-dhamma*). In that context, "perceiving the distinction" means perceiving the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) phenomena. Among those destined for falsehood (*micchattaniyata*), the indeterminate phenomena are common, while the phenomena destined for falsehood are uncommon. Even among those destined for falsehood, [the distinction applies] to those with fixed wrong view (*niyatamicchādiṭṭhika*).
The indeterminate states are common; fixed wrong view is uncommon—it should be understood by one who perceives distinctions according to this method.

Having thus shown the analysis of states through various methods, he now says, beginning with "the plane of seeing," in order to show the analysis of planes and the analysis of proximate causes. Therein, "the plane of seeing" refers to the first path.

However, because at the moment of the first path the noble disciple is said to be "entering the certainty of rightness" (sammattaniyāma), and from that point onward has entered it, it is therefore stated: "The plane of seeing is the proximate cause for the entry into certainty.
Although each preceding path is indeed the cause for the attainment of each subsequent path, [the specific defilements such as] personality-belief (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and so forth—
Because it is impossible to abandon sensual lust, ill will, and so forth without first abandoning them.

Nevertheless, it is said that "the plane of development is the proximate cause for the attainment of the higher fruits" in order to show that the Noble Path is both the specific cause and the proximate cause of its own fruit.
When there is a combination of such conditions, the pleasant way of practice with quick direct knowledge leads to the supreme state of knowledge.

And because it exists [therein], that [first path] is said to have insight as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*). However, the other three modes of practice (*paṭipadā*) likewise bring about serenity (*samatha*).
Since all-encompassing malleability (*sabbamudutā*) has been demonstrated in those [three], the remaining qualities are thereby demonstrated as well; thus he says:
"The painful mode of practice with sluggish direct knowledge has serenity as its proximate cause."
“Basis for meritorious action consisting in giving” (*dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu*): giving itself is “consisting in giving. It is “merit” (*puñña*) in the sense of producing a fruit worthy of honor;

it is “action” (*kiriyā*) because it is something to be performed; and it is a “basis” (*vatthu*) because it serves as the foundation for the perfection of the application and so forth—thus it is the “basis for meritorious action consisting in giving.
“From the voice of another” means from hearing the Dhamma. “Common” means not like a seed [is common] to a sprout; rather, it refers to the stage of vision and so forth.

The intention is that [the hearing of another's voice] is not an exclusive cause for such things as the entry into the path of assurance (*niyāma*), but rather a common one, since it can also proceed from other causes besides those.
In this regard, some maintain that the donor’s practice of expressing appreciation for the gift is the cause for the hearing of another's voice;
they say that the donor, desiring the purification of the offering (*dakkhiṇāvisuddhi*), [praises] the specific virtues of the gift, such as generosity and moral discipline.
“Being engaged in the hearing of the Dhamma when the occasion arises” means that giving is stated to be the cause for hearing the Dhamma.

“One endowed with virtue, being concentrated through the absence of remorse, is capable of reflecting on the Dhamma”; thus he said “consisting of virtue,” etc., meaning that virtue is the cause for knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya-ñāṇa*).
“Consisting of cultivation” refers to that which consists of cultivation known as serenity (*samatha*). “In those consisting of cultivation” [means...]
[This is] by means of that consisting in development, namely, higher jhāna and insight. For each preceding [factor] is the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for each subsequent one.

Now, since giving, virtue, and mundane development are not only conditions for the aforementioned "voice of another" and so forth, but are also, respectively, conditions for mastery of the scriptures, great learning, application to the meditation subject, and right view on the path;
Therefore, in order to demonstrate that same method, he further expanded the teaching with the words beginning, "consisting of giving" (*dānamaya*).

Likewise, because dwelling in a suitable locality and so forth are the causes for bodily seclusion, mental seclusion, and so on, he said "dwelling in a suitable locality" and so forth in order to show this method.
In that context, "investigation of the wholesome" (*kusalavīmaṃsā*) means contemplation through reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā*). "Abandoning the unwholesome" (*akusalapariccāga*) means...

By this, the full understanding through abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*) has been stated. "Of the faculty of concentration" means of the path-faculty of concentration (*maggasamādhindriya*). The rest is easy to understand.
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Analysis (*vibhattihāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
9. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Reversal (*parivattana-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā*)
35. In this context, what is the Mode of Conveying Reversal? This is the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Reversal.

In this regard, when a discourse is being expounded, the determination—by way of the state of being abandoned and so forth—of unwholesome and wholesome states that stand as opposites to the wholesome and unwholesome states as they have been specified, is a reversal by way of opposition. Therefore, [it is said]: "For one of right view..."
The passage beginning with “For a person, wrong view has been worn away” is commenced.
Therein, one whose view is right (sammā), praised, and beautiful is a “right-viewed one” (sammādiṭṭhi); [the text refers to] him.

Furthermore, his state of having right view should be understood either as preliminary right view or as supramundane right view. Regarding the phrase “wrong view has been worn away,” according to the former method:

By right view through insight (*vipassanā-sammādiṭṭhi*), they are abandoned; the meaning is that they are suppressed. In the latter method, by the right view of the first path (*paṭhamamagga-sammādiṭṭhi*), they are abandoned;
the meaning is that they are eradicated.

And as for those which have wrong view as their condition (*micchādiṭṭhipaccaya*): these are the lack of desire to see the Noble Ones (*ariya*) and so forth, caused by wrong adherence (*micchābhinivesa*).

Various unwholesome states—such as greed and so forth, and killing and so forth—which are evil in the sense of being blameworthy and unwholesome in the sense of being produced by lack of skill, might arise.

For this noble one who has begun insight meditation, these phenomena—namely, the phenomena of serenity and insight, or the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment—whether previously unarisen, now arise;
or, having arisen, they reach the fulfillment of their development.
They go. The meaning of "right intention" and so forth should also be understood by this same method. However, this is the distinction:

those with right liberation and so on, while being actually unliberated due to wrong liberation, perceive themselves thus: "We are liberated," or they perceive liberation where there is no liberation.
In this context, the etymological meaning is as follows: *micchā* means evil; *vimutti* means liberation or release.

"Of this" refers to wrong liberation (*micchā-vimutti*). The eight factors of wrong liberation proceed by way of wrong adherence in the manner already described, and they are characterized by the two extremes.

Right liberation (*sammā-vimutti*), however, is a fruit-state (*phala-dhamma*); or else, for one who associates with those of wrong view, there is wrong deliverance (*micchā-vimokkha*) or wrong liberation.
Furthermore, the knowledge and vision of wrong liberation pertains to wrong deliverance through wrong view.
And there is the unwholesome arising of consciousness proceeding by way of grasping, as well as the delusion that arises when one has committed an evil deed and reflects, "I have done well.

Regarding the phrase "of the knowledge and vision of right liberation," it is the knowledge of reviewing belonging to those in training (sekkhā) that is intended here. For that leads to the fulfillment of further development.

36. Having thus shown wrong view and the rest by way of right view and the rest, the passage beginning with “Yassā” (Of whomsoever) is commenced in order to show the replacement of killing living beings and the rest by means of abstention from killing living beings, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct, and so forth.

In that context, the term “kālavādī” (one who speaks at the proper time) is a defining characteristic. He [speaks] at the proper time, with a specific reference, within limits, and connected with the goal. This...
It is said: "He is practicing for the abandoning of idle chatter.
Furthermore, with the words "And whatever [others there may be]," etc., he shows by another method the reversal of wrong view and so forth precisely through the gateway of right view and so forth.
In that context, *sandiṭṭhikā* means directly perceptible; *sahadhammikā* means accompanied by reason; *gārayhā* means censurable.

They are worthy of censure. "Discourses and counter-discourses" (*vādānuvādā*) means both discourses and counter-discourses. There is also a reading, "discourses and follow-up discourses" (*vādānupātā*), which means the continuations of discourses.
"Worthy of honor" (*pūjā*) means those who are to be honored.
"Praiseworthy" (*pāsaṃsā*) means those who are to be praised. Again, with the words "And whoever... and so forth, he shows the turning away from the two extremes toward the middle way of practice.
In this context, the four phrases beginning with "to be enjoyed" (*bhuñjitabba*) should be applied by way of sensual objects (*vatthukāma*).

The pair of phrases "to be developed" (*bhāvetabba*) and "to be practiced frequently" (*bahulīkātabba*) are applied by way of sensual defilements (*kilesakāma*). Regarding these, it may be said that what is called "dhamma" is something to be developed;
yet sensual pleasures are desired as things to be developed by them, whereas abstention from sensual pleasures is the opposite of sensual pleasures. Thus...
The intention is that this constitutes a violation of the Dhamma for them.

"The Dhamma that leads to liberation" refers to the Noble Path together with insight (vipassanā). "Suffering" refers to the mortification of the body undertaken with the thought, "We shall wear away our evil.
"Happiness" refers to the happiness of enjoying blameless requisites. In these sections as well, it is according to the method already stated.

It should be stated that this constitutes a lapse into unrighteousness (*adhamma*). Now, in order to show the overturning of the perception of beauty (*subhasaññā*) and so forth by means of the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*) and so forth, the passage beginning with “Or else” (*yathā vā pana*) was spoken.

It is said, “dwelling in the contemplation of foulness in all conditioned phenomena” (*sabbasaṅkhāresu asubhānupassino viharato*), because for one who has commenced insight (*vipassaka*), the formations of the three planes appear as foul due to the trickling out of the impurities of the defilements (*kilesāsuci*).
With the words “Whatever...,” etc., he clarifies the characteristic of the opposite. Therein, “adhyāpanna” means “adhi-āpanna,” in the sense of having approached, accepted, or fully understood.
The commentary on the analysis of the method of reversal is finished.
10. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Synonyms (Vevacanahāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā) 37.
Herein, what is the analysis of the mode of conveying synonyms? It is the analysis of the mode of conveying synonyms.
To show how there is a demonstration of synonyms therein, it is said: "The Blessed One demonstrates a single state by means of various synonyms."
"By synonyms" means by words of various modes; the meaning of the words has already been explained above.
But why does the Blessed One describe a single Dhamma through many modes? It is said: at the time of teaching, it may be that for someone, in some way, there might be an awakening to that meaning;
thus he uses synonymous expressions, because at that moment there may be those whose minds are distracted or preoccupied with other things.

A figurative statement (*pariyāyavacana*) is for the purpose of making that meaning understood through another method. A figurative statement is also used when a word is spoken again with that same term, so that others might attain understanding therein;
it serves to prevent forgetfulness in those of dull intellect as they repeatedly observe that meaning.
Furthermore, since many meanings may share the same phonetic form (*byañjana*), a figurative statement is employed to preclude the conceptualization of any other meaning.
There may be a synonymous term for the purpose of avoiding [confusion with] that [other word];

there may also be a synonymous term for the purpose of making known various meanings through various designations (*saññā*) when expressing what is not otherwise [specifically designated], as in the case of a glossary (*nighaṇṭu*).
There is also a synonymous term for the easy accomplishment of the composition and the elucidation of the meaning of the texts by those who preach the Dhamma.

The Blessed One teaches this figurative expression either for the purpose of manifesting his own attainment of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and of language, or for the purpose of planting the seed therein for those who are to be trained.
What need for much? It is because of having thoroughly penetrated that element of the Dhamma that the Fully Enlightened Ones [know] all things as they truly are.

His range of knowledge is unimpeded; likewise, regarding all verbal expression, he makes even a single meaning understood through numerous methods, without any slowness or hesitation concerning that meaning.
Nor is there any loss in his teaching of the Dhamma; for this is a unique quality of a Buddha.
Thus, demonstrating this method of teaching by way of synonyms, he said, "Hope," and so forth. In that regard, the meaning...
Explaining this, he said: “‘Hope’ (āsā) is said to be that which pertains to a future benefit,” and so forth.
In this context, “a future benefit” refers to a desired object yet to come. By the phrase “It will certainly come,” etc., he shows the mode of its occurrence.
Craving (taṇhā) directed toward a future object is hope; craving directed toward both future and present objects is longing (pihā). This is the distinction between them.

"Preservation of the accomplishment of the goal" means that by which one preserves—that is, awaits—the accomplishment of the desired goal, or by which one preserves—that is, protects—the goal already accomplished. This is called "rejoicing";
the meaning is that it is the cherishing of the goal as it has been obtained. Having analyzed that accomplishment of the goal by way of the seven formations:
In order to show this, he said: "Or a dear relative," and so forth. Therein, "the dhamma" refers to the dhamma as an object, such as visible forms and so on;
one delights in an extremely desirable object. To show that one also delights in undesirable objects, it is said:

"or one delights because of its non-repulsiveness. For even regarding what is repulsive, through the influence of perversion (vipallāsa), one delights in a being or a formation as if it were not repulsive.
In order to show by way of classification those elements among the "many elements" in which craving functions— craving being thus called "desire for many elements"—
the passage beginning with "eye-element" was stated. Although other multiple elements, such as the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth,
appear in the *Dhātuvibhaṅga* and other texts, eighteen alone are shown here in order to demonstrate that they are all included within these very ones.
The passage beginning with “some are intent on form” (*rūpādhimuttā*) and so forth is a demonstration of how craving (*taṇhā*) operates within those elements (*dhātu*). In this regard,
since the five internal elements and the seven consciousness-elements are included within the mental-object element (*dhammadhātu*), which itself is comprised solely of mental objects,
it should be understood that although eighteen elements are enumerated, only six are analyzed as the actual bases for the operation of craving.

Even those discursive explorations of displeasure based on renunciation—which belong to the side of craving—arise for one who establishes a longing for the unsurpassed liberations, according to the statement:
“With longing as condition, there is displeasure. What need is there to mention those discursive explorations of displeasure based on the household life?
These twenty-four terms are thus said to be “on the side of craving. However, those based on the household life...

“Equanimity is a condition for the persistence of one’s adherence through its state of unknowing”; thus it is said: “The six kinds of equanimity based on the household life belong to the side of views.

(38) Now, showing the aspect of craving (*taṇhā*) regarding those mental explorations (*upavicāra*), he says: “That very [equanimity], in the mode of aspiration, is delight in phenomena (*dhammanandī*),” and so forth.

Furthermore, in order to analyze and demonstrate the "conveying of synonyms" (*vevacanahāra*) by determining the synonymous expressions for mind (*citta*), wisdom (*paññā*), the Blessed One (*bhagavā*), the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, virtue (*sīla*), and generosity (*cāga*),
the passage beginning with "mind, intellect, consciousness" (*cittaṃ mano viññāṇaṃ*) is undertaken. Therein,

by the phrase "and other such types," [it is implied that] wisdom (*paññā*), understanding (*pajānanā*), investigation (*vicaya*), thorough investigation (*pavicaya*), investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicaya*), discernment (*sallakkhaṇā*), and close examination (*upalakkhaṇā*) [are also included].
Discernment, wisdom, skill, sagacity, discrimination, reflection, investigation, vast intelligence, understanding, guidance, insight,
clear comprehension, the goad, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom,
the radiance of wisdom, the lamp of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion— and so forth.
The inclusion of synonymous terms should be understood as being by way of wisdom (*paññā*).
"The five faculties are supramundane" means that the five faculties—beginning with "the knowledge of destruction"—are supramundane;
the meaning is that they are synonyms for supramundane wisdom (*lokuttara-paññā*). "All wisdom" refers to all wisdom spoken of by the other synonyms, which is a mixture of mundane and supramundane.
“Meaning. By the phrase beginning with “Moreover,” he shows that synonyms may also be stated by this method.

“In the sense of predominance” means in the sense of predominance regarding the characteristic of resolve (*adhimokkha*). And “as it is stated in the recollection of the Buddha” means as it is stated in the exposition of the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) by way of the text beginning with “Thus indeed is the Blessed One”:
“The Blessed One is thus indeed an Arahant... [and so on] ...thus indeed is the Blessed One,” through many [epithets].
It is said that the Blessed One is to be recollected by means of his synonyms (*vevacana*).

Following this very method, from "one who has attained the accomplishment of the powers" up to "the illuminator of the radiance of the Dhamma"—having brought forward these terms as synonyms for the Buddha, the Blessed One, which are to be recited in the *Buddhānussati*, the connection [of the text] should be understood. These too are merely a few [of the Blessed One’s...]
Synonyms. For the qualities of a Buddha are incalculable, as are the names of the Blessed One derived from those qualities. Indeed, this was said by the General of the Dhamma:
“Incalsculable are the names Of the Great Sage according to his qualities;
Even a thousand names would not suffice To express fully the name based on his qualities.”
In the recollection of the Dhamma (*dhammānussati*), regarding the terms "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) and so forth:

it is unconditioned because it is not conditioned by any cause. It is infinite because there is no end to its destruction. It is taintless (*anāsava*) because it is not an object for the taints (*āsava*).

It is truth because its intrinsic nature is non-perverted. It is the further shore (*pāra*) because it is the state beyond the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). And it is subtle because it is the domain of refined knowledge and because its intrinsic nature is subtle.
It is "subtle" (*nipuṇa*). It is "very difficult to see" (*sududdasa*) because it cannot be seen by those who have not accumulated the equipment of knowledge.

It is "ageless" (*ajajjara*) because it is not struck by arising and decay. It is "steadfast" (*dhuva*) by virtue of its stability. It is "unfading" (*apalokita*) because it does not wither through aging and death.

It is "non-manifest" (*anidassana*) because it cannot be seen by either the fleshly eye or the divine eye. It is "non-proliferated" (*nippapañca*) due to the absence of the proliferation of passion and so forth. [It is free from] the defilements and volitional formations...
It is "peaceful" (santa) because it is the cause of subsiding.

It is "deathless" (amata) because it is the cause of the deathless and because there is no dissolution [of it]. It is "sublime" (paṇīta) in the sense of being supreme and in the sense of being unsurpassed.

It is "auspicious" (siva) due to the absence of the misfortunes of the round of existence consisting of kamma, defilements, and their results. It is "secure" (khema) because it is free from the calamities of the four bonds (yoga).

It is "the destruction of craving" (*taṇhakkhaya*) because craving is exhausted therein. It is "wondrous" (*acchariya*) because it can only be seen at certain times even by those who have performed meritorious deeds.

It is "marvelous" (*abbhuta*) because it has never occurred before. It is "free from calamity" (*anītika*) because there is no obstruction. It is "of a nature free from calamity" (*anītikadhamma*) because it is the cause for the state of being free from calamity.
It is "unborn" (*ajāta*) because its intrinsic nature is non-origination; for that very reason, it is "unbecome" (*abhūta*). By both terms, it is stated that it is devoid of arising.

It is "without calamity" (*anupaddava*) because it is not afflicted by anything. It is "uncreated" (*akata*) because it is not made by any condition. It is "sorrowless" (*asoka*) because there is no sorrow therein.

It is "free from sorrow" (*visoka*) due to the disappearance of the causes of sorrow. It is "without affliction" (*anupasagga*) because it cannot be afflicted by anything. It is "a state free from affliction" (*anupasaggadhamma*) because it is the cause for the state of being free from affliction.
It is "profound" (*gambhīra*) because it is the domain of profound knowledge. It is [incomprehensible] because it is impossible to see or to attain without right practice.
It is "to be seen" (duppassa). It is "supreme" (uttara) because it stands having transcended the entire world. It is "unsurpassed" (anuttara) because there is nothing superior to it.

It is "unequaled" (asama) due to the absence of anything equal to it. It is "matchless" (appaṭisama) due to the absence of any counterpart. It is "foremost" (jeṭṭha) in the sense of being the highest, or it is "foremost" because of its supreme worthiness of praise.
It is a "refuge" (leṇa) because it is to be resorted to by those who are distressed by the suffering of saṃsāra. It is [a protection] because of protecting from that [suffering].

It is a refuge (*tāṇa*). It is "without conflict" (*araṇa*) due to the absence of strife. It is "without blemish" (*anaṅgaṇa*) due to the absence of defilement. It is "unblemished" (*akāca*) because it is free from fault.

It is "stainless" (*vimala*) through the removal of the stains of passion and so forth. It is an "island" (*dīpa*) because it cannot be overwhelmed by the four floods. It is "bliss" (*sukha*) because of the bliss of the subsiding of saṃsāra.
It is "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) because it lacks any quality that could serve as a measure; it is also "immeasurable" because it is impossible to count it. [In] the ocean of saṃsāra...

It is a "foundation" (patiṭṭhā) by virtue of being a place where one does not sink. It should be understood as "possessing nothing" (akiñcana) in the sense of the absence of the "burdens" (kiñcana) such as lust, and the absence of "possessions" (pariggaha).
In the recollection of the Sangha, it is "the essence among beings" because it possesses the essential qualities such as the essence of virtue; thus, it is the essence among beings. Among beings...

"Maṇḍa" means that, like the cream of ghee among dairy products, he is the essence (*maṇḍabhūta*) among sentient beings. Because he is to be extracted from among sentient beings by virtue of his essential quality (*sāraguṇa*), he is the "extraction" (*uddhāra*) of beings.

By virtue of his immovable quality, he is the "stake" (*esikā*) of beings. By virtue of the splendor of his radiant qualities, he is the "fragrant flower" (*kusuma*) for the "beings" who are like cattle; this is the meaning.
Among all qualities, wisdom is the head; because it is the cause of its adornment, virtue is said to be the adornment of that head.
For one who fulfills the precepts, there is no quality that is not desired; thus it is said: "Virtue is a treasure in the sense of transcending all wretchedness.
This meaning is illustrated by the *Ākaṅkheyya Sutta*. Furthermore, it is said: "It succeeds, monks..."
“The mental aspiration of one who is virtuous is pure. “Craft” means the craft of archery. “Wealth” means that which is to be cherished.
“By way of surveying the Dhamma” means by way of surveying the Dhamma such as serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).

“In the sense of surveying” means it is said that, by standing upon virtue, one is able to survey the world with the eye of direct knowledge (abhiññā-cakkhu), just as one might do from a seven-storied palace or similar structure.
And virtue is "concomitant with all planes" because it follows along even with the wholesome states of the four planes. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Synonyms is finished.
11. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Description.
39. Therein, what is the "mode of description" (paññatti-hāra)? This is the analysis of the mode of description. What, then, is this "description"? It is said:
"It is that teaching which consists of a discourse on the essential nature (pakati-kathā). This is what is meant:

that teaching which, unlike the modes of conveyance such as the "mode of gratification" (assāda), does not specifically determine particular meanings such as gratification, but is the teaching of the Blessed One’s own natural discourse on the Dhamma; the manner of describing that [Dhamma] is the mode of description.
However, because that [exposition] deposits the intended meaning within the mental continuum of those to be trained in such and such a way, it is a "deposition" (nikkhepa).

And since this method of conveying (hāra) makes known the portions—namely, suffering and so forth—by means of its various modes, or establishes them without confusion, it is called "the exposition of deposition" (nikkhepa-paññatti).
Thus, in brief, the teaching is an exposition of the fundamental discourse.
In order to analyze in detail the matter already stated, he asks, "And what is the teaching by way of the fundamental discourse? and then says, "The four truths," and so forth.

Therein, the phrase "this is suffering" is a designation (*paññatti*) which, by way of its state of being contemptible and so on, does not differentiate between the material and immaterial phenomena—such as hardness and contact—which are divided into many categories according to the past and so forth, but rather [designates them] through the commonality of their being oppressive, conditioned, burning, and subject to change.

What is the designation (paññatti) that serves as the cause for grasping [things] together? It is the designation corresponding to that (tajjā-paññatti), which is based upon the designation of names (nāma-paññatti).
Others say it is "simply sound accompanied by a modification of intonation" (viññatti-vikāra-sahito saddo). In this manner, the meaning of designation should be understood in various contexts.
By the phrase "of the five aggregates," etc., he shows the basis (upādāna) of that designation. Of the ten...
"Faculties" (indriyānaṃ) refers to ten: the eight material faculties, the mind faculty, and the feeling faculty.
Feeling is made into a single faculty by virtue of its common characteristic of experiencing; likewise, faith and the others are faculties because they are factors of the path.
"That which is made into mouthfuls" (kabaḷīkāro) is this designation according to its physical basis. It is the nutritive essence by which beings subsist.

This is its designation. For it is "nutriment" (*āhāra*) because it brings about the eightfold materiality consisting of nutritive essence. "Exists" (*atthi*) means that it is present because it has not been cut off by the Path.
"Lust" (*rāga*) is so called in the sense of coloring; "delight" (*nandī*) in the sense of rejoicing;
and "craving" (*taṇhā*) in the sense of stretching forth. All these are merely names for greed itself. "Consciousness is established there and grows" refers to kamma.
Having obtained rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), consciousness is both established and grown by virtue of its capacity to draw that link toward itself.
"Wherein" (*yattha*) refers to the plane of the threefold round of existence (*tebhūmaka-vatta*); or alternatively, this locative case applies to every preceding word.

"Therein there is the growth of formations" (*saṅkhārānaṃ vuddhi*) means those formations which, for one situated within this round of kamma-result (*vipāka-vatta*), serve as the cause for future increase.

Referring to this, it was said: “Where there is the production of renewed existence in the future. That is to say, in whatever place there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there is birth, aging, and death in the future.

Where there is the grasping of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), there is birth, characterized by the manifestation of the aggregates; aging, characterized by their maturation; and death, characterized by their dissolution.
And there is death. This is the designation of the manifestation of both suffering and its origin.

Thus, the aforementioned teaching is the designation of the origination of both the truth of suffering and the truth of its origin; the intention is that it is a description of craving as the condition for both the cycle of kamma-results and the formative forces (*saṅkhāra*).
"There is no lust": because it has been utterly eradicated by the development of the supreme path, there is indeed no lust.

"There consciousness does not become established and does not grow": the meaning should be understood according to the method of the opposite of what was stated previously—that is, by the absence of the capacity to project rebirth-linking after having set the karma in motion, consciousness neither becomes established nor grows therein.

By the phrase “This is the designation of full understanding,” and so forth, he shows that right view of the path functions with respect to the four noble truths by means of a single clear comprehension (*ekābhisamaya*).
“This is the designation of development”: this refers to the contemplation of impermanence regarding the phenomena proceeding through the six sense doors via their respective bases and objects;
it is the designation of the development of the path. “The designation of cessation” refers to cessation—that which is reckoned as cessation—of...
The designation of the complete cessation [of craving] by means of the path. "Designation of arising" (*uppādapaññatti*) is the making known of what has arisen.
"Designation of location" (*okāsapaññatti*) is the making known of a place. "Designation of bringing forth" (*āhaṭanāpaññatti*) is the designation of removal.
Regarding "maggots" (*āsāṭikā*): the eggs laid by blue flies on the wounds of cattle are called maggots. Herein, for whomsoever they have arisen, for that person...

Because they are like gadflies (*āsāṭikā*) in being causes of ruin and calamity for a living being, they are called "gadflies"; [the term refers to] the defilements (*kilesa*). "Designation by way of striking down" means designation by way of total eradication.

41. Having thus shown the analysis of designations regarding the truths by way of the round of existence and its cessation, and by way of the aggregates of clinging as objects of comprehension, he now begins with the words, "This, monks, is 'suffering' for me," etc., in order to show them by way of their three turnings.
Therein, it is "eye" (*cakkhu*) in the sense of seeing; "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*) in the sense of knowing according to the true nature of things;
"wisdom" (*paññā*) in the sense of penetration; "clear vision" (*vijjā*) in the sense of making known; and "light" (*āloka*) in the sense of illuminating. All these are synonyms for wisdom.
This is a designation by way of synonyms (*vevacanapaññatti*). "Designation by way of realization" (*sacchikiriyāpaññatti*) is a designation by way of making something directly evident.

Regarding the verse beginning with *tulamatulañca*: because it is evident to ordinary people (*pacurajana*), that which is weighed and delimited is "the weighable" (*tula*), namely, sense-sphere action (*kāmāvacara-kamma*).
That which is not weighed is "the unweighable" (*atula*), namely, exalted action (*mahaggata-kamma*). Alternatively, since there is no other worldly action equal to it, it is "the unweighable.
Or, sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere action is "the weighable," while immaterial-sphere action is "the unweighable."
"Of little fruit" means measurable; "of great fruit" means immeasurable. "Sambhava" (origin) means that by which something arises; it is that which serves as the cause for arising.
"Bhava-saṅkhāra" (volitional formations of existence) means that which constructs renewed existence. "Avassaji" means he relinquished. "Muni" refers to the Buddha-muni.
"Delighting in the internal" means delighting in one's own internal [states]. "Concentrated" means concentrated by way of access concentration and absorption concentration.
"Like armor he broke through": he broke it as one would break armor. "Born of himself": the defilement arisen within himself.

This is what is meant: he cast off that worldly karma known as the "weighing and the weighed," which is called "becoming" in the sense of having a result, and "formations of becoming" in the sense of constructing existence—just as a great warrior at the head of battle casts off his armor.
Having become inwardly delighted and concentrated, he shattered the defilement that arises from the self, as if [shattering] a balance scale.
Alternatively, "weighing" (*tulanti*) means comparing or examining. "The incomparable and the arising" (*atulañ ca sambhavaṃ*) refers to both Nibbāna and the process of arising.
"Formations of existence" (*bhavasaṅkhāraṃ*) refers to the karma leading to existence. "The Sage abandoned it" (*avassaji muni*) means: "The five aggregates are impermanent; their cessation..."

Weighing [the matter] by way of such passages as “Nirvana is permanent,” the Buddha-Muni, seeing the danger in existence (*bhava*) and the benefit in Nirvana, abandoned with the Noble Path—which brings about the destruction of karma—that formative force of existence (*bhava-saṅkhāra*) which is the root of the aggregates. How so?
"Delighting within. For he, delighting within by way of insight (*vipassanā*) and concentrated by way of serenity (*samatha*), like one wearing armor...
He shattered all the host of defilements—which, because they arise within himself and persist by enveloping his personal existence, have received the name "born of self.
In the absence of defilements, karma becomes "rendered useless" due to its lack of a basis for rebirth;
the meaning is that through the absence of defilements, he abandoned karma.
Because there is no object to be directly known that is exempt from the conditioned and unconditioned elements, it is said: "weighing... [and so on]... of phenomena.
By this, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) is expressed; thus he says: "The designation of relinquishment is the analytical knowledge of phenomena.
With reference to the formative forces of existence belonging to the side of origination, he says: "the designation of relinquishing. This is by way of the side of the truth of suffering.

“Full understanding as a designation”: by way of the state of delighting in the internal, which is distinguished by concentration, it is said, “development as a designation for mindfulness directed to the body.
However, it should be understood that by way of concentration, which is distinguished by the state of delighting in the internal, it is said, “stability as a designation for one-pointedness of mind.
“Breaking out as a designation for the mind” refers to the relinquishing of the life-formations (*āyusaṅkhāra*).

It is a designation for the directing of the mind. "Designation of grasping" means a designation for seizing. "For omniscience" means for the state of being a perfectly enlightened Buddha (*sammāsambuddha*).
By this, he shows that there is no relinquishing of the life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*) by one who is not a perfectly enlightened Buddha.
Showing that the Blessed One abandons karma due to the absence of defilements (*kilesa*), he said: "It is a designation for the breaking open of the eggshell of ignorance."

"He who has seen suffering and its source": he who has undertaken insight (vipassanā) has seen all suffering pertaining to the three planes, and he has also seen that source—that which is its cause—as craving, by way of being its causal condition. "How could such a person bow to sensual pleasures?":
such a person practicing in this way—toward both sensual pleasures with a basis and sensual pleasures consisting of defilements—by what...
There is no such way by which one might bend or lean toward them. Why? Because one has understood that sensual pleasures are a snare in the world;
for there is no bond in this world equal to sensual pleasure. And this was said by the Blessed One: "The wise do not call that a strong bond," and so forth.
Therefore, having understood that conditioned phenomena are a snare in the sense that they entangle, one who possesses mindfulness [should remain detached from them].

"He trains for discipline" means that, through the practice of mindfulness directed to the body, being mindful, he should train heedfully in the three trainings for the sake of the subsiding of those sensual desires; this is the meaning.
"Designation by synonyms" refers to the designation by synonyms for the aggregates and so forth. Furthermore, because it is connected with the word "he saw,"...
It is said: "And it is the designation of the full understanding of suffering. It is the designation of seeing as an enemy because it produces what is disadvantageous;

thus, it is the designation of seeing as an enemy. "Like a mass of blazing fire" means similar to a glowing heap of flames. "Compared to a precipice and a serpent" means compared both to a precipice and to a serpent.
"The world is bound by delusion" means that this world is bound by fetters having ignorance as their cause.
"Appearing as if capable" means that even one whose disposition is corrupted, having concealed his true nature through deceit and guile, shows himself as if he were of a capable nature.
"The fool is bound by acquisitions and enveloped by darkness" refers, however, to that fool.

Likewise, because he is enveloped by the darkness of delusion regarding vision, because he fails to see the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, and because he is bound by the formative forces of the defilements;
being such as this, the fool appears like one devoid of splendor to the wise, standing forth as one utterly lacking in fortune.
All of this arises from the "clutter" (kiñcana) of lust and so forth belonging to the fool. But for the wise man, by means of the eye of wisdom—
"When one has seen that 'there is nothing,' this is the summary meaning. Since the perversions (vipallāsā) are included under the heading of delusion (moha), he says:
"The presentation of the teaching regarding the perversions. "Presentation in a perverted manner" means the making known of that which appears in a distorted way.
The statement "Nirvana exists" is merely a verbal basis for certain recluses and brahmins; whereas "Nirvana does not exist" is [the view] from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramattha).
Regarding the phrase "because its nature cannot be obtained," this was spoken by the Blessed One to refute the wrong views of those who have gone astray:
"Bhikkhus, there is, bhikkhus, that which is unborn, unbecome, unmade, and unconditioned. To show the reason for this, he said, "If, bhikkhus, this were not so," and so forth.
Its meaning is as follows: bhikkhus, if the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) did not exist...

In this case, there would be no escape from all that is conditioned. For when the factors of the Path, such as right view and the rest, proceed by taking Nibbāna as their object, they eradicate the defilements without remainder;
consequently, the threefold round of existence ceases to function. Herein, the intended meaning is as follows:
just as [the Path] is the antidote to sensual desires and material forms, which are surpassed because they are to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*),...

Just as escape is perceived as having a nature contrary to that [of conditioned things], so too there must be an escape for conditioned phenomena—which have that same nature—as an escape characterized by a nature contrary to them;
and that which is this escape is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*).
Furthermore, what more is there? Insight-knowledge has conditioned phenomena as its object; moreover, conformity-knowledge [overcomes] the defilements.

It is not possible to abandon [defilements] by way of their total eradication. Even knowledge regarding the first jhāna and so forth that takes conventional truth (sammutisacca) as its object merely effects suppression; it does not effect the eradication of defilements.
Since it is the noble path-knowledge that effects eradication by abandoning, its object must be something other than the conditioned phenomena of conventional truth.

It is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*). Likewise, the word "nibbāna" should be understood as having an unerring meaning in certain contexts, because it exists through figurative usage (*upacāra-vutti*), just as in the case of the term "lion.
Alternatively, the statement, "Bhikkhus, there is that which is unborn, unbecome, unmade, and unconditioned," has an unerring meaning.
Because it was spoken by the Blessed One. For whatever has been spoken by the Blessed One is of unerring meaning, just as in the case of:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are suffering; all phenomena are non-self.

In this same way, through the application of reasoning, the ultimate existence of the unconditioned element should be understood. Or rather, what is the use of such deliberation on reasoning? Because:
By means of numerous scriptural passages, such as: “Monks, there is, monks, that which is unborn, unbecome, unmade, and unconditioned;

there are phenomena that are conditionless and phenomena that are unconditioned; and, monks, I shall teach you the unconditioned phenomenon and the practice leading to the unconditioned,” the Blessed One has taught that the element of Nibbāna exists in the ultimate sense.
In this context, "presentation by way of application" (*upanayana-paññatti*) is the presentation of the application of the reason (*hetūpanaya*) from the perspective of its opposite.
"Presentation by way of illumination" (*jotana-paññatti*) is the presentation that clarifies the establishment of a meaning already asserted. All the rest is easily understood.
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Presentation (*Paññatti-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā*) is finished.
12. Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Entry (Otaraṇahāravibhaṅgavaṇṇanā) 42.
Therein, what is the mode of entry? This is the analysis of the mode of entry.

Therein, "the liberation of one beyond training" refers to the liberation of the fruit, which is the state of being free from passion regarding the three realms for one beyond training. "Those very same [factors]" refers to those [factors] within this liberation of one beyond training.

"Faith and the others. This is the "entry by way of the faculties": it is the entry by means of the descriptive exposition of the faculties—faith and the rest—which have been determined as the liberation of one beyond training (*asekkhā vimutti*).
"The five faculties are clear knowledge (*vijjā*)," because, like right intention, they are supportive of right view; thus, they are included within the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*).
The four faculties beginning with faith are stated here in terms of inclusion because they are supportive of clear knowledge (*vijjā*).

"Included among formations" means they are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) among the five aggregates. The phrase "those formations that are without taints" (*anāsava*) qualifies that aggregate of formations, because the supreme fruit (*aggaphala*) is intended here.
For that very reason, they are not part of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). They are comprised within the element of mental objects (*dhammadhātu*).

[These] are included within the dhamma-element among the eighteen elements. Although the liberation of one beyond training (asekkhā vimutti), characterized by the absence of lust, was shown previously, the path of seeing is stated here as "not contemplating 'this I am'" in order to demonstrate the practice leading to it.
To show this meaning, the passage beginning with "not contemplating 'this I am'" was spoken. All of this follows the method already explained.
43. "Of one who is dependent there is wavering" means that, by way of craving and views, his karma is unstable.

"Passing away and reappearing" refers to repeated death and rebirth. Extracting the act of depending implied in the word "dependent," he says: "Dependence, namely... "Craving-dependence" is the adherence of craving;
for it serves as the foundation for one whose temperament is dominated by craving. Thus...
Thus it was said. In this way, the reliance on views (diṭṭhinissaya) is also to be understood. Regarding "the volition of one who is lustful":

because the phenomena of the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) have volition as their primary factor, he speaks of craving itself under the heading of volition. For this very reason, he says: "This is the reliance on craving.
Furthermore, since a distorted adherence occurs only when delusion (moha) is powerful, it is said: "The volition of one who is deluded is the reliance on views."
Having thus explained craving and views under the heading of volition (*cetanā*), he now says, "Volition, moreover, is formations (*saṅkhārā*)," taking volition itself in its non-figurative sense.
It was stated [previously] with the consideration that lust underlies pleasant feeling, on the grounds that "the feeling of one who is lustful is pleasant feeling.
Likewise, he said that ignorance underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
—“That feeling of one who is deluded is this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Here, by way of the term “feeling,” volition is expressed.

“By craving” means craving. “By view” means view. Or, just as a person is said to be “dependent on craving” because craving serves as the basis for the remaining states, so too, when craving serves as the condition for the remaining states, the person [is said to be dependent on craving].
He said, "not dependent on craving," because one is called "dependent on craving" when one relies upon it.
"Tranquility" (passaddhi) means the subsiding of distress. "Bodily" (kāyikā) means based on the body composed of the four great elements. "Mental" (cetasikā) means based on the mind.
Since that subsiding of distress becomes manifest only when there is pleasure in both body and mind, therefore [he says]: "That which..."

In order to show that the absence of mental bias (*nati*) is the cause of the tranquility (*passaddhi*) described through the metaphorical application of the fruit—as in the passage beginning with "bodily happiness"—the text says, "one whose body is tranquil," and so forth.
"He" refers to one whose mind is thus liberated, an *āsava*-destroyer.

"Liberated in the destruction of form" means liberated in Nibbāna, which is termed the destruction of all forms. "He does not even approach the thought 'it exists'" means he does not fall into the view of eternalism (*sassata*).
"Self and world" is not approached nor grasped by way of craving and views. "It does not exist" means it is non-eternal.
"It both exists and does not exist" means that some things are eternal and some are non-eternal. "Neither exists nor does not exist" is by way of the endless equivocation (*amarāvikkhepa*).
It is "profound" because of the absence of defilements, which are the causes of superficiality. It is "extinguished" (*nibbuto*) in the sense of "it exists," and so forth.
He has attained final Nibbāna through the subsiding of the defilements that lead to rebirth;
he has become cooled. "Coming here" (idhāgati) means coming here from the other world. "Going" (gati) means going from this world to the other world.
Furthermore, he calls that "renewed existence" (peccabhava). Here, the phenomena of the doors and their objects are shown; therefore, it says "between both."
By the word "phenomena" (*dhamma*), he shows the states that have arisen at the door [of consciousness], saying:

"among phenomena arisen through contact. Its meaning is as follows: among those phenomena—consciousness, feeling, perception, volition, applied thought, sustained thought, and so forth—which have arisen together with contact, having contact as their cause;
therein, one does not see a self because those phenomena are themselves non-self in nature. One becomes dispassionate.
By the phrases "through dispassion one is liberated," he demonstrates that supramundane states possess the nature of dependent origination;
and because they have that as their purpose, he states with the words "supramundane" and so forth that even virtue and the other [faculties] are, in a figurative sense, of that same nature.

(44) "Associated with the name" means mixed with the name. "The element of nibbāna with residue remaining" refers to the fruit of arahantship. And since that has wisdom as its primary factor, he says: "The element of nibbāna with residue remaining is true knowledge. All the rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Descent (*otaraṇa-hāra*) is finished.
13. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Purification (*sodhana-hāra*).

45. Therein, what is the Mode of Conveying Purification? This is the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Purification. Therein, the Blessed One purifies the word (*pada*); thus [it is called] the Mode of Conveying Purification.

When the Blessed One says, “The world is enveloped by ignorance,” he is, as it were, clarifying the statement made by the Venerable Ajita in the form of a question—“By what, indeed, is the world enveloped?”—because he provides the answer to that meaning.
However, he does not yet clarify the undertaking (*ārambha*), because the matter intended to be known has not yet reached its conclusion. Thus, the undertaking remains pure.
The meaning is that the undertaking is purified because the matter desired to be known has been awakened.

For those who have leaped into ignorance or are possessed by doubt, when they ask questions, the subject of their inquiry remains as darkness—unmanifest, like a great thicket, like a vast abyss, and like deep gloom.
But when [the matter] is [clarified] by the Blessed One or by wise men for the Blessed One...
When disciples, by showing the path where there was no path, have cleared away the tangle and the thicket and answered the questions,
it becomes "cleansed"— like a dense thicket that has been overcome and trampled down by a great scent-elephant— standing forth radiant, free from darkness, and purified.
The commentary on the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Purification is finished.
14. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Determination:
46. In this context, what is the Mode of Conveying Determination? It is the analysis of the Mode of Conveying Determination. Therein, "it should be maintained in such a way" refers to...

It should be understood merely as the distinction between the universality and particularity designated by unity and diversity; however, the intention is that nothing further should be conceptualized therein.

The reason for this non-conceptualization has already been stated in the commentary on the section of the exposition. It is called the *magga* because it seeks (*magga-ti*) or searches for each respective fruit;
or alternatively, it is called the *magga* because it is sought or searched for by those who desire that fruit. In the sense of being without delight (*nirati-ṭṭhena*)...
And it is called *niraya* (hell) in the sense of being devoid of refreshment (*nirassāda*). Having gone upward and slanting across, they are called *tiracchānā*;

the animal realm is thus the *tiracchānayoni*. By way of being a *peta*, one is a *petti*; the meaning is "one who has departed from here" (*ito pecca gatabhāvo*). The *pettivisaya* is simply the domain of the *petas*.

They do not rejoice (*na suranti*), they do not speak (*na bhāsanti*), and they do not shine (*na dibbanti*); thus they are *asuras*. The *asurayoni* is simply the realm of the *asuras*. [They are so called] because of divine forms and so forth...

They are called *saggā* because they are excellent (*suṭṭhu*) peaks (*agga*). They are called *manussā* because of the abundance of mind (*manas*). "Vāna" is said to mean craving; since that is not present there, it is *nibbāna*.
One who goes to hell is *nirayagāmī*. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

*Asurayoniyo* means beneficial for the womb of asuras, or one who brings about rebirth in the asura class. One who causes one to go to heaven is *saggagāmiyo*. One who goes among humans is *manussagāmī*.
"Leading to the world of humans. "Cessation through deliberation" (*paṭisaṅkhānirodha*) means cessation through the cultivation of the counteragent after having deliberated;
or, it is the non-arising of what ought to arise when the counteragent does not function in that way.
"Cessation without deliberation" (*appaṭisaṅkhānirodha*) means the natural cessation of conditioned phenomena; the meaning is "momentary cessation."
47. “Form” (*rūpa*) is unity. “Derived from the primary elements” (*bhūtānaṃ upādāya*) is diversity. “Derived form” (*upādārūpa*) is unity.

From the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*) … down to … edible food (*kabaḷīkāro āhāro*), there is diversity. Likewise, “primary form” (*bhūtarūpa*) is unity. From the earth element (*pathavīdhātu*) … down to … the air element (*vāyodhātu*), there is diversity.
The earth element is unity; the twenty modes [of its differentiation] are diversity. The water element is unity.
There is diversity in twelve aspects; there is unity in the fire element. There is diversity in four aspects; there is unity in the air element.
There is diversity in six aspects. Showing this meaning, he said: "He grasps the elements by way of two aspects," and so forth.

In that context, "hair" refers to what is called hair: it is part of the eightfold body derived from clinging (upādinnaka), characterized by hardness, and is a distinct [constituent] within this body.
The earth-element portion: "Hair" ... [and so on] ... "brain" means that which is situated within the body, characterized by hardness;
this is a distinct portion in this body—this is the diversity (*vemattatā*).

The same method applies to the portions beginning with the water-element, such as bile and the rest. However, this is the distinction: "by which" means by which fire-element when it is disturbed. "Is heated" means...
This body is tormented; it becomes heated by the state of one-day-old aging and so forth. "By which it ages" means that by this [fever], this body ages;
it reaches a deficiency of the faculties, a loss of strength, and the appearance of wrinkles, gray hair, and so on.
"By which it is consumed" means that when this [fever] is provoked, this body is consumed, and that person cries out, "I am being consumed! I am being consumed!"
Weeping, he longs for anointing with sandalwood paste from the Satadhotasappi and Gosīta trees and the like,

as well as the breeze from a palm-leaf fan. And by means of which food, drink, chewed food, and tasted food there comes about proper digestion— namely, the food such as boiled rice, the drink such as beverages,
the chewed food such as flour-based snacks, or the tasted food such as mangoes, honey, and molasses— properly...
It undergoes maturation; the meaning is that it undergoes differentiation into the state of nutritive essence and so forth.
And herein, the first three fire elements have a fourfold origination, while the last one has only a kamma-originated origination.
"Upward-moving winds" refers to the upward-ascending winds that set in motion vomiting, belching, and so forth. "Downward-moving winds" refers to those that expel feces, urine, and the like.

The downward-moving winds are the winds that move toward the lower parts of the body. The abdominal winds are the external winds within the intestines. The intestinal winds are the internal winds within the intestines.
The limb-pervading winds are the winds that follow the network of vessels and spread through every limb and member of the entire body, producing such functions as contracting and extending the limbs.
Inhalation (*assāsa*) is the wind entering the nostrils from within. Exhalation (*passāsa*) is the wind exiting the nostrils to the outside. Herein—
And all those preceding [elements] arise from four [causes]. Inhalation and exhalation arise only from mind.

Thus, having presented the four elements by way of analysis through the demonstration of their diversity, he says, "By these forty-two aspects," etc., while connecting them to the contemplation of repulsiveness.
Therein, *na gayhūpagaṃ* means not fit for grasping. *Sabhāvabhāvato* means by way of the characteristic of intrinsic nature.

Having thus shown the attention to repulsiveness (*paṭikkūla-manasikāra*), in order to further show the course of comprehension (*sammasana-cāra*) therein by means of the canonical text itself, the Blessed One said, "Therefore he said: 'And whatever... and so forth. All of that is easy to understand.

48. Having thus shown the mode of apprehension (*adhiṭṭhāna-hāra*) by way of the phenomena of the truths and the path, he now said, "Ignorance (*avijjā*) is unity," and so forth, in order to show it by way of ignorance, clear knowledge (*vijjā*), and the rest as well. Therein, regarding the phrases "ignorance concerning suffering" and so on:
Because ignorance does not allow one to know or penetrate the true essential characteristic of the truth of suffering,
but remains concealing and enveloping it, it is therefore called "ignorance regarding suffering. Likewise,
because [it does not allow one to know] the true essential characteristic of the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the practice leading to the cessation of suffering...
It does not allow one to know or penetrate [the truth], but remains concealing and enveloping it; therefore, it is called "ignorance regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
The "past" refers to the aggregates, bases, and elements that have existed in the past. The "future" refers to those that will exist in the future.
The "past and future" refer to both of these together. "Dependent origination" (idappaccayatā) refers to the causes of volitional formations and so forth.
Ignorance and so forth. Conditionally arisen phenomena (*paṭiccasamuppannā dhammā*) are the formations (*saṅkhārā*) and other factors produced by ignorance and the rest.

In this context, ignorance is so called because it does not allow one to know or penetrate the true nature and characteristics of the past aggregates and so forth, up to all conditionally arisen phenomena; rather, it remains covering and enveloping them.
Therefore, it is said: "Ignorance regarding the past, up to ignorance regarding dependently arisen phenomena. Thus, this ignorance is described both by way of its function and by way of its arising.
For it is described by way of its function because it does not allow one to know or penetrate these eight points;
and it is described by way of its arising because when it arises, it arises in relation to these eight points.
It has been explained. Although it has thus been explained by way of function and origin, it is properly explained only when shown by way of its characteristic;
therefore, to demonstrate it by way of its characteristic, the passage beginning with "ignorance" (aññāṇa) was stated.
Therein, knowledge makes known and clarifies what is beneficial and what is harmful, what is a cause and what is not a cause, and the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
Furthermore, because this ignorance, having arisen, does not allow that which is known to become manifest, it is "non-knowledge" (*aññāṇa*) as the opposite of knowledge.
Wisdom is also called "seeing," for it sees that aspect; but ignorance, having arisen, does not allow one to see, thus it is "non-seeing" (*adassana*).
Wisdom is also called "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*), for it clearly realizes that aspect; but ignorance, having arisen—

"Not allowing one to fully comprehend that" is non-comprehension (*anabhisamaya*). Wisdom (*paññā*)—which is also called "awakening" (*anubodha*), "perfect awakening" (*sambodha*), and "penetration" (*paṭivedha*)—comprehends, perfectly awakens to, and penetrates that aspect.
Ignorance (*avijjā*), however, having arisen, does not allow one to comprehend, perfectly awaken to, or penetrate that;
thus it is non-awakening (*ananubodha*), non-perfect awakening (*asambodha*), and non-penetration (*appaṭivedha*). Likewise with discernment (*sallakkhaṇa*).
Wisdom (*paññā*) is also termed "noting" (*upalakkhaṇa*), "re-noting" (*paccupalakkhaṇa*), and "surveying" (*samapekkhaṇa*);
it notes that mode, notes it closely, re-notes it, and surveys it evenly and correctly. Ignorance (*avijjā*), however, having arisen, does not allow one to do so;
thus it is called "non-noting," "non-re-noting," "non-re-re-noting," and "non-surveying."

There is no direct perception (*paccakkhakamma*) for him; and because he has performed an action without himself reflecting upon it, it is called "action without direct perception" (*appaccakkhakamma*).
The state of being dull-witted is *dummejjha*. The state of being a fool is *bālya*. "Clear comprehension" (*sampajañña*) is wisdom (*paññā*);

it clearly comprehends what is beneficial and what is not, what is a cause and what is not, and the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. However, ignorance (*avijjā*), having arisen, [prevents] one from understanding that cause.

"Not giving" is lack of clear comprehension (*asampajañña*). Through the state of deluding, it is *moha*; through the state of infatuating, it is *pamoha*; through the state of completely bewildering, it is *sammoha*.
It finds what should not be found and does not find what should be found; thus it is ignorance (*avijjā*). It causes one to sink into and descend into the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*);

thus it is the flood of ignorance (*avijjogha*). It yokes one to the round of existence; thus it is the yoke of ignorance (*avijjāyoga*). This is because it has not been abandoned and because it arises again and again.
And there is the underlying tendency (*anusaya*) of ignorance. Just as robbers who have ambushed a traveler on the road, so too does ignorance assail and plunder the wholesome mind;

thus it is called the "outburst" (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) of ignorance. Just as when the crossbar known as the city gate-bar has fallen, the entry of people into the city is cut off, even so, for one in whose "city of personality" (*sakkāya-nagara*) this [ignorance] has fallen, the attainment of Nibbāna is blocked.
Because the movement of knowledge is cut off, it is called "the snare of ignorance" (*avijjālaṅgī*). It is both unwholesome and a root, or the root of unwholesome states;
thus it is an "unwholesome root. Furthermore, that is none other than what is intended here as delusion (*moha*);
thus, "delusion is an unwholesome root" is the extraction of the meaning of ignorance by means of a single term. "This is its diversity" means this is the diversity of ignorance.
*Vijjā*: it is called *vijjā* because it is to be found (*vindiya*), because one finds it (*vindati*), because it pierces (*vijjhana*), and because it makes known (*viditakaraṇa*).

In such passages as “knowledge regarding suffering,” knowledge that knows, sees, and penetrates the specific characteristic of the noble truth of suffering exactly as it is, is called “knowledge regarding suffering” when the noble truth of suffering is its object. This same method applies to the remaining [truths]. *Paññā* (wisdom): *Note: The provided text fragment ends with "Paññāti," which appears to be the beginning of a new section on wisdom.*

It is *paññā* (wisdom) in the sense of making known—that is, making manifest—the meaning of each respective object; or it is *paññā* because it knows phenomena (*dhamma*) through various modes such as impermanence and so forth.
It is *pajānanā* (understanding) in the sense of the act of understanding. It is *vicaya* (investigation) because it investigates impermanence and so forth.

It is *pavicaya* (discernment) because it investigates by way of various modes. It is *dhammavicaya* (investigation of phenomena) because it investigates the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths. [Regarding] impermanence and so forth...
*Sal-lakkhaṇā* (observation) is by way of observing them [the aggregates]. *Paccupalakkhaṇā* (re-observation) is by way of observing each of those individually.

*Paṇḍiccaṃ* (wisdom) is the state of being wise (*paṇḍita*). *Kosallaṃ* (skill) is the state of being skillful (*kusala*). *Nepuññaṃ* (subtlety) is the state of being subtle (*nipuṇa*). *Vibhūta* (discernment) is by way of discerning impermanence and so forth.
*Cintā* (reflection) is by way of reflecting upon those very same things. *Upaparikkhā* (investigation) is because one investigates impermanence and so forth.
“Bhūri” is a name for the earth; furthermore, because it is both subtle and extensive, it is like the vast (bhūrī), and thus it is called “bhūri.
Therefore it is said: “Bhūri is called the earth; one who is endowed with wisdom that is as vast as that earth is ‘one of vast wisdom’ (bhūripañño).
Moreover, this is a designation for wisdom itself. It is called “bhūri” because it delights in the true meaning (bhūte atthe ramati).
It is *medhā* because it clarifies (*medhati*) and destroys (*hiṃsati*) defilements; or else, it is *medhā* in the sense of quick grasping and retention.
It is *pariṇāyikā* because it leads the person in whom it arises toward the practice of what is beneficial or toward the penetration of the characteristics of things as they truly are.
It is *vipassanā* because it sees phenomena through the aspects of impermanence and so forth. It is *sampajañña* because it knows impermanence and the rest in their various modes correctly.

It is called the goad (*patoda*) because it prods the mind—which is like a wild horse running off-course—to bring it onto the right path, just as a goad is used to place a horse that has strayed from the track back onto its path.
It is called a faculty (*indriya*) because it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) over the characteristic of seeing;
thus, the faculty known as wisdom is the "wisdom-faculty" (*paññindriya*). It is the power of wisdom (*paññābala*) because it does not waver due to ignorance.

In the sense of cutting off the defilements, wisdom itself is the sword; thus, it is the "sword of wisdom. In the sense of being loftily risen, wisdom itself is the palace; thus, it is the "palace of wisdom.
In the sense of illuminating, wisdom itself is the light; thus, it is the "light of wisdom.
In the sense of radiance, wisdom itself is the effulgence; thus, it is the "effulgence of wisdom. In the sense of shining forth, wisdom itself is the torch; thus, it is the "torch of wisdom."

Wisdom is a jewel in the sense that it provides delight, bestows delight, generates delight, is highly esteemed, its manifestation is rare, it is incomparable, and it is the enjoyment of extraordinary beings;
thus it is the "jewel of wisdom" (*paññāratana*).

It is non-delusion (*amoha*) because beings are not deluded by it, or because it itself is not deluded regarding its object. The term "investigation of phenomena" (*dhammavicaya*) has already been explained.
But why is this stated again? It is for the purpose of showing that non-delusion (*amoha*) is the direct opposite of delusion (*moha*).
By this it is shown: that which is non-delusion is not merely a phenomenon distinct from delusion;

rather, what is intended here is specifically non-delusion, designated as the investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicaya*), which is the opposite of delusion. "Right view" (*sammādiṭṭhi*) is wholesome view that is in accordance with reality and leads to liberation. [It is] designated as the investigation of phenomena...
The enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*) is that which is praised or beautiful.
It is a "path factor" (*maggaṅga*) because it is a factor—that is, a cause—of the noble path (*ariyamagga*). Because it is included within the noble path, it is said to be "comprised in the path.

The "attainment of non-perception" (*asaññāsamāpatti*) is the attainment that brings about rebirth in the sphere of non-perception, having proceeded by way of the cultivation of dispassion toward perception.

For when a Buddha has not yet appeared, some who have gone forth in various sectarian orders perform preliminary work on the air-kasiṇa, and having attained the fourth jhāna, upon emerging from that jhāna they perceive the defect in perception (*saññā*). They see that while perception exists, there is the suffering of hand-cutting and so forth, as well as all fears;
thus they perceive the defect in perception, thinking: "Enough with this perception! The state of non-perception (*asaññā*) is peaceful. In this way, they perceive the defect in perception.

Having seen this, they develop the fourth jhāna by means of the fading away of perception; then, passing away without having fallen away from that jhāna, they are reborn among the non-percipient beings.
Their consciousness ceases here precisely with the cessation of the death-consciousness, and only the aggregate of material form (rūpakkhandha) is produced there.
Just as an arrow shot by the force of a bowstring travels through the air for as long as the momentum of that string lasts, so too do they remain there.
In exactly this way, those who have been cast up by the force of jhāna remain for as long a time as that force of jhāna lasts after they have been reborn there.
But when the force of jhāna is exhausted, the aggregate of form disappears there, and the perception of rebirth-linking arises here;
it is with reference to this that it is said: "the attainment that produces rebirth in the non-percipient realm. It is called the "attainment in which perception has become non-existent."

The attainment of the base of infinite consciousness. For this is called "the fading away of perception" because it involves the elimination of both the first immaterial-sphere consciousness and the perception of the first immaterial sphere.
Some read "fading away of perception of form" (*vibhūtarūpasaññā*);
according to their opinion, the "attainment of the fading away of form" refers to the remaining immaterial attainments. The other attainments are indeed easy to understand.
The meditator who is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training is an ordinary person (puthujjana) who has attained meditative absorption (jhāna).
The noble-bred meditator is an arahant, or alternatively, all noble persons (ariya-puggala). The "wild-horse" meditator is one whose meditation is like that of a wild horse;
