for just as a wild horse does not submit to training but runs hither and thither according to its own whim, even so is the ordinary person who possesses supernormal powers (abhiññā).
Having relished direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), thinking, "Enough with this much; enough has been done," he does not strive for further higher states.
Driven by the mind of direct knowledge, he runs and wanders hither and thither; such a one is called "a meditator who is like a horse.

"A meditator overcome by views" refers to one who possesses meditative absorption (*jhāna*) but is caught in a wrong view. "A meditator overcome by wisdom" refers to one who, through the contemplation of characteristics (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*)...
The meditator: either everyone who is preeminent in wisdom is a meditator;
or "with conflict" (*saraṇo*) concentration refers to unwholesome one-pointedness of mind, or all contaminated (*sāsava*) concentration.

"Without conflict" (*araṇo*) concentration refers to all wholesome or indeterminate concentration, or specifically supramundane (*lokuttara*) concentration. "With enmity" (*savero*) concentration refers to one-pointedness within states of consciousness accompanied by aversion.

"Materialistic concentration" (*sāmiso samādhi*) is the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (*mettā-cetovimutti*). The same method applies to the following pair as well. "Worldly concentration" (*lokisa-samādhi*) is materialistic;

for it is materialistic because it has not transcended the bait of the round of existence (*vaṭṭāmiṣa*) and the bait of the world (*lokāmiṣa*). "Unmaterialistic concentration" (*nirāmisa-samādhi*) is supramundane concentration.

"Concentration with exertion" (*sasaṅkhāra-samādhi*) refers to that which is difficult of progress and sluggish in direct knowledge, as well as that which is easy of progress but sluggish in direct knowledge. This...
For [this] must be attained with difficulty and exertion by means of a mind that involves volitional effort (*saṅkhāra*) and application (*prayoga*), having suppressed opposing states;
the other is concentration without volitional effort (*asaṅkhāra-samādhi*). "Concentration developed in one way" refers to the concentration of one who practices dry-insight (*sukkha-vipassaka*).
"Concentration developed in both ways" refers to the concentration of one whose vehicle is serenity (*samatha-yānika*). This is the cultivation developed in both ways.

"Concentration" refers to the concentration of one who is a body-witness (*kāyasakkhin*) and of one who is liberated both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*); for he has cultivated the development of both parts.
"The practice that is sunken" means a practice of descending into sensual pleasures; the meaning is the pursuit of sensual happiness.
"The practice that is austere" means a practice occurring by way of the burning up of sensuality and by way of weariness; the meaning is the pursuit of self-mortification.

Regarding the phrases "the practice that is not patient" (*akkhamā paṭipadā*) and so forth: for one who cannot endure cold and other such hardships at the time of exerting effort, it is the "practice" (*paṭipadā*);

because he does not tolerate them, it is "not patient" (*akkhamā*). For one who endures them, however, because he tolerates them, it is "patient" (*khamā*). According to the method beginning with "he does not consent to a thought of sensual desire that has arisen," it is "harmonious" (*samā*) because it harmonizes with wrong thoughts.
It is the "practice of self-control" (*damā paṭipadā*) because it tames the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth.
"Thus" means by the method stated here. "Whatever phenomenon" refers to any phenomenon such as birth and so forth.

"Of whatever phenomenon" refers to another phenomenon, such as aging and so forth, distinct from that [first one]. "The state of being the same" is the state of being identical by way of having the nature of suffering and so forth.

"By way of oneness" means by way of identity, through the unification of the states of suffering and so forth. "It becomes one" means that although it is manifold, it is expressed by the single term "suffering" and so forth.
It becomes one. By this, he states the characteristic of oneness (*ekattatā*). Or, as for "by whatever it is dissimilar" (*vilakkhaṇo*):

whichever phenomenon (*dhamma*) is dissimilar to another phenomenon by whichever state (*bhāva*), by that very state, that phenomenon undergoes differentiation (*vematta*) from that phenomenon—that is, it reaches a state of difference or dissimilarity—by way of the state of suffering (*dukkhabhāvena*).
The meaning is that even though birth and the rest are common [to all], they attain a state of distinction from aging and the rest by way of their specific modes of manifestation and so forth.
By this, he states the characteristic of diversity (*vemattatā*).
Now, in order to demonstrate this by applying it to the domain of unity and diversity, he says: “In the Sutta or in the Exposition (*Veyyākaraṇa*),” and so on.
It has been stated. Therein, "asked" means it was stated by way of a question and by way of a discourse taught in response to that question;
it does not mean that the mode of conveying through determination (adhiṭṭhāna-hāra) is itself the object of a question. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the analysis of the mode of conveying through determination is finished.
15. Explanation of the Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Requisites (Parikkhāra-hāra-vibhaṅga-vaṇṇanā) 49.
In this context, what is the analysis of the mode of conveying requisites?
Herein, having stated the brief definition of a requisite as follows—"That which produces a given state is the requisite for that state"—[the text proceeds] with that...

To show [the distinction] by way of analysis, the passage beginning with “What is its characteristic? was stated. Therein, it is called a *hetu* (cause) because it goes toward (*hinoti*) its own fruit, that is, it becomes the state of being its producer.
It is called a *paccaya* (condition) because the fruit goes toward (*eti*) it by depending upon it (*paṭicca*).

Although the terms *hetu* and *paccaya* both denote a cause, nevertheless, in order to show the specific difference between them through analysis, the passage beginning with “having an uncommon characteristic” was stated.
It has been stated: "Sabhāva" (own-nature) means "hetu" (cause); that is, a common nature, a seed, is the cause. But is it not the case that a seed is not similar to a sprout and so forth?
It is not that it is not similar; for otherwise, such [a result] would not arise from anything else.
By the passage beginning with "Or rather," he clarifies the very distinction between the cause and the condition by showing another illustration.

In this context, "milk" refers to *duddha*. The statement "it becomes curd" is expressed either by way of the principle of identity (*ekattanaya*) or through metaphorical non-distinction (*abhedopacāra*), but not otherwise;
for milk does not literally become curd. Therefore it was said: "There is no simultaneous coexistence of the milk and the curd.
Alternatively, when milk placed in a vessel becomes curd, that curd exists there after some time.

It arises through the conjunction of other conditions; therefore, there is no simultaneous coexistence of milk and curd, because their natures are distinct in terms of taste, maturation, and so forth.

"In the same way" means that just as there is no simultaneous coexistence of the cause, which is the milk, with the result, which is the curd, likewise there is no simultaneous coexistence of any other cause with its result.

It is not so for the condition, for a condition is not necessarily at a different time from its fruit. This is the intended meaning: thus should the distinction between causes and conditions be understood.
Having thus shown the classification of external causes and conditions, he now shows the internal one with the words, "For this saṃsāra... and so forth.
It has been stated. In that context, when it is said, "Ignorance is the cause of ignorance," one might ask:
"Are there multiple instances of ignorance within a single arising of consciousness? He replies: "Prior ignorance is the cause of subsequent ignorance.
By this, he establishes the very point that there is no simultaneous coexistence of cause and fruit at one and the same time. In that regard, by the phrase "prior ignorance," and so forth...
It shows the distinction between ignorance as cause and ignorance as fruit. By the words "like a seed and a sprout," etc., it shows this meaning:
just as a seed, being the cause of a sprout, is a cause by way of being its immediate cause;
and that seed which produces a fruit from itself is a cause of that fruit by way of being its remote cause—so too it is with ignorance.
"It should be seen as being in the state of a cause.
Furthermore, with the words "Or rather," and so forth, he demonstrates the analysis of the causal condition itself. Therein, "thālaka" means a lamp-stand;
"anaggi" means without fire; "dīpetuṃ" means to kindle. Thus, intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) is the cause, as in the case of the kindling of a lamp and so on.
The cause that is like a lamp consisting of fire and so forth is the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), which is the root-cause (*hetu*). The extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*) is the condition (*paccaya*);
in this context, the condition is an intrinsic nature other than the fire itself, such as the pan, the oil, and the wick. "Internal" (*ajjhattika*) means belonging to one's own internal state;

it exists within one's own interior. "External" (*bāhira*) means existing outside of that. "Productive" (*janaka*) means that which brings about origination. "Supporting" (*pariggāhaka*) means that which provides stability. "Unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) means unique or specific.
“Common” (*sādhāraṇo*) means shared with others who have arisen through conditions.
Now, since the cause has been called “requisite” (*parikkhāro*), and the state of being a cause exists in relation to its fruit, therefore [the following should be explained]:
what the causal state of the cause is, how that state comes to be, what the fruit is, what its distinction is, and [the relationship] between the cause and the fruit.
In order to clarify all that [pertaining to] connection (*sambandha*), it was stated: "the meaning of non-interruption" (*avupacchedattha*), and so forth.

Therein, continuity (*santati*) is the state of being connected by way of the relation between cause and fruit. What, then, is the connection there, and what is the relation between cause and fruit? That very thing is the meaning of non-interruption.

That which, having become a fruit, ceases without becoming the cause for another, is said to be "interrupted" (*vupacchinna*); for example: [The text continues with examples of interrupted and uninterrupted continuity.]

That is the death-consciousness of an Arahant. However, that which ceases having served as the cause for its own corresponding fruit is said to be "uninterrupted," because the connection between cause and fruit exists;
thus it is said: "The meaning of continuity is the meaning of non-interruption.
And since what is called a "fruit" is produced from a cause and not unproduced, therefore: "The meaning of production is the meaning of fruit."

It has been said. However, because the aggregates of rebirth that arise by way of linking to the immediately succeeding existence from a previous existence constitute "renewed existence" (*punabbhava*), it was therefore stated: "The meaning of rebirth-linking is the meaning of renewed existence.
Likewise, when defilements arise in a person, they act as a fetter, binding them and not allowing them to practice correctly, until [they are abandoned] by the Path.

As long as they have not been eradicated, they are said to "underlie"; hence it is said: "The meaning of 'obstruction' is the meaning of 'obsession,' and the meaning of 'not being eradicated' is the meaning of 'underlying tendency.
Because, through the realization of full understanding (*pariññābhisamaya*), once [name-and-form] has been fully understood, it will never again be a cause for the sprout of name-and-form, he said:
"The meaning of 'not being fully understood' is the meaning of 'the seed of consciousness. Where there is no cutting off...

In this context, "continuity" (*santati*) refers to the aforementioned non-interruption within the occurrence of the material and immaterial realms; it is there that the conventional term "continuity" is applied.

The statement, "Where there is continuity, there is production," and so forth, is simply a demonstration of the succession of conditions and an elucidation of the relationship between cause and fruit.
Furthermore, by means of the passage beginning with "Or rather, depending on the eye," the very same point already stated—that "intrinsic nature is the cause"—is explained through detailed analysis.

It shows this. Therein, "by way of being a support" means by way of being a decisive support condition (*upanissaya-paccaya*). "Attention" (*manasikāra*) refers to the functional mind-element (*kiriya-manodhātu*).
For that is the cause as a similar state (*sabhāva-hetu*) because it shares the same nature as consciousness in its capacity as consciousness, just as eye-consciousness does.

"Formations are the condition for consciousness, the cause as a similar state" means that meritorious and other types of volitional formations (*puññādi-abhisaṅkhāra*) are the conditions for rebirth-linking consciousness; therein, that which...
Its intrinsic nature is the cause. Here, by "formations" (*saṅkhārā*), all mundane wholesome and unwholesome mental arisings are intended.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood for the remaining terms as well. Thus, whatever is a decisive support (*upanissaya*), all that is an "equipment" (*parikkhāra*);
that is, any condition of the aforementioned classification, because it equips and constructs its own fruit.
The requisite. The exposition of that [requisite] by way of its determination is the "Requisite Mode" (parikkhāra-hāra).
The commentary on the analysis of the Requisite Mode is finished.
16. Commentary on the Analysis of the Mode of Coordination (samāropana-hāra).
50. Therein, what is the method of coordination (*samāropana-hāra*)? This is the analysis of the method of coordination.
Therein, "in one footing" (*ekasmiṃ padaṭṭhāne*) means when any single factor (*dhamma*) serving as a cause has been grasped by way of the Sutta.
"As many footings as descend" (*yattakāni padaṭṭhānāni otaranti*) means as many other factors serving as causes as converge upon that [first] factor. All of those—

"Should be applied" (*samāropayitabbāni*) means that all those bases (*padaṭṭhāna*)—the phenomena (*dhamma*) that serve as bases—should be brought forward by way of correct selection and applied to the teaching;
the sense is that they should be explained as if they had already been included in the teaching.
This is just as it is said in the *Āvaṭṭa-hāra*: "When there is one basis, one seeks the remaining bases," which refers to the case of many bases.
Just as "investigation" was explained [in the previous section], so too here one must apply the coordination of many bases;

showing this, he said, "As in the Mode of Conveying a Conversion. To show that coordination is not to be made merely by way of the bases, but rather also by way of synonyms, development, and abandoning, he said, "In that regard, coordination is fourfold," and so forth.
But why are synonyms for the "footing" (padaṭṭhāna) included here? Is it not the case that this meaning has already been clarified in the Mode of Conveying Synonyms for the Footing?

True, that is so; however, the inclusion of synonyms for the footing here is for the purpose of showing the objective basis for the establishing of development and abandoning, and for the purpose of showing the distinction between their designations.
For in this way, development and abandoning become easy to understand.

And they are easy to explain. "This is the proximate cause" means that these three kinds of good conduct (*sucarita*) are the proximate cause because they serve as the objective basis and foundation for the instruction of the Buddhas' dispensation.

Therein, by means of the three types of good conduct beginning with "bodily," he demonstrates the three aggregates starting with virtue (*sīla*), as well as serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), and the third and fourth fruits of the path.
That is indeed easy to understand. It is called *vana* because one is enticed (*vanīyati*), or because one desires (*vanati*) or seeks after (*vanute*).

In this context, since the five strands of sensual pleasure are the cause for sensual craving; the grasping of signs is the cause for the grasping of secondary characteristics; the internal and external sense bases are the cause for the desire and lust that bind one to them;
and the underlying tendencies are the cause for the obsessions—therefore, regarding that matter:
In order to show this, it was said: "The five strands of sensual pleasure," and so forth.

51. This is "synthesis by means of synonyms": namely, that which is the description of the third fruit by means of these synonymous terms—"the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust," "the fruit of training," "the fruit of non-returning," and "the surmounting of the sense-sphere. Likewise, that which...

The description of the fourth fruit by means of these synonymous expressions— “liberation through wisdom due to the fading away of ignorance,” “the fruit of the one beyond training,” “the supreme fruit,” “arahantship,” and “the transcendence of the three realms”—
and the description of wisdom by means of synonymous expressions such as “the faculty of wisdom,” constitute the coordination by means of synonyms.
"Therefore, bhikkhu, dwell contemplating the body in the body," and so forth;

this should be understood according to the method explained in the commentary on the analysis of the "Stringing Together of Characteristics" (Lakkhaṇahāra-vibhaṅga). The only difference is that in that [text], because they share a single characteristic, it was presented merely by way of showing that even those not explicitly mentioned there are included as having been stated;
here, however, it is presented by way of applying them to the development of meditation (bhāvanā). Contemplation of the body is specifically contemplation of the foul (asubhānupassanā).

Thus, the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*) is the absolute antidote to sensual lust and the defilements associated with it; it is the antidote to those defilements that obstruct the full understanding of physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), namely:

clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), the yoke of sense-pleasures (*kāmayoga*), the bodily tie of covetousness (*abhijjhākāyagantha*), the taint of sense-pleasures (*kāmāsava*), the flood of sense-pleasures (*kāmogha*), and the dart of lust (*rāgasalla*).

It is also the antidote to those defilements that obstruct the full understanding of form-phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), namely: lust for form-phenomena (*rūpadhammesu rāgo*) and falling under the sway of desire (*chandāgatigamana*). These are what it counteracts.
By the passage beginning with “dwelling contemplating the body as a body,” he shows this meaning: that it leads to the abandoning of evil states.
Likewise, the contemplation of feelings is specifically the contemplation of suffering. Regarding that, [it is said]:
“He who saw pleasure as suffering, And saw suffering as a dart;”

"Because of the initial statement: 'He saw that which is peaceful—the neither-painful-nor-pleasant—[as] impermanent,' one who perceives all feeling as suffering [sees] that through the full understanding of the cause of feeling by means of the perception of suffering, there is purification from existence (*bhava*) via [the abandonment of] the defilements that obstruct it, such as [wrong] conduct regarding cattle and so forth;
thus, for one proceeding with craving for feeling, there is the grasping at existence (*bhavupādāna*)."

Through the influence of feeling (*vedanā*), there is the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*); the bodily tie of ill-will (*byāpādakāyagantha*) which proceeds in the manner of thinking "He has done me harm," and so forth;
the dart of hatred (*dosasalla*) which proceeds precisely through the relishing of feeling;

the lust for existence (*bhavarāga*)—comprising the yoke of existence, the state of existence, and the flood of existence—which is the object of feeling and acts as an obstacle to the full understanding of existence (*bhavapariññā*); and the departure toward the realm of hatred.
By the phrase "contemplating feelings in feelings" and so forth, he shows this meaning: that it leads to the abandoning [of the taints].
Likewise, the contemplation of mind is specifically the contemplation of impermanence;

seeing the mind as "impermanent," therein, since beings for the most part perceive permanence, it serves to eliminate the defilements that act as obstacles to the full understanding of the nutriment of consciousness through the perception of permanence.
Precisely because it is the antidote to the adherence to permanence, the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*) is [the counteragent] to the view—

comprised of the yoke of views, the misapprehension of rules and observances, the bodily tie, the taint of views, and the flood of views— to the sign of the perception of permanence, to the mental stiffness proceeding in the manner of "I am superior" and so forth,
to the perception that is the counteragent to the full understanding of perceptions, and to the passion for views that arises because the adherence to views has not been abandoned.
By the passage beginning with "contemplating the mind in the mind," he shows this meaning: that it leads to the abandoning of going to states of fear.
Likewise, the contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) is specifically the perception of non-self (anattasaññā).

It is the antidote to the perception of self regarding formations (saṅkhāra), to the nutriment of mental volition (manosañcetanāhāra), to the underlying tendencies (āsava), to the defilements that are its opposites, to the view of a personal entity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), and to the false adherence that occurs as "this alone is the truth."

By the passage beginning with “dwelling contemplating phenomena among phenomena,” he shows this meaning: that it leads to the abandoning of the defilements that obstruct the full understanding of volitional formations—namely, ignorance characterized by wrong adherence, the bond of ignorance, the taint of ignorance, the flood of ignorance, and the dart of delusion—as well as the abandonment of lust for volitional formations and the falling into the ways of delusion. The rest is self-evident.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Modes of Conveying (Hāravibhaṅga) by way of Coordination is finished.
The commentary on the Analysis of the Modes of Conveying is also finished.
1. Commentary on the Modes of Conveying by Way of Teaching (Desanāhāra).
Thus, as if scattering flowers of various colors upon ground well-prepared;
as if setting various jewel-gems, radiant with networks of diverse rays, into highly polished golden ornaments designed by a master craftsman of refined skill;
as if turning over the great earth and making it eat the essence of *pappaṭaka* mushrooms; and as if pressing a yojana-wide ball of honey—

As if causing [the listener] to drink a most sweet elixir, the Venerable Mahākaccāna, citing various passages from the Suttas and having analyzed the sixteen modes of interpretation (hāra), now began the section on the convergence of the modes (hārasampātavāra), demonstrating how they are all applied within a single Sutta. And as he began it, [he said]:
"In this section on Exposition (niddesavāra)..."
“First, the sixteen modes of conveying (hāra); having surveyed the directions from the perspective of the ‘eye of the directions’;
then, having condensed them by means of the ‘hook,’ one should point out the sutta by means of the three methods (naya).
Thus the verse was spoken. For that section on the analysis of the modes of conveying does not apply here, because the investigation of the methods concerns a scattered subject matter.

And because they are separated [by other sections]. Indeed, the section on the Analysis of the Modes (Hāravibhaṅgavāra) consists solely in showing the classification of the modes through numerous scriptural passages.

However, the section on the Convergence of Modes (Hārasampātavāra) applies them, for it is immediately after having applied sixteen modes to a single scriptural passage that the discussion on the arising of the Guide-Threads (Nayasamuṭṭhāna) is stated.
Therefore, regarding the verse: "The first [section] has sixteen modes."
Having recited [the text], he said: "Where is its exposition (niddesa) to be found? It is in the 'Convergence of Modes' (hārasampāta). The meaning of this is:
"Where is the exposition of that verse to be seen? By this, he shows that the section demonstrating the method of application for the modes (hāra) within the suttas is the "Convergence of Modes.
The meaning of the term *hārasampāta* has already been stated.
"With an unguarded mind" means with a mind that is unprotected due to the absence of the protection of mindfulness at the doors of the eye and so forth.

"Struck by wrong view" means defiled by false attachments such as eternalism and the like. "Overcome by sloth and torpor" means overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, which are characterized by a lack of alertness in both mind and body.
"Falls under the power of Māra" means [falling] at will under the power of the defilement-māra and the others.
"This must be done" (karaṇīyo hoti) is, first of all, the word-meaning of the verse.
Regarding "negligence" (pamādaṃ): the phrase "with an unguarded mind" explains negligence as characterized by the abandonment of mindfulness at the six sense-doors.
"That is the path of Death" (taṃ maccuno padaṃ): that negligence is the path of Māra, who is designated as "Death" because he slays virtuous qualities.
This is the state of mastery; thus, by connecting the first line with the fourth line, he shows: "With an unguarded mind, one goes under Māra’s power.
That perversion is the seeing of the five aggregates—which are impermanent—as "permanent";
that is a perversion, a distorted grasp. For this very reason, he said: "It has the characteristic of grasping things perversely."
“Perversion. Having grasped everything by way of the commonality of perversion, he asks about its specific basis: “What does it pervert?
Since a distinction within a generality is expressed by way of its basis, he says: “Perception, mind, and view. This is to be connected with the phrase “it perverts.
Among these, the perversion of perception is the mildest of all; regarding the impermanent and so forth—
The mere grasping of an appearance presented through the medium of an object by way of error is like the perception that arises in young fawns that grass-stalks are human beings.

A perversion of consciousness (*cittavipallāsa*) is stronger than that; it is like the definitive conclusion that things appearing in the form of jewels and so forth—when they are actually not jewels—are indeed jewels.
A perversion of view (*diṭṭhivipallāsa*) is the mere definitive conclusion regarding permanence and so forth.
But that which is stronger than all is the tendency to adhere— regarding whatever object appears in whatever way— to the view that "only this is true,
anything else is false," by way of eternalism and so forth. In this context, perversion of perception is the cause of perversion of consciousness,
and perversion of consciousness is the cause of perversion of view.
Now, in order to show the locus and the object of the perversion’s occurrence, he said: “Where does it pervert? In the four bases of selfhood.
Therein, “bases of selfhood” refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānakkhandhā*).

For they are called “self” (*attā*) because the conceit “I am” (*ahaṃ-māna*) is placed therein; and because both the intellect and conventional usage arise as “self” with respect to them, they are called “selfhood” (*attabhāva*).

Because they serve as the basis for the perversions (vipallāsa) such as beauty and so forth, and because they are the foundation [of existence], they are called "the bases of personal existence" (attabhāvavatthu).

Having shown their status as the bases of personal existence by way of being the locus for the occurrence of personality-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi)— which is the root of all perversions— through such passages as "one regards form as self," etc.,
[the text] further [describes them] by way of the mode of occurrence of the perversions.
In order to show the objects [of the perversions] by dividing them together with [the perversions themselves], it is said: "Form is the first basis for perversion:
'the beautiful in the ugly'. All of that is easy to understand. Furthermore, in order to show the perversions by dividing them according to their root causes, he says:
"Two things are the defilements of the mind," and so forth. In this context, although there is no craving devoid of ignorance,
Ignorance (*avijjā*) is indeed a condition for the perceptions of beauty and pleasure as well; nevertheless, it is said, "Enveloped by craving...
[and] taking what is suffering to be pleasure," in order to show that craving is their predominant condition. "Enveloped by views" means that ignorance is spoken of under the heading of views;
thus, the meaning is "enveloped by ignorance. Granted, there is no view here that is devoid of craving, yet craving also—

It is indeed a condition for views. Craving (*taṇhā*) is also mentioned—as in "shrouded by views... [and] self"—to show that delusion (*moha*) is a specific condition for the false adherence (*micchābhinivesa*) that occurs in those who emerge from improper reflection (*ayoniso manasikāra*) thinking, "This is permanent, this is self.
As for the "distortion of view" (*diṭṭhivipallāsa*), it refers to the two distortions that occur as "the impermanent is permanent" and "the non-self is self."
Having intended this, he said: “He regards past form... [and so on] ...past consciousness as self.
By this, he shows that the eighteen-fold doctrine of those who speculate about the past occurs by way of the latter two perversions (*vipallāsa*).
“Perversion of craving” (*taṇhā-vipallāsa*) means a perversion rooted in craving. “The beautiful in the ugly, pleasure in the painful.”
He speaks with reference to these two perversions (*vipallāsa*). "One delights in future form" means one delights in future form by way of delighting in [it through] wrong view (*diṭṭhābhinandana*).
The same method applies here for "one delights in future feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness.
By this, the forty-fourfold doctrine of those who speculate about the future (*aparantānukappika*) is also [refuted].

This shows that it generally occurs by way of the first two perversions (*vipallāsa*). By stating "two things are defilements of the mind," he specifically shows that the root cause of the most blameworthy perversion is, in particular, these two things which are defilements of the mind:
craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*); he thus shows them according to their essential nature. The mind is purified by means of those two.
“Is purified” (visujjhati) clarifies that these [perceptions] are indeed defilements by way of their opposites;

for when craving and ignorance are abandoned, no dharma of defilement remains unabandoned. And just as craving and ignorance are the root cause of the perversions, so too they are the root cause of the entire round of existence (vaṭṭa).
Thus, following the sequence of the connection, he concludes the verse with the words beginning “of those” (tesaṃ).
It has been stated. Therein, "of those" refers to those whose minds are unprotected and struck down by wrong view.
By the phrase "obstructed by ignorance," etc., he shows that they wander through the beginningless cycle of existence by falling under the power of Māra.
Regarding the phrase "overcome by sloth and torpor," he shows the essential nature of sloth and torpor by means of the passage beginning with "Sloth is... and so forth.

Since the state of being overcome by those [defilements] is easy to understand, rather than mentioning that separately, it should be understood that by the mention of the "defilement-māra" (kilesamāra) alone, its causes—the formative-māra (abhisaṅkhāramāra), the aggregate-māra (khandhamāra), and the death-māra (maccumāra)—are also included.

Thus, the inclusion of these as well is effected by the word "and" in the phrase "of the defilement-māra and the being-māra. For he, being obstructed, is turned toward the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).

Thus, having fallen under Māra’s power, he remains shrouded by defilements; as long as the bond of Māra is not severed, he is oriented toward *saṃsāra* alone and not toward the disintegration of conditioned phenomena (*visaṅkhāra*).
This is the intended meaning. These two truths were taught by the Blessed One.
How were they taught?
In this regard, discourse is of two kinds: that based on the Abhidhamma and that based on the Suttanta. Among these, that which is based on the Abhidhamma is as follows:
"With an unguarded mind"—here, a lustful mind is unguarded, a hateful mind is unguarded, and a deluded mind is unguarded.
In this context, a lustful mind [is included] among the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed.
It should be understood by way of [the following]: a corrupted mind should be understood by way of the two types of consciousness associated with aversion;
a deluded mind should be understood by way of the two types of consciousness associated with extreme delusion.

As long as there is non-guarding, non-protection, non-preservation, and non-protection of the faculties by way of these types of consciousness, there is negligence, the abandonment of mindfulness, and heedlessness of the mind.
There is non-restraint; thus the mind is unprotected. The mind "struck by wrong view" should be understood by way of the four types of consciousness associated with views.
The mind "overcome by sloth and torpor" should be understood by way of the five types of prompted unwholesome consciousness.
Thus, by including all [these categories] without omission, there are twelve types of unwholesome consciousness.

“Which are the unwholesome states?”—this should be explained in detail by way of the presentation of unwholesome consciousness-arising in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa*, beginning with: “At whatever time an unwholesome consciousness has arisen.
Regarding the phrase “of Māra,” there are five Māras.
Among them, for the defilement-Māra (*kilesamāra*), there are the four taints (*āsava*), the four floods (*ogha*), the four yokes (*yoga*), and the four ties (*gantha*).

The classification should be stated by way of the four kinds of clinging, the eight hindrances, and the ten bases of defilement, according to the method explained in the *Āsavagocchaka* and other sections;

likewise, it should be stated by way of the seven defilements mentioned in the *Khuddakavatthuvibhaṅga*, beginning with "pride of birth, pride of clan, and pride of health. This, then, is the discourse based on the Abhidhamma.
But regarding those based on the Suttas: "With an unguarded mind" means that having seen a form with the eye, one grasps at its general appearance and grasps at its secondary details;

because he dwells with the faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in after him, yet he does not practice for its restraint, nor does he guard it.
The eye-faculty; he does not attain restraint regarding the eye-faculty. By the ear... by the nose... by the tongue... by the body... by the mind...
by the mind-faculty, he attains restraint. In this way, the mind is unguarded.

And "by being struck by wrong view" means that the mind is struck by wrong view either by way of conceptualizing the past limit (*pubbanta*) or by way of conceptualizing the future limit (*aparanta*).
Or, for one who wrongly adheres or improperly emerges [from the teaching] by way of speculating about the past or the future—whatever view there is such as "the world is eternal" ... pe ...
"a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—by that [view] he is struck down and ruined. But as for those [views] which are:
"these four theories of eternalism" ... pe ... "five theories of Nibbāna in this very life," [it is by these that he is not struck down].
The sixty-two views that appear in the *Brahmajāla Sutta* and the *Pañcattaya Sutta* should be explained by way of them as the state of the mind being destroyed by wrong view.
Regarding the phrase "overcome by sloth and torpor": sloth (*thina*) is the unwieldiness of the mind; torpor (*middha*) is the unwieldiness of the three aggregates beginning with feeling.
Likewise, sloth is a lack of energy and fortitude; torpor is a loss of capability. Thus, by means of sloth...
The mind is overcome, overwhelmed, afflicted, and brought to contraction by torpor; it has fallen into lethargy.
It "goes under the power of Māra. Here, "power" (vaso) means desire, greed, intention, preference, longing, command, or injunction.

As for "Māra," there are five Māras: the Māra of the aggregates (khandhamāra), the Māra of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāramāra), the Māra of death (maccumāra), the Māra of the son of a god (devaputtamāra), and the Māra of defilements (kilesamāra).
"He goes" means he goes into their power... [etc. ...he obeys, approaches, enters, conducts himself, follows, and does not transgress their command.
Therefore it is said: "He goes into the power of Māra.
In this context, the unwholesome states already mentioned, or else craving and ignorance themselves, constitute the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*). That which is "power..."
When it was said, "He goes to Māra," those five aggregates of clinging by which he is designated are the five aggregates that constitute the truth of suffering.
Thus, two truths have been taught here by the Blessed One. Therefore, it was said: "Suffering and its origin.
The Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for their full understanding and abandonment; thus, this very meaning is made even more clear.
It is said [that one should act] "for the full understanding of suffering and for the abandoning of its origin. If it is asked, "How does he teach?"—[it is said:
"Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded, whose range is right intention, who places right view foremost, and having understood arising and passing away..."
“A bhikkhu overcome by sloth and torpor would abandon all miserable destinies.

This is the meaning of the verse: because one falls under the power of Māra with an unguarded mind, therefore one should be “one whose mind is guarded” by protecting the six faculties, including the mind, through the restraint of mindfulness.
“Having right intention as his domain” means that—because... [the text continues].
Having applied improper attention in various ways, one whose range of activity consists of wrong intentions such as sensual desire grasps at manifold forms of wrong view.
And for that very reason, with a mind struck by wrong view, one falls under the power of Māra.
Therefore, performing one's work with wise attention, one should have right intentions such as renunciation as one’s range of activity. "Placing right view foremost" means...

Having shaken off wrong views through the range of right intention, and having made right view— characterized by the knowledge of things as they truly are and characterized by the understanding that one is the owner of one’s own kamma—
the forerunner, he applies himself diligently to virtue and concentration. And from that very state, having known the arising and passing away,
and having known the origination and cessation in fifty modes within the five aggregates of clinging, he practices insight.
Having exerted himself and gradually attaining the Noble Path, the bhikkhu who has overcome sloth and torpor through the supreme path abandons all miserable destinies.

Thus, because his defilements are entirely shattered, the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) should abandon all states of existence known as miserable destinies—by way of their association with the three kinds of suffering as appropriate—and should stand beyond them in Nibbāna; this is the meaning.

The abandoning of craving and ignorance is "cessation"; because it serves as the condition for both abandoning and cessation, the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu) is described as "abandoning" and "cessation.
These four truths are those spoken of in two verses: the first two in the preceding verse and the latter two in the following verse; thus, these four are expressed by means of these two verses.
The Noble Truths. Among them, gratification (*assāda*) is through the truth of origin; danger (*ādīnava*) is through suffering; escape (*nissaraṇa*) is through the truths of the path and cessation;
the fruit is the abandoning of all destinations; the means is the guarding of the mind and so forth;

and the Blessed One’s injunction is the enjoining toward the guarding of the mind and so forth by way of prohibiting the non-guarding of the mind and so forth. Thus, gratification and the rest are the meaning of the words that constitute the sustenance of the teaching.
They are to be extracted. For this very reason it was said: "The sequence of the nutriment of the teaching has been applied.
The commentary on the sequence of the nutriment of the teaching is finished.
2. Commentary on the Sequence of the Nutriment of Investigation (Vicaya-hārasampāta).
53. Having thus shown the application of the mode of teaching (*desanāhāra*), he now shows the application of the mode of investigation (*vicayahāra*).

Since the mode of investigation consists in the investigation of the meaning of the terms within the mode of teaching, he begins with the words “In this regard, craving is twofold,” etc., in order to show the application of the mode of investigation by way of analyzing the classification of the wholesome and so forth regarding that craving which was determined as the cause of perversion within the mode of teaching. In this context, “wholesome” (*kusala*) means...
They have wholesome states as their object. Here, the word "wholesome" (*kusala*) should be understood in the sense of being blameless (*anavajja*), as in the *Bāhitika Sutta*.
But why is craving (*taṇhā*) mentioned here by way of the category of the wholesome?

Because in the preceding section on the "Nutriment of Teaching," craving was extracted as the cause of the perversions, and through its influence, the side of defilement was shown. However, due to [the Buddha’s] diverse mode of expression...
Here too, craving has been extracted by way of its wholesome aspect (*kusala-paryāya*) in order to show the side of purification (*vodāna-pakṣa*).
In this context, it "leads to saṃsāra" means it is *saṃsāra-gāminī*; the meaning is that it is the leader of saṃsāra. It "leads to apacaya, which is Nibbāna," thus it is *apacaya-gāminī*.
But how is craving a lead to apacaya? He says: "craving for abandoning. This refers to the abandoning [of defilements] through substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-ppahāna*) and so forth.
Craving is the cause. But how can craving, which is exclusively blameworthy, be wholesome? It is because it is something to be cultivated.
Just as with craving, conceit (māna) is also twofold—both wholesome and unwholesome—and since it is not merely craving, conceit is mentioned here by way of being an illustration for craving.
In that context, in order to show the intended wholesome nature and so forth of conceit, he said: "Depending on which conceit... and so forth.
For this was said by the Blessed One: “O Lord of Devas, I declare that conceit is twofold: that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated,” and so forth.
The statement beginning with “the grief based on renunciation” is spoken for the purpose of showing the specific nature of that craving which was previously called “wholesome.
In that context, what is called “grief based on renunciation” is as follows:
“In this context, what are the six kinds of grief based on renunciation?

Having understood the impermanence of forms themselves, their change, fading away, and cessation, and having seen it as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘Both formerly and now, all these forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,’ one [abides] in the unsurpassed liberations.”

“He arouses longing, thinking: ‘When indeed shall I attain and dwell in that sphere which the Noble Ones now attain and dwell in? Thus, for one who arouses longing for the unsurpassed liberations, longing arises;
conditioned by longing, there arises grief. Such grief as this is called grief based on renunciation.”
Thus, when desirable objects have come into range at the six doors,

one should establish a longing for the noble fruit-dhammas known as the supreme liberation; and for one who is unable to exert themselves by establishing insight (vipassanā) through the aspects of impermanence and so forth in order to attain them—
[thinking] "having exerted myself in insight for this fortnight, this month, or even this year"—

The dejection that arises in one who grieves, thinking, "I was unable to reach the noble plane," is called "dejection based on renunciation" because it arises through renunciation, through insight, through recollection, and as a cause for practice such as the first jhāna and so forth.
This craving is wholesome; this craving, which was described as "longing," is wholesome.

How so? "The liberation of mind through the fading away of lust is wholesome with that as its object. This is what is meant: the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust is not wholesome by way of its own intrinsic nature;
it is wholesome in the sense of being blameless (*anavajja*). However, because craving occurs directed toward that [liberation], it is wholesome by virtue of having a wholesome object.
The liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance is wholesome in the sense of being blameless.
“Of that” means of the liberation by wisdom (*paññāvimutti*). It is by virtue of this that it was stated in the verse, “Therefore, one whose mind is guarded abandons all miserable destinies.

Thus, having completed a long-term residency in insight (*vipassanā*), and because liberation by wisdom has been attained through the painful way of practice and sluggish direct knowledge, the passage beginning with “What is its investigation?
is commenced in order to demonstrate the application of the method of investigation.
In this context, since liberation through wisdom (paññāvimutti) is rooted in the Noble Path, the text states, "Where is it to be seen?
In the fourth jhāna," and so forth, in order to point out the path of arrival for those factors of the Noble Path that have the fourth jhāna as their basis.
Therein, "by means of the perfections" (pāramitāya) refers to the cultivation of the fourth jhāna that has reached its highest excellence. By means of which eight factors...
The fourth jhāna consciousness endowed [with these factors] has been described; in order to show those factors, the words "purified" (*parisuddha*) and so forth were spoken.
Therein, it is "purified" by way of the state of purity of equanimity and mindfulness. Precisely because it is purified, it is "cleansed" (*pariyodāta*); that is to say, it is luminous.
It is "without blemish" (*anaṅgaṇa*) because it is free from the stains of passion and so forth due to the destruction of the conditions for pleasure and the rest. Because it is without blemish...
Thus it is free from defilement; for the mind becomes defiled by blemish (*aṅgaṇa*). The meaning is that, because it is well-developed, it has become supple and attained mastery.
Indeed, a mind that functions under control is called "supple. And precisely because of its suppleness, it is "workable" (*kammaniya*);
the meaning is that it is capable of work and fit for work. For a supple mind is workable; thus, when developed, it is both supple and workable.

"Because this mind, monks, is thus. It is "steadfast" (*ṭhita*) because it stands firm upon these qualities, such as purity of being. Precisely because it is steadfast, it has "reached imperturbability" (*āneñjappatta*);
the meaning is that it is immovable and free from agitation. Alternatively, it is "steadfast" because it stands under its own control through its state of being pliant and workable.
It has "reached imperturbability" because it is embraced by faith and the other [faculties]. For a mind embraced by faith cannot be overcome by lack of faith.
It does not waver: being encompassed by energy, it does not waver through indolence; being encompassed by mindfulness, it does not waver through negligence;
being encompassed by concentration, it does not waver through restlessness; being encompassed by wisdom, it does not waver through ignorance;
having reached illumination, it does not waver through the darkness of the defilements. When encompassed by these six qualities, it has attained imperturbability.
Thus, a mind endowed with these eight factors is capable of being directed toward the direct realization of those states that are to be realized through direct knowledge.
Another method: a mind concentrated by means of the fourth jhāna absorption is purified by the removal of the hindrances.

It is purified by the complete surmounting of applied thought (*vitakka*) and the rest. It is stainless (*anaṅgaṇa*) due to the absence of evil states belonging to the sphere of desire (*icchāvacara*) which are adverse to the attainment of jhāna.
"Belonging to the sphere of desire" means those that range within desire, that have descended through the influence of desire, and that proceed as various causes for anger;
this is the meaning. It is [purified] by the disappearance of mental defilements such as covetousness (*abhijjhā*).
It is free from defilements. Both of these points should be understood by way of the Anaṅgaṇa Sutta and the Vattha Sutta.

It has become pliant through the attainment of mastery; it is wieldy through the attainment of the state of the bases of psychic power; it is steady and has reached imperturbability through the attainment of excellence by means of the perfection of development.
It is "steady" in the sense that it has reached imperturbability, just as it is said to have "reached imperturbability" when it has attained the state of imperturbability.

This is the meaning. Thus, the mind endowed with these eight factors is capable of directing itself toward the direct realization of those states that are to be realized through direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
It serves as the basis and the foundation for the direct realization of those states to be realized through direct knowledge. For this very reason it was said:
"Therein he attains the eightfold [attainment]: the six direct knowledges and two distinctions."
In this context, "he" refers to the yogi who has attained the fourth jhāna. "Therein" means in that fourth jhāna which serves as the basis for his resolve.
"He attains the eightfold [power]" means he attains an eightfold quality.

But what is that eightfold quality? It is said: "The six direct knowledges (abhiññā) and two specific distinctions. These are the power of mind-made form (manomaya-iddhi) and the knowledge of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa). That is the mind.
The fourth jhāna consciousness. By the passage beginning, “Because it is purified, therefore it is bright,” he shows that each preceding factor is the cause for each succeeding one.

“Both of these” refers to those stains (*aṅgaṇa*) such as lust and those defilements (*upakkilesa*) such as covetousness, through the absence of which it is said to be “stainless” (*anaṅgaṇa*) and “free from defilement” (*vigatūpakkilesa*). These...

The "courtyards" and the "defilements"—both of these together constitute craving, because they are of the nature of craving and because they conform to craving; thus, they belong to the side of craving.
And as for "wavering," this is the flickering of the mind due to its lack of concentration. "Instability" means non-abiding.
"This belongs to the side of views": both that wavering and that instability belong to the side of views because they are the cause of wrong adherence.
By the passage beginning with “The four faculties,” he clarifies the fourth jhāna even from the perspective of feeling.
Thus, the consciousness of the fourth jhāna, endowed with eight factors, becomes capable of being directed toward the attainment of the higher direct knowledges (abhiññā).

And that capacity for such direction occurs only for one who has attained mastery through the fourteen modes. Furthermore, that mastery belongs to one who has attained the eight attainments (samāpatti).

The phrase "he attends to the higher attainment as peaceful," etc., is stated by the author in order to show the method of mental attention for the formless attainments, [addressing those] who have not yet attained even the jhānas of the fine-material sphere.

In this context, "the higher attainment" refers to the attainment of the base of infinite space. "He attends to it as peaceful" means that he attends to it as peaceful both in terms of the peace of its factors and the peace of its object.
“He attends to it as peaceful”: for whenever he attends to the formless attainment as peaceful, from that very moment the fine-material-sphere jhāna appears as unpeaceful. Therefore it is said:

“For him, the higher [attainment]... settles. And “discontent and perceptions of resistance”: this refers to the five types of sensory consciousness-perceptions, which are termed “perceptions of resistance.”
Disenchantment settles. By the phrase beginning with "In every way," he shows the attainment of the formless (ārūpya-samāpatti) as a partial [cessation].

Regarding the phrase "the application of higher knowledge is perception of form": these are indeed perceptions belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara); their purpose is merely the application for the sake of higher knowledge, but they are not peaceful in the same way that the formless-sphere attainments are—this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the phrase "the differentiation is perception of diversity": this perception of diversity is a differentiation among various objects of focus.
In this context, the meaning is "the mind's agitated activity. "He transcends" means that, having thus seen the danger therein, he transcends those perceptions.

"And his perceptions of resistance disappear" means that for the yogi who attains the sphere of infinite space, even the ten perceptions of resistance vanish. By this, the first formless attainment is indicated.
"Of one thus concentrated": of one who is concentrated by means of the transcendence of even the one-pointedness of mind in the fine-material-sphere jhāna, according to the method described above.
"Of one thus concentrated": of one who is concentrated by means of the formless-sphere concentration that proceeds with peace.

"The radiance": that which was previously the radiance of the fine-material-sphere jhāna. "It disappears": that radiance of the fine-material-sphere jhāna [disappears] at the time of attaining the formless-sphere jhāna.
"It disappears": even the vision by means of the eye of the fine-material-sphere jhāna vanishes. "That concentration":
that aforementioned concentration of the fine-material and immaterial spheres.

"Endowed with six factors": endowed with the six factors that constitute the nature of the requisites which are beneficial. "Should be reviewed": it should be looked back upon; it should be reflected upon again and again.
This is the meaning. To show the mode of reflection together with its object, it is said: "accompanied by non-covetousness," and so forth.

Therein, "in the whole world" means in the entire world of sentient beings and the world of formations, consisting of all that is dear and pleasant. By this, he speaks of the abandoning of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).

Likewise, by "non-ill will" (*abyāpanna*) and so forth, [he speaks of the abandoning] of ill will (*byāpāda*), laziness (*kosajja*), agitation (*sārambha*), deceitfulness (*sāṭheyya*), distraction (*vikkhepa*), and confusion (*sammosa*).

Abandonment. Furthermore, in order to show those six factors analyzed by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), it was said: "And that which is not accompanied by non-covetousness," and so forth.
All of that is easy to understand. 54.
Up to this point, the preliminary practice for the fruit of arahantship—referred to as "liberation through wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*)—has been shown by way of concentration (*samādhi*).
Having shown that, now, in order to show the concentration of the fruit of arahantship, it is said:

"That concentration," and so forth. Therein, "that concentration" refers to that very right concentration. The concentration which is the fruit of the noble path concentration mentioned previously should be understood as fivefold by means of the five kinds of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa) that will be spoken of hereafter, in the manner of one's own reviewing.
It is to be understood in five ways: “This concentration is pleasant in the present,” and so forth.

The concentration of the fruit of Arahantship is pleasant in the present because it is blissful at every moment of its attainment. It has a pleasant ripening in the future because each preceding moment serves as a condition for each succeeding moment of the bliss of concentration.
It is noble (ariya) because it is remote from the defilements. [It is free] from the bait of sensual pleasures, the bait of worldly gain, and the bait of the world.
It is non-existent and free from worldly taint (*nirāmisa*). It is not practiced by base men because it is practiced by Great Beings such as the Buddhas.
It is peaceful due to its constituent continuity and its continuity in pacifying the distress of all defilements (*kilesa*). It is sublime in the sense of being insatiable.

It is "attained through tranquility" (*paṭippassaddhiladdha*) because it is obtained through the subsiding of the defilements, or because it is obtained by way of the state of the subsiding of the defilements. It is tranquil...

For "tranquillity" (passaddhi) and this [term] are one in meaning. It is "attained through tranquillity" because it is obtained by an Arahant whose defilements have been thoroughly stilled (paṭippassaddha).
It is "attained through singleness" (ekodibhāvādhigata) because it is reached by means of singleness, or because singleness itself has been reached.
This is because, unlike weak, tainted concentration, it has not been reached by suppressing opposing states or warding off defilements with effort and exertion.
"Restrained and checked by the restraint of the formations of the nose":

from whichever stage he enters that concentration, or from whichever stage he emerges, having attained fullness of mindfulness, he enters with mindfulness and emerges with mindfulness; or else, according to the time previously determined, he enters with mindfulness.

One emerges mindful. Therefore, when one reflects upon this as follows: "This concentration is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future," there arises within oneself—without depending on another—a knowledge that is personally realized. This is one aspect.
The same method applies to the remaining [aspects] as well. Thus, by way of these five aspects to be reflected upon, concentration should be understood as fivefold.
Furthermore, with the passage beginning “And whatever concentration,” etc., he shows the distinction between serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) regarding the fruit of arhatship.

Therein, because the bliss of concentration is intended by the term “bliss,” it is said: “Whatever concentration is pleasant in the present, and whatever concentration has a pleasant result in the future—this is serenity.
However, its noble and non-material nature is due to the power of wisdom (*paññā*).
He said, "That which is noble concentration... this is insight," because it is accomplished [through that].

Having thus shown the concentration of the fruit of arahantship by way of its analysis, he now says, "That concentration," in order to show its preliminary practice by way of the analysis of concentration.
Therein, "that concentration" refers to that concentration of the fruit of arahantship.
The concentration of the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere mentioned in the preliminary practice—that is the concentration.

It is to be understood as being of five kinds, according to the five modes that will be explained. In the phrases beginning with “the pervasion by rapture,” wisdom that arises pervading rapture is called “pervasion by rapture” in two jhānas;
wisdom that arises pervading bliss is [so called] in three jhānas.
Wisdom is called "pervasion by happiness" (*sukhapharaṇatā*). Because it arises pervading the minds of others, the wisdom of penetration of minds is called "pervasion of mind" (*cetopharaṇatā*).

Because it arises in the pervasion of light, the wisdom of the divine eye is called "pervasion of light" (*ālokapharaṇatā*). The knowledge of reviewing is called the "sign of reviewing" (*paccavekkhaṇānimitta*).
And this has been said: "In two jhānas, wisdom is 'pervasion by rapture' (*pītipharaṇatā*); in three..."
"Wisdom regarding the jhānas is the pervasion by happiness; knowledge of others' minds is the pervasion by consciousness; the divine eye is the pervasion by light;
and for one who has emerged from various states of concentration, the reviewing knowledge is the sign of review.
Here, in order to show the distinction between serenity and insight, it was said: "And that which is the pervasion by rapture," and so forth. And herein:

The teaching was given by means of wisdom; thus, the commentary was composed by way of wisdom. In such passages as "wisdom is the pervading of rapture," it is understood that these are accompanied by concentration (*samādhi*);

therefore, in that context, serenity (*samatha*) is set forth by way of concentration. Consequently, the pervading of rapture, bliss, and mind succeeds especially through the expansion of concentration;
thus, they are called "serenity. The others [the remaining qualities] are by way of the expansion of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
These are called "insight" (vipassanā).
Now, in order to show that concentration analyzed by way of its objects, it is said: "the ten kasiṇa bases," and so forth.
Therein, the kasiṇas are those consisting of kasiṇa-jhānas; they are so called because they serve as the foundation for the specific types of bliss for the practitioner.

They are called *kasiṇāyatanas* because they are both sense bases (*āyatana*) and the states that constitute the sense base of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense base of mental objects (*dhammāyatana*).

The term "earth-kasiṇa" (*pathavīkasiṇa*) refers to the circle of earth used for preliminary practice (*parikamma*), the learning-sign (*uggaha-nimitta*) and the counterpart-sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) that arise therein, and the meditative absorption (*jhāna*) produced in relation to that sign.
Of these, it is the absorption that is intended here. The "space-kasiṇa" (*ākāsakasiṇa*) refers to the space revealed by removing the kasiṇa.

The first immaterial-sphere jhāna that has arisen is [the basis for the second]. The consciousness-kasiṇa is the second immaterial-sphere jhāna which has the consciousness of the first immaterial-sphere as its object.
With reference to those such as the earth-kasiṇa that proceed by way of pure serenity meditation (samatha-bhāvanā), it is said: "These eight kasiṇas are serenity.
The remaining two kasiṇas, proceeding by way of being the foundation for insight (vipassanā-adhiṭṭhāna), are called "insight."

"In this way" means by this method. "The entire Noble Path" refers to the Noble Path in its entirety, which, though undivided in its nature as right view and so forth, is divided into many distinct types according to the different preliminary practices such as the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
"In whatever aspect" refers to whichever aspect among those such as non-covetousness or present happiness.
It has been said. "By this or that" means: by whichever modes of serenity (samatha) and whichever modes of insight (vipassanā) it is possible to apply them to those respective aspects;
thus, having discerned [the path], the Noble Path should be applied by means of serenity and insight in those respective modes.
"Those" refers to the phenomena (dhammas) consisting of the foundations of serenity and insight. "Comprehended by three phenomena" means by the three phenomena of contemplation (anupassanā).
"Comprehended" means they have been brought into the reckoning. "By which three? He says: "By way of impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
Insight is called "impermanence" because it accompanies impermanence; the same method applies to the remaining two as well.
Developing serenity and insight, he develops the three gateways to liberation; thus, for the sake of attaining the Noble Path...
The yogi, properly engaged, increasing serenity by means of attaining it at the proper time and insight by means of reflecting on it at the proper time,
develops the three contemplations known as the signless door of liberation and so forth. "He cultivates the three aggregates" means that,
bringing about successive distinctions through the three contemplations, he cultivates the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and [the aggregate of wisdom].
"The aggregate of wisdom" means that one increases these three aggregates.
Since the Noble Eightfold Path is comprised within these three aggregates, it is said: "One who develops the three aggregates develops the Noble Eightfold Path.
Now, [this concerns] those persons in whom, while training in this, the doors of deliverance are specifically found, and which defilements...
The three doors to liberation are the opposites [of the three temperaments]; in order to show them together with those [temperaments], it is said, "one of lustful temperament," and so forth.

In that context, "by means of the signless door to liberation" refers to the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*). For that [contemplation] is signless because it eradicates the signs of permanence and so on;
and it is called a "door" because it serves as the entrance to the Noble Path, which has received the name "liberation" due to its being the complete severance of lust and the other [defilements].

Because it serves as the gateway, it is called "the door of liberation that is signless" (*animittavimokkhamukha*). Regarding "in the training of higher mind" (*adhicittasikkhāya*), this refers to concentration (*samādhi*).
"Not approaching a contact to be felt as pleasant" means not approaching with craving a contact that is conducive to pleasant feeling—that is, the cause of pleasant feeling.
"Fully understanding pleasant feeling" means [understanding] that "this pleasant feeling is subject to change, etc."

By fully understanding [them] as "suffering," one has transcended lust for one's own domain. By such expressions as "washing away the stain of lust," he speaks of the abandoning of lust itself through these various methods.
The meaning in passages such as "a person of a hateful temperament" should also be understood according to the method already stated.
For one in whom wisdom predominates, there is the emptiness of self regarding formations, through the resolution of the density of continuity, aggregates, functions, objects, and so forth.
It becomes manifest; thus, because the discernment of the contemplation of non-self is preeminent, it is said: "The door to the void liberation is the aggregate of wisdom.

Likewise, because conditioned phenomena are momentary due to their inherent nature of dissolution, their breaking up right where they arise is manifest specifically to one who is rightly concentrated; thus, the contemplation of impermanence is preeminent.
Because concentration is the primary effort, it is said: "The door of liberation that is signless is the aggregate of concentration.

Likewise, for one who fulfills the precepts and abides having overcome arisen suffering and discontent through abundant patience, the suffering nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) becomes manifest;
thus, because contemplation of suffering is the primary effort regarding the precepts, it is said: "The door of liberation that is desireless..."
The aggregate of virtue. Thus, because the three aggregates are comprised within the three doors to liberation, it is said:
“Developing the three doors to liberation, he develops the three aggregates.
And because the Noble Eightfold Path is comprised within the three aggregates, one who develops the three aggregates [develops] the Noble Eightfold Path.
It is said, “he develops the path. Therefore, showing their inclusion within that [path], he said, “And whatever right speech,” and so forth.
Furthermore, in order to show that the three aggregates (khandhas) possess the nature of serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), he said, “The aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha),” and so forth.
Therein, because the aggregate of virtue is characterized primarily by patience and because concentration is of great assistance to it, it is assigned to the side of serenity.
It should be seen. "Factors of existence" (*bhavaṅgāni*) means the factors of the existence at rebirth (*upapattibhava*). "Two feet" (*dve padāni*) means two steps.
For, by and large, the fifteen factors of conduct are comprised within virtue (*sīla*) and concentration (*samādhi*).

"One who has developed the body" (*bhāvitakāya*) means one whose body has been developed through the fulfillment of the virtue of higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika-sīla*). One whose virtue has been developed through the fulfillment of the virtue pertaining to the beginning of the holy life (*ādibrahmacariyaka-sīla*). Alternatively:
"One who has developed the body" means one whose five doors of the body have been developed through restraint of the sense faculties.

"One who has developed virtue" means one whose virtue has been developed by way of the remaining precepts. When there is right development of the body, the total abandonment of bodily misconduct and the arising of blameless activity are accomplished.
Likewise, when unsurpassed virtue is being perfected, [there is the abandonment] of wrong speech and wrong livelihood in their entirety.

And abandoning becomes perfected. Furthermore, when mindfulness and wisdom are developed, right mindfulness, right concentration, right view, and right intention reach the full perfection of development because they share that same nature and because they have those two as their cause.
He shows this meaning with the words, "When the body is being developed," and so forth.
"He goes to a fivefold attainment" means that the noble path itself is shown by dividing it into five stages according to its specific states.
For the noble path quickly attains, in a single moment of consciousness, what is to be attained by itself regarding the four truths;
thus, unlike a mundane attainment (*lokīyasamāpatti*), it has no need for the task of mastery (*vasibhāvanā*).
Because [the path] exists, there is swift attainment. Because of abandoning those things to be abandoned through absolute liberation, there is the attainment of liberation.
Because of the attainment of the great aggregates of virtue and so forth, which are superior to worldly qualities, there is great attainment.
Because of the attainment of those very same qualities, which yield abundant fruit, there is vast attainment. Because there is nothing whatsoever to be done by oneself that remains incomplete...

"And there is attainment without remainder. But what are these attainments? To show this distinction—that some are through the power of serenity (*samatha*) and some are through the power of insight (*vipassanā*)—the passage beginning with "Therein, by means of serenity" was stated.
Thus, the Great Elder, by way of the verse beginning "Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded," [expounded] by way of the liberation of the fruit of Arahatship.

While explaining the application of the investigative method (*vicaya-hāra*), [the author], by way of demonstrating the various modes of that method through numerous scriptural passages due to his skill in teaching— by means of analyzing the specific cultivations and the benefits of cultivation for the preliminary practice—
has now stated, beginning with "In this regard, he who teaches," in order to demonstrate it also by way of the ten powers of a Tathāgata.

"He does not deceive his disciples with his exhortation" means that he does not mislead or deceive those to be trained—who are called "disciples" because they hear the Dhamma through his own instruction—since, by means of the Noble Path, he has utterly abandoned at the foot of the Bodhi tree all evil qualities that are causes for deception.
"Threefold" means of three kinds; the sense is: by way of three aspects.
"Do this": enter upon and abide in this taking of refuge and in virtue (*sīla*) and so forth. "Do this by this means":
by this method, purifying the refuges and fulfilling virtue and so forth, you should accomplish it. "While you are doing this for yourselves":
while you are practicing this taking of refuge and virtue and so forth, [there will be] the fruits of the present life, the future life, and *nibbāna*.
The meaning is: "You should accomplish those things which, by means of them, will lead to welfare and happiness.

Having thus shown the manner of his exhortation, he said, "So exhorted," and so forth, in order to demonstrate—by analyzing it through the powers of a Tathāgata—the statement that "he does not deceive his disciples with his exhortation.
In that context, "so" (tathā) means by that [method].
"In the manner described" means in the way stated, such as "Do this; do it by this method," and so forth. "Instructed" means exhorted by a teaching of the Dhamma.
"Advised" is a synonym for that same term. "Acting accordingly" means acting in the very way one was advised.
"That plane" refers to both the plane of vision and the plane of cultivation, for the sake of attaining which one was instructed.

"There is no possibility for this" means that such a cause does not exist. For a cause is called a "possibility" (*ṭhāna*) because the fruit stands upon it, since its existence is dependent on that [cause].
In the second instance, "the ground" refers to the ground known as the state of prosperity (*sampatti-bhava*) to be attained by means of the aggregate of virtue (*sīla-kkhandha*).
Now, because the Blessed One’s four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*) also possess an unerring nature, they are [included] in the knowledge of the first fruit.

There is a specific distinction regarding the object; therefore, in order to show that those [qualities] also constitute its object, it was said: "While you were a perfectly enlightened one (*sammāsambuddha*)," and so forth.
In this context, "while you were a perfectly enlightened one" means: by virtue of your claim, "I am a perfectly enlightened one;
all phenomena (*dhammā*) have been fully awakened to by me," you were a perfectly enlightened one. [The thought], "These phenomena have not been fully awakened to..."

"There is no such possibility" means that there is no ground for anyone to say, with a statement consistent with the Dhamma, supported by reason and cause, "These very teachings have not been fully realized by you.
However, those who prattle on like Sunakkhatta are beyond measure.
Therefore, the reason given—that he will counter-accuse him with a statement consistent with the Dhamma—is not possible. This same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. For whom...

"The Dhamma has been taught for their sake" means that for the sake of abandoning whichever [defilements] such as lust (*rāga*) and so forth, the Dhamma—such as the meditation on the foul (*asubha-bhāvanā*)—has been explained.

"For one who practices it" means for one who has practiced accordingly. "The attainment of distinction" means the attainment of distinctions such as the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*).

"Obstructive" (*antarāyika*): an obstruction (*antarāya*) is that which creates an obstacle; those for whom this [obstruction] exists are "obstructive. Or, they are "engaged in obstructions" (*antarāye niyuttā*).

They are called *antarāyika* because they deserve an obstacle to the fruit, or because their purpose is an obstacle. Furthermore, they are fivefold, being divided into [the obstacles consisting of] karma, defilements (*kilesa*), and so forth.
"Not conducive to emancipation" (*aniyyānika*) refers to all phenomena that are contrary to the Noble Path.
"One endowed with right view" (*diṭṭhisampanna*) is a noble disciple who has entered the stream and is endowed with the vision of the Path. "Well-cooked" (*suhatam*) means thoroughly matured.
This too is merely a partial explanation. He does not even perform such acts as giving to the *mataka-peta*s (spirits of the dead) and others.
He is called a *puthujjana* because he is one who produces (*janana*) various defilements (*kilesa*), volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and so forth. For it has been said:
"He is a *puthujjana* because of producing various things through causes such as [defilements]."
"Because he is included among ordinary people, or because this person is many (puthu), thus [he is called] a *puthujjana*.

Regarding the words "mother" and so forth: the mother is the biological mother; the father is the biological progenitor. What is intended here is an *arahant* who has exhausted the taints (*khīṇāsava*) while existing as a human being.
But could a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) deprive others of life? That too is impossible. Even if [the victim] has passed into another existence...
Even if someone were to say to a noble disciple who does not know his own status as a noble disciple,
"Having deprived this ant of life, you shall take over the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch throughout the entire interior of the world-system," he would not deprive it of life.
Yet, they might further say, "If you do not have it killed, we shall cut off your head."

They might even cut off his head, yet he would not kill them. This was said for the purpose of showing the great blameworthiness of the state of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) and for the purpose of illustrating the strength of the state of a noble one (*ariya*). This is the intended meaning here:
"Blameworthy indeed is the state of an ordinary person, wherein one might even commit such immediate retribution offenses (*ānantariya*) as matricide and the like; [yet] it possesses great power."
And there is the state of a noble one, who does not perform these actions.
