"He should cause a schism in the Saṅgha" means that he should cause a schism in the Saṅgha—those who share the same communion—while standing within the same boundary, by means of five causes.
For this has been said: "In five ways, Upāli, the Saṅgha is split: by a formal act (kamma), by a recitation (uddesa), by speaking..."
“By means of proclamation and by means of the drawing of lots.
In this context, “by means of an act” (kammena) refers to any one of the four types of formal acts, such as the act of notification (*apalokana*) and so forth.

“By means of a recitation” (*uddesena*) refers to any one of the five recitations of the *Pātimokkha*. “Speaking” (*voharanto*) means conversing; [he speaks] by means of various appropriate arguments.
By illuminating the eighteen grounds for schism, beginning with the phrase “non-Dhamma as Dhamma,” [the Blessed One said]: “By means of formal proclamation:
‘Do you not know my status as one who has gone forth from a noble family and my state of great learning?

Is it even fitting for you to entertain the thought that someone like me would cause one to adopt what is contrary to the Dhamma, contrary to the Vinaya, and opposed to the Teacher’s instruction? What am I...’”
By whispering words into their ears in such a manner as, "I do not fear the states of misery," and so forth;
and by means of the drawing of lots (*salākaggāha*), that is, having thus announced it, having steadied their minds, and having made them incapable of turning back, [saying], "Take this lot."

And here, the formal act (*kamma*) itself is the recitation or the authority; however, the preliminary stages consist of the consultation, the proclamation, and the distribution of voting sticks (*salākā*).

For even when one who is consulting by way of illustrating the eighteen grounds proclaims it there for the sake of generating consent and has the voting sticks distributed, the Saṅgha remains undivided. But when four or more [monks] have thus [taken] the voting stick...
When they have taken up either a formal act (*kamma*) or a recitation (*uddesa*) that is not shared [with the rest of the Saṅgha], then the Saṅgha is said to be "split.
Thus, it is impossible for a person endowed with right view to split the Saṅgha or create a schism in the Saṅgha.
"With a corrupt mind" means with a mind defiled by a murderous intent. "He should shed blood" means [shed the blood] from a living body.
One might cause even as much blood as could be drunk by a small fly to flow.

By this much, the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariyakamma*), such as matricide and so forth, are shown; these are committed by an ordinary person (*puthujjana*), not by a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*).
"With a corrupt mind" means with a mind defiled by a destructive intent. "A stupa" refers to a shrine (*cetiyam*). "Should destroy" means should ruin it.
"Another teacher": even in another existence, [the thought] "this other founder of a sect is capable of performing the duties of a teacher for me.
"He would acknowledge him": he would take him as "this is my teacher"—such a possibility does not exist.
"He would seek another person worthy of offerings outside of this": outside of this teaching, another external ascetic.
Or [he might approach] a brahmin with the intention: "This person is worthy of offerings; services rendered to him will bear great fruit.

This is the meaning. "One would expect purification through curiosity and auspicious rites" means that because it proceeds on the basis of the thought, "By this, that will happen," one would believe in one's own purification and cleansing through auspicious rites consisting of what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, which are termed "curiosity."
57. "That a woman might be a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) king—this possibility does not exist.

This is because, due to the absence of the female organ being concealed by a sheath and other such marks, her physical characteristics (lakkhaṇa) are not fulfilled; furthermore, because of the absence of the "woman-jewel" (itthiratana), she cannot possess the seven jewels.
Moreover, her personal existence (attabhāva) is not superior to that of all other humans; therefore, [the Buddha said], "A woman... [this possibility] does not exist."
It has been stated. Since the three positions of Sakka and so forth are supreme, while the female gender is inferior, therefore even the status of Sakka and so forth is prohibited for her.
But is it not the case that, just as the female gender does not exist in the Brahma-world, neither does the male gender;
therefore, one should not say that he could be a male Mahābrahmā? It is not the case that he should not be so called. Why? Because here—
Because a male is reborn there. For it is women who, having developed jhāna here and passed away, are reborn in the company of the Brahmapārisajja devas, but not among the Mahābrahmās.
However, it cannot be said that a male is never reborn there.
Even though both genders are absent there, the Brahmās there have the form of males, not the form of females.

Therefore, this is well said: "A woman as a Tathāgata. Let us set aside for now the state of Buddhahood—the capacity to cross over the worlds after having produced the qualities of omniscience—which does not come to pass even through mere aspiration in a woman. [As it is said:
"Human birth, possession of the [male] gender, the cause, and seeing the Teacher;..."

"Going forth, perfection of virtues, qualification, and zeal—through the convergence of these eight factors, the aspiration succeeds. These are indeed the causes for the fulfillment of the aspiration.
Thus, for one who is unable to accomplish even this much of an aspiration...
"How could a woman attain Buddhahood?"—thus it is said: "That a woman could be a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One—such a thing is impossible.
For one whose accumulation of merit is complete in every aspect brings forth a personal existence that is likewise complete in every aspect;
therefore, it is only a man who becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One.

"Of one world-system" means of the ten-thousandfold world-system (*dasasahassilokadhātu*), which is called the "field of birth. For that [world-system] shakes at such times as the Tathāgata’s descent into the womb.

However, the "field of command" (*āṇākhetta*) consists of a hundred thousand million world-spheres (*cakkavāḷa*). It is that which contracts and expands on one side, and wherein the authority of the *Āṭānāṭiya-paritta* and other protective spells prevails. As for the "field of range" (*visayakhettassa*)...
There is no limit. For regarding the Buddhas, it is said: "As much as there is knowledge, so much is the knowable; as much as there is the knowable, so much is knowledge.
Knowledge has the knowable as its boundary; the knowable has knowledge as its boundary.
Thus, there is nothing that is not within their range. Therefore, when the three councils have been held upon these three fields—the Buddha-word contained in the Tipiṭaka—
There is no sutta stating, "Buddhas arise in another world-system, excluding this one," but there is one stating that they do not arise [in the same place].
"Neither before nor after" means they do not arise together—either before or after; rather, they arise either before or after [one another].
This has been stated. In this context, it should be understood that "before" means prior to the descent into the womb.
For from that point onward, by the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world system, the demarcation of the field (*khetta*) is established; there is no arising of another Buddha [within that field].

However, after the final Nibbāna of the relics (*dhātu-parinibbāna*), there is no arising of another Buddha either before or after that time; yet, [the possibility of arising] above that is not excluded.
But why do they not arise neither before nor after one another? Because they would lack the quality of being marvelous.
For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are marvelous persons. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, when one person arises in the world, he arises as a marvelous person," and so forth.
And if many Buddhas were to arise simultaneously, they would cease to be marvelous. Furthermore, there would be no distinction in their teaching.

For whatever Dhamma, such as the divisions of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), one Buddha teaches, that same [Dhamma] would have to be taught by another as well, because there is no dispute [regarding it].
For if many Buddhas were to arise simultaneously, their disciples would quarrel among themselves—just like the pupils of many different teachers—saying, "Our Buddha is more graceful," and so forth.
But what is the use of seeking such reasons? This is simply the nature of things (dhammatā).
Regarding the statement that two Tathāgatas do not arise simultaneously in a single world-system:
just as seeds such as those of the nimba or the kosātakī do not produce a sweet fruit, but rather produce a fruit that is unpalatable and not sweet,
so too bodily misconduct and the like do not produce a sweet result, but only one that is not sweet.

They produce [their results]. And just as seeds of sugarcane, rice, and so forth produce fruits that are sweet and of excellent flavor, not unpleasant or bitter, so too do bodily good conduct and the like produce a result that is sweet, not unsweet. And this has been said:
“As the seed one sows, so is the fruit one reaps;”
"One who performs wholesome deeds [reaps] what is wholesome, and one who performs evil deeds [reaps] what is evil.
Therefore, it was said: "Of the three kinds of misconduct," and so forth.
"Any ascetic or brahmin" refers to anyone who is an ascetic merely by virtue of having gone forth, or a brahmin merely by virtue of birth.
Or: one who has evil desires is a *kuhaka* (a deceiver) because he deceives others with the intention of gaining esteem;
a *lapaka* (a flatterer) by means of speech employed for the sake of obtaining requisites; a *nemittika* (one who hints) by making gestures that produce the acquisition of requisites.
"Making deceit, flattery, and hinting the precursors" means acting as if his faculties were calm and his mind were tranquil, having placed the state of deceit and so forth at the very forefront.
"The five hindrances" refers to the five hindrances beginning with sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). "Without abandoning" means without cutting off.
"Corruptions of the mind" refers to the hindrances; for the hindrances corrupt the mind, making it defiled, obstructing it, and afflicting it.
Therefore, they are called "corruptions of the mind. "Weakening of wisdom" refers to the hindrances.
For when the hindrances arise, they do not allow unarisen wisdom to arise. Therefore, they are called "the weakeners of wisdom.
"With mindfulness unestablished" means that mindfulness is not established in the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). "Without having developed" means without having increased it.
"Unsurpassed perfect enlightenment" refers to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), which has the state of Arahatship as its basis.
In the final section, the phrase "a certain ascetic or brahmin" refers to the Omniscient Bodhisattva.
Therein, "free from all faults" means free from all faults that are contrary to the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*). By this, he demonstrates the state of having fulfilled the perfections.
The foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) are insight (*vipassanā*); the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are the path (*magga*); [and] the unsurpassed...
Perfect enlightenment is Arahantship. The foundations of mindfulness are insight; the factors of enlightenment are mixed; perfect enlightenment is Arahantship alone.
The remainder is to be understood from the opposites stated in the immediately preceding section.

"Knowledge herein" refers to the knowledge that occurs regarding what is a possible case as a possible case, and what is an impossible case as an impossible case, in the manner described above. "By way of cause":
"By way of the cause of what is possible and what is impossible. "Possible" means at that very moment, immediately following the adverting of the mind.
"Without restriction" means by way of the absence of a limit; the sense is that nothing is left out.

Thus, in such phrases as "gone to what is possible and impossible," they have reached the state of being possible and impossible. "All" refers to those whose intrinsic nature is exhaustion, passing away, fading away, and cessation.

Conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*)—which serve as the basis for the designation of "sentient beings"—fall into three categories: some go to heaven, being those who practice in accordance with the Dhamma;
some go to the states of misery, being those who practice contrary to the Dhamma; and some go to Nibbāna, being those who have entered the Noble Path that brings about the destruction of karma.
Now, explaining the meaning just stated, [the Buddha] spoke two verses beginning with: "All beings shall die."
He himself explains its meaning with the words, "All beings... both noble and ignoble," and so forth.
In that context, "having life as their limit, having death as their limit" means that the limit of life is the end, which is defined as death.

Regarding the phrase "they will go according to their karma," the meaning here is that this going of beings according to their karma constitutes the principle of being the owner of one's own actions (*kammassakata*).

The meaning is that by the expression "those who experience the fruits of merit and evil," both the direct manifestation of the fruit of kamma and the non-withdrawal [of that fruit] from those who have performed and accumulated kamma are shown. *Kammanta* is simply *kamma*;
those for whom there is evil *kammanta* are "evil-doers" (*pāpakammantā*). To show the meaning of this:
“Meritorious formations” (apuññasaṅkhārā) is what was said. They are called “meritorious formations” because meritorious formation belongs to them.
Alternatively, it is an ablative expression meaning “due to evil conduct”; the sense is “because of evil conduct. The same applies to “meritorious formations” and so forth.
Furthermore, by means of the two extremes—beginning with “those of evil conduct [go] to hell”—he shows the middle way. Likewise...
By the passage beginning “This is defilement,” three alternative meanings of the verse are shown according to the rounds of existence and its reversal,
the disadvantage and the escape, and the cause and the fruit. Again, by the passage beginning “Hell for those of evil deeds—
this is defilement,” he shows the meaning of the verse according to purification.
59. "By this or that" means by this or that object of attachment, such as existence in the realm of form (*rūpabhava*) or existence in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*).

"Thirty-six" refers to craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*): first, there are six types according to the distinction of objects such as visible forms; likewise, there are eighteen types consisting of craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) and craving for non-existence (*vibhavataṇhā*).
These same [eighteen] applied to internal forms and so forth make eighteen, and applied to external forms and so forth they make another eighteen; thus, there are thirty-six.
"By whatever [means]" refers to [the views] such as "beauty is happiness.
The statement "defilement by craving," and so forth, was spoken in order to show that purification is threefold according to the three aggregates.
Furthermore, the statement beginning with "All beings will die" was spoken to show the meaning of the verses by way of the analysis of the methods of practice (*paṭipadā*).
"Leading to this or that" means leading to Nibbāna in each respective case; the meaning is that it has the nature of going to Nibbāna.
Furthermore, in order to show the distinction between the paths that lead to this or that and those that lead everywhere, the passage beginning with "three groups" was stated.
"That" refers to hell and so forth. It is called "leading everywhere" because it leads to each respective place as appropriate. [This applies] to what is designated as the path...
The Blessed One’s knowledge of the manifestation [of paths] according to their specific divisions— namely, the path leading to demeritorious action, the path leading to meritorious action,

and the path leading to the exhaustion of action— is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the way that leads everywhere. For by means of this knowledge, the Blessed One understands every path exactly as it is.
How so? Even when all the inhabitants of a village are killing a single pig or deer, the volition (*cetanā*) of everyone has precisely the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) of another as its object;
yet that karma differs for them at the very moment of its accumulation (*āyūhana*).
For among them, one acts with earnestness, another acts because he is pressured by others saying, "You too must do it," and another acts out of a shared desire.

Having become like that, he wanders about without being obstructed. Among them, one is reborn in hell by that very kamma, one in the animal realm, and one in the sphere of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya).

The Tathāgata knows this at the very moment of the accumulation [of kamma]: "Because it was accumulated in this manner, this one will be reborn in hell; this one in the animal realm; this one in the sphere of hungry ghosts."
He knows even one being reborn in hell: "This one will be reborn in the eight great hells; this one in the sixteen sub-hells.
He knows even one being reborn in the animal realm: "This one will be legless; this one two-legged; this one four-legged; this one many-legged.
He knows even one being reborn in the sphere of hungry ghosts: "This one will be one of parched thirst..."
He knows: "This one will be hungry and thirsty; this one will live dependent on the gifts of others.
And among those karmas, he knows: "This karma will draw down rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), while this one will not draw it down because it is weak;
having given the rebirth-linking, it will merely ripen within the existing aggregates (upadhi). Likewise, regarding all the inhabitants of a village...
When all are giving gifts on one occasion, the volition of everyone has the object of the gift as its focus;
however, that kamma becomes differentiated for them at the very moment of accumulation (*āyūhana*). For among them, some are reborn in the deva-world and some in the human world.
The Tathāgata knows this at the very moment of accumulation: "Because it was accumulated in this manner, this person will be reborn in the human world."
He knows, "This one will be reborn in the world of the gods. There too, he knows, "This one will be reborn among the Paranimmitavasavatti gods;
this one will be reborn among the earth-dwelling gods (Bhummadeva); this one will be reborn as the chief king of the gods;
and this one will be reborn as an attendant, occupying the second or third rank under him."
And regarding those kamma-formations, he knows: "This one will be able to draw forth rebirth-linking; this one will not be able, being weak;
having given the rebirth-linking, it will merely result in the ripening of the substrate. Likewise, among those who have established insight, he knows:
"Because he has commenced insight in this manner, he will become an Arahant; this one..."
"This one is a non-returner; this one is a once-returner; this one is a stream-enterer; this one is a 'single-seed' person, a 'clansman-to-clansman,' or one who will be reborn seven times at most;
this one will not be able to attain the path and will remain fixed in insight (vipassanā) that takes the characteristics as its object;
this one will remain in the discernment of conditions, this one in the discernment of name-and-form, and this one in the discernment of the formless; this one will define only the primary elements."
“He will not be able to discern anything at all,” he knows. “Even among those performing the preliminary work for the kasiṇas, this one will remain at the mere stage of the preliminary work;
this one will be able to produce the sign, but not absorption.
This one will produce absorption, but this one will attain the jhāna, yet not the higher distinction. This one [will attain] even the higher distinction...”
“He will attain [it]”—thus he knows.

"Of many elements" (*anekadhātu*): it is called "of many elements" because it possesses many elements, such as the eye and so forth, and the earth element and so forth; the meaning is "possessing many elements.
"The world" (*loka*) refers to the world of the aggregates, bases, and so forth. "The eye element," etc., refers to those elements by which the world is said to be "of many elements."

...spoken; [this is] the demonstration of them according to their specific nature. Therein, it is a *dhātu* (element) in the sense of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being (*nissatta*).
"The eye itself is the element" is the "eye-element" (*cakkhudhātu*). The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

Regarding the term "sense-sphere of desire" (*kāmadhātu*), there are two kinds of desire: defilement-desire (*kilesakāma*) and object-desire (*vatthukāma*). From the perspective of defilement-desire, the element associated with desire is the "sense-sphere of desire"; this is a designation for sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*).

This is the name [of the element]. In the case of sensual objects as the basis (*vatthukāma*), however, sense-sphere phenomena (*kāmāvacara-dhammā*) are called "sensual pleasure" (*kāma*) through the elision of the latter member of the compound;
and since it is both sensual pleasure and an element (*dhātu*), it is the "sensual element" (*kāmadhātu*). An element associated with ill will (*byāpāda*) is the "ill-will element" (*byāpādadhātu*);

this is a name for the thought of ill will (*byāpādavitakka*). Alternatively, ill will itself is the element, hence "ill-will element"; this is a name for the aversion (*paṭigha*) whose object consists of the ten bases of resentment (*āghātavatthu*). [An element] associated with cruelty...
The *vihiṃsā-dhātu* is the element of cruelty, which is the thought of cruelty (*vihiṃsā-vitakka*). Alternatively, cruelty itself is the element of cruelty;

this is a name for the harming of other beings. It should be understood that the elements of renunciation, non-ill-will, and non-cruelty are all wholesome states beginning with thoughts of renunciation, as well as loving-kindness (*mettā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*).

The "form element" (*rūpa-dhātu*) refers to existence in the form realm (*rūpa-bhava*), or alternatively, all phenomena consisting of form. The "formless element" (*arūpa-dhātu*) refers to existence in the formless realm (*arūpa-bhava*).

Or they are immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhammā*). The element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*) is the craving for cessation. The element of formations (*saṅkhāradhātu*) refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhatadhammā*). The rest is easy to understand.
Because it possesses various elements that are mutually distinct in their characteristics, it is called "the world of diverse elements" (*nānādhātu*).

For this very reason it was said: "The eye-element is one thing, up to the element of Nibbāna is another. And just as this knowledge [discerns] through the distinctions of the eye-element and so forth...

By way of the world of appropriated formations (*upādinnaka-saṅkhāra-loka*), one understands the world of many elements and various elements; likewise, one understands it by way of the world of unappropriated formations (*anupādinnaka-saṅkhāra-loka*).
For indeed, the Paccekabuddhas and the two Chief Disciples know only the diversity of the world of appropriated formations, and even that only partially, not exhaustively.
[They do not know] the world of unappropriated formations...
However, they do not know the diversity [of these elements]. The Blessed One, however, knows:
"Due to the predominance of this particular element, the trunk of this tree is white; of that, it is black; of that, smooth; of that, rough; of that, thick; of that, thin-skinned.
Due to the predominance of this particular element, the leaf of this tree [varies] by way of color, shape, and so forth."
It is of such a nature: because of the predominance of this particular element, the flowers of this tree are blue, yellow, red, or white; they are fragrant or foul-smelling.
Because of the predominance of this particular element, the fruit is small or large, long or round, well-shaped or ill-shaped, smooth or rough.
"It is fragrant, foul-smelling, bitter, sweet, pungent, sour, or astringent; through the predominance of this particular element,
the thorn of this tree is sharp, or excessively sharp, straight, crooked, black, blue, or white"— in this way,
he understands the state of manifold elements and diverse elements even by way of the world of non-clung-to formations.
For this is the power of the omniscient Buddhas alone, and not of others.

60. "Whatever element" means whatever nature, whether inferior or otherwise. Since what is called "adhimutti" (resolute intention) is the element of inclination (*ajjhāsayadhātu*), therefore "adhimuccana" (the act of resolving) is the occurrence of that inclination by way of an inferior or other nature. And that [occurrence] belongs to that [person] in each respective case.
It is said, "there is resolving and adherence," thus: "they resolve; they resolve upon that very thing and adhere to it.
To show the object of resolution by way of classification, it was said: "some are resolved upon form," and so forth.
This is indeed easy to understand. "Knowledge of the diversity of inclinations" is the knowledge of the diversity of inclinations by way of the inferior and so forth.
"And they become according to their inclinations" means that those beings—whether of inferior inclination or superior inclination—act according to whatever they are inclined toward.
"They undertake various undertakings of action" means that they perform various actions to be undertaken and done by themselves, corresponding to their respective inclinations.
Analyzing those undertakings of action by way of their origination:
He said, “That action is sixfold,” and so forth. In that context, it should be connected thus: “some undertake action by way of greed.
This same method applies to the remaining cases as well. When that [action] is analyzed: being sixfold by way of its origination, it is further twofold when analyzed by way of proceeding and ceasing.
"Whatever action one performs through greed, hatred, and delusion" refers to the ten courses of unwholesome action (*dasākusala-kammapatha*).
For that, because it is defiled, is "black" (*kaṇha*); and because it causes rebirth in the states of misery, it has a "black ripening" (*kaṇhavipāka*).
"Whatever action one performs through faith" refers to the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusala-kammapatha*). For that...
It is called "white" (*sukka*) because it is undefiled (*asaṃkiliṭṭha*). It is "white-resultant" (*sukkavipāka*) because it produces rebirth in heaven and has a white ripening (*vipāka*).
That karma which one performs through greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as through faith, is "black-and-white" (*kaṇhasukka*), meaning mixed karma.
"Black-and-white-resultant" means having pleasure and pain as its ripening. For, having performed mixed karma, by the power of the unwholesome...

One born in the animal realm in the form of a state-elephant experiences happiness through wholesome [kamma], while one reborn even in a royal family experiences suffering through unwholesome [kamma].
Whatever kamma one performs by way of energy and wisdom, this kamma is neither black nor white, and its ripening is neither black nor white; it is that which brings about the exhaustion of kamma.
The volition of the four paths. For if that were black, it would yield a black result; if it were white, it would yield a white rebirth-included result.
However, because it does not yield either of those two results, it is "neither-black-nor-white-resultant"—this is the meaning here. Regarding the undertaking of kamma:
first is the practice of the naked ascetics (acelakas) consisting of the drinking of sensual pleasures; second is that of one with intense defilements, even when weeping with tears on his face...
The practice of the pure holy life while weeping; the third is the practice of the naked asceticism consisting in not falling into sensual desires;
the fourth is the practice of the holy life of the Dispensation for one who possesses the bliss of *jhāna* and *vipassanā*, even when failing to obtain the necessary requisites.
"Whatever kind of undertaking of action of this sort" refers to whatever other action of a similar nature there may be. "By this person," and so forth.
This is the demonstration of the manner in which the Blessed One’s knowledge functions regarding that ripening of kamma.
In this context, "accumulated" (*upacita*) means performed in such a way that the kamma becomes capable of yielding its fruit; it is thus "accumulated.

"Unripened" (*avipakka*) means its result has not yet matured. "Present for the sake of ripening" (*vipākāya paccupaṭṭhita*) means it has been given the opportunity to grant its result. And "not capable of going forth to liberation" (*na ca bhabbo abhinibbidhā gantuṃ*) means...

Because he has no capacity to attain the Noble Path—which is termed "emergence" (abhinibbidhā) due to its breaking out from the formative forces of the defilements—the Blessed One does not instruct him.
Thus, the Blessed One does not instruct such a person, who is shrouded by the obstruction of karmic fruition (vipākāvaraṇa), with a view toward the penetration of the Truths;
however, for the sake of creating a latent predisposition (vāsanā), He still teaches the Dhamma even to such individuals.
"Thus," as in the case of Ajātasattu and others.
"Accumulated" means having begun to be performed. For this very reason he said: "but it has not yet reached completion.

By this, he shows its incapacity for the fixed course of wrongness (micchattaniyāma). "Before it reaches completion" refers to the state of being capable of producing the fruit, which is "completion."
He goes before he might attain [the fruit]. By way of being fixed in falsehood (*micchattaniyatatā*), he immediately produces a state of being unfit for the dharma of the fruit before [it arises].
For this very reason it was said: "Before he transcends the state of being trainable (*veneyyatta*).
There is also a reading, "Before he transcends the indeterminate (*aniyata*)," which has the same meaning. "In the incomplete" means when the karma is not fulfilled, or those two are not fulfilled.

61. Having thus shown the obstacle of karma mixed with the obstacle of defilement (*kilesantarāya*), [the text] now says, “And of this person,” etc., in order to show the unadulterated obstacle of karma. That is exactly according to the method already stated.
“Of all” refers to all the karmas mentioned in this exposition of power (*balaniddesa*). “Weak, medium, and intense” means the state of being weak, medium, and strong.
For it is by virtue of the weak and other states of the karmas themselves that their respective results (*vipāka*) become weak, medium, or intense.

The intended meaning is "it is understood. Regarding the terms *diṭṭhadhammavedanīya* and so forth: the fruit to be experienced in the present life, that is, in this current personal existence (*attabhāva*), is *diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*.
The fruit to be experienced in the next rebirth, that is, in the immediately following personal existence, is *upapajjavedanīya*.
That which is to be experienced in another personal existence—that is, in any other personal existence subsequent to this—is [the third type].

The fruit is to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparāpariyavedanīya*). For within a single impulsion series (*ekajavanavāra*), among the seven volitions (*cetanā*), the first volition is called "to be experienced in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*);
the final volition is called "to be experienced upon rebirth" (*upapajjavedanīya*); and the five volitions in between are called "to be experienced in subsequent lives.
"Knowledge of the diversity of ripening" (*vipākavemattatāñāṇa*) is knowledge regarding the distinctions in ripening due to the diversity of ripening. Now, as for this ripening of kamma:

The excellence of rebirth, the failure of rebirth, the excellence of the physical basis, the failure of the physical basis, the excellence of the time, the failure of the time, the excellence of the application, and the failure of the application are the causes.
And this causal nature of theirs is to be understood from such scriptural passages as:
"There are certain undertakings of evil kamma that, being obstructed by the excellence of rebirth, do not ripen."
62. In order to show that the jhānas and so forth are included by the very phrase "undertaking of kamma" mentioned in the *Anantarabalaniddesa*, it is said:
"of such undertakings of kamma," and so on. The jhānas and so forth occurring within the mental continuums of trainees (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) constitute kamma.
In this context, "of such undertakings" refers to [kamma] that is "bright, with bright result, and pleasant in the present."
In the case of kamma undertaken in such ways as "with a result of happiness in the future," etc., *saṃkileso* (defilement) is the state of being stained by way of opposing states;
*vodānaṃ* (cleansing) is purification by means of those opposing states; and *vuṭṭhānaṃ* (emergence) is both the emergence of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and the proficiency of that cleansing.
In phrases such as "it becomes defiled in this way," the meaning is precisely this: in this manner, jhāna and so forth become defiled or cleansed.
“He emerges” refers to the knowledge of knowing; it is the Blessed One’s unobstructed knowledge, for there is no obstruction to it.
The passage beginning with “How many jhānas? is commenced in order to show the jhānas and so forth by way of classification.

“Four jhānas” is said with reference to the fine-material-sphere jhānas according to the fourfold method. “Eleven” refers to the eight [attainments] beginning with “one possessing form sees forms,” and the three...
This is stated by way of the emptiness liberation (*suññatavimokkha*) and so forth. "Eight" refers to those eight [liberations] excluding the supramundane (*lokuttara*) liberation among them.

"Seven" refers to those same [eight] excluding the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). "Three" refers, according to the method of the discourses (*suttantapariyāya*), to the three beginning with the emptiness liberation.
"Two" refers, according to the method of the Abhidhamma, to the remaining two, because the signless liberation (*animittavimokkha*) is not possible [in that context]. Herein...

Furthermore, they are called "liberations" (*vimokkha*) because, in their respective sequence, at each moment of absorption, they are liberated from adverse states by way of suppression and because they resolve upon their objects.
The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), however, is called "the liberation by departure" (*apagamavimokkha*) because it is liberated from all perceptions and feelings.
And the supramundane [paths] are [liberations] by way of the total eradication of the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path.
Because it is liberated, it is called "liberation"—this distinction should be understood.

Among the meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), according to both the fourfold and fivefold systems, the concentration of the first jhāna is called "concentration with applied thought and sustained thought" (*savitakka savicāra samādhi*).

In the fivefold system, the concentration of the second jhāna is called "concentration without applied thought and with sustained thought only" (*avitakka vicāramatta samādhi*). In the fourfold system...
In the fivefold method as well, in the remaining jhānas, concentration is called "concentration without applied thought and sustained thought" (avitakka-avicāra-samādhi).
Among the attainments, for the eight attainments in their successive order, the name is both "concentration" (samādhi) and "attainment" (samāpatti). Why?

Because of the presence of one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā). In the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), because that [one-pointedness] is absent, it does not bear the name "concentration."
The attainment of perception (*saññāsamāpatti*) and so forth have already been explained above.

Regarding "concentration partaking of decline" (*hānabhāgiyo samādhi*): for one who has emerged from the first jhāna and so forth that lack proficiency, the intrusion of sensual desire and other defilements through perceptions and mental attention constitutes the state of being "partaking of decline" for that concentration of the first jhāna and so forth. [As it is said: "Of the first jhāna..."
Because it is stated that "sensual lust and ill will are defilements," this should be applied by way of the second jhāna and so forth.
"Kukkuṭa" is said to mean the supreme state [of meditation] by way of the mouth of disgust for what is unworthy. "A kukkuṭajhāyī" refers to persons;
thus, it is said that the jhānas are mentioned [here], namely the first and second jhānas. One who, having produced either the first or the second jhāna...
Thinking, “Enough with this much,” he falls into despondency and does not strive further; his four jhānas are called “hen-jhānas,” and one who possesses them is a “hen-jhāyer.
Among those, the first two are described as being of the nature of defilement because their adversaries are near and powerful, and because they lack the quality of distinction.
However, the others, although lacking the quality of distinction, [are not so described].
It should be understood that these are described as having the nature of purification because they are the adversaries of dullness.

Regarding "concentration partaking of distinction": for one who has emerged from the first jhāna and so forth when they are proficient, the leaping forward into the second jhāna and so forth through perception and attention, as well as the emergence from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) with a purified state of proficiency, is called "emergence" (vuṭṭhāna).
For each lower jhāna that has been mastered is the proximate cause (padatthāna) for each higher one;

therefore, purification (vodāna) is also called "emergence" (vuṭṭhāna). Since emergence from all jhānas occurs by way of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the life-continuum is both purification and emergence.
Furthermore, because of mastery over emergence, [one remains] in attainment for as long as the time has been delimited.
Emergence occurs; therefore, skill in emerging from attainment is here termed "emergence. 63.
"Of that very concentration" refers to the concentration described by way of the synonyms such as "jhāna" and so forth in the exposition of the immediately preceding power.
"Requisites" means equipment. "Faculties" refers to the faculties of faith, mindfulness, and wisdom. "Powers" refers to [the powers] together with moral shame and moral dread.
They are together with those very same [factors]. The separate mention of energy (*vīriya*) is for the purpose of showing its great assistance to the powers (*bala*).
For it is through the support of energy that faith and the other faculties become unshakable by their opposites. Therefore he said: "The powers come to be by way of energy.
"Of these" refers to the faculties. "Weak, medium, and superior" means: not clear is weak; not very clear is medium; very clear is superior.
That which is excessive and powerful is called "sharp" (*tikkha*).
To show that the Blessed One’s delivery of the teaching conforms to the faculties (*indriya*) of those to be trained (*veneyya*), the passage beginning with "Therein the Blessed One...
was stated. In that context, "by way of brief and detailed exposition" means by way of a detailed exposition of what is brief; or alternatively, "by way of the brief."

"By mere recitation" means by the brief [recitation]. "In brief and in detail" means by way of the summary (uddesa) and the exposition (niddesa). "In detail" means by way of the summary, the exposition, and the sub-exposition (paṭiniddesa).
"Gently" means lightly, without making it heavy by way of censuring [the student] through fear of the states of woe, fear of the round of existence, and so forth.

"Gentle yet sharp" means not excessively sharp; rather, it makes [the teaching] weighty by way of generating a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) through the bases for such urgency. "He teaches calm" (samathaṃ upadisati).
The intention is that he teaches by making serenity (samatha) predominant, and not insight (vipassanā) in that way;
for the penetration of the Truths is not possible through serenity alone. "Serenity-and-insight" refers to serenity-and-insight in equal measure.
He teaches "insight" as insight that is preeminent. And because those with sharp faculties and so forth are precisely those who understand through a condensed explanation (ugghaṭitaññū) and so on.

Therefore, it is said: “He points out the escape for one of keen faculties,” and so forth. In that context, regarding the phrase “by means of the training in higher wisdom” (*adhipaññāsikkhāya*), this refers to the training in higher wisdom itself.
As for the clause “the knowledge which [arises] herein”: here, the knowledge that arises due to the dull, medium, or superior state of the faculties should be connected as follows:
“this is called the knowledge of the diversity in the mastery over the faculties of other beings and other persons.”
In order to show the manner in which that knowledge functions, it is said: "This person has gone to this plane," and so forth.
Therein, "this person has gone to this plane and to purification" means that this individual has gone, goes, and will go to this defilement-habituation, purification, and life-continuum;
this is because there is no intention to specify a particular time, just as one says "milk" [to refer to milk in general]. At this moment...

At this time, by means of this instruction distinguished as soft, medium, and sharp. "Of such an element" means having such an inclination, having such a disposition, according to the classification of inferior and so forth.

"And this is his underlying tendency (*āsaya*)" refers to the underlying tendency of this person, which takes the form of eternalism or annihilationism, or the form of receptivity (*khanti*) conforming to knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtañāṇa*). For it is here that beings have these four kinds of underlying tendencies.

That which they dwell upon is called their "abode" (*āsaya*). Furthermore, the Blessed One, knowing the abodes of beings, knows even at the moment when those views, insight-knowledge, and the knowledge of the ownership of one's own actions (*kammassakatā*) are not occurring. And this has been said:
"He knows one who indulges in sensual pleasures: 'This person is heavy with sensual pleasures, has an abode in sensual pleasures, and is intent on sensual pleasures. Kāma...
He knows one who cultivates renunciation: "This person values renunciation, is inclined toward renunciation, and is intent upon renunciation.
He knows one who cultivates renunciation... ill will... non-ill will... sloth-and-torpor... the perception of light:
"This person values sloth-and-torpor, is inclined toward sloth-and-torpor, and is intent upon sloth-and-torpor."
"This underlying tendency" means this underlying defilement, such as sensual lust and so forth, which has not yet been abandoned in this person.
For an underlying tendency (*anusaya*) is a defilement that has become firmly rooted precisely because it has not been abandoned. "Of other beings" refers to preeminent beings.

"Of other persons" refers to those other beings who are inferior; this is the meaning. Alternatively, these two terms have the same referent, being used according to the needs of those to be trained (*veneyya*).

It is stated in two ways. Regarding "knowledge of the diversity in the penetration of others' faculties" (*indriyaparopariyattavemattatāñāṇa*): *paropariyattaṃ* refers to both the state of being another (*parabhāva*) and the state of not being another (*aparabhāva*), with the letter *a* changed to *o*;

the diversity of that is "diversity in the penetration of others" (*paropariyattavemattatā*). The analysis of the compound should be understood as: "knowledge of the diversity in the penetration of others' faculties" (*indriyaparopariyattavemattatāñāṇa*), meaning the knowledge of the diversity in the penetration of the faculties such as faith and the rest.
In this context, "that which" refers to the Blessed One’s knowledge by way of recollecting his manifold former existences;
the connection is that "this is the eighth power of a Tathāgata. "Manifold" (*anekavihitam*) means of many kinds, or having proceeded in many ways.
"Former existence" (*pubbenivāsam*) refers to what one desires to recollect—namely, the immediately preceding past of oneself and others.
"Taking existence as the beginning" means the continuum dwelling here and there [in various births].

"He recollects" means he remembers by following the sequence of births in this manner: "one birth, two births," and so on; or it means he remembers immediately, in the sense that he remembers as soon as his mind is directed toward it.
For the Blessed One has no need for preliminary work (*parikamma*); he remembers by mere adverting (*āvajjana*) alone.
“Seyyathidaṃ” is a particle used in the sense of indicating the manner in which something has begun.

“Ekampi jātiṃ” means even a single birth, that is, a single continuum of aggregates (khandhasantāna) comprised within one existence, beginning with rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and ending with death (cuti). This same method applies to the phrases “two births,” and so forth.

However, in the phrases “many eons of dissolution” (saṃvaṭṭakappa) and so on, an eon that is contracting is a “eon of dissolution” (saṃvaṭṭakappa), while one that is expanding is an “eon of evolution” (vivaṭṭakappa).

It should be understood. In this context, by means of the contraction (*saṃvaṭṭa*), the period of subsistence during contraction (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*) is included because it has that as its root; and by means of the expansion (*vivaṭṭa*), the period of subsistence during expansion (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*) is included.
For when this is so, all those [periods] which were stated thus—"Bhikkhus, there are these four incalculable eons of a kappa. Which four?
The eon of contraction, the period of subsistence during contraction, the eon of expansion, and the period of subsistence during expansion"—are fully encompassed.

[They] exist. "In such-and-such a place," and so forth, is a demonstration of the mode of recollection. Therein, "in such-and-such a place" means in such-and-such an eon of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭakappa*), or in such-and-such a state of existence, a womb, a destination, a station of consciousness, an abode of beings, or a class of beings.
"Of such a name" means Tissa or Phussa. "Of such a clan" means Bhaggava or Gotama. "Of such a complexion" means...
"Fair-skinned or dark-skinned": thus he is one whose food is such; that is, one whose food consists of boiled rice with meat or one who subsists on wild fruits.
"Experiencing pleasure and pain in this way": he is an experiencer of various kinds of bodily and mental pleasure and pain, distinguished as being both carnal and non-carnal.
"Having such a limit to his lifespan": having such a limit to his lifespan, whether it be a maximum of a hundred years or a maximum of eighty-four thousand eons.

"Or: 'Having passed away from there, I arose elsewhere' means that having passed away from that state of existence or from that class of beings (*sattanikāya*), I arose again in such-and-such a class of beings.
Or else: 'I existed there,' meaning in that state of existence or in that class of beings. The phrase "of such a name," etc., has already been explained.

Regarding the passage beginning with "by the divine" (*dibbena*), it is called "divine" because it resembles the divine. For even though it is produced by the kamma of good conduct performed by deities, it is not [produced] by bile, phlegm, blood, and so forth.
The divine eye of clear vision (*pasādacakkhu*) is unobstructed because it is free from defilements, and it is capable of grasping objects even at a distance.

This eye of knowledge (*ñāṇacakkhu*), which is produced by the power of the development of energy (*vīriyabhāvanābala*), is exactly like that; thus, it is "divine" because it resembles the divine eye.
Alternatively, it is "divine" because it is obtained through the practice of the divine abidings (*dibbavihāra*), and also because it itself is supported by the divine abidings.

It is "divine" (dibba) because it possesses great radiance through its grasping of light; it is also "divine" because it has a vast range through its seeing of forms located beyond walls and so forth.
All of this should be understood according to the science of grammar (*saddasattha*). It is "the eye" (*cakkhu*) in the sense of seeing.

It is also "the eye" because it performs the function of the eye, as if it were an eye. It is "purified" (*visuddha*) because it is a cause for the purification of view through the seeing of death and rebirth. For whoever...
One who perceives only death and not rebirth adopts the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-diṭṭhi*).
One who perceives only rebirth and not death adopts the view of the manifestation of new beings (*nava-satta-pātubhāva-diṭṭhi*).
However, one who perceives both of these transcends both of those types of views; therefore, that vision of his is for the sake of purification of views (*diṭṭhi-visuddhi-hetu*).
It exists. And the Blessed One sees both of these. Therefore it was said: "It is purified because seeing the passing away and rebirth is a cause for the purification of view.
Or else, it is purified because it is free from the eleven defilements.
As it was said: "Anuruddha, having understood: 'Doubt is a defilement of the mind,' I [abandoned] doubt..."
He abandoned the defilement of the mind. Having understood: “Inattention is a defilement of the mind... lethargy and drowsiness... trepidation... elation... coarseness...
over-exertion of energy... under-exertion of energy... longing... perceptions of diversity...
and excessive preoccupation with forms is a defilement of the mind,” he [abandoned] excessive preoccupation with forms.
"...abandoned the defilement of the mind," and so forth.

Thus, it is pure by virtue of being free from these eleven defilements. It is "surpassing the human" because it sees forms after having transcended the range of human beings, or because it has surpassed the fleshly eye (*maṃsacakkhu*). By means of that divine...
"With the purified eye that surpasses the human":
he sees beings; that is, like a human with the fleshly eye, he sees and observes beings.
Regarding the phrase "passing away and being reborn," it is not possible even for the divine eye to see [beings] at the precise moment of death or at the precise moment of rebirth.
However, those who are near death and will pass away now, as well as those who have already taken rebirth and have just been born, are intended by the phrase "passing away and being reborn.
It is regarding such beings passing away and being reborn in this way that [the text speaks].

"Inferior" means despised and held in contempt by way of low birth, family, wealth, and so forth, due to being associated with the outflow of delusion (*moha*). "Superior" means [the opposite], due to being associated with the outflow of non-delusion (*amoha*).

The opposite of that [is the case for the following]. "Beautiful" (*suvaṇṇa*) means possessing a color that is desirable, lovely, and pleasing because it is associated with the outflow of non-hatred (*adosa*).
"Ugly" (*dubbaṇṇa*) means possessing a color that is undesirable, unlovely, and displeasing because it is associated with the outflow of hatred; the meaning is "whether handsome or deformed.

"Well-gone" (*sugata*) means having gone to a good destination, or being wealthy and possessing great riches because it is associated with the outflow of non-greed (*alobha*). "Ill-gone" (*duggata*) means having gone to a bad destination, because it is associated with the outflow of greed (*lobha*).
Or [as] poor, with little food and drink. "According to their deeds" (*yathākammūpaga*) means that they have gone according to whatever karma has been accumulated.

Therein, by the preceding terms beginning with "passing away," the function of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*) is stated; but by this term, the function of the knowledge of rebirth according to one's deeds (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*) is stated.
Furthermore, the knowledge of rebirth according to one's deeds and the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*) both have the divine eye as their basis.
They succeed together with the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).

Regarding the phrases beginning with "bodily misconduct" (*kāyaduccarita*): it is "misconduct" because it is practiced badly, or because it is a bad practice due to being rotten with defilements (*kilesa*).

Bodily misconduct is misconduct committed by means of the body, or misconduct that proceeds from the body; thus it is "bodily misconduct. Verbal and mental misconduct are to be understood in the same way.

They are to be seen. "Endowed with" means possessed of. "Slanderers of the noble ones" refers to those who, by means of even the final category [of offenses] or by disparaging their virtues, revile, abuse, and censure the noble ones, beginning with the Buddha, including even lay stream-enterers.
"Holding wrong views" means having a perverted perspective. "Engaged in deeds based on wrong views" means having undertaken various kinds of kamma that have wrong view as their cause.
And those who encourage others in bodily actions and so forth rooted in wrong view.

In this context, although the reviling of the Noble Ones and wrong view are already included by the mention of verbal and mental misconduct, they are mentioned again for the purpose of showing their extreme blameworthiness.
For the reviling of the Noble Ones is extremely blameworthy, being like an immediate offense (*ānantariya*). As it has been said:
“Sāriputta, just as a bhikkhu endowed with virtue, endowed with concentration,
and endowed with wisdom might attain final knowledge in this very life, so too, Sāriputta, I say that one who does not abandon that speech,
does not abandon that mind, and does not relinquish that view is deposited in hell just as he was brought there.”
There is indeed nothing more blameworthy than wrong view. As it is said:

"Monks, I do not see even a single thing that is so blameworthy as wrong view, monks; wrong views are the supreme blameworthiness. "With the breakup of the body" means with the relinquishing of the aggregates that have been grasped.
"After death" means immediately thereafter, at the taking up of the newly produced aggregates.
Alternatively, "with the breakup of the body" means the cutting off of the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). "After death" means after the moment of death (*cuti*).

"The state of deprivation" (*apāya*) and so forth are all synonyms for hell (*niraya*). For hell is called *apāya* because it is devoid of the "gain" (*āya*) of merit that serves as the cause for heaven and liberation, or because it lacks the gain of happiness.
It is called a "bad destination" (*duggati*) because it is a resort (*gati*) or refuge (*paṭisaraṇa*) for suffering.

A *duggati* (bad destination) is a state of existence produced by an action corrupted by an abundance of hatred. It is a *vinipāta* (fall) because those who have committed evil deeds fall there helplessly (*vivasā*).
It is a *niraya* (hell) because there is no pleasure (*āyasaññita*) to be found therein.
Alternatively, by the mention of the *apāya* (woeful states), he indicates the animal realm; for the animal realm is indeed an *apāya*, as it is far removed from a happy destination.

Because they have departed [from the human state]. It is not an "evil destination" (*duggati*), because great beings such as the Naga kings and others can be born there. By the term "evil destination," he indicates the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*);
for that is both a state of loss (*apāya*) and an evil destination, as it has departed from a "good destination" (*sugati*) and is a place where suffering goes.
However, it is not a "fall" (*vinipāta*), because those like the Asuras do not fall [into it], for even celestial palaces (*vimāna*) are produced for hungry ghosts of great psychic power.

By the inclusion of the term *vinipāta* (the fallen), he indicates the host of *asuras*; for that, in the sense already stated, is called a *vinipāta* because it is both an *apāya* (a state of loss) and a *duggati* (an unhappy destination), owing to its falling away from the heights of happiness.
By the inclusion of the term *niraya* (hell), he indicates hell itself in its many varieties, such as *Avīci* and the rest.
*Upapannā* means "gone to" (*upagatā*), the intended meaning being "reborn there. This is the opposite of what was previously stated.
The bright side (sukkapakkha) is to be understood.

However, this is the distinction: here, by the inclusion of "a happy destination" (sugatī), one includes the human destination as well; by the inclusion of "heaven" (sagga), one includes only the divine destination.

In that context, a "happy destination" (sugati) is a beautiful destination. A "heaven" (sagga) is a place where one is excellently supreme (suṭṭhu aggo) through sense objects such as forms and so forth.
Thus, the etymological meaning is that the entire world (*loka*) is so called in the sense of breaking up and dissolving.

By combining the functions of the eighth and ninth powers of knowledge (*bala-ñāṇa*), it is shown that "due to what was accumulated by such-and-such a person in a previous aeon, they have now, or in the future, become one who goes to heaven or one who goes to a state of misery.
This is likewise the case in passages such as "even in a hundred thousand aeons," and so forth. For this very reason, he said: "These are two knowledges of the Blessed One."
“Māra was slain at the foot of the Bodhi tree”: Māra of the defilements was slain and utterly cut off at the root of the Bodhi tree.
This is the Blessed One’s tenth power; this slaying and cutting off of Māra of the defilements is the Blessed One’s tenth power.
Therefore it is said: “The knowledge of the total destruction of all taints. For when, by means of the path of Arahantship, [the taints] along with their latent tendencies...
When all taints were exhausted, it was then that the Blessed One attained omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*); therefore, it was said, "That which is the attainment of omniscience," and so forth.
This, first of all, is the teachers' exposition of the identical meaning here. However, an opponent says:

"There is no such thing as a separate 'knowledge of the ten powers' (*dasabalañāṇa*), because it is stated that 'having attained omniscience, all phenomena were known'; therefore, this [is merely] of the knowledge of omniscience itself."

Regarding the statement "the distinction," it should not be viewed in that way. For the knowledge of the ten powers (*dasabala-ñāṇa*) is indeed one thing, and the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññuta-ñāṇa*) is another.
The knowledge of the ten powers knows only its own respective functions, whereas the knowledge of omniscience knows those as well as what remains beyond them.
Among the knowledges of the ten powers, the first knows only what is a cause and what is not a cause; the second knows only the delimitation of kamma.
The third [chapter] concerns the diversity of elements (*dhātu-nānatta*) alone; the fourth, the underlying disposition and resolution (*ajjhāsaya-adhimutti*) alone;

the fifth, the interval between the maturation of kamma (*kamma-vipāka-antara*) alone; the sixth, their defilement and so forth together with the jhānas and other states; the seventh, the sharpness or dullness of the faculties (*indriya*) alone;

the eighth, the continuity of the aggregates in previous existences (*pubbenivuttha-khandha-santati*) alone; the ninth, the passing away and rebirth of beings (*sattānaṃ cutūpapāta*) alone; and the tenth—

It performs only the function of defining the truths. However, the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa) understands both what is to be known by these [other knowledges] and what lies beyond them;
yet it does not perform all their specific functions. For that [knowledge], being unable to enter as jhāna, cannot exercise transformation through psychic power (iddhi);
and being unable to act as the path, it cannot eradicate the defilements (kilesas).

Furthermore, the opponent should be asked: "Is this so-called knowledge of the Ten Powers with applied thought and sustained thought, or without applied thought and with sustained thought only, or without applied thought and without sustained thought;

is it of the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere; is it mundane or supramundane? Knowing the answer, he would say: "In sequence, the first seven are with applied thought and sustained thought, and the two following them are without applied thought and without sustained thought."

The knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa) may be with applied thought and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra), it may be without applied thought and with sustained thought only (avitakka-vicāramatta), or it may be without applied thought and without sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra).

Likewise, he will state that there are seven mundane knowledges belonging to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) in succession, followed by two belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), and finally one supramundane (lokuttara).
However, the knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) is exclusively with applied thought and sustained thought, belongs exclusively to the sense sphere, and is exclusively mundane.
The conclusion must be reached here.
The commentary on the section on the Mode of Conveying Investigation is finished.
3. Commentary on the Section on the Mode of Conveying Reasoning (Yuttihāra).

65. Having thus expanded upon the application of the Mode of Conveying Investigation through various methods, the following section beginning with “In this regard, what is the application of the Mode of Conveying Reasoning?
is now commenced in order to demonstrate the application of the Mode of Conveying Reasoning and so forth.

Therein, the word-meaning of the verse “Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded... has already been explained in detail. [It means that] for one whose mind is guarded, there will be the range of right intention.

"It is fitting" (*yujjati*): for one who dwells having closed the doors—the six sense faculties including the mind—with the bolt of mindfulness, there is no opportunity at all for wrong intentions such as sensual thoughts;

thus, it is fitting that only right intention, consisting of thoughts of renunciation and so forth, shall become his range and sphere of activity. By way of this reasoning, it is joined and harmonized.
The meaning is "he comes together. One whose range of activity is right intention will become one of right view;
according to the method already stated, a person whose range of activity is right intention will, through his thoughts, become one of right view without error.
Dwelling with insight-knowledge—known as right view—preceding him, he will penetrate, through path-knowledge, the arising and passing away of the five aggregates without delusion.
And one who penetrates thus will abandon all states of existence known as the miserable destinies because they have suffering as their intrinsic nature;
consequently, one will transcend all fear of the lower realms and all fear of saṃsāra. Thus, this entire meaning is entirely logical.
The commentary on the Mode of Conveying Logical Connections is finished.
4. Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Footings (Padaṭṭhāna-hārasampātavaṇṇanā) 66.
One’s intention becomes well-ordered as if it were one’s own prosperity. Since guarding the doors of the sense faculties is a proximate cause for the fulfillment of good conduct, he said:
"Of one whose mind is guarded" is the footing for the three types of good conduct. This is the meaning.
“Of one whose mind is guarded”: this is a statement regarding the foundation for the three types of good conduct.

For one who abounds in the intention of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*) and so forth, the abandoning of hindrances such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is easy; thus, the intention of renunciation and the others are proximate causes for serenity (*samatha*).
Therefore it is said: “The domain of right intention is the foundation for serenity. Regarding the right view of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakatā-sammādiṭṭhi*):

And standing in right view that sees name-and-form as conditioned, one perceives the suffering of saṃsāra as dependent upon a self and undertakes insight (vipassanā) as the means to transcend it; thus, he says:
"Having right view as the foremost is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for insight," because it is the specific cause for insight. One who exerts oneself in the vision of arising and passing away...

"One enters the certainty of rightness" means that this is the cause for the attainment of the first path; thus it is said: "Having known arising and passing away is the proximate cause for the plane of vision.
Overcoming sloth and torpor through the application of attention to the perception of light and so forth is the immediate cause for energy;
thus it is said: "A bhikkhu who has overcome sloth and torpor is the proximate cause for energy."

Even though, at the moment of the Noble Path, abandoning and cultivation are simultaneous because a single clear realization (*ekābhisamaya*) is intended, nevertheless, since there is no fulfillment of cultivation in the absence of the abandoning of what is to be abandoned, cultivation is described as having the aspect of abandoning:
“‘Abandon all miserable destinies’ is the proximate cause for cultivation. Alternatively: “All miserable destinies...”
The words “Just as... are the Blessed One’s statement praising the benefits for the purpose of generating enthusiasm in yogis;
thus it is said that they are the specific cause for development: “All... [the foundation]...
The commentary on the Mode of Conveying Foundations (padaṭṭhāna-hārasampāta) is finished.
5. Explanation of the Convergence of the Modes of Conveying Characteristics (Lakkhaṇahāra) 67.

Regarding the sense faculties, guarding the doors is the restraint of mindfulness (*satisaṃvara*). And because one becomes abundant in thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhamma-vitakka*) and so forth through the power of mindfulness, it is said:
"Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded, 'the domain of right intention' is this faculty of mindfulness. This is its meaning.

Regarding the passage, “Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded, the range is right intention,” here, through the metaphorical application of the cause to the effect, these five faculties are included within the faculty of mindfulness because they share a single characteristic—either by the characteristic of a faculty or by the state of bringing liberation to maturity.
This is the intended meaning. As for the phrase “is included,” it is here by way of the characteristic of the Path.
Since grasping [the path] is easy to understand, the passage beginning with “For from right view, right intention arises” was stated in order to show how it is grasped by way of its causes.
Precisely for that reason, after stating that the Noble Eightfold Path has been grasped, liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation are also mentioned.
The commentary on the application of the method of characteristics is concluded.
6. Explanation of the Convergence of the Fourfold Array of Modes (Catubyūhahārasampātavaṇṇanā) 68.
It is "guarded" (*rakkhita*) because it is protected (*rakkhīyati*). This is the etymological derivation based on the word-form (*padavasena*).

However, since when the etymological derivation is stated according to the meaning (*atthavasena*), the derivation based on the word-form is already implicitly stated, [the author] says: "It is guarded; it is fully preserved—this is the etymology (*niruttī*)."

It has been stated. In that context, the word *iti* signifies "beginning with" (*ādi*) or "manner" (*pakāra*). By this, it is meant that this etymological derivation (*nirutti*) begins with these [terms] or is of such a manner.

Therefore: it thinks, thus it is *citta*; it accumulates its own continuity, thus it is *citta*; it is variegated by conditions, thus it is *citta*; in the sense of being variegated by consciousness, it is *citta*;
in the sense of making consciousness, it is *citta*. The etymology should be understood through such expressions as "it intends rightly, thus it is right intention" (*sammāsaṅkappo*), and so forth.

“This is the Blessed One’s intention here” means that the Blessed One’s intention in this verse—when he speaks of the restraint of the sense faculties and so forth, as well as the abandoning of miserable rebirths, by saying “one whose mind is guarded,” etc.—is as follows. “For Kokālika... and so forth is the explanation of the introduction (*nidāna*).
Therein, the word *hi* (for) indicates a reason. This is what is meant: because Kokālika, due to his lack of mental restraint, [was reborn] among the foremost disciples...

Having corrupted his mind, he was reborn in the Paduma hell; therefore, one who desires to abandon the miserable destinies should have a guarded mind—this is the meaning of the Blessed One’s statement that one endowed with a mind protected by mindfulness abandons all miserable destinies.
The statement in the Sutta, “The mind should be guarded by mindfulness,” is shown as the connection between the teachings.
The commentary on the "Convergence of the Mode of Conveying the Fourfold Array" is finished.
7. Commentary on the "Convergence of the Mode of Conveying the Conversion. 69.
One who is abundant in the intention of renunciation, having attained one-pointedness of mind—whether by means of the kasiṇas or by means of loving-kindness and so forth—[is described as follows:]
Having placed the mind within the casket of the mind, or having protected the mind from defilement by means of whatever concentration has been attained, one is said to be "one whose mind is guarded.
Thus it is said: "Therefore, for one whose mind is guarded, right intention is the range; this is serenity (samatha).
Regarding insight (vipassanā), which has wisdom as its primary factor, he says: "Right view is the foremost; this is insight. By means of the Noble Path...
When the truth of suffering has been fully understood, the vision of its arising and passing away is said to have reached its culmination; thus it is said:

"Having known arising and passing away, there is the full understanding of suffering. For this is the demonstration of the occurrence of path-knowledge: "Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease. These are the four truths;
this is the turning [of the mind] by way of the Dhamma of the Four Truths.

It brings it to completion. In this context, it should be understood that by means of the first two methods of establishing the truths, there is a turning-back (*āvatta*) by way of dissimilar states, and by means of the latter [two], there is a turning-back by way of similar states.
The commentary on the section on the Mode of Conveying Turning-Back is finished.
8. Explanation of the Convergence of the Divisions (Vibhattihārasampātavaṇṇanā) 70.
"The side of the wholesome should be demonstrated by means of the side of the wholesome": thus, for one whose mind is guarded, there is "restraint through mindfulness" (*satisaṃvara*).
This is sixfold according to the doors, from restraint at the eye-door up to restraint at the mind-door. Right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) is threefold.
—The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, and the intention of non-cruelty. Right view is eightfold:
knowledge regarding suffering … [and so on] … knowledge regarding phenomena that have arisen dependently through specific conditions. Knowledge of arising and passing away is fiftyfold:
from the arising of ignorance comes the arising of form … [and so on] … even when one sees the characteristic of change in the aggregate of consciousness.
We see it thus: the overcoming of sloth and torpor is fourfold by way of the four paths. Therein, the restraint of mindfulness is twofold, being mundane and supramundane.
Of these, the mundane is restricted to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*); the supramundane is twofold, distinguished as that of seeing and that of cultivation.
Each of these is further fourfold, distinguished by the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*). This same method applies to right intention and the other factors as well.
This, however, is the distinction: right intention should also be brought out as belonging to the fine-material sphere by way of the first jhāna.

The analysis of the proximate cause should be stated according to the method explained in the "Conveying of the Proximate Cause" (Padaṭṭhāna-hāra). On the side of the unwholesome, there is non-restraint: non-restraint of the eye...
[and so on] ...non-restraint of the body, non-restraint of the mobile body, non-restraint of speech, and non-restraint of the mind.
It is eightfold. Wrong intention is threefold by way of sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth. Ignorance is analyzed as eightfold by way of “ignorance regarding suffering” and so forth.
Wrong view, being the opposite of right view, should be understood as sixty-two-fold.
Sloth and torpor are fivefold according to their spheres of arising. Thus should the analysis on the side of the unwholesome be understood.
The commentary on the Section on the Convergence of the Modes of Conveying by Analysis is finished.
9. Commentary on the Section on the Convergence of the Modes of Conveying by Reversal (Parivattana-hārasampāta): 71.

Regarding the Mode of Conveying by Reversal, instead of determining serenity and insight according to the method stated for the Mode of Conveying by Conversion, [it is said]: "By means of serenity and insight..."
He said, "Because it has been cultivated. And here, mundane serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) are to be understood.

"By the opposite" means by the opposite of the verse beginning with "with an unguarded mind"; this is the intended meaning. Alternatively, the sense is: by the opposite of the unwholesome side (akusalapakkha) as demonstrated in the section on analysis (vibhattihāra).
The commentary on the Mode of Conveying Reversal is finished.
10. Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Synonyms 72.
“Mind, heart, lucid [mind], consciousness, the aggregate of consciousness, the mind-consciousness element”—thus [are the synonyms] of the mind.
Synonyms: for right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*), there are “reasoning, applied thought, purpose, absorption, sustained application, and the directing of the mind.
For right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*), there are “wisdom, understanding, investigation, thorough investigation,” and so forth.
For sloth (*thina*), there are “sloth, sluggishness, sluggishness of mind, unwieldiness, inflexibility, obstruction, envelopment, and inward contraction. [Also] unwieldiness and inflexibility.
“Lassitude of body, sleeping, the act of sleeping, and the state of having slept”—this refers to *middha* (drowsiness). “A mendicant, a monk,” and so forth, refers to the term *bhikkhu*.
“An evil destination, a state of loss, a downfall, the suffering of the round, and saṃsāra”—by such phrases, the synonyms for *duggati* (an evil destination) are to be understood.
The commentary on the section on the method of synonyms is concluded.
11. Commentary on the Mode of Conveying Descriptions (Paññattihārasampātavaṇṇanā) 73.
Because the mind that is protected by mindfulness—which has established its resolve—is, as it were, the very resolution of that mindfulness itself, it is said:
“‘Of one whose mind is guarded’ is a description by way of proximate cause (padaṭṭhānapaññatti) for mindfulness. The rest in this [section]...

In the convergence of the Mode of Conception (*paññatti-hāra*), as well as in the subsequent convergences of the Modes of Entry (*otaraṇa*) and Purification (*sodhana*), there is nothing new; they follow exactly the method explained above.
The commentary on the convergence of the Mode of Conception is concluded.
14. Commentary on the Convergence of the Mode of Determination (*adhiṭṭhāna-hāra*).

76. In the convergence of the modes of conveying (hāra) through resolution, right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*)—defined as "knowledge regarding suffering" and so forth—is shown to possess diversity by way of its object, which consists of the four truths categorized as cause-and-cause-arisen and condition-and-condition-arisen.

Furthermore, the phrase "the knowledge and vision according to reality here and there" illuminates the diversity of that very [right view] by way of the remaining objects within the text and the meaning of the text. In this context, "that which is the arrival at the truths" refers to...
The arrival of the object in its true and unerring nature is what is meant by "attainment" (*adhigama*).
There is also a reading, “yaṃ paccāgamanaṃ,” which means the successive arrival of the object; the sense is that it is the attainment of each respective object.
As for the rest here—what needs to be said regarding the arrangement and application of the requisites—it is self-evident, as it follows the method already explained previously.
The commentary on the convergence of the modes of conveying by way of determination is finished.
The commentary on the convergence of the modes of conveying by way of combination should also be understood by this same method:
“Mental phenomena are preceded by the mind, have the mind as their chief,
and are made of the mind. If one speaks or acts with a pure mind,
happiness follows one even as a shadow that never departs.”
In this context, what is the convergence of the nourishment of the teaching? Regarding the verse, "Mind precedes all phenomena" (*manopubbaṅgamā dhammā*):

by means of the definition of the aggregates (*khandha*), he teaches the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*). By means of the definition of the sense bases (*āyatana*), he teaches the mind base (*manāyatana*). By means of the definition of the elements (*dhātu*), he teaches the element of consciousness (*viññāṇadhātu*).
By means of the definition of the faculties (*indriya*), he teaches the mind faculty (*manindriya*). What phenomena are preceded [by the mind]? Six phenomena are preceded [by the mind].
