The roots of the wholesome for wholesome states, the roots of the unwholesome for unwholesome states, the dominant influence for those states accompanied by a dominant influence, and the faculties for all mental arisings.
Moreover, in this sutta, "mind" (mano) is intended. Just as the king is the precursor of an army, even so mind is the precursor of phenomena.
In that regard, mind is the precursor in three ways: through the desire for renunciation...
By the desire for non-ill will and the desire for non-cruelty. In this context, the mind is preceded by the desire for renunciation as the basis for non-greed;
the mind is preceded by the desire for non-ill will as the basis for non-hatred; and the mind is preceded by the desire for non-cruelty as the basis for non-delusion.
"Mind is foremost" means that the mind is the best, the most distinguished, the highest, the most excellent, the root, and the leader among those phenomena.
Because the mind is the leader, it is said: "the mind is supreme. "Mind-made" means made by the mind, fashioned by the mind, produced by the mind;
the mind is their condition, therefore they are called "mind-made. Furthermore, those phenomena are brought about by desire, originated by untroubled intention, and conditioned by contact;
they are the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of mental formations.
“With a mind serene” means: faith, believing, conviction, and profound confidence.
Thus, one who is endowed with, fully endowed with, possessed of, fully possessed of, perfected in, and equipped with this serenity is said to be “with a serene mind.

This is mental action (*manokamma*). “Speaks” refers to verbal action (*vacīkamma*). “Acts” refers to bodily action (*kāyakamma*). Thus, the ten paths of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*) are shown.
"From that": because of having performed and accumulated the ten kinds of wholesome kamma. "Him": that person who has performed merit, performed what is wholesome, and performed a refuge from fear.
"Happiness": happiness is twofold—bodily and mental. "Follows": it accompanies him.

Here, suppose there is a man who has not abandoned his underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) and who contemplates gratification in things that lead to fetters; he [is thus bound] by those things that lead to fetters.
Contemplating gratification in phenomena, he aspires for a state of existence in accordance with what he has seen and heard.
Thus, ignorance and craving for existence become bound to him;
aspiring for a state of existence in accordance with what he has seen and heard, he inspires confidence, places faith, and resolves his mind upon an inspiring object. With a confident mind, he...
He practices the three bases for performing merit—consisting of giving, morality, and mental development—by way of body, speech, and mind.
He experiences the result thereof either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in subsequent successive states.
Thus, for him, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition...
Name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases, contact productive of pleasant feeling;
conditioned by contact, feeling. When this is so, that pleasure follows along. As feeling thus turns from one state to another, craving arises.
Conditioned by craving, clinging... [and so on] ...there is the arising [of suffering].
In this context, that which is the mind, those mental phenomena preceded by the mind, and that which is pleasure—these are called the five aggregates;
they constitute the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca*). Ignorance and craving for existence, which serve as their prior causes, constitute the truth of the origin (*samudayasacca*).
For the sake of fully understanding and abandoning these, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma: for the full understanding of suffering and for the abandoning of its origin.
That by which one fully understands and that by which one abandons is the Path. That wherein the Path operates is Cessation.
These Four Noble Truths should likewise be determined by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and faculties (*indriya*).

In this context, gratification (*assāda*) is understood through Origination, danger (*ādīnava*) through Suffering, and escape (*nissaraṇa*) through the Path and Cessation. The fruit is the consequence of pleasure, [to be known] by the mind.

The exertion of body and speech by one who is confident is the means; since all phenomena are preceded by the mind, one who desires their own happiness and is confident should engage in verbal and bodily action with a confident mind—this is the Blessed One’s injunction. This is the sequence of the nutriment of teaching.

In this regard, what is the sequence of the nutriment of investigation? It is called "mind" (*mano*) because of its measuring and because of its cognizing of objects. In that which has the characteristic of measuring...

Among associated states, they are "foremost" because they exercise sovereignty; they are "phenomena" (*dhammā*) in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being or a soul due to the absence of striving.
They are "mind-foremost" (*manoseṭṭhā*) because the mind is their chief in the sense of being preeminent, just as a village headman is among villages.

They are "mind-made" (*manomayā*) because they are produced by the mind acting as a co-nascent and other conditions. [They arise] from a state of clarity and through the manifestation of vocal intimation resulting from the mind's conviction regarding the object.
It speaks likewise because of its relishing. It acts likewise because of the expansion of the body that supports it and because of its relishing.

It is said to be "from that" because of its being directed toward that and its non-difference from that. It is said to be "pleasure" (sukha) because of its being pleasant, its state of being agreeable, and its state of being desirable.
It is said to "follow" (anveti) because it has been accumulated through action and because its ripening has not yet matured. This is because its existence is dependent upon causes.
And because there is no transmigration, it is said: "Like a shadow, never departing. This is the application of the method of investigation by way of successive analysis.
In this regard, what is the application of the method of reasoning (*yuttihārasampāta*)? It is logical that the mind possesses primacy due to its sovereignty over mental phenomena (*dhamma*).
For that very reason, it is logical that mental phenomena have the mind as their chief, because they follow after the mind. This is by way of such conditions as co-nascence (*sahajātādi-paccaya*).
The "mind-made" nature of phenomena is logical because they are produced by the mind. It is logical that bodily and verbal actions arising from a clear mind possess a wholesome state.
It is logical that whatever wholesome karma has been accumulated follows after one like a shadow, bringing happiness. This is the application of the method of reasoning (*yuttihāra*).
In this context, what is the sequence of the mode of conveyance as a basis? The mind is the basis for mental explorations.
Mental states preceded by the mind are the basis for the entire side of wholesome factors. "He speaks" refers to right speech; "he acts" refers to right action;
these two are the basis for right livelihood. Right livelihood is the basis for right effort. Right effort...
Right mindfulness is the proximate cause for right concentration. Right mindfulness is the proximate cause for right concentration.
Regarding the phrase "with a serene mind," here "serenity" is the faculty of faith; that is the proximate cause for virtue. Virtue is the proximate cause for concentration.

Concentration [is the proximate cause] for wisdom, and so on, up to the knowledge and vision of liberation—thus it should be applied. This is the convergence of the mode of conveyance of the proximate cause.
In this context, what is the application of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-hāra-sampāta*)?
By the statement, “States have mind as their precursor,” the fact that states have desire as their precursor, energy as their precursor, and investigation as their precursor is also expressed;
for by way of the characteristic of predominance, desire and the others share the same characteristic as the mind. Likewise, they also have faith and the other [faculties] as their precursors.
It is said [to be characterized] by the characteristic of the faculties because faith and the others share a single characteristic with the mind.
Just as the possession of clarity by the mind is the characteristic of the blamelessness of bodily and verbal actions originated by it— as in the phrase "If one has a clear mind"—
so too the possession of mindfulness and the rest by the consciousness is the characteristic of their blamelessness, by virtue of being originated through appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*).

Because they share a single characteristic (*ekalakkhaṇattā*). By the expression "happiness follows," there is stated the following of agreeable forms and so forth, which serve as conditions for happiness;
for these too share a single characteristic by virtue of having kamma as their condition. This is the application of the Mode of Conveying Characteristics (*lakkhaṇahārasampāto*).

In this regard, what is the application of the Mode of Conveying the Fourfold Array (*catubyūho hārasampāto*)? [It concerns] the words "mind" (*mano*) and so forth in such passages as "preceded by mind" (*manopubbaṅgamā*).

Etymology (*nibbacana*) is linguistic derivation (*nirutta*); it should be understood by way of the explanation of word-meanings (*padatthāna*). And the meaning of the words is easily understood according to the method already stated.
For those who desire happiness, bodily, verbal, and mental actions should be performed with a confident mind—this is the Blessed One’s intention here.
Having become a forerunner for others in the performance of meritorious deeds, therein for them...

The "introducers" (*sammā-upanetāro*) are the source (*nidāna*) of this teaching. The "connection of the teaching" (*desanānusandhi*) is the coordination of this teaching through such correlations as:
"The king is the lord of the six doors; the states of mind follow upon the mind; all are subject to the power of that single state, the mind.
As for the connections between the words (*padānusandhiyo*), they are easily understood. This is the "fourfold array" (*catubyūha*) method of exposition.
In this context, what is the sequence of the modes of conveying (*hārasampāta*) through the method of turning back (*āvaṭṭa*)? Regarding the statement, "Phenomena are preceded by the mind":

therein, the three roots of wholesomeness are the cause for the eight rightnesses. Those which are the rightnesses constitute the Eightfold Path. That mentality-materiality (*nāmarūpa*) co-arising with the mind is suffering (*dukkha*).
Ignorance and craving for existence, produced previously and not yet cut off, are the origin (*samudaya*). Wherein...
The abandoning of these is cessation; these are the Four Truths. This is the convergence of the modes of conveying.
In this context, what is the convergence of the mode of analysis? Regarding the verse: "States are preceded by mind;
if one acts with a serene mind, happiness follows after it"—this is not to be understood according to the literal meaning alone. For as for the ascetic or brahmin...

Or, if one gladdens one's own mind toward one who takes life, holds wrong views, or has entered upon a wrong course, and with a gladdened mind speaks in praise of non-existent qualities or performs an act of homage toward them, happiness does not follow from that;
rather, only suffering follows it, like the track of a wheel following the footstep of a draught animal. Thus...

For this is to be answered by way of analysis (*vibhajjavyākaraṇīya*). If one speaks or acts with a mind full of confidence (*pasanna*), and that verbal or bodily action is to be experienced as pleasant—why is that?
Because [actions] proceeding from rightness (*sammatta*) are to be experienced as pleasant, while those proceeding from wrongness (*micchatta*) are to be experienced as painful.
But how is this "confidence" to be understood? This is not actual confidence; it is a counterfeit of confidence.
"But I say it is wrong resolve. This is the convergence of the method of analysis (*vibhattihāra*).
In this regard, what is the convergence of the method of reversal (*parivattano hārasampāto*)? It is the passage beginning with "Mind is the forerunner," and so forth.
That which one speaks or does with a corrupted mind leads to suffering; for this Sutta is the direct opposite of that [previous statement]. This is the convergence of the method of reversal.

In this context, what is the convergence of synonyms (*vevacana-hārasampāta*)? Regarding the phrase "preceded by mind" (*manopubbaṅgamā*): "mind" (*mano*), "consciousness" (*citta*), "mind-base" (*manāyatana*), "mind-faculty" (*manindriya*), "mind-consciousness" (*manoviññāṇa*), and "mind-consciousness-element" (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) are synonymous terms. "Preceded by," "going before," and "going ahead" are synonymous terms.
"Phenomena" (*dhammā*), "self" (*attā*), and "intrinsic nature" (*sabhāva*) are synonymous terms. "Best," "foremost," and "excellent" are synonymous terms.
"Synonymous expression" (*pariyāyavacana*): "mind-made," "produced by the mind," and "arisen from the mind" are synonymous expressions.
"With a serene mind," "believing," and "confidently resolved" are synonymous expressions. "Pleasure," "delight," and "feeling" are synonymous expressions.
"Follows," "pursues," and "keeps company with" are synonymous expressions. This is the "descent of synonyms" (*vevacano hārasampāto*).
In this context, what is the application of the method of description (*paññattihārasampāta*)? "Mind precedes [all phenomena]"—this is a description of the function (*kicca-paññatti*) of the mind.

"Dhammas"—this is a description of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva-paññatti*), and a description of the wholesome paths of action (*kusalakammapatha-paññatti*). "Mind is chief"—this is a description of preeminence (*padhāna-paññatti*). "Mind-made"—this is a description of co-nascence (*sahajāta-paññatti*).

"By one with serene faith"—this is a description of being endowed with the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya-paññatti*), and a description of the exclusion of lack of faith (*assaddhiya-paṭikkhepa-paññatti*).
"Either speaks or acts"—this is a designation for the presentation of right speech and right action.

"Then happiness follows him"—this is a designation for the continuity of the fruit of karma, and a designation for the non-perishing of karma. This is the inclusion of the method of designation (*paññattihāra*).

In this regard, what is the inclusion of the method of entry (*otaraṇahāra*)? "Mind" is the aggregate of consciousness (*viññāṇakkhandha*). "Phenomena" (*dhammā*) are the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations (*vedanā-, saññā-, saṅkhārakkhandhā*).

"Either speaks or acts" refers to bodily and verbal intimation (*kāyavacī-viññatti*). Their support consists of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); thus, this is the entry by way of the aggregates (*khandha*).
"Mind" refers to formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*); by the inclusion of "mind," formations conditioned by ignorance (*avijjā-paccayā saṅkhārā*) are thereby included.
"Conditioned by formations, consciousness... and so on, up to "...there is an origination"—this is the entry by way of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
"Entry" (*otaraṇa*): this is the sequence of the mode of conveying through entry.

In that regard, what is the sequence of the mode of conveying through purification (*sodhana*)? "Mind" (*mano*) is the starting point; it is neither purification of the word nor purification of the starting point.

"Preceded by mind" (*manopubbaṅgama*) is purification of the word, not purification of the starting point. Likewise, from "phenomena" (*dhammā*) up to "happiness" (*sukha*) is purification of the word.

There is no purity of undertaking. However, the phrase "Happiness follows" refers both to purity of word and purity of undertaking. This is the sequence of the purifying mode of conveyance (*sodhana-hārasampāta*).

In this regard, what is the sequence of the mode of conveyance of determination (*adhiṭṭhāna-hārasampāta*)? In the passage "States are preceded by mind, mind is their chief, they are mind-made," there is unity (*ekattatā*).
In the passage "If one speaks or acts with a pure mind," there is diversity (*vemattatā*); likewise, in the passage "If one speaks or acts with a pure mind," there is unity.
"Either speaks or acts"—this is diversity (*vemattatā*); "if with a serene mind"—this is unity (*ekattatā*).

That serenity is twofold: internally, through the suppression of ill-will (*byāpāda*), and externally, through full confidence (*okappanā*). Likewise, there is diversity in that it is both a cause for a fortunate existence (*sampattibhava*) and a cause for growth (*vaḍḍhi*).
This sutta should be resolved in two ways: by way of the cause (*hetu*)...
And that which is with a clear mind, and that which is to be experienced as pleasant by its ripening. This is the convergence of the modes of conveying through the foundation.
In this regard, what is the convergence of the modes of conveying through the requisites? In the phrase "mind precedes," "mind" here refers to wholesome consciousness.
And for that [consciousness] associated with knowledge, there are three associated roots: non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; for that dissociated from knowledge—
Non-greed and non-hatred are the two associated roots. For all [these states], wise attention is the root without distinction;

the four wheels of success are the condition. Likewise, hearing the true Dhamma is a condition, as are the objects to be given and so forth for that [hearing] which proceeds by way of giving and the rest.
And here, "phenomena" (dhammā) refers to desirable objects and so forth for feelings and the other [mental factors]. Likewise, the three...

Consciousness is the condition for feeling and the other [mental aggregates]; the sense-faculty is the condition for feeling; wholesome volitional formations regarding an object worthy of faith are the condition for resultant pleasure.
This is the "accessory" (parikkhāra) method of exposition.
In this context, what is the "correlation" (samāropana) method of exposition? Regarding the verse "Mind precedes all phenomena," "mind" refers to a meritorious state of consciousness.
That is threefold: consisting of giving, consisting of virtue, and consisting of development. Among these, non-greed is the proximate cause for that which consists of giving;
non-hatred is the proximate cause for that which consists of virtue; and non-delusion is the proximate cause for that which consists of development.
For all of them, full confidence is the proximate cause. The Sutta passage, “Having become endowed with faith, he approaches; approaching, he pays respect,” should be quoted in detail.
Wholesome consciousness is the proximate cause for pleasant, desirable fruition. Wise attention is the proximate cause for wholesome consciousness.
For one who attends wisely, wholesome consciousness becomes established and wholesome consciousness is developed;
he generates desire for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states, and for the abandoning of arisen [evil, unwholesome states].
“He strives for the abandoning of unwholesome states... [and so on] ...he exerts himself for the maintenance of wholesome states that have arisen.
As he thus develops the four right efforts, the four foundations of mindfulness reach fulfillment by development, and so on up to the noble eightfold path. This is the application of development.
Since mindfulness is established through development, its abandoning is also accomplished as a matter of course. This is the “convergence” method of exposition.
Likewise:
“For one who gives, merit increases; for one who restrains himself, enmity does not accumulate.
The skillful person abandons evil; through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished.”
In this context, "merit increases for one who gives" refers to the basis for meritorious action consisting in giving (*dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu*).
"By restraint, enmity is not accumulated" refers to the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue (*sīlamaya-puññakiriyavatthu*).

And "the skillful one abandons evil" speaks of the abandoning of greed, hatred, and delusion; by this, the basis for meritorious action consisting in mental development (*bhāvanāmaya-puññakiriyavatthu*) is stated.
"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished"—this refers to final Nibbāna through non-clinging.
"Merit increases for one who gives"—this is the wholesome root of non-greed (*alobha*). "For one who restrains himself, enmity is not accumulated"—this is the wholesome root of non-hatred (*adosa*).
"And the wise man abandons evil"—this is the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha*). Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he...
"Extinguished" (*nibbuto*) is stated as their escape.

"Merit increases for one who gives" is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*). "By restraint, enmity is not accumulated" is the proximate cause for the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*).
"And the skillful one abandons evil" is [the proximate cause] for the aggregate of wisdom (*paññākkhandha*) and the aggregate of liberation (*vimuttikkhandha*).

The proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) is as follows: by means of giving (*dāna*), there is the abandoning of gross defilements (*kilesa*); by means of virtue (*sīla*), of those that are middling; and by means of wisdom (*paññā*), of those that are subtle.
"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished" (*rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbuto*) shows the stage of one who has accomplished what was to be done (*katāvī-bhūmi*).

"Merit for the giver... [etc. ...he abandons evil" shows the stage of the trainee (*sekkha-bhūmi*). "Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished" states the highest fruit (*aggaphala*).

"Merit for one who gives... and so forth, up to "...is not accumulated," refers to the mundane root of skillfulness (*lokīyakusalamūla*). "The skillful person abandons evil" refers to the supramundane root of skillfulness (*lokuttarakusalamūla*).
"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished" refers to the fruit of the supramundane root of skillfulness.

"Merit for one who gives... and so forth, up to "...is not accumulated," shows the stage of the worldling (*puthujjanabhūmi*). "The skillful person abandons evil" shows the stage of the trainee (*sekkhabhūmi*). "Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished" shows the stage of the adept (*asekkhabhūmi*).

“Giving... [and so on]... it does not accumulate” refers to the practice leading to heaven. “The skillful one abandons evil” refers to the liberation of those still in training (*sekkhā-vimutti*). “Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished” refers to the liberation of those beyond training (*asekkhā-vimutti*).
“Giving... [and so on]... it does not accumulate” expresses the discourse on giving, the discourse on virtue, and the discourse on heaven—the teaching of mundane phenomena.
“The skillful one abandons evil” expresses the preeminent teaching of the Dhamma together with the contemplation of the world’s dangers (*ādīnavānupassanā*).
"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished"—this states the fruit of that teaching.
"Merit increases for one who gives" refers to both the gift of the Dhamma and the gift of material goods.

"Enmity is not accumulated by one who restrains himself" refers to the gift of fearlessness to beings through abstention from taking life. In this way, all the training precepts (sikkhāpada) should be elaborated upon.
And by means of that restraint of virtue, being established in virtue, he restrains his mind; thus his serenity (samatha) reaches fulfillment.
Thus, established in serenity, through application to skill in insight (vipassanā), he becomes skilled and abandons evil:
he abandons lust, he abandons hatred, he abandons delusion; and by means of the Noble Path, he abandons all evil unwholesome states. Thus...

"And practicing, through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished"—this means that by the complete exhaustion of lust and the other defilements, one attains both kinds of liberation;
this is the exposition of the Sutta.
In that regard, what is the sequence of the presentation of the teaching? What is taught in this Sutta? Two happy destinations: gods and [humans].
The five strands of sensual pleasure pertaining to humans and those pertaining to the devas;
the five aggregates of clinging pertaining to humans and those pertaining to the devas—this is called the noble truth of suffering.
By way of being its cause, craving produced successively in the past is the noble truth of the origin. This is called both the gratification and the danger.
The exposition of the entire [verse] is by means of the first two phrases: “As he gives... it is not stored up. “The skillful one abandons evil” refers to the Path.
“Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished” refers to the two elements of Nibbāna:

that with residue remaining and that without residue remaining. This is the Escape. The Fruit and so forth, however, should be understood according to their respective contexts. This is the sequence of the presentation of the teaching.
Regarding "Investigation": by the first phrase, "Merit increases for one who gives," the threefold basis for the performance of merit—consisting of giving, virtue, and meditation—is stated.
The relinquishing of all ten kinds of objects worthy of being given is thus mentioned, as well as the relinquishing of the sixfold objects of sense, beginning with visible forms.
By the second phrase, "For one who restrains himself, enmity does not accumulate," [the same is shown].
By the first phrase, the practice that is free from enmity, free from adversaries, and free from ill will is stated.

By the third phrase, “And the skillful one abandons evil,” the arising of knowledge, the cessation of ignorance, the entire Noble Eightfold Path, and all the factors conducive to enlightenment are stated.

By the words, “Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished,” the deliverance of mind through fading away of lust (*rāgavirāga-cetovimutti*) by means of the destruction of lust is indicated.
"Through the destruction of delusion and the fading away of ignorance, liberation by wisdom is said to occur.
This is the application of the mode of analysis (*vicayahāra*). Regarding "reasoning" (*yutti*): standing in generosity, one fulfills both—the abandoning of stinginess and the outflow of merit;
this is the reasoning here. Standing in the restraint of virtue, one fulfills both—access concentration and absorption concentration; this is the reasoning here.
"Reasoning" (*yutti*): "While abandoning evil states, one fully understands suffering, realizes cessation, and develops the path"—this is the meaning of this reasoning.
"When lust, hatred, and delusion have been completely exhausted, one attains final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue"—this is the meaning of this reasoning.
This is the inclusion of the method of reasoning (*yuttihāra*).
"Foundation" (*padaṭṭhāna*) means: "Merit increases for one who gives"—this is the foundation for the foundation of generosity (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*).

"By restraint, enmity is not accumulated"—this is the foundation for the foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*). "The skillful one abandons evil"—this is the foundation for the foundation of wisdom (*paññādhiṭṭhāna*).
"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished"—this is the foundation for the foundation of peace (*upasamādhiṭṭhāna*). This is...
The basis is the sequence of the modes of conveying the meaning (*hārasampāta*).

Regarding the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*): it should be understood that by the word "of one giving" (*dadato*), the quality of pleasant speech (*peyyavajja*), beneficial conduct (*atthacariyā*), and impartiality (*samānattatā*) are shown, because they share a single characteristic by way of being the bases for social integration (*saṅgahavatthu*).
By the word "of one restraining oneself" (*saṃyamato*), patience, loving-kindness, non-violence, compassion, and so forth [are shown].
It should be understood that [the opposite qualities] are shown by virtue of having the same characteristic as the non-arising of enmity (*vera*).

By the phrase "enmity is not accumulated," shame (*hirī*), moral dread (*ottappa*), fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*), contentment (*santuṭṭhitā*), and so forth are shown, because they share the same characteristic as the non-increase of enmity.

Likewise, shamelessness (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), and so forth are shown by virtue of having the same characteristic as the state of being blameworthy (*acetabbabhāva*). By the term "skilled" (*kusala*), through the illumination of skillfulness (*kosalla*)...
Right intention and the others are shown by way of being path-factors and so forth because they possess a single characteristic.
By the phrase "he abandons evil," full understanding, clear realization, and so forth are also shown because they possess a single characteristic through the nature of clear realization.

By the phrase "through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion," the destruction of the remaining defilements and so forth is also shown because they possess a single characteristic through the state of being destroyed; this is the characteristic.
Regarding the verse beginning with "Catubyūho ti dadato," what is the Blessed One’s intention?
Those who will aspire to great wealth will give gifts for the sake of abandoning poverty. Those who desire freedom from enmity will abandon the five kinds of enmity.
Those who have a longing for wholesome qualities will cultivate the Eightfold Path. Those who wish to attain nibbāna...
"The Blessed One’s intention here is that they will abandon lust, hatred, and delusion. Thus should the derivation, the source, and the connection be stated.
This is the "fourfold array" (*catubyūha*).
As for the "turning back" (*āvatta*): it refers to the stinginess of one who does not give, the enmity of one who lacks self-restraint, and the unwholesome evil...

Non-abandonment is the origin [of suffering] described by way of its opposite. Its abandonment through non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—namely, these three roots of the wholesome—is the path. The condition for these is the eight rightnesses;
this is the path. That which is the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion is cessation. This is the turning [of the mind].
"Analysis" (*vibhatti*) means: "Merit increases for one who gives"—this is not an absolute rule.
For one who gives out of fear, who gives out of lust, or who gives for the sake of some small material gain, his merit does not increase.

Furthermore, in the case of giving a staff or a weapon for the purpose of harming others, demerit increases for him. However, when one gives with a wholesome mind, either out of compassion or out of reverence...
One gives food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps;
or one gives the gift of fearlessness to all beings; or, with a mind of loving-kindness, an intention for their welfare, and perceiving the state of liberation, one teaches the Dhamma.
"From restraint, enmity does not accumulate"—this refers exclusively to the non-accumulation of enmity in one who has desisted from causing fear. What is the reason?
One who is incapable [of committing such acts], being restrained by fear, fears the consequences in this very life, thinking: "May kings not seize me and cut off my hand...
[or] even impale me alive on a stake. By that restraint, one accumulates non-enmity.
But he who, being thus, does not accumulate enmity—yet he who undertakes such a vow [knows]: "The ripening of the taking of life is evil."
Both in this very life and in future lives, thus he desists from all that is unwholesome;

by this restraint, enmity is not accumulated. Restraint is called virtue (*sīla*). That is fourfold: virtue as volition (*cetanā-sīla*), virtue as mental concomitant (*cetasika-sīla*), virtue as restraint (*saṃvara-sīla*), and virtue as non-transgression (*avītikkama-sīla*). And "the wholesome one abandons evil" refers to those things which abandon evil.
The thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā) should be spoken of. This is the analysis (vibhatti).
As for the reversal (parivatta): merit increases for one who gives, and merit also increases for one who does not give; it is not merely consisting of giving.

Enmity is not accumulated by one who restrains himself, nor is enmity accumulated by one who does not restrain himself—that which [is accomplished] through giving and the power of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānabala).

By the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*). The skillful one abandons evil, but the unskillful one does not abandon it. Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished (*nibbuto*);
through their non-destruction, there is no extinction. This is the "reversal" (*parivattana*).
As for synonyms (*vevacana*): merit increases for one who gives; from relinquishment, the wholesome (*kusala*) accumulates; even by rejoicing, merit [accrues].
It increases through both clarity of mind and the performance of services. "Through restraint" means through the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*) and through gentleness (*soracca*).
"Enmity is not accumulated" means evil does not increase; unwholesomeness (*akusala*) does not increase.
"The wholesome one" means the wise, the skillful, the intelligent, the investigator. "He abandons" means he cuts off, he eradicates. This is a synonym (*vevacana*).
"Description" (*paññatti*): "Merit increases for one who gives" is a description of the relinquishing of greed, a description of the establishing of non-greed.
"By restraint, enmity is not accumulated" is a description of the suppression of hatred, a description of the establishing of non-hatred.
"And the skillful one abandons evil" is a description of the eradication of delusion, a description of the cultivation of non-delusion.
The designation of the abandoning of lust, hatred, and delusion; the designation of the development of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.

"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished" is the designation of the subsiding of the defilements and the designation of the realization of Nibbāna. This is the designation (*paññatti*). As for the entry (*otaraṇa*):
"Merit increases for one who gives"—this gift arises through the faculties such as faith, and so forth. This is...
"Entry by way of the faculties" (*indriyehi otaraṇo*). "By restraint, enmity is not accumulated"—this refers to the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) called "restraint";
this is "entry by way of the aggregates" (*khandhehi otaraṇo*). "The skillful one abandons evil"—the abandonment of evil occurs through the three liberations (*vimokkha*);
their means are the three gateways to liberation (*vimokkhamukha*); this is "entry by way of the gateways to liberation. [This leads to] the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion.

"He is extinguished" (*sa nibbuto*) refers to the aggregate of liberation (*vimuttikkhandha*). This [aggregate] consists of the element of mental phenomena (*dhammadhātu*) and the sphere of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*);
thus, this is the entry by way of elements and spheres. This is the "entry.

"Purification" (*sodhana*) refers to the purification of words such as "giving" (*dadato*), which is not the purification of the undertaking (*ārambhasuddhi*). "He is extinguished through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion" (*rāgadosamohakkhayā sa nibbuto*)—this is both the purification of words and the purification of the undertaking. This is the "purification."

"Resolution" (*adhiṭṭhāna*)—namely, "giving"—is unity; the varieties are the eight kinds of giving: the gift of Dhamma, the gift of material things, the gift of fearlessness, and so forth, which should be explained in detail.
"Restraint" (*saṃyama*) is unity; the varieties are the restraint of the *pātimokkha* and the restraint of mindfulness.
"The skillful person abandons evil" is unity; the variety is [the abandonment of] the view of a self-existent body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
"This abandons doubt, this abandons [it]" and so forth—this is diversity (*vemattatā*). "Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished"—this is unity (*ekattatā*).
"The element of Nibbāna with residue remaining" and "the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining"—this is diversity. This is the basis (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
As for the requisite (*parikkhāra*): joy is the condition for giving; non-greed is the cause, while shame and dread of blame are the conditions for self-restraint.
Proper attention and non-hatred are the cause; concentration and the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are are the conditions for the abandoning of evil.

The three contemplations are the cause; for Nibbāna, right view of the path is the cause, while right intention and the other factors are the conditions. This is the requisite. As for the application and the convergence of the modes of exposition:
"Merit increases for one who gives" refers to the basis for performing meritorious deeds consisting in giving.
That is the proximate cause for virtue. "From restraint, enmity is not accumulated" refers to the basis for meritorious action consisting of virtue;
that is the proximate cause for concentration. For by virtue, as well as by meditation, the defilements such as lust and the rest are not accumulated.
Furthermore, those taints, afflictions, and fevers that might arise on account of them do not exist for him. And the skillful one abandons [them].
"Evil things" refers to the full understanding through abandonment (*pahāna-pariññā*); that is the basis for meritorious action consisting in cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya-puññakiriyavatthu*).
"Through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished" means: through the destruction of lust, through the destruction of hatred, and through the destruction of delusion.

In this context, "lust" (*rāga*) is that which is lust, intense lust, the lustfulness of the mind, greed, the act of being greedy, the state of being greedy, covetousness, greed, and the unwholesome root of greed.
"Hatred" (dosa) means that which is hatred, the state of hating, the condition of being hateful, ill will, mental malice, hatred, and the unwholesome root.

"Delusion" (moha) means that which is ignorance, non-seeing, lack of clear comprehension, lack of awakening, lack of penetration, dullness, childishness, lack of situational awareness, delusion, and the unwholesome root.
Thus, the destruction, cessation, relinquishment, extinguishing, and extinction of these [defilements] such as lust and the rest.
"Parinibbāna," "the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining," and "the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining"—this is the convergence of the mode of treatment known as "Convergence.
The commentary on the convergence of the mixed mode of treatment is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the section on the origin of the methods.

79. Having thus demonstrated the analysis of the strings (*hāra*) by way of various suttas and by way of a single sutta, the following is now commenced in order to demonstrate the analysis of the methods (*naya*):
“In this regard, what is the arising of the methods? and so forth. But why, in this context, is there no exposition of the strings (*hāra*) in the manner of [the previous section], such as:
“In this regard, what is the string of teaching? It is the verse beginning with ‘The gratification and the danger. This string of teaching teaches what? and so on?

Why is it that [the *Nandiyāvaṭṭa* method] is commenced not by beginning with such questions as, "In this context, what is the *nandiyāvaṭṭa*? What does the verse beginning 'Craving and ignorance' lead to?
and so forth, but rather by way of the heading of "origination" (*samuṭṭhāna*)? It is said:

because of the difference in the scope of the *hāra* (modes of conveying) and the *naya* (guiding methods). For while the *hāras* are commentaries on the meaning of the Sutta by way of the phrasing (*byañjana*), the *nayās* are not so.

However, when the meaning of suffering and so forth is understood through the method (*naya*) by connecting the four truths with the root terms such as craving and ignorance—which have been extracted from various suttas—that is the "method.
For it leads (*nayati*) and brings about the knowledge of the path; thus it is called a method.

Furthermore, according to the three types of disciples to be trained—namely, those who understand through a brief indication (*ugghaṭitaññu*), and so forth—it is divided into three ways based on the analysis of the root terms.

Furthermore, because each individual [factor] herein leads [to a result], and because of the distinction between those factors of defilement (*saṃkilesa*) and purification (*vodāna*), the scope of the methods of extraction (*hāra*) and the guiding principles (*naya*) is divided into groups of two, four, and eight, and so forth. For it has been said:

"The *hāras* are the investigation of the phrasing (*byañjana-vicaya*); the *nayās* are the threefold meaning of the Sutta. Thus, because their scopes are distinct, the *hāras* and *nayās* are different from one another.
Pointing out the method, he said: "In this regard, what is the origin of the method?
and so forth. Herein, this is the etymological analysis: that by which things arise is an "origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*). What arises? The methods (*naya*).
The origin of the methods is the "origin of the method" (*nayasamuṭṭhāna*). And what is that? It is the application of the Four Noble Truths to each respective root-term.
For it is called the "source" (*samuṭṭhāna*) and the "ground" (*bhūmi*) because it is the place of origin for the methods such as the Conversion of Delight (*nandiyāvaṭṭa*).
And so he will say: "This is called the ground of the method of the Conversion of Delight.
The passage beginning with "The prior limit of ignorance and craving for existence is not known" is the demonstration of the ground of the method of the Conversion of Delight.

In this context, "the prior limit is not discerned" means that it cannot be found that ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) arose at the time of such-and-such a Buddha, Blessed One, or such-and-such a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*), and that they did not exist before that; thus, no initial boundary for ignorance and craving for existence is apprehended. Why?
Because saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning. For this has been said:
“Bhikkhus, this saṃsāra is without discoverable beginning; its prior limit is not apparent,” so it is said in detail.

“Therein” refers to ignorance (*avijjā*), existence (*bhava*), and craving (*taṇhā*). Although the state of being a fetter (*saṃyojana*) is ascribed to ignorance and the state of being an hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*) to craving in the Canon, nevertheless, the meaning here is that craving fetters one to existences whose dangers are concealed by ignorance.
For the purpose of showing this, it is said: "obstructed by ignorance and fettered by craving.
"Associated with ignorance" means mixed with ignorance, or bound to the bases of misapprehension by means of ignorance.

"Wandering along the side of ignorance" means wandering along the side of ignorance—that is, accompanied by ignorance—by way of the twelvefold perversion regarding those things that have become the bases of misapprehension.

They operate upon an object. They are called "those of speculative temperament" (*diṭṭhicarita*); being overcome by ignorance, they adhere to form and so forth as permanent and so on, and thus they are called "those of speculative temperament"—the meaning is "those whose temperament is dominated by views.

By the side of craving, that is, by means of the eight hundred modes of craving’s wandering (*taṇhāvicarita*). Having analyzed the practice regarding both the wandering of views and the wandering of craving—

To demonstrate this, it is said: “those of speculative temperament,” and so forth. Therein, “devotion to self-mortification” means the practice of afflicting one’s own body and the way of life involving self-torment.
“Devotion to sensual pleasure” means the practice of clinging to sensual pleasure and the state of being intoxicated by sense-desires.
Even though outsiders know that “suffering is craving,” and they recognize, “This is suffering; this is the extent of suffering,” yet [they do not understand] “this... [is the origin of suffering].”

“Craving is this; its fading away is that”—yet they do not know it in terms of what is to be fully understood and what is to be abandoned. Thus, they do not even know the mere occurrence of existence and its cause.
What need is there to speak of the cessation of existence and its causes? Therefore, he said: “Outside of this, there is no defining of the truths,” and so forth.
In that context, “the manifestation of the truths” means the teaching of the truths. “Skill in serenity and insight” refers to [skill] regarding serenity and insight.
Skill in cultivation (*bhāvanākosallaṃ*), or skill in the study, inquiry, hearing, and mental attention regarding those [teachings].

Here, "the basis for insight" (*vipassanādhiṭṭhāna*) is intended to mean serenity (*samatha*). "Attainment of the bliss of peace" (*upasamasukhappatti*) is the achievement of the bliss resulting from the subsiding of the defilements (*kilesa*).

"One whose mind is perverted" (*viparītacetā*) means one whose mind is wrongly adhered to. "There is no bliss through bliss" refers to that which [is attained] by means of the bliss of enjoying blameless conditions.
Having brought tranquility to the distress of both body and mind, he rejects that bliss of peace (upasama-sukha) which is to be attained by the Noble Ones.
"By means of suffering" means by means of the suffering of bodily exhaustion.
"He increases the world" means that by indulging in sensual pleasures, he causes the world—consisting of his own personal existence (attabhāva)—to grow and expand.
Because the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is not cut off through the succession of sons and grandsons, he increases the world of beings.
"He produces much merit" means that by satisfying himself with the five strands of sensual pleasure and by seeing the face of his son, he generates much merit.
Because his adherence is not excessively firm, he has such a perception; because it is firm, he has such a view: "Happiness [is found] through suffering."
It should be connected thus: "They dwell aspiring for and devoted to self-mortification, perceiving sensual pleasures as merit, and devoted to the pursuit of sensual pleasure.
"Those who perceive them as peaceful" means those who have such a perception.
"They increase only their own disease" means they increase only the disease of their own personal existence (*attabhāva*).
Or they cause the very disease of the defilements (*kilesa*) to increase further and further. The same method applies to the abscesses and arrows (*gaṇḍasalla*).
"Pierced by diseases" means afflicted by the aforementioned diseases. "Oppressed by abscesses" means tormented by the aforementioned abscesses.

"Transfixed by arrows" means pierced by the aforementioned arrows. "Emerging and submerging" refers to births and deaths. "Striking and counter-striking" [refers to the rising and falling of the breath].
"High and low states. "Medicine for the disease, the tumor, and the dart" refers to the treatment of the aforementioned diseases and so forth;
he speaks with reference to serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Therefore he says: "Serenity and insight are the medicine that destroys disease.

In this context, "destroying disease" means the pacification of disease. By means of the passage beginning "Defilement is suffering," he explains the Truths in terms of their being fully understood and so forth.
In this context, "defilement is suffering" means that the form and formless bodies—
which possess the defilements of devotion to self-mortification and devotion to sensual pleasures, or which become defiled by those two— are the Noble Truth of Suffering.
"Clinging to that is craving" means that craving is given the names "clinging" (abhisanga) and "attachment" (āsanga) with respect to that [suffering].

80. Now, in order to show the difference in the way that those of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*) and those of craving temperament (*taṇhācarita*) proceed in their viewing of personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), it is said:

“Those of speculative temperament,” and so forth. Therein, “those of speculative temperament approach form as self” means that because of the strength of their adherence to views, those of speculative temperament grasp form as “self. For their adherence to a self is powerful.
There is no such strong adherence to [form] as one's own (attaniya). This same method applies to feeling and the other aggregates as well.

Those of craving-temperament (taṇhācarita) hold that "the self possesses form" (rūpavantaṃ attānaṃ); because their adherence through craving is powerful, those of craving-temperament establish form in the state of being a possession or a hindrance to the self, and then grasp the remaining factors—feeling and so forth—as "the self.
Or, "form in the self" (attani rūpaṃ) means form that has the self as its support (attādhāraṃ). In form...

Or "self" means a self based on form (*rūpa*). The same method applies to the phrases "possessing feeling" and so forth. For in these cases, the adherence to "what belongs to a self" (*attaniya*) is strong, whereas the adherence to "a self" (*atta*) is not.
Therefore, having imagined whatever has been obtained as "belonging to a self," they grasp what is other than that as "the self.
This is called the twenty-based personality view (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*); it [occurs] within the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).
In each [of these], by way of four sets of four graspings, there are twenty bases for mindfulness within the body, which is comprised of the five aggregates;
or, when mindfulness exists therein, the views that exist there are "personality-view" (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*).
"Supramundane right view" refers to the right view of the first path. "Conformable" means following after right view.
When right view functions by way of abandoning the view of a personal body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), the meaning is that [the other factors] function in accordance with it.

But what are they? He says: "right intention," and so forth. By the phrase "those three aggregates," etc., he distinguishes serenity and insight from the perspective of the aggregates within the Noble Path. The section beginning with "Therein, the personal body... is the distinction of the Four Noble Truths.
All of that is easy to understand.

Furthermore, by means of the phrase "In this regard, those who approach form as self," and so forth, he determines the two extremes—namely, annihilationism and eternalism—and the middle way, by way of the view of a personal body (*sakkāya-diṭṭhi*).
In that context, these are called "annihilationists" because they [view] these things, beginning with form...
Those who approach the five aggregates as a self, and because of the impermanent nature of form and the other aggregates, adhere to the view that "the self is annihilated, it perishes,
and does not exist after death," are called "annihilationists" (ucchedavādino).
Those called "eternalists" (sassatavādino) are those who [hold] by way of the passage beginning "the self possesses form," etc., that there is some self other than form and the rest.
Because they approach [the world] by adhering to the view that "it is permanent, stable, and eternal," they are called "eternalists" (*sassatavādino*).
The determination of truth—such as "Both annihilationism and eternalism are extremes; this is the process of saṃsāra"—is easy to understand.
Briefly stated, annihilationism and eternalism constitute the twenty-based personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), namely: "the self is annihilated" and "the self is eternal."

And because it proceeds from a beginning, the view of annihilationism and eternalism is, in brief, simply the twenty-based personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*). For every doctrine of self is included within personality-belief.
In detail, there are sixty-two types of views; that is, the sixty-two types of views set forth in detail in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.
"Of these" refers to the views of annihilationism and eternalism, which possess both concise and detailed aspects. "The antidote" means the antidote that abandons them.

"The forty-three factors conducive to enlightenment" are as follows: the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the four foundations of mindfulness... [and so on] ...up to the noble eightfold path; these constitute the forty-three.
The factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyā dhammā*).

Having thus shown the opposing side by way of insight (*vipassanā*), it was further stated by way of serenity (*samatha*) that "there are eight liberations (*vimokkha*) and ten bases of totality (*kasiṇāyatana*).
The sixty-two types of views are the net of delusion; [this refers to] the sixty-two types of views.
And it is the "net of delusion" because it has the net of delusion as its cause. It is "occurring without beginning or end":

it is "without beginning" (anādi) because there is no prior limit; it is "occurring without end" (anidhanappavatta) because it proceeds without interruption by way of a continuum so long as its opposite has not been attained.
Furthermore, since the various speculative views have the net of delusion as their cause, they are shattered when the net of delusion is shattered. Therefore—
It is said: “The forty-three factors conducive to enlightenment are the diamond of knowledge that shatters the net of delusion.

Herein, “diamond of knowledge” means knowledge that is like a diamond. The diamond of knowledge is the knowledge of insight and the knowledge of the path, which have been brought to a state of sharpness by entering and mastering the eight attainments. Indeed, it is this very knowledge that has proceeded from the Blessed One.

It is called "the great diamond-like knowledge" (*mahāvajirañāṇa*). However, showing it together with its constituent factors, he said: "the forty-three states conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiyā dhammā*).

"The shattering of the net of delusion" refers to the shattering of ignorance and the craving for existence—by way of suppression in the preliminary stage and by way of total eradication at the moment of the Path.
[This occurs] regarding form and so forth, which are divided into the categories of past and so on, as well as regarding one's own personal identity and so forth.
Because it proceeds by way of binding together, the craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) is a "net. For that craving has the designations "the netter," "the binder," and "the net.

Thus, having analyzed ignorance (*avijjā*) and craving (*taṇhā*) according to their specific synonyms as the "net of delusion" (*moha-jāla*)—by way of determining self-mortification, devotion to sensual pleasure, views, adherence through craving, eternalism, and annihilationism—one [continues] according to the sequence of the text.

Concluding the section on the side of defilement (*saṃkilesapakkha*), he said: "Therefore it is said that no prior limit is discerned for ignorance (*avijjā*) and the craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*).

(81) Therein, by the passage beginning with "one whose temperament is dominated by views" (*diṭṭhicarito*), he shows the side of purification (*vodānapakkha*). Therein, "one whose conduct is continuously refined" (*sallekhānusantatavuttī*) means one whose conduct of refinement (*sallekhavutti*) is untroubled.
Why? Because he possesses intense reverence for refinement. For one whose temperament is dominated by views [proceeds] by means of asceticism, self-disgust, and so forth.

Even by means other than the formal methods, he mostly conducts himself with the intention of effacing the defilements; therefore, having gone forth in the Dispensation, he fulfills the practice of effacement by way of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). "One whose conduct is continuous with the training" means one whose conduct of the fourfold purification of virtue is unbroken.
"The occurrence of wisdom similar [to that] in its own domain regarding view": as he becomes purified, he becomes preeminent in wisdom; thus it is said: "one whose temperament is dominated by view."

"One entering the certainty of rightness becomes a follower by Dhamma. Because there is wrong liberation through craving, one whose temperament is dominated by craving, while being purified, possesses a predominance of faith;
therefore it is said: "One whose temperament is dominated by craving, entering the certainty of rightness, becomes a follower by faith.
The passage beginning with "one whose temperament is dominated by views [enters] the pleasant way" is the description of the ways of practice (*paṭipadā*).
This has already been presented below in the *Vibhaṅga* on the "Nutriment of Teaching," and its meaning has also been stated there in every respect.

However, regarding the previously unstated passages: "being analyzed" (*viveciyamāno*) means being liberated (*vimociyamāno*). "He emerges" (*paṭinissarati*) means he goes forth; the sense is that he is liberated.
"And he understands the Dhamma slowly" is said with reference to one of craving-temperament who possesses dull wisdom. One of sharp wisdom...

"But he understands the Dhamma quickly. By the passage beginning with "Beings are also twofold," he again demonstrates the classification of the way of practice (*paṭipadā*) according to the classification of the faculties (*indriya*); that is easy to understand.
By the passage beginning with "Whosoever," he demonstrates the absolute certainty of those ways of practice regarding deliverance at all three times.
In this context, "by these very four ways" means by these very four ways, because there is no other way apart from them.
"The fourfold path" refers to the fourfold way, for the way is indeed the path.
Alternatively, "the fourfold path" refers to the path consisting of the four directions of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa diagram. Those four—
They will come from every direction according to the method of observing the directions. But for what purpose does he prescribe the fourfold path? He says: "served by ignorant people," and so forth.
Therein, "served by ignorant people" means served by unwise people. "Beloved by fools" means desired by foolish people. "Dwelling among those who delight in passion":
she dwells among those who are overcome by passion (*rāga*), thus she is one who dwells among those who delight in passion; [he refers] to her. "By those who rejoice" means therein...

In that context, it is called "delight" (*nandī*) in the sense of relishing. "Turning back" (*avaṭṭana*) means the sense of cutting off. This is called the "ground of the method of the turning-back of delight" (*nandiyāvaṭṭa-naya*);

this refers to the application of the Four Truths to the two directions on the side of defilement by way of craving and ignorance, and likewise the two directions on the side of purification by way of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). This is the method of the turning-back of delight.
"Because it is the source of this method, it is the 'ground' (bhūmi).
(82) Having thus demonstrated the ground of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method, he now demonstrates the phenomena that constitute its directions.
Since the method of "surveying the directions" is already implicitly stated when those phenomena constituting the directions are explained, [the author says]: "In the Veyyākaraṇas..."

Having referred by way of a partial definition to the characteristic of "discerning directions" as "those which are wholesome and unwholesome," the passage beginning with "they are to be examined in two ways" is commenced.

Therein, "they" refers to those phenomena that have become the directions. "In two ways" means in this twofold manner: "these are defiled phenomena (saṃkilesadhammā), these are purified phenomena (vodānadhammā).

"To be examined" (upaparikkhitabbā) means they are to be looked at thoroughly from the standpoint of their arising; that is, according to their respective status as directions through their connection with specific phenomena.
The meaning is that they are to be seen and to be observed.
He shows what mode was intended when it was said, "they are to be examined in two ways," by stating:

"that which conforms to the world’s cycle (saṁsāra) and that which conforms to the world’s dissolution. Its meaning is as follows: the world itself is the cycle; thus, it is the "world-cycle" (*lokavaṭṭa*). By way of being the world-cycle...
It follows and proceeds along with it, thus it is "following the world-cycle" (*lokavaṭṭānusārī*); the meaning is that it is a phenomenon of defilement (*saṃkilesadhamma*).

The turning away from the world or from the world is the "turning away from the world" (*lokavivaṭṭa*), which is Nibbāna. It follows that and goes toward it by way of conformity, thus it is "following the turning away from the world" (*lokavivaṭṭānusārī*);
the meaning is that it is a phenomenon of purification (*vodānadhamma*). For this very reason it was said: "The cycle (*vaṭṭa*) is called saṃsāra; the turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) is Nibbāna."
"How is that to be seen?"—if one asks, "In what manner or by what means is it to be seen? it is by way of accumulation (*upacaya*).
Just as an action performed becomes capable of yielding its fruit, so too that which is performed is said to be "accumulated.

Thus, in the state of being accumulated, it is called "kamma," meaning it becomes the cause for the cycle of rebirth (*vipākavaṭṭa*). All defilements (*kilesa*) [are included] within the four perversions (*vipallāsa*).
They should be demonstrated, because all ten defilements serve as causes for the perversions.
To the question, "Where are they to be seen?"—that is, where are those perversions to be observed—he says: "In the heap of defilements having ten bases.

The meaning is: in a collection of defilements consisting of ten kinds of causes. In this context, both the defilements themselves are "bases of defilement," and the phenomena that serve as conditions for the defilements are also "bases of defilement."
Among these, the defilements established previously as causes are also "bases for defilement" because they serve as conditions for subsequent defilements in others.
Likewise, improper attention and those phenomena conditioned by improper attention should be understood as "bases for defilement" because they function as the causes for the arising of defilements.

Regarding the phrase "four nutriments" (*cattāro āhārā*): here, by way of the headword "nutriment," the defilements (*kilesā*) that have that as their object are also intended. The same principle applies to the phrase "four stations of consciousness" (*catasso viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo*).
By the passage beginning with "In the first nutriment," etc., he shows that within this heap of defilements consisting of ten bases, each preceding one is the cause for each succeeding one.
Therein, "in the first nutriment" means in the first [nutriment] which has become the object.
The meaning is that the first perversion occurs with respect to food. This same method applies to the remaining types of nutriment as well.
"When the first perversion" means that when the first perversion has not been abandoned, the first clinging occurs;
this same method applies to the remaining phrases as well. Whatever else needs to be said here, we shall explain it in the exposition itself.
83. Now, dividing the mass of defilements consisting of ten bases into two portions by way of craving (*taṇhā*) and ignorance (*avijjā*), he says:

“And whatever is material food,” and so forth. Therein, for one of craving-temperament who does not fully understand material food and contact-food, there arises, respectively, intense desire and lust for the body and for feelings; thus, [this is] regarding the defilement.
Because they serve as the cause for desire and lust, edible food and contact-food are said to be the defilements for a person of craving-character.
Likewise, one of view-character, not fully understanding mental volition-food and consciousness-food, perceives a self and permanence in them;
thus, by that same method, those two are [defilements] for the person of view-character.
These are said to be the defilements of the person (*puggala*).

Likewise, the first two distortions (*vipallāsa*), as well as the first two pairs of clinging (*upādāna*), yokes (*yoga*), ties (*gantha*), taints (*āsava*), floods (*ogha*), arrows (*salla*), stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), and ways of going (*agatigamana*), are said to be the defilements of one whose temperament is craving (*taṇhācarita*), because they have craving as their primary factor, because they have the nature of craving, and because they have craving as their object.
However, the latter [pairs] have view (*diṭṭhi*) as their primary factor.
It should be understood that they are called "defilements of the view-temperament" because of their identity with views and because they are the objects of views. 84.
Regarding the "perversion of perceiving the beautiful in the unattractive" in the case of physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*):

among the four nutriments and the four perversions, the perversion of perceiving the beautiful in the unattractive is to be understood as applying to physical nutriment, because physical nutriment is by nature unattractive.

And because it originates from the unattractive (*asubha*). Likewise, because the nutriment of contact (*phassāhāra*) has suffering as its intrinsic nature and is a condition for suffering, there specifically occurs therein the perversion of perceiving "pleasure" in what is suffering. Similarly, beings for the most part perceive permanence in consciousness and a self in formations (*saṅkhāra*);
and since formations have volition as their primary factor, it is said: "In the nutriment of consciousness... [and so forth]."
“...the perversion of ‘self. Established in the first perversion, one clings to sense-pleasures;

thus, one who grasps erroneously at the beautiful in the ugly takes hold firmly of objective sense-pleasures by means of the defilement of craving. This is called clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*);
this very grasping of sense-pleasures is what is called clinging to sense-pleasures. One who grasps erroneously at pleasure in suffering [clings] by means of rules and observances...

One firmly grasps at the view that "purity in future existence" is the bliss of extinction (*nibbāna*). One who grasps perversely by taking "the impermanent to be permanent" firmly grasps at the view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*), which delights in *saṃsāra*, thinking:
"All existences are permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change.
One who grasps perversely by taking "the non-self to be self" [thinks]: "If there is no self, to whom does this fruit of action belong?"
"Therefore, he acts; he experiences"—by this [statement], beginning with "standing in the second perversion," it shows that one firmly grasps the view of self (attadiṭṭhi).

This is called the "yoke of sensual desire" (kāmayoga), by which clinging to sensual pleasures (kāmupādāna)—consisting of sensual lust—a being, together with the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthukāma),...
That by which one is bound—this sensual lust—is called the "fetter of sensuality" (*kāmayoga*).

That by which a being is bound together with existence (*bhava*) through the clinging to existence (*bhavupādāna*), which is termed the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*)—this craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) is called the "fetter of existence" (*bhavayoga*).

That by which [one is bound] through evil views, such as the view of no-cause (*ahetukadiṭṭhi*) and so forth, or through the remaining views such as the view of a self-existent body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and so forth—this is called the "fetter of views" (*diṭṭhiyoga*).
And that by which a being is bound together with suffering—this evil view is called the "fetter of views.
This is called the "fetter of ignorance": that by which, through the clinging to a self-doctrine, a being is bound together with the entire suffering of the cycle of existence;
this ignorance is called the "fetter of ignorance."
However, because the bond of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*) and the others are the conditions for the bodily tie of covetousness (*abhijjhākāyagantha*) and so forth, it is said:

"Established in the first bond, one ties the body with covetousness," and so on. In this context, "one ties the body with covetousness" means that by means of covetousness—characterized by the coveting of what belongs to others—one ties or obstructs the mental body (*nāmakāya*). Likewise [it is said] regarding the longing for existence (*bhavapatthanā*).
Because beings defile their minds toward the bases of resentment due to the presence of the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*) and lust for existence (*bhavarāga*), it is said:
“One established in the second yoga binds the body with ill-will (*byāpāda*).

Likewise, because one adheres to the notion that purification comes through rules and observances (*sīlabbata*) due to views and ignorance (*avijjā*), and clings to the thought “this alone is truth, all else is vain,” it is said: “In the third... [etc.]”
“By the adherence to ‘this is the truth,’ one binds the body.
“Of him” means of that person endowed with covetousness and so forth. “Bound in this way” means having remained bound to the mental body (nāmakāya) by means of covetousness and the rest.
“They flow” means they proceed as an outflow (āsava). And from what [perspective] are they said to flow?
But from what cause do those defilements flow? Thus he asks about the cause of the outflows (*āsava*).

Since the defilements, having obstructed the arising of the wholesome and remaining by seizing the mind, become the cause for the arising of the outflows—either as underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) or as active obsessions (*pariyuṭṭhāna*)—therefore it is said:
"Either through underlying tendency or through obsession. Through the bodily tie of covetousness, there is the outflow of sensual desire.

Since covetousness (*abhijjhā*) is established as a bodily tie (*kāyagantha*) by virtue of its nature being identical to sensual lust (*kāmarāga*), the taint of sensuality (*kāmāsava*) is thereby established.
Because one who is depressed over some particular object yearns for an object that is its opposite, or for a state of existence (*bhava*) abundant in such objects, it is said:

"By the bodily tie of ill-will (*byāpāda*), there is the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*). By the bodily tie of misapprehension (*parāmāsa*), there is the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*); specifically, by the bodily tie of misapprehension of rules and observances (*sīlabbata-parāmāsa*).
The taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*) is established for one who, by means of a settled conviction, binds themselves to various successive views due to their inherent nature.

As for the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*), it arises through the bodily tie of dogmatic adherence (*idamsaccābhinivesakāyagantha*); that is, for one who adheres with the thought "this alone is the truth, all else is vain," the taint of ignorance arises together with numerous unwholesome states due to improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). This applies to all [beings].

Or, because unwholesome states are preceded by ignorance (*avijjā*), the taint of ignorance—which is established as their cause—is proven by means of the "body-fetter" consisting of the adherence to the view that "this is the truth.

Furthermore, since it is the taints themselves that, having swelled up, carry one away and sink one down in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), they are called "floods" (*ogha*); therefore it was said: "These four taints of his," and so forth.
"Accompanied by underlying tendencies" (*anusayasahagatā*) means having proceeded or arisen without rejecting the state of underlying tendency, or being of the nature of underlying tendencies.

"Inclination" (*ajjhāsaya*) refers to the mind. "Pervaded" (*anupaviṭṭhā*) means plunged into. "Remaining striking the heart" (*hadayaṃ āhacca tiṭṭhanti*) means remaining after striking the heart, which is reckoned as the interior of the mind.
For it is said in the *Aṭṭhasālinī*: "The heart in the sense of being internal."
Therefore they are called "arrows" (salla) because, having entered into one's underlying intention (ajjhāsaya), they remain striking the heart;
thus they are called "arrows. Their nature as arrows consists in producing affliction and being difficult to extract.
Since the grasping "I am this" occurs by way of the grasping "This is my self," one arouses conceit even by relying on views; hence he says, "by the flood of views, the arrow of conceit."
“Exhausted” (*pariyādinna*) means grasped on all sides without leaving room for anything else.
“It settles upon four things” means it becomes established upon those four things that have become objects by way of being object-conditions.
He shows these in their specific form as “in form, feeling, perception, and formations. “With the sprinkling of delight” (*nandūpasecana*) refers to [the craving] associated with greed.

“With delight as its sprinkling” means that for one [type of consciousness] there is sprinkling by way of the factor of co-nascence (*sahajāta*), and for the other, by way of the factor of decisive support (*upanissaya*); thus it is “with delight as its sprinkling,” and by means of that sprinkling of delight.
But by what is it sprinkled with delight? He says: “by consciousness which has the dart of lust and is sprinkled with delight.

Therein, “by the dart of lust” means by the dart of lust acting as a cause; “by consciousness which is sprinkled with delight” is used in the sense of a characteristic of a state so described (*itthambhūtalakkhaṇe*).

The word *karaṇa* means "instrument" (or "means"). "Bases of consciousness that have gone to form" (*rūpūpagā viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo*) means that they are called bases of consciousness that have gone to form because form itself must be approached as an object (*ārammaṇa*), and because consciousness is established (*patiṭṭhā*) therein. It is called a "base" (*ṭhiti*) because consciousness stands (*tiṭṭhati*) there.

For in the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*), the volitional consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*) stands supported by the aggregate of form. "By the dart of hatred" means by the dart of hatred that is co-nascent (*sahajāta*).

When the station of consciousness associated with feeling is spoken of, then consciousness should be understood as being moistened by delight from the perspective of the decisive support condition (*upanissaya-koṭi*).

And that feeling is indeed a feeling of mental distress (*domanassa-vedanā*). Furthermore, when the station of consciousness associated with feeling is spoken of by means of the sting of hatred acting as a decisive support condition, then it should be understood from the perspective of the co-nascent condition (*sahajāta-koṭi*) and the perspective of the decisive support condition.

Or consciousness should be seen as being sprinkled by the "Nandi" (delight). Feeling, however, is all three [types of feeling], because they serve as the object-condition (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*) for those three feelings.
Therein, the first method is stated by way of the volitional formation-consciousness (*abhisankhāra-viññāṇa*) that has displeasure (*domanassa*) as its object;
the second should be understood by way of that which has all feelings as its object.
"By the dart of the mind" means by that which is co-nascent with the dart of the mind, or by that which serves as its decisive support (*upanissaya*).

"By the dart of delusion"—here too the same method applies. And herein, in this beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), men and women delight in forms; thus, the first station of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) is associated with the dart of lust (*rāga*).
Since there is a sense of suffering inherent in every kind of feeling, and because there is aversion toward suffering, [the second station is associated with the dart of hatred].
"It underlies" (anuseti) refers to the second [station of consciousness] by way of the sting of hatred (*dosasalla*). "The conceit 'I am better'" arises by way of perception;

thus, the third station of consciousness should be understood as being associated with the sting of pride (*mānasalla*). The fourth station of consciousness is joined with the sting of delusion (*mohasalla*) because among the formations (*saṅkhāra*), there is a massed compactness that is difficult to disentangle.
"Supported" (*upatthaddha*) means propped up by those stations of consciousness which have become the objects of clinging. And that karma...
That which was previously stated as "volition is a mental factor" (cetasika). And these defilements refer to these ten-based defilements.
The remainder is indeed easy to understand. 85.
Now, in order to define the nutriment and other categories according to their directional aspect within the side of defilement, [it says]: "These four..."

The passage beginning with “the directions,” and so forth, has already been explained. Furthermore, the section beginning with “edible food” (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) was undertaken to analyze and demonstrate which specific individuals possess defilements (*upakkilesa*) regarding the nutriments (*āhāra*) and other factors.
In that context, the phrase “of ten suttas” is stated using a collective designation for a portion of them; for a conventional term applied to a whole is also seen to apply to its individual parts.
“As a cloth is burnt, as the ocean is seen. This is said because it accomplishes a single meaning (*ekassa atthassa nipphādanato*).
Regarding the phrase “only the phrasing (*byañjana*) is different,” it should be understood that by the mention of “phrasing,” the meaning of the phrasing (*byañjanattha*) is also included.
By all ten sutta passages, craving (*taṇhā*) together with its basis is stated. And craving [quickly] [characterizes] a person of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*).
