He says, "They defile," meaning: "These are the secondary defilements (upakkilesa) of a person of lustful temperament (rāgacarita).

Just as the states described under the first heading are the secondary defilements of one of lustful temperament, so too are the states described under the second heading those of one of hateful temperament (dosacarita).
The states described under the third and fourth headings are, respectively, those of one of deluded temperament (diṭṭhicarita) who is dull-witted and one who is sharp-witted.
And the defilements have been stated. Their status as defilements is to be understood according to the method already described.

Although the perversions regarding nutriment and the rest are all, as appropriate, to be fully understood and abandoned in the prior stage by means of all three doors to liberation, nevertheless, for one whose contemplation of suffering frequently proceeds in the aspect of suffering regarding the first two types of nutriment, [it is particularly so].
By virtue of that, it is said that both edible food and contact as food reach full understanding through the door of liberation that is the wishless (*appaṇihita*).
This same method applies to the remaining [nutriments]. And this is so, not otherwise.

For there can be no fixed rule regarding what is to be fully understood and what is to be abandoned by the doors of liberation, as there is for the noble paths regarding what is to be abandoned. Thus...
The conclusion is: "All phenomena that follow the cycle of the world lead out from those worlds by means of the three doors to liberation.

Its meaning is as follows: thus, all such things as the nutriments mentioned above, which are phenomena following the cycle reckoned as the world, lead out from that world-cycle—which is itself the world—by means of the three doors to liberation, namely, the contemplations of impermanence and so forth.

86. Having thus demonstrated the phenomena that constitute the directions on the side of defilement (*saṃkilesa*), the text now says, “The four modes of practice” (*catasso paṭipadā*) and so forth, in order to show the phenomena that constitute the directions on the side of purification (*vodāna*).
In this context, the “divine, brahmā, noble, and imperturbable abidings” (*dibba-brahma-ariya-āneñja-vihāra*) refer to the four abidings.
The abandonment of conceit, the uprooting of attachment, the abandonment of ignorance, and the pacification of existence are the four wonders (*acchariya*) and marvels (*abbhuta*).
The phenomena (dhammā) are as follows: the four foundations (adhiṭṭhāna), beginning with the foundation of truth;

the four developments of concentration (samādhibhāvanā), beginning with the development of concentration through desire; the four phenomena conducive to happiness (sukhabhāgiya), which should be understood as: the virtue of merit consisting in the restraint of the faculties (indriyasaṃvara); the development of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgabhāvanā); and Nibbāna, which consists in the relinquishment of all acquisitions (sabbūpadhipaṭinissagga).

The passage beginning with "the first way" (*paṭhamā paṭipadā*) and so forth is a demonstration of the non-differentiation of the foundations of mindfulness as a way of practice (*paṭipadā-satipaṭṭhāna*) and the rest.
If this is so, why has there been a separate mention [of them]? It is for the purpose of showing that they are the antidotes (*paṭipakkha*) to the mass of defilements consisting of ten bases;
thus, the exposition of the tenfold way of practice is given. For he will say: "The four nutriments have their antidote in the four [foundations of mindfulness]."

“...the way of practice,” and so forth. Although there is no fixed rule among the four foundations of mindfulness stating that “this particular foundation of mindfulness is accomplished only by this specific way of practice,” nevertheless, it is stated thus— “the first way of practice, the first foundation of mindfulness”—
precisely on account of their possible occurrence, since the first foundation of mindfulness can arise through the first way of practice.

However, since there is no difference in meaning between the foundations of mindfulness and the paths of practice (patipadā), etc., as there is between the distortions regarding nutriment and so forth—
because it is simply the foundations of mindfulness themselves that, when practiced in various ways, receive such names as "the painful path" or "slow direct knowledge"— therefore,
just as on the side of defilement one speaks of "the first distortion regarding the first nutriment," and so on, by way of a distinction of loci;
Thus it was said; and so, without making a distinction among the legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), it was stated: "The first way, the first foundation of mindfulness," and so forth.
The same method applies to the others as well.
A marvel (*acchariya*) is that which arises only occasionally, like a blind man climbing a mountain; it is called a marvel because it is worthy of a *accharā* (a finger-snap).
*Porāṇa* means ancient. *Abbhuta* means that which has never occurred before has now occurred; both terms are designations for what brings about wonder.
For nothing else is found to be more difficult to accomplish or more marvelous than the abandonment of conceit and so forth;
one resolves by means of this, or it is the very act of resolving upon this, thus it is called *adhiṭṭhāna*. It is both truth and a resolve, hence *saccādhiṭṭhāna*.
Or, it is the resolution upon truth (*sacca*); or, that which has truth as its resolution is "resolution upon truth" (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*).
The same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well. Concentration itself, by virtue of being something to be developed, is "development of concentration" (*samādhibhāvanā*).

One who partakes of happiness is "one who partakes of happiness" (*sukhabhāgiyo*); or, one who is beneficial to the portion of happiness, that is, to the constituent element of happiness, is "one who partakes of happiness. The development of foulness (*asubhabhāvanā*) and so forth, even for a single sentient being...
Because it does not stop at one part but proceeds until there is no remainder, it has no measure; thus it is called "immeasurable" (*appamaññā*).
When the first way of practice is developed and cultivated, it fulfills the first foundation of mindfulness;
the meaning is that the development and cultivation of the first way of practice is the fulfillment of the development of the first foundation of mindfulness.

The same method applies to the remaining sections as well. For just as when the Noble Path is developed, all the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma), such as the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, are indeed developed, so too should this be understood.
Because contemplation of the body is the direct antidote to sensual lust, it is said: "When the first foundation of mindfulness is developed and cultivated..."
It is said: “One fulfills the first jhāna as the opposite of sensual desire. Likewise, the second foundation of mindfulness proceeds by way of experiencing rapture (*pīti*) and so forth;
the third foundation of mindfulness proceeds by way of gladdening the mind of the second jhāna which is accompanied by rapture;
and [the fourth] proceeds by way of impermanence, dispassion, and so forth toward the pleasure of the third jhāna which has reached its peak.
The fourth foundation of mindfulness, which is equanimous toward formations during their occurrence,
leads to the fulfillment of the fourth jhāna because of its state of purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

Furthermore, because the first fine-material-sphere jhāna [is the basis] for the fine-material-sphere attainments, and the second jhāna [is so] through the distancing of ill-will, applied thought, and so forth...
The third jhāna, through its happiness born of the fading away of rapture, becomes the basis for insight among the divine abidings (brahmavihāras);
the fourth jhāna, having reached imperturbability through the purity of equanimity and mindfulness, is specifically the condition for the imperturbable abidings (āneñjavihāras).
Therefore, "the first jhāna, when developed and cultivated, [is the condition] for the first abiding..."
"‘He fulfills it,’ and so forth, was said. Thus, it should be understood that whatever is a specific condition for something is said to fulfill it.
87. Now, in order to define the path and the rest as directions within the side of purification, ‘In this regard, these are the four directions,’ and so forth, was said.
That is indeed easy to understand. Again, regarding the fourfold sets beginning with the path, such as ‘The first path,’ and so forth..."
This has been undertaken in order to demonstrate, by way of analysis, which purification belongs to which individual. That follows the same method as explained below.

Although there is no fixed rule among the three gateways to liberation that "this specific gateway to liberation succeeds only through this particular practice," for those individuals who [succeed] through the first two practices by means of the desireless gateway to liberation...

It is the attainment of the Noble Path. Likewise, this correlation between the modes of practice and the doors to liberation is made by way of those individuals who attain the Noble Path through the door of the emptiness liberation via the third mode of practice, and those who attain it through the door of the signless liberation via the fourth mode of practice.
This same method applies to the correlation between the foundations of mindfulness and so forth with the doors to liberation as well.

"Of them, the sport" means the sporting or dwelling of lions—namely, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha—due to their possession of specific qualities such as fearlessness, speed, and prowess.

This refers to the accomplishment of the path and so forth within one's own and others' continuums by way of transcending the bases of defilement, such as nutriment. Now, [regarding] the manner in which nutriment and the rest are transcended by means of the path and so forth:
Demonstrating their state of being opposites, he said: "The four nutriments have as their opposite the four paths," and so forth.

Therein, their state of being opposites consists of both the state of being abandoned and the state of being the abandoner. Furthermore, the state of being abandoned here refers to the nutriments and the persistence of consciousness;
this should be understood by way of the desire and lust that bind them. In this context, "sport" refers to meditation (*bhāvanā*).
And as for the phrase “realization,” etc., this is its summary meaning:

“Their sport” refers here to that which is called sport—the cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) that are to be developed, and the realization of the fruits and Nibbāna that are to be realized.
Likewise, [there is the abandoning] of the mass of defilements consisting of ten bases, by means of the abandonment through substitution of opposites (tadaṅga), and so forth.
"Abandoning, making an end, without remainder. Now, showing this in brief, he said: "The play based on the faculties (*indriyādhiṭṭhāna*) is the non-basis for inversion (*vipariyāsānadhiṭṭhāna*).
"Based on the faculties" means the engagement with, the cultivation of, and the realization of the faculties. "Non-basis for inversion" means...

The non-occurrence of the perversions is their abandonment and non-arising. "The faculties have the true Dhamma as their domain" means that here the faculties intended are those such as faith-faculty (saddhindriya) and so forth, which have become the domain of the true Dhamma and are the causes for its occurrence.
"Perversions have the defilements as their domain" means that the perversions (vipallāsā) are the locus of the occurrence of the side of defilement and are the causes for its occurrence.
This is called the "ground" of the Lion’s Play method (*sīhavikkīḷita-naya*).

It is the determination—by way of revealing both defilements and purification—of ten tetrads on the side of defilement, beginning with "the four nutriments," and of ten tetrads on the side of purification, beginning with "the four paths," for those of craving-temperament and so forth; this is what is known as the ground of the Lion’s Play method.

88. Now, desiring to clarify the ground of the Tipukkhalanaya by way of the three types of persons—namely, those who understand through a condensed statement (ugghaṭitaññū) and so forth—it should be understood that since it is intended for the various methods (nayā) to enter into one another, the Tipukkhalanaya emerges from the Sīhavikkīḷitanaya;
therefore, by way of the analysis of the path, the four types of persons constitute the ground of the Sīhavikkīḷitanaya.

Having thus demonstrated [the path], he then began the passage beginning with "Therein, those who [follow] the painful way" in order to distinguish the three types of persons, such as the one who gains knowledge by a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*).
Therein, "these two persons" refers to two persons by way of the two aforementioned ways of practice;
this same method applies to the other cases as well. Again, the passage beginning with "Therein, those who [follow] the painful way" is [taken] from the previously mentioned tetrad of persons.
This was stated in order to distinguish the triad of persons beginning with the one who gains knowledge through a condensed explanation (*ugghaṭitaññū*). Therein, the connection is as follows:

"He who sets out by means of the common [path]—that is, by the painful practice with quick direct knowledge (*khippābhiññā*) and by the pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge (*dandhābhiññā*).
But how can these two practices occur for a single person? This should not be viewed in that way; for it is possible for a single person, at one time...

"Two modes of progress (paṭipadā) occur. Now, regarding the two modes of progress mentioned above, the intended meaning here is that whoever proceeds by whichever one is "one who knows by exposition" (vipañcitaññū).

However, since it was stated as "it wavers" in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* during the investigation into whether the mode of progress wavers or does not waver, therefore, even for a single person, between the intervals of jhānas and the intervals of paths—

"The distinction of the path is intended" means that by the passage beginning with "Therein, the Blessed One," the Teacher clarifies that very same classification of persons through the divisions of the teaching;

this follows the method already explained above. In that context, "higher mind" (*adhicitta*) refers to the training in higher mind (*adhicittasikkhā*), where the word "and" (*ca*) has been elided in the compound.
The meaning is that by means of that [teaching], he explains the training in higher mind and the training in higher wisdom to one who is to understand through exposition (*vipañcitaññū*).
The same method applies here for "higher virtue" (*adhisīla*). It should be construed as: "the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
The statement "having been four, they become three" is expressed with a change of gender; the meaning is that having been four persons, they become three persons.

"This is defilement" (saṃkilesa): this refers to the group of twelve factors beginning with the unwholesome roots; it is called "defilement" because one is defiled by means of these. "This is cleansing" (vodāna): here too the same method applies. "Having been three, they become two":

this was stated for the purpose of showing the phenomena that constitute the direction of the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method. For this very reason he said: "Craving and ignorance," and so forth; all of that is indeed easy to understand.
Why, however, has the exposition here not been made according to the sequence of the enumeration of the methods? It is for the purpose of showing the arising of methods from methods.
Indeed, because the third method arises from the first method by way of a person-based designation (puggalādhiṭṭhāna),
and the second method arises from the third method, the third method is explained immediately after the first method, and the second method is explained immediately after the third method,
in order to demonstrate this distinction. However, by way of a dharma-based designation (dhammādhiṭṭhāna), the second method [arises] from the third method, and from the second method...
The first method is also possible; therefore, in order to show this distinction, the basis for the first method is shown at the end with the words, "Craving and ignorance," and so forth.
For it is precisely for this reason that it was said: "Having been four, they become three;
having been three, they become two. If that is so, [one might ask]: "Having been two, they become four; having been two, they become three..."
"Having been three, they become four"—should this method also be stated? This is true;

however, it was not mentioned because this method has already been shown by way of its meaning. For since the mutual inclusion of the three methods of meaning is intended, and when there is inclusion, emergence from them is likewise possible.
And this meaning should be clarified by means of the *Peṭakopadesa*.
Herein, this is the exposition starting from the beginning: there are four types of persons. One of craving-temperament is twofold:

one of dull faculties and one of keen faculties. Likewise, there is one of view-temperament. Among these, the one of craving-temperament with dull faculties goes forth by means of the painful way with sluggish direct knowledge;
the one with keen faculties goes forth by means of the painful way with swift direct knowledge.
But one of speculative temperament with dull faculties is led out by the pleasant way with sluggish direct knowledge,
while one with sharp faculties is led out by the pleasant way with quick direct knowledge. Thus, among these ways,
the four nutriments are to be abandoned by those of craving-temperament and speculative-temperament who abide therein as appropriate, through the abandoning of the desire and lust that bind them.
"Having developed the four foundations of mindfulness, the four perversions are to be seen"—the entire method as previously stated should be followed here.
In this regard, the text is as follows: "In that case, those beings who are of a speculative temperament (diṭṭhicarita) hold a view of aversion toward sensual pleasures;
yet, because their underlying tendencies (anusaya) toward sensual pleasures have not been uprooted, they dwell devoted to the pursuit of self-mortification. To them, the Teacher or the Dhamma..."
Or another venerable fellow-celibate teaches them, saying, "There is no purpose in sensual pleasures.
Since they were already previously indifferent to sensual pleasures, they relinquish sensual pleasures without difficulty and are not obsessed by mental suffering.
Therefore, this is called the "pleasant way of practice. However, those beings who are of craving-temperament are obsessed with sensual pleasures.
The Teacher or a certain monk teaches them the Dhamma, saying, "There is no purpose in sensual pleasures.
They relinquish what is dear through suffering. Therefore, it is called "the painful way of practice.
Thus, all these beings converge upon two ways of practice: the painful and the pleasant.
In that regard, those beings who are of speculative temperament (diṭṭhicarita) are of two kinds: those with keen faculties (tikkhindriya) and those with dull faculties (mudindriya).
Among them, those beings of speculative temperament who have keen faculties relinquish [the hindrances] easily and realize [the path] quickly.
Therefore, it is called "the pleasant way with quick direct knowledge" (sukhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā). Among them, those beings of speculative temperament who have dull faculties...
First, compared to those with sharp faculties, they realize [the goal] more slowly;
they relinquish with ease, yet they realize it slowly. Therefore, it is said: “The pleasant way of practice with slow direct knowledge.
In that regard, beings of craving-temperament are of two kinds: those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties. Among them, those beings of craving-temperament who have sharp faculties—
They relinquish through suffering and attain realization quickly. Therefore, it is called "the painful practice with quick direct knowledge.

In that regard, those beings of craving-temperament who have dull faculties and attain realization more slowly than those with sharp faculties relinquish through suffering and attain realization slowly. Therefore...
It is called "the painful practice with slow direct knowledge. These are the four practices, no fifth and no sixth.
For whoever has been extinguished, is being extinguished, or will be extinguished, they do so by means of these four practices and no others.
This practice indicates the defilements by way of the fourfold path. That which is to be indicated among the noble qualities by way of the fourfold path—
This is called the method known as "The Lion’s Play.

In this regard, there are these ten terms: the four nutriments (*āhāra*), the four perversions (*vipallāsa*), the clingings (*upādāna*), the yokes (*yoga*), the ties (*gantha*), the taints (*āsava*), the floods (*ogha*), the arrows (*salla*), the stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), and the ways of going to ruin (*agatigamana*).

This is the correlation of the sutta. Regarding the four nutriments: therein, the nutriment of physical food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*) and the nutriment of contact (*phassa-āhāra*) are to be abandoned by one of craving-temperament (*taṇhā-carita*). Therein, the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanā-āhāra*) and the nutriment of consciousness (*viññāṇa-āhāra*) are to be abandoned by one of view-temperament (*diṭṭhi-carita*).

In this regard, the first nutriment is the first perversion, the second nutriment is the second perversion, the third nutriment is the third perversion, and the fourth nutriment is the fourth perversion; these four perversions are neither a fifth nor a sixth.
And these are the four nutriments by way of measure.
Therein, one who stands in the first perversion clings to sense pleasures; this is clinging to sense pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).

One who stands in the second perversion clings to future existence; this is clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*). One who stands in the third perversion clings to perverted views; this is clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*).
One who stands in the fourth perversion clings to the aggregates as a self.
This is the clinging to a theory of self (*attavādupādāna*).
Therein, one who stands in clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) is bound by covetousness for sense-pleasures; this is the bodily tie of covetousness (*abhijjhākāyagantha*).

One who stands in clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*) is bound by ill-will; this is the bodily tie of ill-will (*byāpādakāyagantha*). One who stands in clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*) is bound by misapprehension; [this is the bodily tie of misapprehension].

This is the bodily tie of dogmatic adherence (*parāmāsa-kāyagantha*). Established in the clinging to a self-doctrine (*attavādupādāna*), one who proliferates conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) ties himself;

this is the bodily tie of insistence on "this alone is the truth" (*idaṃsaccābhinivesa*). From his being bound by these ties, the defilements (*kilesa*) flow out. What is it that is said to "flow out"? It is regrets (*vippaṭisāra*). Those regrets are the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). In this context, through the bodily tie of covetousness (*abhijjhā-kāyagantha*), the influx of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) [flows]; through the bodily tie of ill-will (*byāpāda-kāyagantha*), [the influx of existence flows].
The taint of existence (*bhavāsava*) is through the bodily tie of clinging to views; the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*) is through the bodily tie of adherence to "this is the truth.

When these four taints have reached full development, they become floods (*ogha*); therefore, they are called "floods. Among them, the taint of sensual desire is the flood of sensual desire, the taint of existence is the flood of existence, the taint of ignorance is the flood of ignorance, and the taint of views is the flood of views.
These four floods, having entered the underlying tendency and being accompanied by latent dispositions, are called "arrows" because they strike the heart.
They persist. Therein, the flood of sensual desire is the dart of lust; the flood of existence is the dart of hatred; the flood of ignorance is the dart of delusion;
and the flood of views is the dart of views.
Consciousness, gripped by these four darts, persists in four things: in form, in feeling... [and so on].
[And] in perceptions regarding volitional formations. These are the four stations of consciousness. Therein, consciousness that has reached form stands, moistened by delight through the barb of lust;
[consciousness] that has reached feeling [stands] through the barb of hatred; [consciousness] that has reached perception [stands] through the barb of delusion;
and consciousness that has reached volitional formations stands, moistened by delight through the barb of views.
Through the four stations of consciousness, beings go to the fourfold wrong destination out of desire, hatred, fear, and delusion.

Through desire, one goes to a wrong destination because of lust; through hatred, one goes to a wrong destination because of aversion; through delusion, one goes to a wrong destination because of ignorance;
and through views, one goes to a wrong destination because of fear. Thus, these actions and these defilements are the cause of saṃsāra.

In this regard, these are the four directions: edible food, the perversion that there is beauty in the foul, clinging to sensual pleasures, the yoke of sensual pleasure, the bodily tie of covetousness, the taint of sensual pleasure, the flood of sensual pleasure, the dart of lust, the station of consciousness that leads to the realm of form, and going on the wrong path through desire—this is the first direction.

Contact as nutriment, the perversion that there is pleasure in the painful, clinging to rules and observances, the yoke of existence, the bodily tie of ill will, the taint of existence, the flood of existence, the dart of hatred, the station of consciousness that leads to the realm of feeling, and going on the wrong path through hatred—this is the second direction.
The nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*) is the perversion of regarding what is non-self as self;

it is the clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*), the bond of views (*diṭṭhiyoga*), the bodily tie of misapprehension (*parāmāsakāyagantha*), the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*), the flood of views (*diṭṭhogha*), the sting of views (*diṭṭhisalla*), the station of consciousness associated with perception (*saññūpagā viññāṇaṭṭhiti*), and going to a bad destination out of fear. This is the third direction.

The nutriment of consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*) is the perversion of regarding what is impermanent as permanent; it is the clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*), the bond of ignorance (*avijjāyoga*), and the bodily tie of adherence to "this is the truth" (*idaṃsaccābhinivesokāyagantha*).

The taint of ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the dart of delusion, the stations of consciousness that lead to formations, and the going to a bad destination through delusion—this is the fourth direction.
Thus, by the first term of these ten suttas, there is the surveying of the first direction;
by the second term, of the second direction; by the third term, of the third direction; and by the fourth term...
The illumination of the fourth direction—this is called the illumination of the directions. In this manner, all defilements are to be assigned to the four locations.

This is the unwholesome side. [The opposites are] the four ways of practice, the four jhānas, the four foundations of mindfulness, and the four abodes: the divine, the sublime, the brahma-like, and the taintless.
The noble imperturbability; the four right efforts; the four wonderful and marvelous qualities; the four foundations;
the four concentrations—namely, concentration through desire, concentration through energy, concentration through mind, and concentration through investigation;
and the four factors conducive to happiness, which are none other than the factors of enlightenment, austerity, restraint of the sense faculties, and [right] view.
All relinquishings, the four immeasurables.
Therein, the painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge, when being developed and cultivated, fulfills the first jhāna;
the first jhāna, when fulfilled, fulfills the first foundation of mindfulness; the first...
The fulfillment of the foundation of mindfulness fulfills the first abiding;
the fulfillment of the first abiding fulfills the first right exertion; the fulfillment of the first right exertion fulfills the first wonderful and marvelous quality;
the fulfillment of the first wonderful and marvelous quality fulfills the first...
He fulfills the foundation; when the first foundation is fulfilled, it fulfills concentration through desire (*chandasamādhi*);

when concentration through desire is fulfilled, it fulfills restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara*); when restraint of the sense faculties is fulfilled, it fulfills the first immeasurable (*appamāṇa*).
In this way, up to the relinquishment of everything, it fulfills the fourth immeasurable.
Therein, the first way of practice, the first jhāna, the first foundation of mindfulness, the divine abiding, the first right exertion,
the first wonderful and marvelous quality, the resolution upon truth, concentration through desire,
restraint of the faculties, and the immeasurable loving-kindness— this is the first direction.
The second path, the second higher knowledge, the second jhāna, the second foundation of mindfulness,
the second divine abiding, the second right effort, the second wonderful and marvelous quality,
the foundation of generosity, concentration of mind, austerity, compassion, and the immeasurable— this is the second direction.
The third way is of slow direct knowledge; the third jhāna; the third foundation of mindfulness;
the noble abiding; the third right exertion; the third wonderful and marvelous quality; the resolution upon truth; energy and concentration;
the enlightenment factors; and the immeasurable state of sympathetic joy. This is the third direction.
The fourth path, the fourth jhāna, the fourth foundation of mindfulness,
the imperturbable abiding, the fourth right effort, the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality,
the basis of tranquility, the concentration of investigation, the relinquishment of all, equanimity, and the immeasurable— this is the fourth direction. Of these...
The surveying of the four directions is called the method known as "surveying the directions" (*disālocana*).
Herein is the application: the four nutriments, the four paths, the four perversions, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four clingings, the four jhānas, and the four yokes.
And the four abidings, the four ties, the four right endeavors, the four taints,
the four wonderful and marvelous qualities, the four floods, the four foundations,
the four arrows, the four concentrations, the four stations of consciousness, and the four things conducive to happiness.
The phenomena, the four ways of going to ruin, and the four immeasurables. Thus is the application by way of the opposition between the wholesome and the unwholesome sides.
This is the method of "the Lion’s Play" regarding the surveying of directions.
Its conclusion consists of the four fruits of recluseship; therein, the fruit of stream-entry belongs to the first direction.

The conclusion [of the first] is the fruit of stream-entry; the second, the fruit of once-returning; the third, the fruit of non-returning; and the fourth, the fruit of arhatship is the conclusion. In this regard, what is the Tipukkhalanaya method?

Among the four types of persons distinguished by their mode of practice (*paṭipadā*), he who proceeds by means of a pleasant practice with swift direct knowledge (*khippābhiññā*) is one who gains knowledge through a condensed teaching (*ugghaṭitaññū*).
He who [proceeds] by means of a pleasant practice, or... with sluggish direct knowledge (*dandhābhiññā*)... [is one who gains knowledge through an expanded teaching].
One who goes forth by means of the painful practice with quick direct knowledge is one who gains knowledge through what is condensed (*ugghaṭitaññū*).
One who goes forth by means of the painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge is one who is led (*neyyo*). Thus, having been four, they become three.

Among them, insight preceded by serenity (*samatha*) is suitable for one who gains knowledge through what is condensed. For one who is led, serenity preceded by insight [is suitable]. For one who gains knowledge through what is expanded...
Calm and insight are yoked together. For one who gains knowledge through a brief indication, the teaching is gentle; for one who must be led, the teaching is sharp;
for one who gains knowledge through detailed exposition, the teaching is both sharp and gentle.

For one who gains knowledge through a brief indication, there is the training in higher wisdom; for one who gains knowledge through detailed exposition, there is both the training in higher mind and the training in higher wisdom.
And for the person to be guided (neyya), there is the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
Thus, for these types of persons, there is deliverance by means of four paths.

In this regard, this is the side of defilement: the three unwholesome roots, the three kinds of contact, the three feelings, the three modes of mental application, the three defilements, the three types of thought, the three fevers, the three characteristics of the conditioned, and the three kinds of suffering.
The three unwholesome roots are: greed as an unwholesome root, hatred as an unwholesome root, and delusion as an unwholesome root.
The three types of contact are: contact to be experienced as pleasant, contact to be experienced as painful, and contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
The three feelings are: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. The three modes of mental engagement are:
The three explorations of mental states are: exploration accompanied by joy, exploration accompanied by grief, and exploration accompanied by equanimity.
The three defilements are: greed, hatred, and delusion. The three types of thought are: sensual thought, ill-will thought, and cruelty thought.

The three fevers are: born of lust, born of hatred, and born of delusion. The three characteristics of the conditioned are: arising, persistence, and passing away. The three kinds of suffering are: [suffering as pain, suffering as change, and suffering as formations].
The suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of formations.
Therein, greed, which is an unwholesome root, arises with a pleasant object.
Dependent upon that very same pleasant object, a contact to be experienced as pleasant arises; dependent upon that contact to be experienced as pleasant, [greed] arises.
There is pleasant feeling; dependent on pleasant feeling, there arises the mental exploration of joy; dependent on the mental exploration of joy, lust arises;
dependent on lust, sensual thought arises; dependent on sensual thought, the fever born of lust arises;
dependent on the fever born of lust, arising—the characteristic of the conditioned—arises.
In dependence upon the characteristic of the conditioned, which is arising, there arises the suffering of change.
Hatred, an unwholesome root, originates from an unpleasant object.
In dependence upon that very same unpleasant object, there arises contact to be experienced as painful; in dependence upon contact to be experienced as painful, there arises pain.
Feeling: dependent on a painful feeling, there arises the mental exploration of grief; dependent on the mental exploration of grief, there arises hatred;
dependent on hatred, there arises ill-will directed thought; dependent on ill-will directed thought, there arises fever born of hatred;
dependent on the fever born of hatred, there arises the alteration of what stands, which is the characteristic of the conditioned.
The characteristic of the conditioned (*saṅkhatalakkhaṇa*), namely change while standing, gives rise to the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*).
Delusion, which is an unwholesome root, arises by way of an object that is a basis for equanimity (*upekkhāṭhāniya*).

Dependent upon that very same object which is a basis for equanimity, there arises contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*adukkhamasukhavedanīyo phasso*), [and] that which is to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant...
Dependent on contact, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises; dependent on neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the investigation of equanimity arises;
dependent on the investigation of equanimity, delusion arises;
dependent on delusion, a thought of cruelty arises; dependent on a thought of cruelty, a fever born of delusion arises; [dependent on] that which is born of delusion...
In dependence on fever (pariḷāha), there arises passing away (vaya), which is a characteristic of the conditioned;

in dependence on passing away, which is a characteristic of the conditioned, there arises the suffering inherent in formations (saṅkhāradukkhatā). Thus, this is the exposition of the defilements by way of three aspects.
Whatever belongs to the unwholesome side, all that is subsumed within the three unwholesome roots.
In this regard, what is the side of the wholesome? There are three roots of the wholesome: non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. There are three kinds of wisdom:

that consisting of hearing, that consisting of reflection, and that consisting of cultivation. There are three concentrations: with applied thought and sustained thought, without applied thought and with sustained thought only, and without applied thought and without sustained thought.

There are three trainings: the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom. There are three signs: the sign of serenity, the sign of exertion, and the sign of equanimity.
The sign of exertion, the sign of equanimity. Three types of thought: the thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill will, and the thought of non-cruelty. Three faculties:
the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has known.
Three modes of mental exploration: exploration of renunciation, exploration of non-ill will, and exploration of non-cruelty. Three searches...

The search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search for the holy life. There are three aggregates: the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom.

In this context, the wholesome root of non-greed fulfills the wisdom consisting of what has been heard. Wisdom consisting of what has been heard, when fulfilled, fulfills concentration accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought.
Concentration accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, when fulfilled, fulfills the training in higher virtue.
The training in higher virtue, when fulfilled, fulfills the sign of serenity; the sign of serenity, when fulfilled, fulfills thoughts of renunciation;

thoughts of renunciation, when fulfilled, fulfill the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"; the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," when fulfilled, fulfills the investigation based on renunciation;
and the investigation based on renunciation, when fulfilled, [abandons] the search for sensual pleasures.
He abandons it. The abandoning of the search for sensual pleasures fulfills the aggregate of virtue.
Non-hatred, as a root of the wholesome, fulfills wisdom born of reflection; wisdom born of reflection, when fulfilled, fulfills concentration free from applied thought but with sustained thought;
concentration free from applied thought but with sustained thought, when fulfilled, fulfills the training in higher consciousness.
The training in higher consciousness, when fulfilled, fulfills the sign of equanimity; the sign of equanimity, when fulfilled, fulfills thoughts of non-ill will;
thoughts of non-ill will, when fulfilled, fulfill the faculty of final knowledge; the faculty of final knowledge, when fulfilled, fulfills the investigation of non-ill will;
and the investigation of non-ill will, when fulfilled, abandons the search for existence.
The abandoning of the desire for existence fulfills the aggregate of concentration.

The wholesome root of non-delusion fulfills wisdom consisting in development; when wisdom consisting in development is fulfilled, it fulfills concentration without applied thought and sustained thought;
when concentration without applied thought and sustained thought is fulfilled, it fulfills the training in higher wisdom.
The training in higher wisdom, when fulfilled, fulfills the sign of exertion;
the sign of exertion, when fulfilled, fulfills thoughts of non-harming; thoughts of non-harming, when fulfilled, fulfill the faculty of one who has known;
the faculty of one who has known, when fulfilled, fulfills the investigation of non-harming; the investigation of non-harming, when fulfilled—
It fulfills the quest for the holy life; the fulfilled quest for the holy life fulfills the aggregate of wisdom.
Thus, these three states—those belonging to the unwholesome side and those belonging to the wholesome side—are demonstrated by the triple sets of definitions.
This is called the Direction of the Tipukkhalanaya. Its conclusion consists of the three liberations: the wishless, the void, and the signless. This is the second method, named Tipukkhalo.

In this regard, among these three types of persons— the one who gains knowledge through a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*), the one who gains knowledge through an elaboration (*vipañcitaññū*), and the one who is led to understanding (*neyya*)—
two of these persons lead out by means of the pleasant way of practice with quick direct knowledge and the pleasant way of practice with sluggish direct knowledge;
and only two persons lead out by means of the painful way of practice with quick direct knowledge and the painful way of practice with sluggish direct knowledge.

And they attain deliverance through sluggish direct knowledge; these are the four. Specifically, there are two: the one of speculative temperament (*diṭṭhicarita*) and the one of craving temperament (*taṇhācarita*).
These four, becoming three, and these three, becoming two.

For these two types of persons, the corruption consists of ignorance (*avijjā*), craving (*taṇhā*), lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), lack of mindfulness (*asati*), and lack of clear comprehension (*asampajañña*).
The hindrances, the fetters, attachment, adherence, the notion of "I," the notion of "mine," lack of faith,
difficult-to-correctness, laziness, improper attention, doubt, ignorance, not hearing the true Dharma, and non-attainment.

In this context, ignorance, lack of moral shame, lack of moral dread, the hindrances, attachment, the conceit "I am," lack of faith, laziness, doubt, and not hearing the true Dhamma—this is one direction.

Craving, lack of moral dread, lack of clear comprehension, the fetters, dogmatic adherence, the conceit "mine," difficult speech, improper attention, ignorance, and failure to attain meditative absorption—this is the second direction. [This concludes] the ten dyads.
The first direction consists of ten terms that should be formulated. They indicate the meaning in brief;
the second direction consists of ten terms, which are ten pairs of opposites belonging to the dark side (*kaṇhapakkha*).

What therein is the wholesome side (*kusalapakkha*)? It is serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), true knowledge (*vijjā*) and conduct (*caraṇa*), mindfulness (*sati*) and clear comprehension (*sampajañña*).
Moral shame and moral dread, the abandoning of the conceit "I am," the abandoning of the conceit "mine," right effort,
wise attention, right mindfulness, right concentration, wisdom, disenchantment, meditative attainment, hearing the true Dhamma, gladness,
and practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
The first ten terms, beginning with the methods of settling (*samatha*) and ending with mental joy (*somanassa*), constitute the first direction among the ten pairs.
The second ten terms, beginning with insight (*vipassanā*) and ending with practice in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammānudhammapaṭipatti*), constitute the second direction.
Thus, there are four directions for the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method regarding both the unwholesome side and the wholesome side.
Among those, on the side of the wholesome, through serenity (*samatha*) and so forth, craving (*taṇhā*) and the rest on the side of the unwholesome go to abandonment;

through their abandonment comes the liberation of mind (*cetovimutti*) by fading away of lust (*rāga-virāga*). On the side of the wholesome, through insight (*vipassanā*) and so forth, ignorance (*avijjā*) and the rest on the side of the unwholesome go to abandonment;

through their abandonment comes the liberation by wisdom (*paññāvimutti*) by fading away of ignorance (*avijjā-virāga*). Thus, these two liberations are the conclusion in the "Joyous Turn" method (*nandiyāvaṭṭa-naya*).
In this context, there are four terms: craving (*taṇhā*), ignorance (*avijjā*), serenity (*samatha*), and insight (*vipassanā*). Within these, eighteen root terms converge.
How so? The five terms—serenity, non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adosa*), the perception of foulness (*asubhasaññā*), and the perception of suffering (*dukkhasaññā*)—belong to serenity.
Insight, non-delusion (*amoha*), the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*), and the perception of non-self (*anattasaññā*) [belong to insight].
And these four terms—“craving,” “grasping,” “clinging,” and “becoming”—belong to insight (*vipassanā*). Thus, nine terms that are wholesome converge into two categories.
Five terms—“craving,” “greed,” “hatred,” “perception of beauty,” and “perception of pleasure”—belong to craving;
and four terms—“ignorance,” “delusion,” “perception of permanence,” and “perception of self”—[belong to ignorance].
The terms belong to ignorance. Thus, the nine unwholesome terms converge into two terms.
In this way, the Tipukkhalo method and the Sīhavikkīḷita method enter into the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method.
How do the other two methods enter into the Tipukkhalo method? Insight (vipassanā) and non-delusion (amoha) are the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā).
And the perception of non-self—these four terms constitute non-delusion (*amoha*).
Serenity, non-greed, the perception of the foul, and the perception of suffering—these four terms constitute non-greed (*alobha*). Non-hatred is simply non-hatred itself.
Thus, these nine wholesome factors converge into three categories. Craving, greed, the perception of beauty, and the perception of pleasure—

These four terms—greed (*lobha*), ignorance (*avijjā*), delusion (*moha*), and the perception of permanence (*niccasaññā*), as well as the perception of self (*attasaññā*)—these four terms constitute delusion.
Hatred (*dosa*) is simply hatred itself. Thus, these nine unwholesome terms converge within three categories.
In this way, within the "three-pronged" method, the other two methods are included.
How do the eighteen root-terms converge within the four bases? Craving and the perception of beauty—this is the first perversion.
Greed and the perception of pleasure—this is the second perversion. Ignorance and the perception of permanence—this is the third perversion.
Delusion and the perception of self—this is the fourth perversion. Thus, nine...
The unwholesome factors converge upon four bases. Tranquility and the perception of foulness constitute the first foundation of mindfulness;
non-greed and the perception of suffering constitute the second foundation of mindfulness; insight and the perception of impermanence constitute the third foundation of mindfulness;
and non-delusion and the perception of non-self constitute the fourth foundation of mindfulness. Thus, there are nine wholesome factors.
They converge upon four points. Thus, in the Lion’s Play method (*sīhavikkīḷitanaya*), the other two methods enter into it.
For whatever grounds constitute the range of the three methods, each enters into a single method.
Therefore, when unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*) are understood within any one method, the opposite should be sought; having sought the opposite, that method—

It is to be demonstrated. When that method has been demonstrated, just as in one method the root-terms of the other methods have entered therein, they must be extracted from here and there and demonstrated. For within each individual method, the eighteen root-terms have entered.
Therein, when each single phenomenon is understood, all phenomena become understood. Of these three methods—
Regarding the method of the Lion’s Play, there are four fruits as its conclusion: the first fruit is the conclusion of the first direction,
the second fruit is the conclusion of the second direction, the third fruit is the conclusion of the third direction,
and the fourth fruit is the conclusion of the fourth direction.
In the Tipukkhalā method, the three liberations are the conclusion: for the first direction, the desireless liberation; for the second, the void liberation;

and for the third, the signless liberation is the conclusion. In the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method, the two kinds of deliverance are the conclusion: for the first direction, the deliverance of mind through the fading away of craving;
for the second direction, the deliverance by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance is the conclusion. In these three methods, regarding the eighteen...
The examination of the words is the method of Directional Survey (*disālocana-naya*). The correct application, by one who has surveyed both the wholesome side and the unwholesome side and knows:
"This state is associated with that state," is the method of the Hook (*aṅkusa-naya*). These are the five methods.
The commentary on the section concerning the origin of the methods is concluded.
Commentary on the Section on the Foundation of the Dispensation (Sāsanapaṭṭhānavāra-vaṇṇanā) 89.
Having thus analyzed the arising of the methods in every respect, he now analyzes the foundation of the Dispensation.
Since, in the sections on the Compendium (Saṅgahavāra) and so forth, the foundation was compiled by means of the root terms alone and was not shown in its own form, therefore—just as...
The *Paṭṭhāna* is to be extracted from the root-terms; likewise, it is for the purpose of showing that the root-terms are also to be extracted from the *Paṭṭhāna* that he said:
"Where are the eighteen root-terms to be seen? In the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*. For the mutual inclusion of the root-terms and the *Sāsanapaṭṭhāna* has already been demonstrated previously.
Now, what is the etymological meaning of *sāsanapaṭṭhāna*? Of the teaching (*sāsana*)...

*Paṭṭhāna* means the foundation of the Dispensation (*sāsanapaṭṭhāna*). The Dispensation is the teaching; its "foundation" (*paṭṭhāna*) is its establishment and occurrence through various modes in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained, for the purpose of accomplishing their welfare and happiness.
Here, however, it should be understood as "the foundation of the Dispensation" in the sense of demonstrating that very nature [of the teaching].
Alternatively, the Dispensation consists of the training in higher virtue and so forth. They are established (*patiṭṭhahanti*) because this [work] serves as the means for their occurrence.

“By these” refers to the *paṭṭhānas*, which are the phenomena of defilement and so forth. Because they reveal these [phenomena], the discourses (*suttas*) are called *paṭṭhānas* by metaphorical extension.
However, because this section of the treatise is a collection of them, it is called *paṭṭhāna*.

Another method: in what sense is it *paṭṭhāna*? In the sense of being established (*paṭṭhita*) and in the sense of proceeding (*gamana*); such is the meaning. “Those which are *goṭṭhā*... [and so on].
For in the passage where it says, "the cattle have set out," the basis by which those cattle are called "herds that have set out" is,

in actual meaning, "going. Thus, among the methods of extraction (*hāranaya*) that are not overly prolix, because one gains the methods in their detailed exposition— whether they pertain to the knowledge of teaching regarding the "unimpeded going" (*anissaṅgagamana*),
or to the classifications such as the "partaking of defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and the "worldly" (*lokiya*), or to the mixed combinations of both— one attains the detailed method.

Because they proceed by way of non-attachment, those [factors]— namely, the categories beginning with the "partaking of defilement" (saṃkilesabhāgiya) and the mundane (lokiya), etc.— whether taken individually, collectively, or in combination,
constitute what is called the *Paṭṭhāna* (the Foundation) by virtue of being the basis (*adhikaraṇa*).
This section of the treatise should be understood as the *Paṭṭhāna* because it elucidates them.
Regarding the terms beginning with “partaking of defilement” (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*): it is called *saṃkilesa* because one is defiled by means of it.
That which occurs in the part of defilement, in the section of defilement, is “partaking of defilement. *Vāsanā* is the cultivation of merit;

that which occurs in the part of cultivation is “partaking of cultivation,” or it is called “partaking of cultivation” because it causes one to partake in cultivation. *Nibbijjhana* is the shattering of the mass of greed and so forth.
*Nibbedha* means penetration. That which occurs in the portion of penetration, or that which causes one to partake in penetration, is "conducive to penetration" (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).

Those whose training is fully completed are the *asekkhas*; that which occurs in the state of being an *asekha*, or that which causes one to partake in the state of an *asekha*, is "conducive to the state of an *asekha*" (*asekkhabhāgiya*).

Among these, that in which the defilement consisting of craving and so forth is analyzed is "conducive to defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*). That in which the bases for meritorious action such as giving [are analyzed]...

That in which [the factors] are analyzed is the portion dealing with purification by virtue (*vāsanābhāgiya*). That in which the aggregates of virtue and so forth of those in training (*sekkha*) are analyzed is the portion dealing with penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
However, that in which the aggregates of virtue and so forth of those beyond training (*asekkha*) are analyzed is the portion dealing with the beyond-training (*asekkhabhāgiya*).
The others are stated by way of their mixed method.
These, moreover, consist of six dyads, four triads, one tetrad, and another tetrad, making twelve in total.
Among these, four dyads and two triads have been extracted; the others have not been extracted, though there is no reason for their omission.
It should be understood that they were abbreviated in the text because they can be grasped by this same method. For he will say accordingly:
—“These four suttas, when made common, become eight,” and so forth.

In this context, because in some suttas only the corruption of craving (*taṇhā-saṃkilesa*) is demonstrated, in some only the corruption of views (*diṭṭhi-saṃkilesa*), and in some only the corruption of misconduct (*duccarita-saṃkilesa*), the discourse dealing with corruption (*saṃkilesabhāgiya-sutta*) is taught by dividing it into three types: “that dealing with the corruption of craving... [and so on].

By the passage beginning with "sutta," and so forth, it is shown that since purification (*vodāna*) occurs only when defilement (*saṃkilesa*) exists, the discourse pertaining to purification (*vodānabhāgiya-sutta*) is likewise taught in three ways according to the classification of defilement, beginning with "the discourse pertaining to the purification of craving" (*taṇhā-vodānabhāgiya-sutta*).
However, in terms of its actual meaning, this is nothing other than the discourse pertaining to the residual impression (*vāsanābhāgiya*), and so on.
Furthermore, this method is not found in some manuscripts.

“In that regard, defilement is threefold,” and so forth; this is undertaken for the purpose of showing the scope of suttas such as those dealing with the side of purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*), by way of distinguishing serenity (*samatha*) and the rest through their opposition to defilement.
Therein, “if attachment arises toward states of existence” means: if a longing for existence arises in one who is unable to abandon desire and lust for states of existence.
“Thus they experience” refers to that person in this manner.
This constitutes a basis for meritorious action consisting in the cultivation of serenity and insight, because it produces the fruit of a state of existence worthy of honor.
"It leads to rebirth there" means that it leads to rebirth in various such states of existence.
"These four discourses" refers to these four discourses beginning with those dealing with defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya). They are made common [to all]... and the discourse dealing with defilement...
The "pertaining to habituation" (vāsanābhāgiya), the "pertaining to defilement" (saṃkilesabhāgiya), and the "pertaining to penetration" (nibbedhabhāgiya);

the "pertaining to defilement" and the "pertaining to the state beyond training" (asekkhabhāgiya); and the "pertaining to habituation" and the "pertaining to penetration"—thus they are made mixed by way of joining different terms.
"There are eight" means that the four preceding ones and these four [others] thus make eight.

Those same eight suttas become sixteen when made common; that is, those same eight suttas as previously stated are [treated] with respect to the portion dealing with purification (vāsanābhāgiya), the portion dealing with the Asekhas (asekkhabhāgiya), and the portion dealing with penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya);

and [the portions dealing with] the Asekhas, the portion dealing with defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya), and the portion dealing with purification; and [the portions dealing with] penetration, the portion dealing with defilement, and the portion dealing with purification.
That which pertains to the state of one beyond training (*asekkha*), that which pertains to defilement (*saṃkilesa*), and that which pertains to penetration (*nibbedha*);
or that which pertains to the state of one beyond training, that which pertains to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and that which pertains to penetration;

or that which pertains to the state of one beyond training, that which pertains to defilement, and that which pertains to habitual tendencies; or that which pertains to penetration, that which pertains to the state of one beyond training, and that which pertains neither to defilement nor to habitual tendencies; and that which pertains neither to habitual tendencies nor to penetration.
And "not pertaining to those beyond training" (na asekkhabhāgiyaṃ): thus, when the previous eight and these eight are combined as common categories, there are sixteen.
Among them, one should understand the following classification: four singles, six pairs, four triads, one tetrad, and another tetrad.
Furthermore, it should be understood that among those, two pairs, two triads, and two tetrads are not included in the canonical text (pāḷi).
Now, in order to clarify how this *Paṭṭhāna* encompasses the entire Teaching (*sāsana*), it is said:
"By these sixteen types of suttas being analyzed, the ninefold sutta becomes analyzed. The meaning of this is as follows:

by these sixteen suttas, beginning with those dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and so forth, which are analyzed according to the method of the *Paṭṭhāna*, the ninefold scripture (*pariyatti-sāsana*) known as Sutta, Geyya, and so on, is [encompassed].

The Sutta is divided into sixteen parts. The intention is that there is no portion of the scriptural teaching (pariyatti-sāsana) not included within these sixteenfold matrices (paṭṭhāna). But how is the state of being "pertaining to defilement" (saṃkilesabhāgiya), and so forth, to be understood?
He says: "A verse is to be inferred from a verse," and so on. Therein, "a verse is to be inferred from a verse" means:

Just as this verse, so too all verses should be inferred—whether they pertain to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*), to purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*), to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), or to the state of one beyond training (*asekkhabhāgiya*).
The meaning is that they must be known by inferring them one by one and conjecturing them.
This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. And here, all the scriptures (*pariyatti*) excluding the commentaries on the verses are included under the term "by the Sutta."
They should be understood as being "included.

Now, in order to clarify by way of examples the discourses dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and so forth exactly as they were indicated, the passage beginning with "In this context, what is a discourse dealing with defilement?
is commenced. Therein, [the verse] begins: "Blinded by desire, covered by a net..."

The meaning of the verse has already been stated above. Just as with this one, we shall not further comment on the meaning of those that follow which have already had their meanings explained or whose words are self-evident.

"Ways of going astray" (*agatigamanāni*) means ways of proceeding improperly by way of body and so forth; the meaning is "performing what should not be done. "Desire" (*chanda*) means for the sake of desire.
Conditioned by desire. "He goes to a bad destination" means he goes to a destination that should not be gone to; the meaning is that he does what should not be done.
"The Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the virtuous noble ones. "He transgresses" means he oversteps it by violating it.
"He is brought low" means he declines. "Fame" refers to both reputation and retinue.
In the verse beginning “Mind precedes all phenomena” (*manopubbangamā dhammā*), although “mind” (*mano*) refers to all consciousness belonging to the four planes—
including the wholesome states of the sense-sphere and so forth— in this particular context, only the consciousness associated with aversion is applicable,
as it arose when the Elder Cakkhupāla was a physician in a previous birth. That mind is the precursor.
"These have mind as their precursor" means they are endowed with the mind that goes first. "Dhammas" refers to dhammas in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being or a soul;
these are the three formless aggregates (khandhas), beginning with feeling. For these indeed have mind as their precursor.
But how is it that the mind, arising simultaneously with them in the same physical basis, the same object, and at the same moment, is their precursor?

Why is it called "arising"? In the sense of being a condition for arising. For just as when many people are performing acts such as plundering a village together, if one asks, "Who is their leader?", that person who is their condition—relying upon whom they perform that deed, whether he be Datta or Mitta—is called their leader; this should be understood in the same way.
Thus, because mind is the forerunner of these in the sense of being the condition for their arising, they are "mind-forerunners" (*manopubbaṅgamā*).
For they are unable to arise when the mind does not arise; yet the mind itself certainly arises even when some mental factors do not arise.
Because mind is supreme among them by way of dominance, they are "mind-superiors" (*manoseṭṭhā*). Just as, for example, there are chief thieves and so forth among thieves and the like.
Just as the lord is the best, so too is their mind the best.

Furthermore, just as goods produced from wood and other materials are called "made of wood" and so forth, so too these [beings] are called "mind-made" (*manomaya*) because they are produced from the mind.
"With a corrupted mind" means with a mind defiled by faults such as covetousness; speaking or acting with such a mind, he indeed speaks in four ways.
He speaks only verbal misconduct; even while acting, he performs only the threefold bodily misconduct;
and by not speaking and not acting, through a mind corrupted by covetousness and the like, he fulfills the threefold mental misconduct.
In this way, his ten unwholesome courses of action reach completion. "Then suffering follows him" means from those three kinds of misconduct.
Suffering follows that person by the power of their misconduct; they pursue suffering in the four states of woe.
How so? "Like the wheel follows the hoofprint of the ox that draws the cart.
Just as the wheel follows the hoofprint of the ox pulling a cart as it strikes the ground, even so does suffering follow that person.
In the verse, “When one is drowsy,” *middhī* means overcome by sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*).

*Mahagghaso* means one who eats much, like any one of those such as the *āharahatthaka*, *alaṃsāṭaka*, *tatravaṭṭaka*, *kākamāsaka*, or the one who eats until full. *Niddāyitā* means one whose nature is to sleep.
*Samparivattasāyī* means one whose nature is to lie down turning over and over, due to being devoted to the pleasure of the bed and the pleasure of the side.
"Fed on fodder" means nourished by the food of pigs, such as *kuṇḍaka* (broken rice) and so forth.
For a domestic pig, having been raised since its youth, when its body becomes fat, it is unable to go outside the house;
it merely lies down, turning over and over on the floor beneath the bed and so forth, breathing in and out. This is what is meant: when a person is drowsy...

Furthermore, if he is a glutton, like a great boar stuffed with fodder, unable to maintain himself through any other mode of conduct, and is habitually sleepy, rolling and tossing about in his sleep, then he is unable to attend to the three characteristics—"impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
Due to his lack of such mental attention, one of dull wisdom enters the womb again and again; he is not liberated from dwelling in the womb.
In the verse, “Like rust from iron,” *ayasā* means from iron. *Samuṭṭhitaṃ* means arisen. *Tato uṭṭhāya* means having arisen from that. *Atidhonacāriṃ*:
*dhonā* is said to be the wisdom that uses the four requisites after reflecting, “This is sufficient for this purpose;
enough with this. One who acts by transgressing that is called *atidhonacārī*. This is...
This is what is meant: just as rust, having arisen from iron, consumes and destroys that very iron from which it arose, even so,
for one who uses the four requisites without reflection and is excessively unrestrained, those very kamma-formations—
having arisen within his own mental continuum— are his own property, and they lead him to a state of misery.
In the verse beginning “Just as a thief,” the phrase “just as a thief is caught at the entrance of a breach” means that a thief,
having cut through a house wall while entering a home, is seized by royal officers right at the opening of that breach.
“He is struck and bound by his own deed” means that by the action he himself committed, he is both struck with such things as lashes and bound with such things as ropes.
And thus: "This generation, having passed away, goes to another world"—in this way, this evil-doing generation, having fallen from here, in the other world, is "slain and bound by its own karma";
that is, by the very evil karma committed by oneself, one is both slain and fettered in various ways through punishments and the like in the hells and other realms.
Regarding the verse beginning with “Those who desire happiness”: “He who harms with a stick” refers to that person who injures others with a stick, a clod of earth, or similar objects.
“Having passed away, he does not obtain happiness” means that such a person does not obtain either human happiness or divine happiness in the next world;
as for the happiness of Nibbāna, it goes without saying that they do not attain it.
"Of cows crossing over," means when the cows are crossing a great flood. "The leader goes crookedly" means if the bull, the head of the herd, goes in a curved manner.
"They all go crookedly" means all those cows also go only in a curved manner. Why?
Because the leader has gone crookedly; that is, because the leader has gone in a curved manner.
The meaning is: "because it has gone crookedly through the net. For he is indeed their leader and the remover of their misfortune.

In the verse beginning with "Even so," just as this is the case, even so if one who is esteemed for his striving among human beings should be a practitioner of unrighteousness (*adhamma*), all those who depend upon him would likewise become unrighteous. For the attainment of material goods [depends] on the attainment of one's character.
He brings about [this]. And because this is so, therefore the entire kingdom suffers, if the king is unrighteous.

"Truly, they are in great distress" means they have indeed fallen into a state of extreme hardship. "In the acquisitions" (upadhīsu) means in the acquisitions consisting of the strands of sensual pleasure.
"Attached" (rattā) means overcome by lust. "Bitter" (kaṭukaṃ) means suffering.
Because the very cause that produces remorse cuts off the source from which the bowl’s rim originated, the production of fruit leads to the destruction of the plantain tree;
thus it is said: "The fruit indeed destroys the plantain. Likewise, because the fruit is the end of medicinal plants, it is said:
"The fruit [destroys] the bamboo, the fruit [destroys] the reed. An *assatarī* is the name for a mule born to a mare from a donkey.
Having conceived, when the time arrived for birth, she was unable to give birth. She stood striking the ground with her feet;
then, having bound her four feet to four stakes and ripped open her belly, they extracted the foal, and she died right there.
Therefore it is said: "like a mare with her fetus. This is what is meant:

Just as its own fruit destroys the plantain, the bamboo, and the reed, and as the fetus destroys the female donkey, so too does honor— which is itself the fruit of one's own karma— destroy the person of bad character.
"One who values anger and malice" means one who holds in high regard anger, characterized by the act of being angry, and malice, characterized by the act of smearing over the virtues of others.
Having turned it upward, having lifted it up, he moves about. "In a good field" means even in a good field.

"Like a rotten seed" means like a seed that has reached a state of rot. The meaning is that it is corrupted by the defect of the seed due to not having been treated with manure, liquid fertilizer, drying, or proper storage.

91. "With his own mind" means with his own consciousness (*citta*). "His mind" refers to the consciousness of that person. "Having delimited" means having circumscribed. "He moves" means it proceeds. "As brought" means as something has been brought and placed there.
“Mā akattha” means “do not do. “Na pamokkhatthī” means there is no escape. “Upeccāpi” means even intentionally; the meaning is “even with prior awareness.
Although he said “by unrighteousness,” he further said “by false speech” in order to show that false speech is a very grave offense. For this very reason he said:
“For one who has transgressed a single principle,” and so forth; likewise, “Thus small indeed, Rāhula, is their...”
“‘Asceticism’ refers to those who have no sense of shame regarding intentional lying,” and so forth. “How will that be? means:
in what manner will that wealth belong to them? Because it was accumulated by them through unrighteousness (*adhamma*), it does not remain with them for long;
this is the meaning. “There will indeed be obstacles” means that obstacles such as those from kings will arise due to their unrighteous dealings and the like.
*Sūti* is merely a particle. Regarding the phrase "what has been gathered perishes": the "gathering" (*sambhataṃ*) refers to what has been prepared or accumulated;
it perishes. *Saggaṃ* means a happy destination (*sugati*). For that is intended as "heaven" (*sagga*) because it is the foremost (*agga*) due to its beautiful qualities such as forms and so forth.
"To this extent" means by the loss of benefits pertaining both to the present life and the future life. "Destroyed" (*hatā*) means ruined.

"Vivaṭṭate" means it turns back. "One digs one's own self with greed" means that by performing unwholesome deeds on account of greed, one is said to "dig up" oneself through bodily misconduct and the like. "He wastes away through friends" means he declines in his state of friendship.
"They wander" means they roam about performing only what is unwholesome through the four modes of conduct.

"Fools" (bālā) refers to those here who do not know the welfare of this world or the welfare of the next world; these are called fools here. "Dull-witted" (dummedhā) means lacking wisdom (*paññā*). For there is no such thing as a corruption of wisdom itself.
There is a name for it. "By one who is like an enemy" means by one who has become like an adversary or a foe. "Bitter fruit" means sharp fruit;

the sense is that it results in suffering. "That deed done is not good, having done which one regrets" means that deed which is capable of producing rebirth in the hells and other realms, which gives rise to suffering, and for which one regrets at every moment, whether remembered or not.
One grieves; that which was done is neither good, nor beautiful, nor auspicious.
"With tearful face" means one who, with a face wet with tears, weeping, experiences and undergoes the result.

"Difficult to do" refers to the impossibility of performing the morality of higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika-sīla*) through the fulfillment of duties such as the major and minor observances (*vatta-paṭivatta*).

It is difficult to perform. From the moment of undertaking it, it is hard to endure because one must reach the final consciousness of the higher life (*brahmacariya*) without breaking it, or because it is impossible to accomplish it without making the restraints of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*) and so forth flawless.
Furthermore, it is hard to endure by way of the restraint of patience (*khanti-saṃvara*), because those things that must be endured are difficult to bear. "By the unskilled" means...
By one of dull wisdom. *Sāmañña* means the state of being a recluse (*samaṇa*). *Tattha* refers to that state of being a recluse.

*Sambādha* refers to the crowded conditions such as being jostled by women who are poorly clothed or poorly dressed, and so forth. *Yattha* refers to those dissimilar objects and the like, designated as "crowded," which act as obstacles to the restraints of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*) and so on.
Alternatively, in order to show the meaning of the word *dukkara*, it is said to be *duttitikkha*. *Duttitikkha* means difficult to endure.
"Difficult to dwell with. "By the untrained" means by the foolish. "The state of a recluse" (*sāmañña*) means the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
This is what is meant: that which wise sons of good family—[practicing] for ten years, twenty...

[or] even sixty years—with teeth set against teeth, pressing the tongue against the palate, restraining the mind with the mind, and subsisting on a single meal at a single sitting—[find difficult to dwell with].
"Practicing the holy life to the end of the aeon, they perform the state of a recluse; the foolish and incompetent are unable to do so.
"Therein, there are many obstructions" means that in this noble path termed "the state of a recluse," there are many obstructions;
the meaning is that for one practicing for the attainment of the path, there are many dangers.

"Measuring the immeasurable" means measuring a person whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsavapuggala*) by thinking, "This one has such-and-such virtue, such-and-such concentration, and such-and-such wisdom.
"What wise man would conceptualize?"—this explains that who here is a wise and intelligent person who would conceptualize?
Only one whose taints are destroyed could conceptualize while measuring another whose taints are destroyed. "He thinks [the other] is obstructed" refers to the worldling (*puthujjana*).
When he begins to speak, I consider him one whose wisdom is covered and turned downward. "Akissava": *kissavā* is said to be wisdom;
the meaning is "devoid of wisdom. "An axe" (*kuṭhārī*):
harsh speech is like an axe in the sense that it cuts oneself. "It cuts": [it cuts] what is known as the roots of wholesome merit.
"It cuts right at the root. "Like the halāhala poison" means like the poison known as *halāhala*.
"Thus it causes one who has failed to fall" means that it causes a person who has failed—that is, one who has erred—to fall into the states of misery (*apāya*).
"Just as speech is ill-spoken" means just as speech is ill-spoken by way of reviling the Noble Ones (*ariya*).

92. They censure one who is censurable; or he censures one who is praiseworthy—that person who, by virtue of his distinguished qualities, is worthy of praise—and he reviles him by imputing such things as evil desires (*pāpicchatā*). "He accumulates" means he piles up. "Fault" (*kali*) means an offense.
"This fault" means this transgression. "In dice" refers to the dice used for gambling. "Even with all [his wealth]" means even together with everything.
"By oneself" means both by one's own wealth and together with oneself.

"Among the Sugatas" refers to those designated as Sugatas—the Buddhas and others—because they have gone to a beautiful state, because they have gone to an excellent place, because they have gone rightly, and because they have spoken rightly.
"Whoever would corrupt the mind": it is said that for whoever would corrupt the mind, this very corruption of the mind is the greater evil.
It is so. Why? Because [the Blessed One said]: "A hundred thousand... [and] evil. In that context, "a hundred thousand" means one hundred thousand *nirabbudas*.
"Thirty-six" refers to another thirty-six *nirabbudas*. "And five" means five *abbudas* according to the *abbuda* calculation.
Therefore, by way of counting years, such is the duration of time during which one who reviles the Noble Ones [remains there].
Having directed the mind toward evil, one goes to hell; it is said that there one is cooked.
This is the measure of the lifespan in the Paduma hell in brief; however, it will be explained in detail later.
Regarding "the quality of greed" (*lobhaguṇe*): because it is perceived as a "quality" (*guṇa*) by fools and because it occurs many times, greed itself is called the "quality of greed."
