"In that quality of greed" means "in craving. "Addicted" (*anuyutta*) means addicted to each [of them]. "One who does not know how to speak" (*avadaññū*) means one who does not know how to speak, because he does not accept even the instruction of the Buddhas.
"Miserly" (*maccharī*) means miserly with the five kinds of miserliness.
"Addicted to slander" (*pesuṇiyaṃ anuyutta*) means addicted to slander by causing a schism between the two Chief Disciples. For while [the Buddha] was exhorting Kokālika as he was dying—
These verses were spoken by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. "Mukhadugga" means one with a distorted mouth.
"Vibhūta" means one who has departed from reality, a speaker of falsehoods. "Anariya" means a non-noble person, an unworthy man. "Bhūnahū" means a destroyer of beings, one who ruins his own wisdom.
"Purisanta" means the lowest of men. "Kalī" means an unlucky or wretched man. "Avajātakaputta" refers to [the son] of the Blessed Buddha.
"O you of low birth! Do not speak much here; you are one born for hell.
You scatter dust"—you cast the dust of the defilements (*kilesa*) upon yourself. "The peaceful ones"—those whose defilements are stilled and whose taints are exhausted.
"A doer of evil"—a perpetrator of wicked deeds. They fall into hell.

"This is that which pertains to defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) should be understood as a sutta pertaining to defilement shown by way of example through numerous scriptural passages, in order to demonstrate its many divisions according to the distinction of the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of craving and so forth, and according to the distinction of their stages (*avasthā*).
"With a clear heart" (*pasanna*) means with one who has faith in karma, its fruit, and so on.
"Prosperous" (*iddha*) means enriched with hand-held ornaments, head-ornaments, and so forth, as well as with gems, gold, and the like. "Thriving" (*phīta*)...
"Abounding" means abundant with oil, honey, molasses, and so forth, as well as with wealth, grain, and the like. "Crowded with people" means densely populated with humans.

"With congested thoroughfares": "thoroughfares" (byūhā) refers to unpierced streets; those through which one can exit only by the path already entered are "congested thoroughfares," and because such thoroughfares exist there, it is called "with congested thoroughfares.
By this [description] as well, the dense settlement of that city is indicated.
He illuminates [this]. "With turbulence" means with one who has not attained self-control, wandering here and there.
"Not evil" means blameless. "With verified confidence" means with unshakable confidence, with the confidence that has arisen from the penetration of the Truths.

"And having passed away, he obtains" means that the person who does not harm living beings with punishment obtains human happiness when born as a human in the next world, divine happiness when born as a deity, and, transcending both, the happiness of Nibbāna—this is the meaning.
94. "He will set out on a journey" means he will go on a tour of the countryside (*janapada-cārikā*). But for what reason does the Blessed One travel on a tour of the countryside?
Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, travel on a tour of the countryside for seven reasons:
for the sake of training those to be converted who have gone to other regions; to arouse longing in those staying there; and for the sake of [visiting] practitioners in a single location...
The Blessed Buddhas undertake a journey through the countryside for seven reasons: to avoid residing in one place permanently; to demonstrate their lack of attachment to those locations;

to establish the status of certain places as *cetiyas* (shrines) because they were sites where a Perfectly Enlightened One dwelt; to cause a flood of merit to flow forth among many beings through their being seen and approached;
and to pacify calamities such as drought. It is for these seven reasons that the Blessed Buddhas travel on tour through the countryside.
It should be understood that they were traveling.
"Isidatta and Purāṇa" refers to Isidatta and Purāṇa; among them, Isidatta was a once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*), and Purāṇa was a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*).
"At Sāketa" means in his own village of wealth, which had acquired the name "Sāketa. "They stationed a man on the road" refers to those [two].

It seems that the Blessed One’s route passed through the village gate; therefore, thinking, "If the Blessed One should pass while we are asleep or negligent, we would not get a chance to see him," they stationed a man in the middle of the road.
"They followed" means they did not follow from a distance, but followed closely behind him. For the Blessed One was traveling on foot in the middle of the cart-track.
He went; the others followed along on both sides. "Having stepped off the path":
for Buddhas, while traveling with anyone, perform friendly greetings; they stand with some and sit even for a portion of the day with others.
Therefore, the Blessed One thought: "These are dear to me in the Dispensation; they have attained the fruit. Together with them—"
"Having sat down, I will perform a friendly greeting for half the day.
Having descended from the road, he approached the foot of a certain tree and sat down on the prepared seat.

It is said that they had come along, having had him take with them an umbrella, sandals, a walking staff, oil for rubbing his feet, eight kinds of beverages, and a couch made of *sarabha* wood. Then, [he sat] upon that couch.
Having prepared them, they gave them [to the Buddha]. The Teacher sat there. They sat down to one side means:
having said, "Give parasols, sandals, and so forth to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus," and having paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
The entire passage beginning with "He set out on a walking tour from Sāvatthī among the Kosalans" is spoken specifically with reference to the Middle Country.
Why? Because of his fixed habit. For the Blessed One’s wandering was restricted to the Middle Country alone.
Even if he went to a border region, it was his fixed habit that he would cause dawn to break only within the Middle Country; therefore, it is stated specifically with reference to the Middle Country.
"In Kāsī" means from the kingdom of Kāsī. Likewise, "in Magadha" means from the kingdom of Magadha. "Near us," O Blessed One.
Regarding the phrase "it will be," their joy arises not only because of its proximity; rather, their joy arises from the thought:
"Now we shall be able to give gifts, perform worship with perfumes, garlands, and so forth, listen to the Dhamma, and ask questions."

"Therefore, masters of the household, the home life is a confinement. Masters of the household, since there is no small measure of dejection in you when I am far away, and no small measure of joy when I am near, for this reason too it should be understood that 'the home life is a confinement.
Indeed, it is through the fault of the home life that such feelings arise in you. But if one were to abandon the home life—"
He spoke thus while illustrating this meaning: "If you were to go forth, then even as you are going and coming together with me, that [distress] would not happen to you.
In this context, "constriction" (sambādhatā) should be understood in the sense of being possessed of belongings and possessed of obstacles.
For even for one living in a large house, the household life is indeed a constriction in the sense of being possessed of belongings and possessed of obstacles.
The "dust-path" (*rajopatha*) is the path for the arrival of the dusts such as passion (*rāga*); the meaning is "the place of arrival.
"Open space is renunciation" (*abbhokāso pabbajjā*): renunciation, moreover, is open space in the sense of being without possessions and without impediments.

For even in a four-cubit room, when two monks sit with their cross-legged postures touching one another, it is still called "renunciation" in the sense of being without possessions and without impediments.

"An open space" means it becomes an open area. "And it is enough for you, venerable ones, to be diligent" means that while living in such a cramped dwelling, it is fitting for you to practice only diligence.
"Nāgas" refers to elephants. "Opavayhas" are those fit for a king to mount. "Let one sit in front and one behind" means [let them be seated thus].
It is said that both of those women, adorned with every ornament, had those two women seated upon two elephants;
placing the king’s elephant in the middle, they proceeded on both sides. Therefore, they spoke thus:

"The elephant must also be protected" means it must be guarded in such a way that it does not perform any particular act [of aggression]. "Those sisters too" refers to how they were to avoid negligence.
They do not incur [offenses]; thus they must be protected. "One's own self" means that one's own self must also be protected by those who do not engage in laughing, talking, or distracting behavior.
For one who acts in such a way may be restrained on the grounds that "this person is a traitor.
Therefore, O chamberlains, because the King constantly entrusts you with royal property, for that reason as well it is a matter of great delicacy.

The household life is a path of dust; however, since there is no one who can provide such protection for a monk who wears rag-robes, therefore the open air is the state of renunciation—this applies in all respects.
Furthermore, he shows: "O householders, it is enough for you to be heedful; practice indeed heedfulness. "One who has relinquished attachment" means one who has abandoned stinginess.
"Pure-handed" means one whose hands are washed for the purpose of giving to whoever comes. "Delighting in relinquishment."
"Delighting in relinquishment, which is characterized by self-surrender. "Devoted to begging" (*yācayoga*) means one who is engaged in being asked for alms.

There is also a reading, "devoted to sacrificing" (*yājayoga*), which means one who is intent on giving. "Delighting in giving and sharing" means that having obtained even a small thing, one delights in sharing it from that very source.
"Unapportioned" (*appaṭivibhatta*) means not divided in this way: "This shall be ours; this shall be for the noble ladies."
The meaning is that everything must indeed be given. "Ariyan disciple endowed with these four qualities is a stream-enterer" means that one who possesses these qualities is a stream-enterer.
By this, he shows that these four qualities are invariably found in a stream-enterer.
Having thus shown by way of a figurative explanation that those *thapatis* were endowed with these four qualities, he now said, “You, indeed, *thapatis*,” and so forth, in order to show it directly.
95. “A thousand koṭis of *kappas*” means there were a thousand individual existences (*attabhāva*).
There is also a reading, “eighty koṭis of *kappas*,” which means there were eighty koṭis of lifespans. But where did they exist? He says: “Among the gods and...”
"Among humans" means among both gods and humans. "Fully grown" means grown by the taking up of sprouts on all sides.
"I obtained" means I, [the speaker], obtained. "Today is the thirtieth kappa from that" means that from that kappa until today, this present kappa is the thirtieth.
"From the impression of that perception" means from the impression of that perception directed toward the Buddha.
"Destroyer of craving" means one who cuts off craving. "Ear-ornament" means an ear-flower made of blossoms.
"Adorned with all flowers" means decorated with various kinds of flowers. "From between the lips" means from the space between the upper and lower lips.
"Radiance" means light. "Disappear within the head" means vanish inside the head. "Dispel doubt" means remove uncertainty. "In whom that [radiance] [arises] regarding all phenomena..."
The phrase "knowledge always proceeds" (*sadā ñāṇaṃ pavattati*) is merely a conventional expression (*nipātamatta*). The connection is as follows:
for him whose knowledge always proceeds because it is bound to his wish regarding all phenomena, that omniscient Blessed One spoke thus to the Elder Ānanda.
"A king shall arise in the realm" means he will become king over the entire realm. "The last" (*carima*) refers to the final existence (*carimabhava*).
"Having realized" means having made it directly manifest. "The principle of the Dhamma" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths or to Paccekabodhi (the enlightenment of a solitary Buddha).
"A ship with a golden covering" refers to a golden ship that is adorned on both sides with golden ornaments.
Regarding the phrase "When asked a question, she answered; thus have I heard from Sakka," this refers to how that deity [responded] to the question.
When questioned by Sakka, she replied; and thus the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna told the Blessed One what he had heard himself, saying, "Thus have I heard.

Regarding the phrase *paṃsuthūpesu*: these are mounds made of earth after the bodily relics have been placed within. For it is in this way that they are said to be "dedicated to the Blessed One"; therefore he said, "in those mounds dedicated to the possessors of the Ten Powers."
97. "Devaputtasarīravaṇṇā" means having a complexion like that of the body of a son of the gods. "Subhagasaṇṭhiti" means a physical form endowed with great fortune.
"Uḷāraṃ vata taṃ āsi" means "truly sublime was that merit performed by me. "Yāhaṃ" means "I, who.
"Satasahassaṃ kappe, mudito thūpaṃ apūjesi" means that after worshipping the stupa, for a hundred thousand aeons, I remained joyful.

The meaning is as follows: "Not coming back to the lower realms" means not having undergone rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*). "That eye" refers to the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*). "Directed" means established.
"I am one whose mind is liberated" means my mind is liberated. "With the taint shaken off" means with the taint of craving shaken off;
the meaning is that craving has been utterly cut off.
"98. 'Sāmākapatthodanamattan'ti means a mere handful of grain from *sāmāka* grass. 'Akhile'ti means without the five mental obstructions (*cetokhila*).

'And in him he placed faith in the supreme Dhamma'ti means that in that Paccekabuddha he believed in the supreme Dhamma, the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha, thinking: 'This must indeed be the supreme Dhamma. "And in that Dhamma..."
With the words “I made a mental aspiration,” he means: “I directed my mind with the thought, ‘May I too realize the Dhamma thus attained.
And with the words ‘And may I never have longing for existence,’ he made an aspiration with his mind, thinking, ‘May I not have longing for any state of existence whatsoever’—this is the connection.”
"Among the Kurus" means among those in Uttarakuru. "Long-lived" is said because their lifespan is one thousand years. "Selfless" means without possessions.
"Beings" refers to sentient beings. "Not lacking in what they had gained" means that for as long as they lived, they did not fall away from the prosperity they had obtained.
"He was reborn among the Thirty-Three" means he was reborn as a member of the Tāvatiṃsa [gods], or he was reborn among the Thirty-Three in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

"Approached among distinguished bodies" means having approached among those with distinguished bodies, that is, among those with bodies of various colors. "Among the illustrious" means among those possessing a retinue.

"By those who have transcended the beneficial and the harmful" means by those who have gone beyond the wholesome and the unwholesome. "This word is indeed evident" is the intended meaning: this statement is indeed directly manifest.
*Sakāsī* means he performed it. *Balimābhihārī* means he brought an offering of worship. *Patitassa ekaṃ* means one flower fell from his hand.
*Upariṭṭhaṃ* means standing above in the air. *Ariṭṭhaṃ* refers to the Paccekabuddha named Ariṭṭha.
*Ajjhattañca bahiddhā ca* means both those with internal objects and those with external objects. *Ye me vijjiṃsu* means those who previously existed for me.

They have come to be. Regarding the phrase "the cycle of birth and death; there is now no further becoming": the cycle (*saṃsāra*), which consists of being born again and again and passing away, is called "further becoming" (*punabbhava*);
the meaning is that this [cycle] no longer exists.

This is known as a discourse pertaining to the portion of purification (*vāsanābhāgiya-sutta*); it should be understood as a discourse pertaining to the portion of purification, shown by way of examples from various scriptural passages that clarify the merit belonging to the portion of purification.

99. “Above, below... [etc. ...for the sake of non-becoming again”: this is called a sutta pertaining to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), because the function of the Noble Path is the crossing over of the floods (*ogha*). “No volition is to be made” means that no thought is to be generated. “The nature of things” (*dhammatā*) means the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*).
100. “When indeed” (*yadā have*) means at whatever time. “Manifest” (*pātubhavanti*) means they arise.

“Phenomena” (*dhammā*) refers to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) which accomplish the penetration of the modes of favorable conditions. Or, “manifest” means they become evident, becoming clear through the process of direct realization (*abhisamaya*).
"Dhammas" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. "Austerity" (ātāpa) is said to be energy (vīriya) in the sense of burning away the defilements.

"Austere" (ātāpino) means one who possesses the energy of right exertion. "Meditating" (jhāyanto) refers to one who is meditating with jhāna characterized by contemplation of the object and characterized by contemplation of the [three] characteristics.
"Of the brahmin" (brāhmaṇassa) means of one who has banished evil and whose taints are destroyed. Then his doubt...

"‘They clarify everything’—thus, for one in whom the Dhamma has appeared in this way, there arises a doubt regarding the mode of conditions (paccayākāra), such as in the method beginning: ‘Venerable sir, who touches?

‘That is not a fitting question,’ said the Blessed One; and likewise in the method beginning: ‘Venerable sir, what is aging-and-death, and to whom does this aging-and-death belong? ‘That is not a fitting question,’ said the Blessed One."
Those sixteen doubts that have arisen—beginning with "Did I exist in the past?

due to the failure to penetrate the very nature of conditioned relations—and the eight doubts that have come forth—beginning with "He doubts the Buddha, he doubts the Dhamma"—all these vanish, depart, and cease. Why?
Because one understands phenomena together with their causes; that is to say, because [one understands] by means of ignorance and so forth...
By means of the cause, he understands, has understood, and penetrates this entire mass of suffering, beginning with volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*),
as being "with cause. Because he has known, understood, and penetrated Nibbāna— which is designated as the destruction of conditions— by knowing the destruction of conditions, therefore,
when these aforementioned phenomena become manifest for that ardent, meditating brahmin.
Then, whatever doubts might arise for him due to his lack of knowledge regarding Nibbāna, all those doubts are dispelled.

"In the forest" means belonging to the forest-dwelling life. "Subsisting on gleanings unknown" means subsisting by the practice of alms-gathering (*piṇḍacariyā*) among families, remaining always a stranger and unrecognized;
or else, [subsisting] in the houses of prominent people who are well-known, [avoiding] the accumulation of pungent condiments...

For one seeking fragrant food, "gleaning" (uñchana) means knowing the proper way of gleaning; however, the mixed food obtained by standing at the door of houses in regular succession is called "other gleaning" (aññātuñchana).
This is what is intended here. "Sustaining oneself with that" means subsisting on that.
"Without regard for sensual pleasures" means being free from longing for both sensual objects (vatthukāma) and the defilements of sensual pleasure (kilesakāma).
"Having cut" means having destroyed. "He sleeps in peace" means he sleeps happily because he is not being consumed by the fever of anger.

"He does not grieve" means he does not sorrow because his mental distress has been destroyed by the elimination of anger. "Of that which has a poisonous root" refers to that which results in suffering.
"Of that which has a sweet tip" refers to the pleasure that arises when one reviles one who has reviled him, or strikes back at one who has struck him.
Referring to that, it is called "the sweet peak" (*madhuragga*). For in this context, the conclusion is called the "peak" (*agga*). "Noble ones" (*ariyā*) refers to the Buddhas and others.

"Should strike" (*haneyya*) means he should strike. "Arising" (*uppātitaṃ*) means not yet eradicated; it refers to that which is arising by way of non-suppression, or arising as a manifestation, or proceeding as a current activity. "He should dispel" (*vinodaye*) means he should remove it from his own mental continuum. (101) "With a sword" (*sattiya*) is a mere figure of speech for the teaching;
the meaning is "with a weapon such as a single-edged blade. "Struck down" (*omaṭṭho*) means beaten.
For there are four kinds of blows: *omaṭṭha*, *ummaṭṭha*, *maṭṭha*, and *vimaṭṭha*.
Among these, a blow delivered from above with the hand facing downward is called *omaṭṭha*; a blow delivered from below with the hand facing upward is called *ummaṭṭha*;
one made by piercing through like a door-bolt or a needle is called *maṭṭha*; and all the rest are called *vimaṭṭha*. In this [context]...
However, it was taken from an improper place. For that arrow is most cruel, difficult to extract, hard to treat, and possesses internal defects;
it remains filled with pus and blood. Without the pus and blood being discharged, they remain covering the opening of the wound.
Those wishing to remove the pus and blood must tie the patient down on a bed and keep him with his head downward; [otherwise] death—
Or he encounters suffering amounting to death. "Paribbaje" means he should dwell [in this way].

What is stated by this verse? Just as a man struck by a spear exerts effort, applies means, and strives for the sake of extracting the dart and treating the wound; and just as when one's head is burning...

"Just as one whose head is on fire exerts energy, applies effort, and strives to extinguish it, even so, O Blessed One, a bhikkhu should dwell mindful and vigilant for the sake of abandoning sensual lust"—thus he spoke.
When the deity had spoken thus, the Blessed One then thought: "This deity has brought forward a simile that has been made firm."
However, she remained grasping only a minor point. For even though she spoke again and again, she would have been speaking only of the suppression and abandonment of sensual lust;
and as long as sensual lust has not been eradicated by the Path, it remains a persistent follower.
Taking that very simile, the Buddha turned the deity away from her position by means of the first Path, showing: "As if struck by a sword."
He spoke the second verse. Its meaning should be understood according to the method previously explained.

"Worldly bait" (*lokāmisa*) refers to the strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*). "One who looks toward peace" (*santipekkho*) means one who looks toward *nibbāna*, the subsiding of all conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*).

"Possessing wisdom" (*paññavā*) means being endowed with wisdom. "With mind sent forth" (*pahitatto*) means one whose consciousness is directed toward *nibbāna*. "Detached from the perception of sensual pleasure" (*virato kāmasaññāya*) means [detached] from whatever [perception of sensual pleasure].
He is detached from the perception of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*) through the abandonment consisting in complete cutting off (*samucchedavirati*), which is associated with the fourth path.
The reading *viratto* (dispassionate) also occurs. However, in the case of *kāmasaññāya*, it is a locative expression. In the *Sagāthāvagga*, the reading is *kāmasaññāsu*.
Because the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*) have been transcended by means of all four paths, he has transcended all fetters (*sabbasaṃyojanātīta*). This is by means of the fourth path alone.
Or, having transcended the higher fetters, because he has crossed over craving— which is designated as "delight"— due to his lack of delight here and there,

and because the three states of existence have been completely exhausted, he is one for whom delight and existence are exhausted. Such a bhikkhu, whose taints are destroyed, does not sink in the deep ocean of saṃsāra.

"He has faith" means that he has faith in the Dhamma by which the Arahants—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha—attained Nibbāna. This Dhamma consists of the categories of good bodily conduct and so forth in the prior stage, and the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment in the subsequent stage.
By having faith in that Dhamma of the Arahants for the sake of attaining Nibbāna, one gains mundane and supramundane wisdom; yet this is not achieved through faith alone.
But because one who has conceived faith approaches, and approaching pays respect, and paying respect lends an ear,
and lending an ear hears the Dhamma, therefore, starting from the approach and continuing through to hearing the Dhamma,
one obtains the desire to hear and wisdom.

What is meant? Even after having faith in that Dhamma, and even after approaching the teachers and preceptors from time to time and attending upon them by performing the proper duties, when they—having had their minds won over by such attendance—are desirous of saying something, then one who, having developed a desire to hear what has been attained, lends an ear and listens, thus obtains it;
in this way, there is also "desire to hear" (*sussūsā*).
Only one who is heedful through not being separated from mindfulness and discerning through the knowledge of what is well-spoken and ill-spoken attains [this], and no other.
Therefore he said: "heedful and discerning.
"One who acts appropriately" means one who, without neglecting the place, time, and so forth, employs the appropriate means for the attainment of mundane and supramundane Dhamma.
One who acts accordingly is a "doer of what is fitting. One who bears the burden is "steadfast," meaning one who does not cast off the yoke by virtue of mental energy (*cetasika-vīriya*).
One who exerts himself is "energetic," meaning one endowed with physical energy (*kāyika-vīriya*) and unremitting effort.

"He finds wealth" means he attains mundane and supramundane wealth. "By truth" refers to both verbal truth and ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*). [This applies to] Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*).
Those attaining *nibbāna* certainly attain fame as well. "Giving" means that by giving others whatever they desire or long for, one binds friends, accomplishes them, and establishes them.
Alternatively, by giving what is difficult to give, one "binds";
it should be understood that by way of giving, all four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*) are included. Through these, one makes friends. From this world...
"To the other world, he indeed does not grieve after passing away"— the meaning is that whichever person possesses these qualities beginning with faith,
having gone from this world to the other world, he does not grieve, for there is no cause for his grief.
"In whomsoever these four qualities exist, in the faithful seeker of the home..."
“Truth, Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity—he indeed does not grieve after passing away.

Having set aside the remainder of the verse, this was recited. For in the *Āḷavaka Sutta*, these verses were spoken by the Blessed One when he was questioned by Āḷavaka with the words, “How indeed does one obtain wisdom?
and so forth. “In whatever way” means by whatever cause or manner. “Living together” means in one place.
“Living together” means meeting. “Him”—that person who has thus met and is worthy of compassion. “With a mind serene”:
with a mind serene through the serenity inspired by compassion (*karuṇā*). “One is not fettered by that”:
one does not become fettered by the aforementioned instruction in the sense of being bound by the fetters such as sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*). “That which is compassion” is pity (*anuddayā*).
The meaning is: "compassion" (*karuṇāyanā*) and "loving-kindness" (*mettāyanā*) by way of bringing about the Noble Path.
102. "Greed and hatred" (*rāgadosā*): greed and hatred are as explained in the method below. "From what source? (*Kutonidāna*): from what source, from what cause?
This is the substitution of *to* for the singular case-ending; it should be understood that there is no elision of the case-ending in this compound. "Discontent and contentment" (*arati ratī*).

"From where is this horripilation born? From where are these three things born, from where do they arise?"—this is the question: namely, that aversion and dissatisfaction toward secluded lodgings and toward higher wholesome states;
that delight, attachment, infatuation, and playfulness toward the five strands of sensual pleasure;
and that mental terror termed "horripilation" because it originates from horripilation. From where [do these arise]?

"From where do they arise? means from what source do they originate? "Mind" refers to wholesome consciousness (*kusala-citta*). "Thoughts" (*vitakka*) refers to sensual thoughts (*kāma-vitakka*) and so forth.

"As children release a hawk" means: just as children playing might bind a crow to its leg with a string and release it—that is, let it fly—so too, from where do unwholesome thoughts arise and release the wholesome mind? This is the question.

"Passion, too... is the second verse; this is its explanation. Therein, "from this" is said with reference to the personal existence (*attabhāva*). For passion and hatred have their source in personal existence;
discontent, delight, and horripilation are born from personal existence. Discursive thoughts of sensual desire and the like, arising precisely from personal existence, discharge the unwholesome mind.
Thus, by that [statement], he rejects any other cause such as primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and so forth.
He said: "From this as their source, from this as their origin. The grammatical derivation here should be understood according to the method stated in the preceding verse.

Now, regarding the meaning expressed in the phrases "from this as their source" and so forth—namely, that they have the personal existence (*attabhāva*) as their source, are born from the personal existence, and originate from the personal existence—he says, "Born of affection, arisen from self," in order to establish that.
For these [defilements], beginning with lust and ending with discursive thought (*vitakka*), are indeed thus.

They are born from the moisture of craving (*taṇhā*). And as they are thus being born, they arise within the self (*attā*)—which is designated as the personal existence (*attabhāva*) consisting of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcupādānakkhandha*).
Therefore he said: "Born of moisture, arisen from the self. Now he shows a simile that illuminates this meaning:
"Like those born on the trunk of a banyan tree (*nigrodha*). In that context, "born on the trunk" refers to the offshoots (*pāroha*) produced upon the trunks. This is what was stated.

It is as follows: just as the shoots designated as "trunk-born" arise in a banyan tree when there is the moisture designated as "sap," and while arising, they come into being in various parts of the branches of that very same banyan tree;

so too, these [defilements] such as lust arise when there is the moisture of craving internally, and while arising, they come into being in various parts such as the eye, etc., within that very same personal existence.
They arise in relation to desirable objects. Therefore it is said: "Born of affection, produced from oneself.

As for the phrase "clinging separately to sense pleasures": since lust occurs by way of the five strands of sensual pleasure and so forth, hatred by way of the bases of resentment and so forth, and discontent and the rest by way of their respective varieties—all these defilements exist in every respect as manifold and diverse.
They are "clinging" (visattā) because they adhere and become entangled in various ways within those respective sensual pleasures by way of their bases, doors, objects, and so forth.
Like what? Just as the *māluvā* creeper, when spread through a forest, becomes clinging, adhering, and entangled among the various branches and twigs of trees;
even so are these defilements (*kilesa-dhammā*). Therefore, regarding these manifold varieties...
Attached to sensual pleasures, it is a thicket of defilements.
Those who understand it, from what source it arises, they dispel it; listen, O yakkha! Its meaning is this:
those beings who understand that thicket of defilements—"From this source this arises"—they [dispel] it, which is moistened by the moisture of craving.
"Knowing that it arises within one's own person, they dry up that moisture of craving with the fire of the knowledge of meditation—such as the contemplation of danger—and thus dispel and abandon it.
'In this way, O Yakkha, listen to what we say.
They cross over this flood so difficult to cross, which was never crossed before, for the sake of non-renewal of existence; for those who dispel the thicket of defilements will certainly [succeed]."
They develop the path. For there is no dispelling of the defilements apart from the development of the path.

Developing the path in this way, they cross over—by means of this [path]—the fourfold flood, such as the flood of sensual desire, which is difficult to cross by ordinary knowledge, and which during this long period of time has never before been crossed or transcended even in a dream, for the sake of Nibbāna and the non-renewal of existence.

"Difficult, Blessed One. It is said that a certain son of the gods, a former practitioner of yoga, having suppressed his defilements through diligent application despite their abundance, performed the duties of a recluse;
yet, because the power of his past causes was weak, he died without reaching the plane of the Noble Ones and was reborn in the world of the gods.
Having approached the Tathāgata, he spoke of the difficulty [of the practice].

Thus he spoke. Therein, "difficult to do" means that the performance of the entirely pure ascetic practice (*samaṇadhamma*) for ten years... [and so on] ...even for sixty years is indeed difficult to do.
"Learners" (*sekkhā*) refers to the seven learners (*satta sekkhā*). "Concentrated by virtue" (*sīlasamāhitā*) means endowed with and possessed of virtue.
"Firmly established" (*ṭhitattā*) means having a stable nature. Having thus answered the question asked, [he continued:]
In order to raise a further question, he said: "Of one who has entered the homeless life," and so forth.

Therein, "of one who has entered the homeless life" (*anagāriyupetassa*) means of one who has gone to the state of homelessness (*niggehabhāva*), that is, of one who has gone forth (*pabbajita*). "Contentment" (*tuṭṭhi*) is satisfaction with the four requisites.

"By cultivation" (*bhāvanāya*) means by the cultivation of the tranquility of the mind. "Having cut the net of Death"—referring to those [who practice] day and night for the tranquility of the sense faculties.
Those who are devoted apply their minds, which are difficult to concentrate, to concentration.
Those whose minds are concentrated do not weary while fulfilling contentment with the four requisites. Those who are content do not weary while fulfilling virtuous conduct.
Those seven trainees established in virtue—those Noble Ones—proceed after cutting through the net of defilements known as the net of Death.
“Duggama, this is indeed true, venerable sir: those who delight in the calming of the faculties compose their difficult-to-compose minds;
those whose minds are composed, fulfilling contentment with the four requisites, do not grow weary; those who are content, fulfilling virtue, do not grow weary;
and those seven trainees who have grasped the supreme goal in virtue—those noble ones [do not grow weary] of the net known as Death.”
Having cut through the net of defilements, they go forth. Why would they not go? Yet, because this path is difficult to traverse, he said, "The Blessed One’s is an uneven path.
In that regard, although the Noble Path itself is neither difficult to traverse nor uneven, its preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipadā*) involves many perils;
therefore, it was described in this way. "With their heads downward" means having their heads turned downward by means of the head of knowledge (*ñāṇasira*).
They fall down. Because they are incapable of ascending the Noble Path, they are said to "fall on the path.

That very path is "equal for the Noble Ones" (ariyānaṃ samo maggo); thus, it is equal for the Noble Ones. "Equal even on the uneven" means that they remain indeed equal even amidst the uneven body of beings.
103. "This indeed is that Jeta’s Grove"—Anāthapiṇḍika, the son of a deva, [refers] both to Jeta’s Grove and to the Buddha and the others.
Having come for the purpose of praising [the place], he spoke thus. "Resorted to by a host of seers" means inhabited by the community of monks (*bhikkhusaṅgha*).
Having thus described the praise of Jetavana with the first verse, he now speaks the words beginning with "Action, knowledge... while describing the praise of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*).
Therein, "action" (*kamma*) is the volition of the path; "knowledge" (*vijjā*) is the wisdom of the path; and "Dhamma" is concentration (*samādhi*).
Or, the factors conducive to concentration (*samādhipakkhika-dhammā*). "Virtue is the supreme life" shows that for one established in virtue, life itself is supreme.

Alternatively, "clear knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to right view and right intention; "the Dhamma" refers to right effort, mindfulness, and concentration; "virtue" refers to right speech, action, and livelihood.
"The supreme life" means that for one established in this virtue, life is indeed called supreme. "By this, mortals..."
By this, "they are purified," it is meant that beings are purified by means of this Eightfold Path.
Therefore—because they are purified by the path and not by lineage or wealth—for that reason.

"One should wisely investigate the Dhamma" means one should investigate the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) through skillful means. "In this way, one is purified therein" means in this way, within that Noble Path.
He is purified. Alternatively, "one should wisely investigate the Dhamma" means one should investigate the Dhamma of the Noble Truths by means of the proper method.
"Thus one is purified therein" means one is purified in those four Noble Truths.
Now, while speaking in praise of the Elder Sāriputta, he said, "Sāriputto," and so forth. Therein, "Sāriputto" is a term of emphasis; by these [qualities]...
He says that Sāriputta alone is superior by virtue of wisdom and the other [faculties]. By "tranquility" he means the subsiding of the defilements.

By "gone to the further shore" he means one who has reached Nibbāna; he says that no other bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna is like him, and that he is the ultimate limit, for there is no disciple superior to the Elder.
"Past" refers to the five aggregates of the past. "One should not pursue it" means one should not follow after it by way of craving and views.
"One should not long for it" means one should not desire it by way of craving and views. "Whatever is past" is the statement of the reason here:
because whatever is past has been abandoned, ceased, and come to an end, therefore one should not pursue it. And because whatever is future therein—
Since that has not been reached, not yet arisen, and not yet produced, one should not long for it either.
"There, there" means that whatever present phenomenon has arisen in this or that place, one contemplates it with the seven contemplations beginning with the contemplation of impermanence;
or else, one contemplates it in various locations such as the forest and so forth. It is unshakable and unagitated.

This is stated for the purpose of showing insight (*vipassanā*) and further-insight (*paṭivipassanā*). For insight is "unshakeable" (*asaṃhīrā*) and "unagitated" (*asaṃkuppā*) because it is not shaken or disturbed by lust and the other defilements; the meaning is that one should cultivate, increase, and further-insight that [insight].
Alternatively, Nibbāna is "unshakeable" and "unagitated" because it is not shaken or disturbed by lust and the other defilements; that...
A wise, learned bhikkhu should cultivate it; the meaning is that by repeatedly entering the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) which has that as its object, he would cause it to increase.
For the sake of that cultivation, one must exert oneself this very day;

"ardor" (*ātappa*) is the name given to energy (*vīriya*) through the burning and scorching of the defilements, and it should be practiced this very day. Who knows if death will come tomorrow? Or if life will continue until tomorrow?
"Who knows whether there will be life or death? I shall give a gift this very day, or I shall guard my virtue, or I shall perform some other wholesome deed.

Without giving rise to the thought, "There is still time for delay today; I shall decide tomorrow or the day after," one should exert effort with the resolve, "I shall do it this very day"—this is what he shows. By "Mahāsena": [the rest of the passage follows].
For there are many causes of death for him, such as snakes, scorpions, poison, weapons, and so forth;

thus, by means of that great army, he dwells with Death—who possesses such a vast host—thinking, "Wait for just a few days while I perform my own supporting tasks, such as making offerings to the Buddha," or in the manner of a friendly greeting, "This hundred... or...

There is no compact consisting of the offering of a bribe, such as "take a thousand [pieces of gold] and wait for a few days," nor is there a compact consisting of a gathering of forces, such as "we shall repel [the enemy] with this mass of troops.
For "compact" (saṅgara) is a term for making friends, giving bribes, and assembling a force;
therefore, this meaning has been stated. "Untiring" (atandita) means not lazy, but industrious. Because he has practiced in this way...

"One who has a single auspicious night" is *bhaddekaratta*. Thus, the Blessed One—the Sage of the Buddhas, who is "peaceful" due to the subsiding of passion and the other defilements—declares that a person practicing in this way is "one with an auspicious night.

"With the eye and with wisdom" means both with the eye and with wisdom; or, with wisdom that has become the eye. "With mindfulness and with wisdom" means both with mindfulness and with wisdom; or, with wisdom distinguished by mindfulness. "With the body" means with the mental body (*nāmakāya*).
"The divine eye is perfectly purified" means that the divine eye is thoroughly cleansed; the intention is that which one realizes.
"Past lives" refers to the aggregates (khandhas) dwelt upon in previous births. "The modes of psychic power" refers to the various divisions of supernormal power (iddhi).
"Cessation" is Nibbāna. The rest is easily understood.

104. “Whose mind is like a rock”: because it cannot be shaken by the winds of worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*)—just as a solid, single-mass rock cannot be moved by natural winds—one’s mind is like a rock.
Therefore he said: “Stable, it does not tremble. Regarding “in things that cause passion,” this refers to gain and so forth;
regarding “in things that cause anger,” this refers to loss and so forth. How could suffering come to him? To one whose mind has been thus developed...
Suffering caused by worldly conditions will not follow that Supreme Person who has transcended worldly conditions.

As for the one called a "brahmin," he is a brahmin because he has banished evil states; he does not claim to be a brahmin merely by birth while remaining possessed of evil states such as making oaths, uttering "hum" sounds, or other such practices, nor through mere adherence to auspicious sights. That brahmin, because he has banished evil states...

He is *nihuṃhuṅka* because he has abandoned the utterance of "huṃ" and "huṃ. He is *nikkabha* because of the absence of the impurities such as lust (*rāga*). He is *yatatta* because his mind is restrained through the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*).
He is a *vedantaga* because he has reached the end—Nirvana—by means of the knowledges known as the four paths, or because he has gone to the end of the Vedas.
He is one who has *vusitabrahmacariya* because he has lived out the holy life of the path. By means of the Dhamma, he [proclaims] the Brahma-discourse.
“He would speak” means he would utter that speech, “I am a brahmin.

The meaning is that in his entire dwelling within the world, there is not even in regard to a single object any such excesses (ussada) as the excess of lust, the excess of hatred, the excess of delusion, the excess of conceit, or the excess of views. “He does not stand firm” means he does not take a footing.
“The floods” refers to the floods known as the *sukka* (the white). If [this applies] to the moon, the sun, and so forth...
Anticipating the doubt that "there is no light there, but only darkness," he said, "darkness is not found there.

And when it is said, "when one finds it by oneself," and so forth: when one finds such Nibbāna through knowledge that is directly realized by oneself, then one becomes liberated from both material and immaterial phenomena, as well as from pleasure and pain.
"In one's own states" means in the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhas) comprised within one's own personal existence.

For, as a general rule, the application of insight (vipassanā) is directed inwardly. "This demon" refers both to the demon Ajakalāpaka and to the demon of the defilements (kilesapisāca) mentioned by you.
"Disharmony" refers to the disorder created by you and the act of causing such disorder. "Transgresses" means it oversteps [its bounds].
"He does not rejoice at her coming" means he does not welcome his former wife as she arrives, nor any other woman;
he does not accept them with his mind. "He does not grieve for her as she departs" means he does not sorrow over her leaving.
"The victor in battle, freed from bonds" refers to the monk who has conquered the battle and is liberated from the fivefold fetter.
"Bahvettha" means "many people bathe here"; the intention is that he does not become pure by that alone.

"Jātibalaṃ" refers to the refutation of the power of birth; it is that which negates the power of birth. "Sahāyā vata" means "indeed companions," in the sense of proceeding together with the cultivation of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
By way of hearing the suitable Dhamma from time to time, for a long duration...
“Those who have long been united” means those for whom there is a meeting or coming together [with the goal]. “Exerting slackly” means having made their energy slack.

(105) “In that regard, monks, what is the distinction? This refers to the absence of distinction—both above and below—in terms of the preliminary practice consisting of disenchantment with the five aggregates of clinging and so forth, as well as liberation through non-clinging.
It shows this. For it has been said: "There is no diversity in liberation. In that context, the phrase "What is the distinction here? refers to the absence of any difference.
"Adhippāyāsa" means excessive application. And "nānākaraṇa" (differentiation) is also said to be simply a distinction.
"This, monks, is the distinction" means, monks, that although there is indeed a distinction between the disciple’s liberation and that of the Teacher...

There is no [such thing as this], but rather, having exhausted all defilements along with their latent tendencies through self-awakened knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*) and having fully awakened to perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), there is the conjunction of all the qualities of omniscience, such as the production of the noble path (*ariyamagga*) that had not yet arisen in the mental continuum of another.

This is the distinction of the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) from one liberated by wisdom (*paññāvimutta*). In this context, "that which has not arisen" means that which is not currently occurring. For the noble path...
The Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa brought it forth. There was no other teacher in the interval who could be called a bringer-forth;
therefore, this Blessed One is called the bringer-forth of the path not yet brought forth. "Unarisen" is a synonym for that same thing. "Unproclaimed" means unspoken.
He knows the path, thus he is "one who knows the path" (*maggaññū*). He has made the path known, understood, and manifest, thus he is "one who understands the path" (*maggavidū*).
"One skilled in the path and the non-path" means one who is an expert regarding the path (*maggakovida*). "Followers of the path" means those who follow the path.
"Attained later" means: "I was attained first; the disciples were attained later.

Regarding the phrase "born into a low family," and so forth: it is called "darkness" (*tamo*) because it is joined with darkness. This is because through bodily misconduct and the like, one again goes to the darkness of hell.

“Having darkness as his final resort”: thus, by both [of these terms], only the darkness of the aggregates is described. By the phrase beginning with “born into a wealthy family,” he is joined with light;
that is to say, he has become like light. Because he goes toward rebirth in a heavenly state through bodily good conduct and so forth, he has light as his final resort.
In this same manner, the other two [types of persons] are also to be understood.
Regarding the phrase "The wise say that is not a strong bond": here, "the wise" refers to the Buddhas and other learned persons.
They do not call "strong" that which is made of iron—known as a shackle—and that which is made of wood—known as a wooden bond—or the rope-bond fashioned by making a cord from jungle grass;
for these can be cut with swords and other weapons, and thus they are not called "firm."
The meaning is as follows: *Sārattarattā* means being attached after having become attached; the sense is "colored by intense passion.
*Maṇikuṇḍalesu* means among jewels and earrings, or among earrings inlaid with jewels.

*Etaṃ daḷhaṃ* means that for those who are intensely attached to jewels and earrings, whatever passion there is toward them, and whatever craving there is regarding children and wife—this is a bond consisting of defilements.
Wise men call it "firm.
It is called "dragging down" (*ohārina*) because it drags one away and causes one to fall into the four states of misery; it carries one off and takes one downward.

It is "loose" (*sithila*) because, at the place of binding, it does not disturb the skin and so forth, nor does it even make known the state of being bound, [whether] on water routes, land routes, or elsewhere.
"It allows one to act" means it is lax. "Difficult to release":
for a bond of defilement that has arisen even once through the power of greed is difficult to free from its place of attachment, like a tortoise [from its shell]; thus it is "difficult to release.
"Having cut this too": having severed even this firm bond of defilement with the sword of wisdom, and being without longing, one abandons sensual pleasure.
The meaning is: they wander about, they set out, and they go forth.

(107) "He intends" means he intends by way of unwholesome volition (*akusalacetanā*). "He plans" means he plans that very same unwholesome volition by way of bringing it to the state of bodily and verbal action.
"It underlies" means the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) such as lust, etc., underlie the continuum (*santāna*) because they have not been abandoned.
"This becomes an object for the persistence of consciousness" means that this volition (*cetanā*), planning (*pakappanā*),
and underlying tendency (*anusaya*) serve as the condition for the persistence and occurrence of formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*). "When there is an object,
there is a foundation for consciousness" means that when the aforementioned conditions exist, [the object] causes the formative consciousness to set its karma in motion.

It is a foundation because it provides the capacity to draw forth rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "There is the production of renewed existence in the future" means that there is the production of consciousness and the other factors known as renewed existence in the future.
By the passage beginning with "If, monks, one does not intend," he rejects unwholesome kamma alone. This, then, is the summary meaning here:
Even if, at some time, unwholesome volition does not arise due to wise attention, the underlying tendencies (anusaya) have nevertheless not been abandoned;
thus they certainly serve as the basis for wholesome formative consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa).

And when there is formative consciousness, it is indeed appropriate to say that there is the production of renewed existence in the future. The third section is to be understood by way of the opposite of what has been stated.
108. “This, monks, is not the ocean in the discipline of the Noble One,” and so forth.

This was said to show that if the term “ocean” were to be applied on the grounds of being difficult to fill, difficult to sink into, or difficult to cross, then this same principle applies even to the eye and the other [faculties] by a hundredth or even a thousandth part. Therefore he said: “The eye, monks...”
“The ocean is for a man; its surge consists of forms. This means that because beings are drawn toward forms, the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) itself is the surge, the surge of the eye.
“He who withstands that surge consisting of forms” refers to the bhikkhu who, together with the object, regards the eye as impermanent and suffering.
Contemplating it as non-self, becoming disenchanted with it, becoming dispassionate toward it, and being liberated from the net of defilements to which it is bound, he overcomes it.
This, monks, is called "one who has crossed the ocean of the eye";
this monk is said to have crossed the ocean known as the eye.
Another method: "The eye, monks, is an ocean in the discipline of the Noble One.
Whether it is an ocean in the sense of being difficult to fill or in the sense of surging together, the eye itself is the ocean.

For from the earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma-world, the blue and other objects of perception that flow into it cannot bring it to a state of fullness. Thus, it is an ocean in the sense of being difficult to fill.

It is an ocean (*samudda*). Furthermore, it is an ocean in the sense of "arising" (*samudana*): because when it is unrestrained, the eye arises toward various objects such as blue and so forth, and by being a cause for the arising of defilements, it proceeds with a state of impurity (*sadosa*).

Likewise, because the eye is a gateway for the arising of the streams of craving and so forth, it is an ocean in the sense of "arising" and in the sense of "moistening" (*temana*) the continuum by means of them.

The ocean. Its "material surge" should be understood as an immeasurable, material surge—just like the immeasurable surge consisting of waves in the ocean—that belongs to this ocean of the eye, occurring by way of the objects (ārammaṇa) classified as blue and so forth that flow into it.
"He who endures that material surge" means he who endures that material surge flowing into the ocean of the eye.

One endures by means of equanimity (*upekkhaka-bhāvena*), not giving rise to defilements such as lust and so forth—namely, lust for an agreeable form, hatred for a disagreeable one, and delusion toward that which is neither.
Regarding the terms *saūmi* and so on:

it is "with waves" (*saūmi*) because of the waves of defilement; "with whirlpools" (*sāvaṭṭa*) because of the cycles of defilement; "with crocodiles" (*sagaha*) because of the crocodiles of defilement; [and] "with *rakkhasas* of defilement" (*sarakkhasa*) because of the *rakkhasas* of defilement.
It is "with ogres" (sarakkhasaṃ) by way of the distress of anger. It is "with waves" (saūmiṃ) by way of the strands of sensual pleasure.
It is "with whirlpools" (sāvaṭṭaṃ) and "with crocodiles" (sagahaṃ) by way of women. For this has been said: "Bhikkhus, 'fear of waves' is a designation for the distress of anger.
Likewise, bhikkhus, 'whirlpools' is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure."
“‘A female ogre,’ monks, is a designation for women. The same method applies to the other doors as well.

“He has crossed over the difficult-to-traverse [ocean] with its dangers from waves” means he has transcended that which is fearful due to the dangers of the waves of impermanence and so forth, and is thus hard to cross. “One who has reached the end of the world” means one who has gone to the end of the world of saṃsāra. “He is called ‘one who has gone beyond’” means he is said to have reached Nibbāna.
“Hooks” (baḷisa) are like hooks because they are a cause of harm to sentient beings. “For misfortune” (anayāya) means for what is harmful. “For affliction” (byābādhāya) means...
To suffering. "Desirable" means desirable either because it has been sought after or because it has not been sought after, owing to its being an object of pleasure.

It is "lovely" (*kantā*) in the sense of being desirable. It is "agreeable" (*manāpā*) in the sense of increasing the mind. It is "of a lovely nature" (*piyarūpā*) because of its quality of being dear.

It is "connected with sensual desire" (*kāmūpasaṃhitā*) because it is accompanied by the defilement of sensual desire. It is "provocative of lust" (*rajanīyā*) because it colors the mind in the sense of generating passion. "And that" refers to that objective field of form.

For although the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) is divided into many types by way of blue and so forth, it does not transcend its single nature as an object of form and as something cognizable by the eye-consciousness;
thus, taking that commonality of intrinsic nature, it is said, "If he...
He "rejoices" (*abhinandati*) means he delights facing toward craving accompanied by rapture, which is itself rejoicing. He "speaks in praise" (*abhivadati*) means: "Oh, what happiness!"
He assents by way of craving when she makes him say, “Oh, what happiness! He “remains clinging” means he remains having swallowed and digested it.

“This, monks, is called a monk who has swallowed Māra’s hook”—this means, monks, that this monk is said to remain having swallowed the craving for forms, which is the hook belonging to the defilement-māra. The same applies to the remaining sections.
The meaning should be understood according to this method. *Abhedi* means he split [it]. *Paribhedi* means he split it in every part. The rest is self-evident. 109. *Ayaṃ loko santāpajāto*:

the meaning is that this world of beings has become subject to torment—tormented by birth, and possessing the torment of sorrow arisen through such things as the loss of relatives, as well as the torment of feverish passion arisen through lust and so forth. *Phassapareto*: overcome by numerous painful contacts.
"Overwhelmed": he speaks while weeping because, being unable to endure through the lack of bodily cultivation each suffering touched by himself, he laments, saying, "Oh, what suffering!
May such suffering never befall even my enemy," and so forth. Why?
Because "in whatever way they conceive it, it turns out otherwise than that," for these [beings].
In whatever manner beings imagine a remedy for their suffering and hope for it, that suffering must be treated by a method other than that.
Or, in whatever manner they imagine their own prosperity, there is instead only misfortune;
thus, what is cultivated in such a contrary way leads only to the frustration of one's desires.
This "clinging being" (*bhavasatta*) refers to the world of beings (*sattaloka*) attached to existence, such as existence in the sense-sphere and so forth;

nevertheless, it delights only in existence and does not become disenchanted with it. That which it delights in is "fear": that existence in the sense-sphere and so forth which it delights in is "fear" in the sense of being exceedingly terrifying because it is followed by numerous calamities such as aging and death.
"That from which one fears" refers to that [existence] from which one fears, namely, aging, death, and so forth.
It is called "suffering" because it is the basis of suffering and because of its nature as the suffering of suffering.
"For the abandoning of existence" means for the purpose of relinquishing existence (*bhava*). "Kho" is a particle used in the sense of emphasis. This is what is meant:
this has been attained by me solely for the purpose of abandoning existence—such as sensual desire and the rest—by means of abandoning its origin.
"The holy life is lived under the guidance of the Path.
Having thus shown that the Noble Path leads exclusively to liberation, he now says "Whosoever... and so forth, rejecting the possibility that any other path leads to liberation.
In this context, "by existence" means either by the form-sphere existence (*rūpabhava*) or the formless-sphere existence (*arūpabhava*).
"Bhava" means *saṃsāra*. "Vippamokkha" means liberation from existence (*bhava*); the meaning is purification from *saṃsāra*.

Although those ascetics and brahmins perceive that as *nibbāna*, they speak of purification from existence by means of existence—namely, through the form and formless meditative absorptions which lead to existence, and through the rebirth-existence produced thereby—thus claiming liberation from existence by means of existence.
They indeed say [this]. Therefore he said: “I declare that all of them are not liberated from existence (bhava).

Alternatively, by “existence” (bhavena) is meant the view of existence (bhavadiṭṭhi). For since the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi) proceeds by way of the thought “it exists, it persists, it is eternal,” it is called the “view of existence.
This very view of existence is expressed as “existence” (bhavo) through the elision of the latter member of the compound, just as in the case of “craving for existence” (bhavataṇhā) and so forth.
For here, through the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*), some imagine that a particular state of existence itself is liberation from existence.
As the Brahmā Baka said: "This is permanent, this is stable, this is eternal, this is not subject to change.

Through non-existence (*vibhava*) means by way of the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). For the annihilationist view is so called because it proceeds [with the thought]: "It ceases, it perishes, it is cut off."
In the manner already stated, it is called "non-existence" (*vibhava*). "They spoke of the escape from existence" means they spoke of the purification of *saṃsāra*.
For here, some speak of the purification of *saṃsāra* by way of the annihilationist view (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*). Thus it has been said:

"But when, sir, this self—possessing form, composed of the four great elements... [and so on] ...having attained and dwelling in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—at that point, sir, this self is completely annihilated."

“Unreleased” means not having emerged. He states the reason for this: “For it is in dependence on acquisitions (*upadhi*) that this suffering arises. Here, “acquisitions” refers to the acquisitions consisting of the aggregates (*khandha*), and so forth.

What is meant? Where these proponents of views perceive [something] as Nibbāna, there the acquisitions of the aggregates, the acquisitions of defilements (*kilesa*), and the acquisitions of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*) have been attained and known. How, then, could there be an escape from suffering for them?
But in order to show that which is the ultimate escape from suffering, it is said: "With the destruction of all clinging, there is no arising of suffering.
"Behold this world," the Blessed One addresses his own mind. "Puthū" means individually. "Ensnared by ignorance" means overcome by delusion.
"Bhūta" refers to the pentad of aggregates. "Bhūtarata" refers to women delighting in men, and men delighting in women.
Thus, beings are mutually attached to one another; for that very reason, they are not liberated from existence (*bhava*).

For whatever existences there may be—whether of short duration or long life, whether accompanied by pleasure or pain—all such existences are included. "In all places" (*sabbadhi*) means everywhere: above, below, and across.

"By way of all" (*sabbatthatāya*) means by way of every mode of being. Regarding the passage beginning with "all those existences," [it refers to] the teaching that "all existences are impermanent," and so forth.
For one who sees without error through the wisdom of the path accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*), craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) is abandoned and ceases;
he does not delight in nor long for non-existence or annihilation (*vibhava*). Because all his cravings cease completely through the path, Nibbāna is his extinguishment (*nibbuti*).
For that bhikkhu thus extinguished, there is no further clinging to the formative forces of the defilements (*kilesābhisaṅkhāra*).
Through non-clinging and non-grasping, there is no further becoming. For one who has become thus, the fivefold Māra is overcome;
he has won the battle with this Māra, has transcended all states of existence, and has attained the characteristic of equanimity toward the desirable and undesirable, and so forth.
The worldling who goes with the stream and the noble worldling who goes against the stream; the trainee whose mind is established;
and the other, the one beyond training. 110. "Lineage" refers to births. One of dark lineage is one born into a dark, low family.
"He gives birth to dark states" means he produces and performs the tenfold state of immorality, which is black; having given birth to that, he is reborn in hell.
Regarding the phrase "the bright dhamma": thinking, "In the past, because I did not perform meritorious deeds, I was reborn into a low family;
now I shall perform merit," one gives birth to the bright, pure dhamma known as merit (*puñña*). Through that, one is reborn in heaven.
Regarding "neither dark nor bright, Nibbāna": for if Nibbāna were dark, it would yield a dark result.
One might give what is bright, with a bright result. However, because it is not given by either of these two, it is said to be "neither black nor bright.
And here, "Nibbāna" refers to Arahantship; for it is called "Nibbāna" because it is born at the end of the extinction of the defilements (*kilesa-nibbāna*).
One "is born into," produces, and accomplishes that. "Bright-born" (*sukkābhijātiko*) means one born into a bright, noble family. The rest...

This should be understood in the manner already stated. The meaning of the fourfold classification of kamma beginning with "black with black result" has already been analyzed below in the section on the Convergence of Modes (Hārasampāta). 111.
"Human state" (mānusatta) means the human condition; the sense is "human womb. "Two" refers to what is to be done and what is not to be done.

Two [tasks]. This shows that only duties (*kicca*) are to be performed, and no non-duty (*akicca*) is to be done. "Good duties" and so forth is the demonstration of the specific nature of those things referred to as "duties.
"Exertions" (*padhānāni*) means supreme or distinguished.
In the first instance, "among those who have gone forth," the locative case is used in the sense of a sphere. In the second...
In the section on the "legal case" (*adhikaraṇa*). Herein, "Nirvana" is intended to mean Arahatship.

But why is the relinquishing of material things (*āmisa*) here taught as being of equal weight to Arahatship? It is for the purpose of showing that a gift (*dakkhiṇā*) bestowed upon those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*) yields great fruit.
"By whatever basis whatsoever" means by a basis such as annihilationism (*uccheda*) and so forth. "Attached" means attached by way of craving for existence (*bhava-taṇhā*) and the like.
"In the second [case], 'by whatever basis' refers to the basis of endless equivocation (*amarāvikkhepa*) and so forth.
'By this unwholesome result of kamma' means by an unwholesome, inauspicious result of kamma, because it is the ripening of unwholesome kamma such as bodily misconduct.
'This characteristic of a fool is produced' means that due to being possessed of misconduct in a previous existence..."
The characteristic "this one is a fool" arises as a mark. This is a discourse pertaining to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya-sutta*);
such is the discourse that proceeds in this manner, called "pertaining to defilement.
The meaning here should be understood according to the method explained in the passage beginning with "by means of this beauty. In that context, "the marks of a Great Man" (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*)...
The characteristic of a wise person (*paṇḍitalakkhaṇa*). "By means of the planes of defilement" (*kilesabhūmīhi*) means by means of the locations of defilement or the states of defilement.

"Obsession arises for one who has underlying tendencies" (*sānusayassa pariyuṭṭhānaṃ jāyati*) means that for one whose underlying tendencies have not been abandoned, lust and the other defilements arise by way of obsession when the appropriate conditions converge.
"Being obsessed, he is fettered" (*pariyuṭṭhito saṃyujjati*) means that he whose mind is obsessed by lust and the rest is fettered by sensual lust and the other fetters.

"Name. One who "binds" (saṃyujjanto) grasps (upādiyati); that is, one who is bound by the fetters such as sensual lust (kāmarāga-saṃyojana) and so forth, grasps the clinging to sense-pleasures (kāmupādāna) and so forth, as well as unwholesome kamma.
The rest is clear in all respects. 112.
Having thus analyzed the *Paṭṭhāna* of the Dispensation in its sixteenfold manner by way of examples from various suttas, now...

Since this analysis of the *Paṭṭhāna* as well is comprised by the root-terms (*mūlapada*), and there is no portion of it that is not included therein, [the author], in order to show the root-terms and their analysis, first extracts the root-terms by way of the question: "In this regard, what are the eighteen root-terms? and so forth.

By the passage beginning with “mundane and supramundane,” the twenty-eightfold foundation of the Dispensation (*sāsanapaṭṭhāna*)—namely, the ninety-one [texts] and the *Thava* (Hymn)—has been enumerated.
Therein, “mundane” (*lokiya*) means that which is connected to the world (*loke niyutta*), or that which is known in the world (*loke vidita*).
However, in this context, a discourse (*sutta*) in which a mundane matter is stated is called “mundane. The same applies to the “supramundane” (*lokuttara*). Furthermore, in whichever discourse...
In one part it is mundane, and in another part it is supramundane; thus it is both mundane and supramundane.
That which is taught by way of the designation of beings, having taken beings as its basis, is "based on beings" (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*).
That which is taught solely by way of the phenomena (*dhamma*) is "based on phenomena" (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*). That which is taught by way of both is "based on beings" and "based on phenomena. By this—
The meaning in all instances should be understood according to this method. However, a discourse that proceeds by way of extolling the virtues of the Buddha and others is called *thava* (praise).
In that context, *sajjukhīraṃ* refers to the fresh, warm milk that has just issued from the udders of a cow at that very moment. *Muccatīti* means it transforms [into curds].
This is what is meant: just as the milk issuing from the cow’s udder at that very moment...
It is not released, it does not transform, and it does not become curd;

however, through contact with sour substances such as buttermilk, at a later time it abandons its original nature and reaches the state of curd. In the same way, even an evil deed (*pāpakamma*) does not ripen at the very moment of its performance.
If it were to ripen then, there would be no room for the specific characteristics of the various realms of existence (*gati*), and no one would [ever] commit an evil deed.
One would not be able to do so. However, as long as the aggregates produced by wholesome karma continue to function, they protect that person;
yet upon their dissolution, it ripens by causing rebirth in the states of misery (*apāya*).

And as it ripens, it follows after the fool like a burning fire, just like a fire covered by ashes. For just as a glowing ember hidden by ash might burn even one who steps on it, so too does this karma follow the fool.
Because it is covered by ashes, it does not burn immediately; however, having heated the ashes, it proceeds burning everything from the skin onwards up to the brain.
In the same way, the evil kamma also follows the fool who committed it, burning him as he is reborn in the hells and other realms in his second or third existence.

Regarding the phrase "whose faculties": this is the meaning in brief. For that bhikkhu whose six faculties have reached a state of being tamed, calmed, and rendered harmless—just like horses well-tamed by a skilled charioteer—he has abandoned the ninefold conceit;
because he stands having abandoned conceit, and because he is free from the four taints due to the absence of those taints, he abides in the state of equanimity (*tādibhāva*).
Even the gods envy one who stands in such a state; even humans surely long for the sight of him and his arrival.
"When there is nutriment" means when desire and lust bound to nutriment have not been abandoned.
"Having traversed all quarters with the mind" means having gone around the ten directions with the consciousness. "He did not find" means...
One would not find anything dearer. "Dearer" means exceedingly dear. "To oneself" means as one's own self.
Thus, because no one else’s self is found to be dearer than one’s own, the self of each and every other being is likewise dear.
And since this is so, therefore one who desires their own welfare—that is, one who desires their own happiness—should not harm another.

“Have been” means born or produced. “Will be” means will be produced. Alternatively, “have been” refers to those whose taints are destroyed; for they are indeed “beings” (bhūta) because existence has been abandoned by them. “Will go” means they will go to the other world. But those whose taints are destroyed [go] to Nibbāna without residue. “And he becomes dear”:
one who is endowed with perfectly pure accomplishment in virtue and perfectly pure accomplishment in view becomes dear and beloved.
For this has been said: “One endowed with virtue and vision, established in the Dhamma, a speaker of truth;”
“People hold dear that person who performs deeds for their own sake.

He is *garu* (venerable) because he is to be held in high esteem, like a stone parasol. He is *bhāvanīyo* (to be cultivated) because he is to be honored on account of his superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
Alternatively, his state of being dear, venerable, and so forth, should be understood by way of his virtue of moral discipline (*sīlaguṇa*). For it has been said: “If one should desire...”
“Monks, when a monk thinks, ‘May I be dear, pleasing, respected, and esteemed by my fellow practitioners of the holy life,’ he should be one who fulfills the precepts themselves. Regarding “conduct”:
having established within himself the five qualities beginning with “I shall speak at the proper time,” he acts for the sake of uplifting his fellow practitioners of the holy life.

*Vattā*: One who stands firm. *Vacanakkhamo*: When addressed by any fellow practitioner of the holy life, one is patient with their words because one is well-spoken and accepts their speech with deference;
thus, one is "patient with words. Alternatively, *vattā* means one whose habit is speaking by way of discourse on the Dhamma. *Vacanakkhamo*:
While praising the Dhamma, one is not shaken by others and is patient with the words of their questions; thus, one is "patient with words."
"He speaks profound discourse" means he speaks on such topics as the Truths and Dependent Origination, or other profound discourses.
"He does not direct one to what is improper" means that because he explains the Dhamma and Vinaya, etc., solely by way of the Dhamma and Vinaya, etc., rather than by way of non-Dhamma and non-Vinaya,
etc., he does not direct one to what is improper.

Regarding the phrase "having killed mother and father": here, craving (taṇhā) is called "mother" because, according to the statement "craving gives birth to the person," it generates sentient beings within the three realms of existence.

Conceit of self (asmimāna) is called "father" because conceit arises in dependence upon a father, such as [thinking], "I am the son of such-and-such a king or a royal minister. Just as the world [depends] on a king...
All positions of view fall into two categories: the views of eternalism and annihilationism;
therefore, these two views are called the "two Kṣatriya kings. The twelve sense-bases (āyatana), because they are extensive and resemble a kingdom, are called the "kingdom.
Craving for delight (nandirāga), which depends upon them like a subordinate official who accomplishes the king's aims, is called the "attendant."

"Anigho" means free from suffering. "Brāhmaṇo" means one whose taints are destroyed. For by this, craving and the rest have been struck down and expelled by the sword of the knowledge of the path to arahantship. "Yāti" means that the brāhmaṇa, having become free from suffering, goes forth.
"Kāye" refers to the body born of karma. "Cittam" refers to the mind of the foundational jhāna.
"Samodahati" means he places [the mind] therein. The meaning is: when he wishes to go with a visible body, he then resolves the mind of the foundational jhāna to follow the course of the body.
"He absorbs the body into the mind": when he wishes to go quickly, he then inserts the body into the mind of the foundational jhāna;
the meaning is that he resolves the body so that it follows the movement of the mind. "Having entered upon the perception of bliss and the perception of lightness in the body":
just as if a strong man were to stretch out his bent arm, or... [stretch out his bent arm].

Or, as it is said in the passage beginning “or he might bend his arm,” the possessor of supernormal power (iddhimā), having entered into the perception of pleasure and the perception of lightness regarding the body, goes to the desired place in a single moment of consciousness while observing delightful parks and groves with a body visible to others. 114.
That which is called “supramundane knowledge” (lokuttara-ñāṇa) is so termed because it stands having transcended and overcome the entire world.

But it is not because it belongs to the supramundane plane. It is said that "it occurs at all times" because its activity is bound to adverting (āvajjana), not because it occurs continuously and uninterruptedly.
