For it cannot be said that the omniscient knowledge of the Blessed One arises at every single moment.
"I will show you peace": because it is the cause for the subsiding of all defilements, I shall demonstrate peace, which is Nibbāna.
"In this very life" (*diṭṭhe dhamme*): in the phenomena such as suffering that are seen, or in this very personal existence (*attabhāva*).

"Not based on hearsay" (*anītihanti*): it does not proceed by way of mere tradition (*itikirāya*); the meaning is that it is directly perceived by oneself. Having known this, they live mindfully, [saying]: "All..."
Having become mindful by way of the method beginning with "formations are impermanent," and having realized that peace through the Noble Path,

one should cross over the attachment in the world; the meaning is that one should cross over— that is, transcend— the craving known as "attachment" because it spreads throughout the world of formations.
"I rejoice in that" means: "I desire that speech of yours which has been spoken in the manner described and which indicates peace," or rather, Dhota says, "I rejoice in that very supreme peace.
Regarding the phrase "above, below, across, and in between": here, "above" (*uddhaṃ*) refers to the future and what is high;
"below" (*adho*) refers to the past and what is low; and "across, and in between" (*tiriyañcāpi majjhe*) refers to the present.
"And all around. Having understood this as "the source of attachment," one knows that this—namely, the future and so forth—is the place where attachment arises.
"For the sake of various states of existence" means for the sake of both small and great existences, or for the sake of eternalism and annihilationism.

"Of the noble truths" means of those truths which produce the state of a Noble One (*ariya*). "Through non-awakening" means through not waking up, through lack of knowledge. "Through non-penetration" means...
"By not penetrating. "Run about" means run about from one existence to another.
"Wandered on" means wandered on by way of going again and again. "Both mine and yours" means both by me and by you.
Alternatively, "run about and wandered on" means that the running about and the wandering on was both mine and yours.

Meaning: “The guide to existence” (bhavanetti) refers to the rope of craving (taṇhārajju) capable of leading one from one state of becoming to another. “Transmigrated” (saṃsitaṃ) means having wandered through cyclic existence.
“Completely eradicated” (samūhatā) means thoroughly struck down, severed, and rendered non-functional.
“All formations are impermanent”: the five aggregates (pañcakkhandhā), which receive the name “formations” (saṅkhārā) because they are conditioned by causes, are thus described.

They are impermanent because they have a beginning and an end, because they are subject to termination, because they are merely temporary, and because they are limited to a single moment; thus they are not permanent.
"When one sees with wisdom" means when one sees with the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*). Then one becomes disenchanted with this suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*);
becoming disenchanted, one penetrates the Truths by way of the full understanding of suffering and so forth. This is the path to purification.
This penetration of the truths in the manner described is the path for the sake of purification. "All conditioned phenomena are suffering":
all conditioned phenomena are suffering in the sense of being constantly oppressed and in the sense of exhaustion. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
"All phenomena are non-self": all phenomena belonging to the three planes are non-self because they are other-dependent, empty, void, coreless, and lack mastery.
And [the view] "it is not-self. The rest is exactly as before.
"Superior" means distinguished or excellent. "Equal" means the same. "Inferior" means base. For even disparagement occurs by way of deprecating oneself and by way of exalting others.
Therefore it is said: "I am inferior. What else could this be other than [knowing] things as they truly are?

"Non-seeing" (*adassana*) means: since material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*), by their very nature of momentary dissolution and absolute lack of stability, cannot be elevated by way of [pride such as] "I am better" and so forth, what other cause for this could there be than non-seeing—that is, ignorance—of them as they truly are?
The meaning is that there is no other cause for it whatsoever. This same method applies to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates as well. By the reverse of what was stated [above]:
The bright fortnight is to be understood.

115. "Those who discern the noble truths" means that by means of the light of wisdom, they dispel the darkness of the defilements that conceal the truths—such as suffering and the rest—and make them luminous and manifest to themselves.
"By one of profound wisdom" means by virtue of having immeasurable wisdom.
"By the All-Knowing One" means by him whose wisdom finds no foothold even in the world including the devas.

"Well-taught" means well-expounded through various methods, such as concise and detailed expositions. "Even though they may be exceedingly negligent" refers to those persons who have discerned the Noble Truths;
although they might occupy positions of negligence such as the sovereignty of the devas or the kingship of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), [they remain steadfast].

Having approached [the world], they become greatly negligent; nevertheless, through the knowledge of the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa) and the cessation of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa), because name-and-form (nāma-rūpa) which would otherwise arise in the beginningless cycle of existence (saṃsāra) throughout seven existences have ceased, they do not take up an eighth existence.
Rather, having begun insight (vipassanā) precisely in the seventh existence, [they attain liberation].
The meaning is: "they reach arahantship.
Regarding the phrase *yathindakhīlo* ("like the city-gate bolt"): here, *yathā* is a word of comparison.

*Indakhīlo* refers to a solid wooden post made of heartwood, which is driven into the ground after digging eight or ten cubits into the earth within the threshold (*ummāra*) for the purpose of securing the city gate.
This is a designation for a pillar. "It might be fixed in the earth" means that it would enter deep into the ground and be established upon the earth by means of its deep-rimmed base.
"By the four winds" means by the winds coming from the four directions. "Unshakable" means incapable of being shaken or moved.
"One who sees... like that" refers to one who, through wisdom, perceives the Four Noble Truths.

Having plunged deep, he sees; that true person, the supreme person, because of seeing him thus, is like the aforementioned post of Indra in its unshakability by the winds of the doctrines of all other sectarians—this is the meaning.
"By means of the factors of stream-entry" means by those things which constitute the factors for becoming a noble stream-enterer. "A noble disciple" refers to a disciple of the noble Buddha.
He is a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) because he was born at the end of hearing the Blessed One’s true Dhamma. "I am one for whom hell is exhausted" means: "I am one whose hell has been destroyed.
"Exhausted are the states of deprivation, the bad destinations, and the fallen realms"—this is stated by way of synonyms for hell and the others.

For hell and the rest are called "states of deprivation" (*apāya*) because they have departed from "gain" (*āya*), which is a term for prosperity. They are "bad destinations" (*duggati*) because they are the resort and refuge of suffering.

They are called *vinipātā* because those who commit wrongdoings (*dukkata*) fall into them helplessly. One is a *sotāpanna* because they have reached and attained the stream (*sota*), which is the Noble Path, from the very beginning.
Because of the unshakable nature of the paths and fruits, one is of a nature not to fall into the "disfigurement" (*virūpa*) known as the state of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*);

thus, one is "of a nature not to fall" (*avinipātadhamma*). For that very reason, due to being fixed by the fixedness of the Dhamma, one is "fixed" (*niyata*). [This applies to] those characterized by the three higher paths...
"Having enlightenment as his supreme goal" means that enlightenment is his ultimate destination, resort, and refuge because it is necessarily to be attained.
The words "settled," and so forth, are merely synonyms for one another. "Fellow-practitioners of the Dhamma" refers to those living the holy life together (*sabrahmacārī*).
"Dear to the Noble Ones" means dear, beloved, and pleasing to the Noble Ones. For the five precepts are dear to the noble disciples, even in other lives.
This was said with reference to those [precepts] because they are not abandoned. However, every kind of restraint (saṃvara) is indeed obtainable here.

The statement, "I am a stream-enterer," is merely a conventional designation for the teaching. Those who are once-returners and so forth likewise declare themselves according to the same method, saying, "I am a once-returner," and so on.
Therefore, for all of them, declaring oneself in a manner consistent with the training rules (sikkhāpada) in an appropriate context is indeed permitted.
"Whose faculties": the faculties, such as faith and the rest, belonging to that noble person (*ariyapuggala*).
"Well-developed": thoroughly developed by means of the cultivation of the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*). "Internally and externally": by way of abandoning the lower and higher fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Therefore he said, "in the whole world. "Having become disillusioned": having become disillusioned and having penetrated through [it].

"Dhammapadāni" means sections of the Dhamma. "Non-covetousness" (*anabhijjhā*) as a Dhamma-section refers to non-greed (*alobha*), or alternatively, the jhānas, insight, paths, fruits, and Nibbāna attained by way of the ten kinds of foulness (*dasasu asubhesu*);

these jhānas and so forth are the Dhamma-section of non-covetousness. Those attained by way of the four divine abidings (*catubrahmavihāra*) are the Dhamma-section of non-ill will (*abyāpāda*). [Those attained] by way of the ten recollections (*dasānussati*), the perception of repulsiveness in food (*āhāre paṭikkūlasaññā*), and so forth...
The Dhamma-foot of right mindfulness has been attained. The Dhamma-foot of right concentration has been attained by way of the ten kasiṇas and mindfulness of breathing.
"He cuts off five": a person might cut with a sword the rope bound to his feet, which leads to rebirth in the lower realms;
so too, one should cut the five lower fetters that lead to rebirth in the lower realms by means of the three lower paths. "He abandons five": [those] which lead to the higher world of the devas.
The five higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) should be abandoned and severed by means of the path of Arhatship, just as a man would remove a rope tied around his neck;

this is the meaning. "One should further develop the five" means that for the sake of abandoning the higher fetters, one should further develop the five faculties beginning with faith (*saddhā*). "One who has transcended the five attachments": when this is so, of the five...

By transcending the attachments of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and views, a bhikkhu who has become one who has gone beyond the five attachments is called "one who has crossed the flood" (*oghatinno*);
the meaning is that he is called "one who has crossed over the four floods.

For one who is practicing with the thought, "I shall know, I shall understand," the Dhamma of the Four Truths not yet known or penetrated, or the very state of the Deathless (*amatapada*)—[for such a person...]
The faculty of one standing on the first path is the "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" faculty (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*).

For that knowledge of the first path is spoken of in this way by way of its preceding stage. One who understands—meaning one who knows without overstepping the boundary of what is known through the first path—is "another" (*añña*);
his faculty is the "faculty of knowing" (*aññindriya*). This is a designation for the knowledge in the three lower fruits and in the three higher paths.
The faculty of one who has already known is the faculty of one who has already known (aññātāvindriya), belonging to the Arahant who has completed his task regarding the four truths;

this is a designation for the knowledge of the supreme fruit (aggaphala-ñāṇa). "Of that which has not been fully realized" means of that which has not been penetrated. "For the sake of full realization" means for the sake of penetration. 116.
"Characteristics of a fool" means the causes by which a fool is characterized. "Signs of a fool" means [those by which one knows] "this person is a fool."
To grasp the signs means to grasp the causes. "The ancient deeds of a fool" refers to the long-standing, accumulated karmas of a fool.
Regarding the phrases beginning with "one who thinks ill-thought thoughts": one who thinks covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view is "one who thinks ill-thought thoughts.
One who speaks false speech and so forth is "one who speaks ill-spoken words. One who performs the deed of killing living beings and so forth is "one who performs ill-done actions."
The bright fortnight (the waxing moon) should be understood by reversing what has been stated.
"Bhiyyo" means further and further. "Pakujjheyuṃ" means they would oppose; there is also a reading, "pakuppeyyuṃ. "Bhusena" means strongly.
"Daṇḍena" means by the infliction of punishment. "Dhīro" means wise, one of a nature endowed with discernment. "Nisedhaye" means he would ward off.
The meaning is: "He would be unable to do or say anything further. *Paraṃ* means an adversary.
"Who, being mindful, attains peace" (*yo sato upasammati*)—the meaning is: for one who, possessing mindfulness, attains peace, I consider that very peace to be the restraint of the fool.
*Vajjaṃ* means fault. "When he conceives it" (*yadā naṃ maññati*) means because he conceives it. "He climbs over" (*ajjhāruhati*) means he overwhelms.
"More than a cow, he flees": just as in a herd of cattle, two cows fight while the rest of the herd stands looking on until one flees;
but when one flees, then the entire herd of cattle more fully overwhelms that fugitive—so too, the foolish person more fully overwhelms the one who forgives. This is the meaning.
"Having one's own welfare as the supreme" means having one's own purpose as the supreme. "Nothing exists superior to patience":
among those purposes for which one's own welfare is supreme, no other purpose is found that is more excellent than patience.

"They call that patience supreme": when one who is strong exercises endurance, they call that patience of his supreme. The "strength of a fool" is the strength of ignorance; that [strength] belongs to whom...
That which is strength is indeed no strength; they do not call it strength, nor speak of it, nor point it out.

"Of one protected by the Dhamma" means of one guarded by the Dhamma, or of one protecting the Dhamma. "An opponent" means one who speaks back in opposition, or one who might say whatever he pleases after having opposed you.
But there is no one capable of shaking one who stands firm in the Dhamma. Of him alone...
"By that, it is worse"—by that anger, evil accrues to that very person. To whom? To him who returns anger for anger.
In this context, "to the angry one" (*kuddham*) is used in the accusative case where the dative is intended; the meaning is "to the angry one. "Those who wish to heal" (*tikicchantānam*):
the plural form is used for the singular; the meaning is "one who wishes to heal. "People think"—such [is their thought].

“Those who are unskilled in the Dhamma”—meaning those who are not proficient or expert in the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths—they think thus of the person who heals and accomplishes the welfare of both himself and others: “This person is a fool.
This is the meaning. Only blind, foolish worldlings (puthujjana) conceive such a notion.

117. "They fall" means that the requisites of sensual pleasure (*kāmūpakaraṇa*) already attained and currently being experienced are what must be attained; thus, those very same things are to be attained and experienced in the future.
"Both of these are strewn with dust" means that both are scattered with the dust of passion (*rāga*) and so forth.
"Of one who is afflicted" means of one afflicted by the defilements (*kilesa*) such as passion. "Learning after" means learning after individuals who abound in defilements.
And those who take the training as their essence are those who stand having grasped the training—consisting of virtue, vows, and so forth—as they have been undertaken, as their very core.
Therefore he said: "Virtue, vows, livelihood, and the holy life. Therein, that which one refrains from with the thought "I shall not do it" is virtue (*sīla*).

That which consists of such things as eating at the proper time and following the prescribed conduct is the vow (*vata*). "Livelihood" (*jīvita*) means mode of living (*ājīva*). "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*)...
*Abstinence from sexual intercourse*. "Having service as their core" means that these [virtues] such as moral discipline (*sīla*) have non-performance as their core.
The meaning is that they stand having grasped those [virtues] as a core, thinking, "By these alone is there purification from *saṃsāra*.

Thus, "these two extremes": by way of the adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*), there is devotion to self-mortification; and by way of the perception of blamelessness in sensual pleasures...
And "devotion to the pleasure of sense-desires"—these are the two extremes.

These, respectively, are to be practiced by those who, being afflicted by the defilements, follow after others who are attached to the strands of sensual pleasure—which are strewn with the dust of passion and so forth, both as they are presently obtained and as they are to be obtained in the future—and by those who themselves are likewise afflicted by the defilements;
and for that very reason, they increase the cemetery, leading from one state to another through aging and death.

"Those whose nature is to increase in the charnel ground" means they exclusively increase the cemetery; while increasing it themselves, they cause others to increase it by exhorting them toward the two extremes—this is the meaning.
"Not understanding both extremes" means not knowing the two extremes as they have been described. "Some shrink back" means [they hold that] "the self is eternal..."
"Both self and the world," some sink down due to the adherence of craving characterized by sluggishness.
"Some overreach" means that others go beyond due to the adherence of overreaching, thinking, "Self and the world are annihilated and destroyed.

They did not conceive [these views] because they have abandoned such conceivings as craving and the rest. Precisely for that reason, because of their parinibbāna through non-clinging, there is no threefold round of existence for them to point out.
“Jaññā” means he would know. “Saṃyuje” means he would bind himself. “Mānusaṃ” means belonging to humans (mānussa); it is that which is included within human existence.
“Kiṃ hi tassa sakaṃ hoti?”—for what else is called one’s own property for that being entering the jaws of death, other than wholesome kamma?
For beings are the owners of their kamma. Therefore he said: “Therefore, one should do what is wholesome,” and so forth.
In this context, "pertaining to the future life" (*samparāyika*) means that which produces the fruit of the future life.
"These phenomena" (*ime dhammā*) refers to these wholesome or unwholesome phenomena. "Thus acquired" (*evaṃ-gahitā*) means thus undertaken or produced.
"This fruit" (*idaṃ phalaṃ*) refers to this fruit of desirable or undesirable ripening. "This benefit" (*ayaṃ attho*) refers to this growth.
"This is a loss" is the meaning. "And anything else of this kind" refers to what is to be declared categorically (*ekamsavyākaraṇīya*).

Regarding the phrase "they might not know according to their wish," he says—"What does the Blessed One wish for?"—because the wish of the Blessed One is not within the domain of others; thus he says, "This is not to be answered. "To such an extent" means having that as its measure.
"In the aggregate of virtue" (*sīlakkhandhe*) means by reason of the aggregate of virtue; there is also a reading: "by the aggregate of virtue" (*sīlakkhandhena*).
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. "They move" (*iriyanti*) refers to bodily and verbal conduct. "They manifest" (*pabhāveti*) refers to their power (*ānubhāva*).

"With loving-kindness" (*hitesitāya*) means with *mettā*. "With psychic power" (*iddhiyā*) means with the various modes of psychic power (*iddhividha*). Such are the qualities of a Buddha, and each of these possesses such power.
Likewise, the paths, fruits, and *nibbāna* possess such majesty. And the Noble Saṅgha is endowed with such qualities.
The great majesty of the Three Jewels is not the domain of others in every respect;
it is the domain of the Blessed One alone. Thus he said: "The domain of the Buddha is unanswerable. By this, he shows that whatever other matter is the domain of the Buddha, that too is unanswerable.
For this was said by the Blessed One: "The domain of the Buddha is inconceivable; it should not be thought about. One who thinks about it..."
“He would partake of madness and frustration. Regarding the question, “What is the prior limit?”—it is unanswerable.
The question posed by someone asking, “What is the prior limit? is unanswerable. Why? Because there is no prior limit to saṃsāra.
For this very reason it was said: “The prior limit, monks, is not discerned. In that context, “is not discerned” means it is not seen.

The meaning is "it is not apprehended. Regarding the statement, "It is not discerned," this was said with the intention that it does not fall within the range of another's knowledge, as in the passage:

"It is not discerned because of the deficiency in the knowledge of the disciples," and so forth. In that context, *attūpanāyikā* means "that to which the self is to be applied" (*attā upanetabbo etissā*).
By the phrase, "There is no lack of understanding on the part of the Blessed Buddhas,"...
He shows that because of the very non-existence of a prior limit, it is not perceived, and there is no obstruction of knowledge therein.
However, to show that whatever exists—even if immeasurable for others—is not immeasurable for the Blessed One, and thus to demonstrate the Blessed One’s unimpeded knowledge everywhere, he said:
"Just as the Blessed One, concerning the bhikkhu Kokālika... and so forth.
In that context, "a certain bhikkhunī" refers to one whose name and clan were not well-known.
She spoke thus to a certain bhikkhu who was seated after having asked the question:
"Venerable sir, how long indeed is the lifespan in the Paduma hell? Here, the remainder of the text is as follows: "Long, bhikkhu, is the lifespan in the Paduma hell; it is not easy to calculate."
“for so many years,” or “for so many hundreds of years,” or “for so many thousands of years,” or “for so many hundreds of thousands of years.
“But is it possible, Bhante, to provide a simile?
“It is possible, bhikkhus,” the Blessed One said. “Suppose, bhikkhu, there were a Kosalan cartload of sesame seeds consisting of twenty khāris. From that, a man...”
At the end of every hundred years, one should remove a single sesame seed.
By this method, monk, that Kosalan sesame-cartload of twenty khārīs would more quickly reach exhaustion and depletion than even a single Abbuda hell. Just as with twenty Abbuda hells, monk...
"Thus there is one Nirabbuda hell," and so forth.
In that context, "twenty khāris": according to the Magadhan *pattha*, four *patthas* make one *pattha* in the kingdom of Kosala;
by that [Kosalan] *pattha*, four *patthas* make an *āḷhaka*, four *āḷhakas* make a *doṇa*, and four *doṇas* make a *mānikā*.
Four *mānikās* make one *khārī*. Twenty *khārīs* of that measure constitute a load of sesame seeds (*tilavāha*). A "load of sesame seeds" refers to a cartload of sesame seeds.

Regarding the "Abbuda hell": there is no separate individual hell named Abbuda; rather, it is a specific location within Avīci itself where beings are tormented according to the count of *abbudas*, and thus it is called the "Abbuda hell.
This same method applies to the Nirabbuda and other such hells as well.
In this regard, the calculation of years should be understood as follows:

just as one hundred thousand times one hundred thousand makes a *koṭi*, so too one hundred thousand times one hundred thousand *koṭis* is called a *pakoṭi*. One hundred thousand times one hundred thousand *pakoṭis* is called a *koṭipakoṭi*.

One hundred thousand times one hundred thousand *koṭipakoṭis* is a *nahuta*. One hundred thousand times one hundred thousand *nahutas* is a *ninnahuta*. One hundred thousand times one hundred thousand *ninnahutas* is one...
The Abbuda hell. Twenty times that is the Nirabbuda. This same method applies everywhere.

And it is said—“it is not easy to calculate”—because this reckoning is difficult for those who are unacquainted with it. Some, however, say: “These names were obtained because of the various kinds of lamentation and the various kinds of torture in each respective place. Others say: “These are cold hells.”
"Having corrupted the mind" means having defiled the mind.

"How does he conquer? is a question regarding the manner. "By what does he conquer? is a question regarding the cause. He asks: by what cause, by what reason, by what practice of conduct does he conquer?
Furthermore, "how" [implies] in what manner; does it refer to those of the past, or rather...
He asks, "Is he a conqueror (jina) by means of the abandoning of future and present defilements? Therefore, that [question] is said to be "answerable.
He asks, "Who is the conqueror? Is it form that is the conqueror, or is it feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that is the conqueror?
Or is there another, distinct from form and the rest, who is called the 'self' and is the conqueror? With reference to this matter, he says it is "unanswerable" (avisajjanīya).
"To what extent" means by what measure or what dimension.

"There is a Tathāgata" means there is a being. Because it is this venerable one—who is designated in dependence upon the five aggregates as "having such a name" and "having such a clan"—that is intended here, it is said that [the question] "is to be answered. Form...
It is stated that "it is not to be answered" because the question is asked on the basis of the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), taking the Tathāgata to be a form or a self.
In this same manner, the meaning is to be understood in all the following passages.
120. In phrases such as "a fool mounted upon a stool," the accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī-attha*). "Misconduct by way of the body" refers to...
"Done badly with the body. "Hanging down" (*olabbhanti*) means they hang down or spread out.
The remaining two phrases are synonyms for that same term. For they appear in the manner of hanging down and so forth; therefore, it is stated thus. "Great" (*mahataṃ*) means of the great ones.
"Hanging down upon the earth" means they spread out upon the surface of the earth. The remaining two phrases are synonyms for that same term.
For this is indeed the manner of spreading out [the mat]. In that regard, monks, "of the fool" means that in that manner of attending, it occurs thus to the fool.
"A gain for you, monks"—monks, those gains of human status, the acquisition of faith, and so forth, which have been obtained by you;
they are truly gains, just gains for you. "Well-obtained" refers to this very accomplishment of the fourfold purification of virtue and so forth, having gone forth into homelessness.

What has been gained, that too is well-gained. "The opportune moment has been obtained by you" means that this ninth moment, free from the eight inopportune moments (*aṭṭha-akkhaṇa*), has been obtained for dwelling in the holy life of the Path. By the partial indication beginning with "I have seen," he clarifies the eight inopportune moments.

121. "Wherever"—that is, whichever miserable destination (*duggati*) one goes to; "that which is unrighteousness" refers to the person who has practiced that which is unrighteousness (*adhamma*). "It strikes" means it afflicts.

"Of little influence" (*appesakkhatā*) means having little power. "Ugly" (*dubbaṇṇatā*) means deformity or repulsiveness. "Unwise" (*duppaññatā*) means lacking wisdom; it is the state of being like a dull-witted goat due to a rootless rebirth-linking (*eḷamūgatā*). 122.
"Guarded in speech" (*vācānurakkhī*) means one who guards speech by avoiding the four types of verbal misconduct.
"Well-restrained in mind" means not giving rise to covetousness and the other [unwholesome states]. By abandoning killing and so forth, one does no unwholesome deed with the body.
One should act; thus one should purify these three courses of action.
For by purifying them in this way, one will accomplish the Noble Eightfold Path proclaimed by the Sages, such as the Buddha, who are the seekers of the aggregate of virtue and the other perfections.
"Dukkaṭa" refers to that unwholesome, blameworthy action—whether by body, speech, or mind—which has suffering as its outcome and leads to rebirth in the lower realms.
There is none. "Restrained in three ways" means it is closed off by these three causes through the prevention of the entry of bodily misconduct and so forth;
him I call a "brahmin. "Utter immorality" refers to the state of being exclusively immoral.
Even a householder, from birth onwards, [abstains from] the ten unwholesome courses of action...
One who commits a grave offense (garukāpatti) from the day of his full ordination (upasampadā), whether as a novice or a monk, is called "extremely immoral" (accantadussīla).
However, what is stated here refers to the state of immorality that has followed one through successive existences—specifically, one who has been immoral in two or three previous lives.
Furthermore, in this context, "state of immorality" refers to the six doors of the immoral person through which [unwholesome states] arise.
Craving is to be understood. "As the māluvā creeper envelops the sal tree" refers to that person whose immorality is termed craving.

Just as the māluvā creeper, having enveloped a sal tree, covers it entirely by breaking it apart and catching the rainwater with its leaves when it rains, so too does that [craving] stand having enveloped and covered the personal existence (attabhāva).
The meaning is: just as a tree, having been broken by a *māluvā* creeper, falls to the ground,
so too one who has been broken by that craving known as immorality and is falling into the states of misery (*apāya*) makes oneself exactly as one who desires one's harm wishes.
The summarized meaning of the verse beginning with “By oneself indeed is it done” is as follows:

Just as a diamond, which is made of stone and originates from stone, consumes its own source—the stone from which it arose—by making that very stone-jewel perforated, broken, and shattered into pieces so that it becomes unusable; even so, [the evil deed] done by oneself [consumes] within oneself.
The evil born from one's own self destroys, carves up, and shatters the foolish person lacking wisdom within the four states of misery;
this is said because it is to be cultivated [as an enemy].
"Censure" means worthy of reproach. "Of dull intellect" means of weak understanding. "And through the exhaustion of karma..."
Because of the exhaustion of karma through the knowledge that brings about the destruction of karma.

"With mind liberated" means one whose mind is liberated by both the liberation of total eradication (*samuccheda-vimutti*) and the liberation of subsiding (*paṭippassaddhi-vimutti*). "They go out like a flame when the fuel is exhausted":
just as a fire goes out when it has no further fuel, even so does consciousness—which is a formative process—go out through its complete and remainderless exhaustion.
123. Regarding the verse beginning with “Just as the bee,” *bhamara* refers to any species of honey-bee.

*Pupphaṃ* means that while wandering in a flower garden, it moves about without harming the flower, its color, or its fragrance; the meaning is that it moves about without injuring or destroying them.
Having moved in this way, *paleti rasamādāya* means that after drinking as much nectar as it requires, it departs for the purpose of making more honey.

Having taken the sap, it moves on. Having entered a certain dense forest thicket, it deposits that sap mixed with dust within the hollows of trees and other such places; gradually, it transforms it into sweet honey.
Yet, because of its roaming in the flower garden, neither the flower, nor its color, nor its fragrance is destroyed; rather, the flower remains exactly as it was before.

"Thus should a sage wander in the village": the meaning is that a trainee (sekha) or one beyond training (asekha), a sage who has gone forth from the home life, should wander through the village in succession from house to house for alms.
For him, there is no loss of faith or loss of wealth due to wandering in the village; both his faith and his wealth remain as they were. And having wandered thus, he should depart from the village.

Having spread out his outer robe in a place convenient for bathing outside the village and sitting down, he consumes his almsfood while reflecting upon it by way of the similes of greasing an axle, an ointment for a wound, and the flesh of one’s own son.

Then, having entered a suitable forest grove, he comprehends the internal meditation subject and brings the paths and fruits into his very hands. The Asekha Sage, however, devotes himself to dwelling in happiness in this very life.
This is his resemblance to the honey-bee (*madhukara*). However, it is one whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*) who is intended here.
"He dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha": that which protects (*pāti*), guards, and liberates (*mokkheti*) from the sufferings of the states of woe and so forth is the *Pātimokkha*.
That very [restraint] is so called because it restrains and shuts off bodily and verbal transgression.
Restraint. Being restrained and endowed with that restraint of the Pātimokkha, he conducts himself in all modes of behavior.
"Perfect in conduct and resort" means perfect in both conduct and resort. "In even the slightest" means in those that are minor.
"Faults" means unwholesome states. "Seeing danger" means seeing fear. "Having undertaken, he trains in the training rules" means...
Having correctly undertaken whatever is to be trained in among the training rules, he trains in it all.

Regarding the phrase "endowed with wholesome bodily and verbal action, pure in livelihood," although wholesome bodily and verbal actions are already included by the very mention of "conduct" (*ācāra*) and "range of activity" (*gocara*), this virtue of purity of livelihood is nevertheless not [included] among such things as the sky.
It arises, however, only at the doors of body and speech; therefore, in order to show the doors of its arising, it is said:
“endowed with wholesome bodily and verbal action. And because one is endowed with that, one has a pure livelihood;
this was said in order to show that purity of livelihood is indeed virtue itself. For this has been said:
“And what, carpenter, are wholesome virtues? Wholesome bodily action and wholesome verbal action;

I also say, carpenter, that a pure livelihood is virtue. One who has aroused energy is called “one who has aroused energy,” meaning one whose physical and mental energy has been exerted. In this regard, he who, having dispelled attachment to social crowds...
In the four postures, one becomes solitary by means of the eight bases for exertion; his bodily energy is said to be "aroused.

He who, having dispelled mental clutter, becomes solitary by means of the eight attainments, and having suppressed a defilement that has arisen while walking or otherwise at the very place it arose, brings forth jhāna—his energy is mental.
It is called "undertaken. Thus he is one whose energy is undertaken. "Steadfast" means possessing stability. "Firm in effort" means having stable exertion.

"Not casting off the burden... for the sake of realization": not casting off the burden for the purpose of abandoning defiled states, for the purpose of accomplishing purified states, and for the purpose of making them directly manifest, he dwells instigating energy.
“Possessing wisdom” means being endowed with the wisdom that discerns the arising and passing away of the five aggregates.
Therefore he said, “leading to their arising and passing away.
There is no love equal to that for one’s children; even if their own two sons are ugly, parents regard them as if they were golden images.
They imagine [this love] as if they were wearing a garland of flowers upon their heads and so forth while wandering about.
Even when sprinkled or smeared by them, they experience joy as if receiving perfumes and ointments. Therefore it was said: “There is no love equal to that for a son.
What is meant is that there is no love equal to the love for a son. “Cow-like wealth” (*gosama*) means wealth similar to cattle, like a herd of cows. Another...

There is no such thing as "wealth" [in the ultimate sense]. There is no other radiance equal to the radiance of the sun; there is no other light equal to the sun's radiance. Regarding "those whose limit is the ocean":
whatever other bodies of water exist, they all have the ocean as their limit. The ocean is supreme among them;
the Blessed One says that there is no other source of water like the ocean.
For there is no love equal to self-love. Indeed, even abandoning their mother and father, sons and daughters nourish themselves alone. And there is no wealth equal to grain.
For at such a time, even gold, silver, and the like, as well as cattle, buffaloes, and so forth, [are exchanged] for the sake of acquiring grain from the owners of grain alone.
They go along taking [it] with them. Furthermore, there is no radiance equal to wisdom (*paññā*).

For the sun and other luminaries illuminate only a single region and dispel only present darkness; wisdom, however, is able to make even a ten-thousandfold world-system a single blaze of light and shatters the darkness that obscures the past and so forth. And its voice is equal to a rain from a cloud.
There is no such thing as a lake that is equal to rain. Whether it be a river or a pond and so forth, there is no body of water equal to rainfall.
For when the rain from the clouds has ceased, there is not even enough water in the great ocean to wet a finger-joint;
yet while the rain is falling, everything up to the Ābhassara realm becomes one vast expanse of water. Therefore, the Blessed One [considered] the words of the deity...
Speaking verse by verse by way of rejection, he said: “There is no love equal to self,” and so forth.
(124) “What indeed is it that they fear? means: what is it that they are afraid of? “The path has been proclaimed as having many entrances” means:
the path has been explained through many reasons by way of the thirty-eight objects of meditation; this being so, why is it that these people, out of fear, [cling to] the sixty-two [wrong views]?
"He grasped at views," it is said. "Of vast wisdom" means of much wisdom, of abundant wisdom. "He does not fear the next world":
one going from this world to the next world should have no fear.
"Having set aside" means having laid down. "Living as a householder" refers to those such as Anāthapiṇḍika who live in houses with abundant food and drink.
"Vasanto" means "dwelling. "Saṃvibhāgī" means one whose habit is to eat only after having split even what was taken by a finger-nail with a fingernail and given it to another.
"Vadaññū" means one who knows the speech uttered by supplicants through their begging, or one who is worthy of being addressed.
In this context, "vācaṃ" refers to the four types of verbal good conduct; "manaṃ" refers to the three types of mental good conduct; and "kāyena" refers to the three types of bodily good conduct.
These ten courses of wholesome action are called the "preliminary factor of purification.
By the phrase "dwelling in a house with abundant food and drink," the requisites for sacrifice are included. "Faithful" is one factor, "gentle" is one, "liberal" is one, and "charitable" is one;
referring to these four factors, he said, "established in these four qualities."

Another method: there are three factors consisting of the words “speech,” etc.; by the phrase “abundant food and drink,” the requisites for sacrifice are included; and there is one factor consisting of “faithful, gentle, generous, and liberal.
There is also another method called the “pair-method”: there is one factor consisting of “speech and mind”;

one factor consisting of “dwelling at home while committing no evil with the body and providing abundant food and drink”; one factor consisting of “faithful and gentle”; and [one factor] consisting of “generous and liberal.”
"One who stands firm in these four things is called one who stands firm in the Dhamma. Such a person does not fear when going from this world to the next world.
The passage beginning with "In bodily conduct as well... is a demonstration of restraint according to the Pātimokkha. In that context, "twofold" means of two kinds, or by way of two divisions.
"One should know" means one should understand. Furthermore, this discourse on virtue is presented either by way of the courses of action (kamma-patha) or by way of formal designation (paññatti).

Or it may be explained in another way. Therein, when explaining first by way of the courses of kamma (*kammappatha*), the bodily conduct that should not be cultivated should be explained by means of killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct.
By way of the formal rules (*paññatti*), it should be explained by way of the transgression of the training precepts (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed for the door of the body.

Bodily conduct that should be cultivated should be explained by means of the abstinence from killing and so forth, as well as by the non-transgression of the training precepts prescribed for the door of the body.

The conduct of speech that is not to be cultivated should be explained by way of verbal misconduct such as false speech (*musāvāda*) and the transgression of training rules prescribed for the door of speech.

The conduct of speech that is to be cultivated should be explained by way of abstaining from false speech and so forth, and by way of not transgressing the training rules prescribed for the door of speech.
As for "search," however, it refers specifically to search by means of body and speech; although it is included within the mention of bodily and verbal conduct, [it is treated separately].
Since what is called the virtue of the eightfold livelihood arises only at these two doors and not in space, it is stated separately for the purpose of demonstrating that eightfold livelihood.
Therein, the search that is not to be practiced should be discussed under the ignoble search, and the search that is to be practiced under the noble search.
For this has been said: "And what, bhikkhus, is the ignoble search? Here—"
“Monks, a certain person, being himself subject to birth, seeks only that which is subject to birth,” and so forth. Likewise:

“And what, monks, is the noble search? Here, monks, a certain person, being himself subject to birth, having understood the danger in that which is subject to birth, seeks the unborn, the unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna,” and so forth.

170. Regarding the "Eightfold Path": whether it be the paths of the legs and so forth, or the paths of the sixty-two types of views, among all such paths, it is that which—by means of the eight factors beginning with right view—effects the abandoning of the eight evil states beginning with wrong view;
and having made cessation its object, it accomplishes the task of fully understanding suffering and so forth within all four truths.
The eightfold path is the best, the supreme. Regarding the "four feet of the truths," whether it be the truth of speech mentioned in the passage,

"One should speak the truth and not be angry," or conventional truth (sammutisacca) such as the distinctions between "a truthful brahmin" or "a truthful kshatriya," or the truth of views (diṭṭhisacca) such as "this alone is the truth,
all else is false," or [the ultimate truth] expressed as "for there is one truth, there is no second"— [all these are included].

Whether it be the ultimate truth (paramatthasacca) that has been stated, for all these truths, by way of being fully understood, abandoned, realized, developed, and by way of their single penetration and their true penetration, the four terms beginning with "the noble truth of suffering" are indeed called "supreme. As it is said:
"Dispassion is the supreme among states," and so on, up to: "Bhikkhus, to whatever extent..."
Because of the statement, “Whether phenomena are conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (virāga) is declared the foremost among them,” dispassion,
which is synonymous with Nibbāna, is the most excellent of all phenomena.
And because he is “the one with eyes among bipeds,” the Blessed One alone is the most excellent of all bipeds— whether gods, humans, or others— by virtue of possessing the five kinds of vision.

"Foremost" means the most excellent. "As many as" means however many there are. "Footless" refers to those such as snakes and fish, who lack feet. "Two-footed" refers to those such as humans and birds.

"Four-footed" refers to those such as elephants and horses. "Many-footed" refers to those such as centipedes. "Material beings" refers to sentient beings of the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere.
"Non-percipient" refers to sentient beings reborn in the non-percipient realm. "Neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient" refers to sentient beings reborn at the peak of existence.
"It is called 'the foremost' because it is declared to be the foremost, the highest, and the best by virtue of its qualities.
'Of the unconditioned' refers specifically to Nibbāna. 'Dispassion' and so forth are also names for Nibbāna itself;
for by resorting to it, all defilements become dispassionate, and all intoxications such as lust and pride become de-intoxicated—that is, they reach non-existence."
All thirsts are brought to cessation; all attachments are uprooted; the rounds of existence are cut off;
craving is exhausted; all fevers are stilled; the suffering of the round ceases and goes out.
Therefore, it receives these names.
"And the Dhamma is characterized by skill": the Dhamma of that Teacher is skillful and blameless;
precisely because it is blameless, it is unassailed by its opposites—the defilements such as lust and so forth—and by the doctrines of all other sectarians. "These three excel":
these three jewels excel all other jewels in the world; the meaning is that they surpass the entire world by virtue of their qualities.
The "assembly" (gaṇa) refers to a multitude consisting of noble recluses who resemble lotuses.

For "lotus" (paduma) is the name for a water-born flower possessing a full hundred petals. And because noble persons possess qualities that are complete in every respect, they are said to be like lotuses.
"Honored by the wise" means honored by the learned and wise. "Tamer of the best of men."
The meaning is: "the best of men" and "the tamer and leader of men. "Supreme in the world" means standing above the world;
the meaning is that they are the highest in all the world.
"Without fever" means without the fever of passion (*rāga-pariḷāha*) and so forth. "Of true name" means having a name that is not false, by virtue of qualities corresponding to reality.
He whose name has been proclaimed. "All-conqueror" (*Sabbābhibhū*): he stands having overcome the entire world with his own virtues.
"Truth-dharma" (*Saccadhamma*): the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, together with the scriptures, which is non-false because it is the absolute escape from the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*);
for that very reason, there is no other Dhamma superior to him, meaning there is no other Dhamma with qualities greater than his.
The meaning is as follows: the Noble Saṅgha alone is constantly, at all times, honored by the wise, that is, by all the learned.
In the verse beginning with “ekāyanaṃ,” *ekāyana* means the single path. For regarding the path, it is said:
“Path, way, road, track, the straight course, the journey, the passage.”

"A boat, a causeway, a raft, a mat, and a crossing."—These are many names, but here it is spoken of by the name "way" (*ayana*). Therefore, "one-way" (*ekāyana*) means a single path, not one that has become a forked road.
Alternatively, it is "one-way" because it is to be traveled by one alone. Having abandoned the company of crowds, by way of seclusion, one who is secluded...
The meaning is "that which is to be practiced. Or, it is called a "path" (*ayana*) because one goes by means of it; the meaning is that they go from saṃsāra to Nibbāna.
Alternatively, it is "the single path" (*ekāyana*) because it is the path of the Blessed One, the best of all beings.
For although others also go by it, nevertheless, that path belongs to the Blessed One alone, since it was brought forth by him. As it is said: "For that, O Brahmin..."
“The Blessed One is the arouser of the unarisen path,” and so forth. Or, it is called *ayana* because it is a way (*ayati*);
the meaning is that one goes along it or proceeds by means of it. It is the "sole way" (*ekāyana*) because this way exists only in this very Dhamma and Vinaya, and not elsewhere.
As it was said: "In this Dhamma and Vinaya, Subhadda, the Noble Eightfold Path is found. Furthermore, in the preliminary stage...
Although it proceeds by way of various doors of meditation, it goes toward and arrives at only one destination, namely Nibbāna; thus it is "the single path" (*ekāyana*), and that is the "single path.
"One who sees the end of birth" (*jātikhayantadassī*): the "end of birth" (*jātikhayanta*) is the end consisting of the destruction of birth.
Nibbāna is the absolute end of birth; one who sees that is "one who sees the end of birth. There is also a reading: "The compassionate one understands the path."
The meaning of this is as follows: the Blessed One understands with his self-dependent knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*) the path known as the "single way" (*ekāyana*) of the kind already described;
and understanding it, he has compassion for beings through each respective benefit.

Now, in order to clarify the state of being a "single way" of that path and its absolute deliverance throughout the three times, [the text says]: "By this path they crossed over in the past, they will cross over..."

"And those who cross the flood," he said. Its meaning is this: those who in the past crossed the fourfold flood of sensual desire and so forth, those who will cross it in the future, and those who are crossing it now—all of them do so by this very path and not by another.
"Seeking purity" means the ultimate purity, Nibbāna, through the crossing over of the four floods.
"Longing for" means "desiring to attain final Nibbāna.

Having thus analyzed the two-fold foundation of the Dispensation by citing various sūtra passages, [the author] now begins with the words "a worldly sūtra" and so forth, in order to demonstrate it by correlating it with the sections on defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya) and the rest.
Therein, by means of the section on vision (dassanabhāgiya)...
"And by that which pertains to development" means by that which pertains to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
For it is precisely that which pertains to penetration which is shown divided into two parts: that which pertains to seeing (*dassanabhāgiya*) and that which pertains to development.

"Both mundane and supramundane" means that both mundane and supramundane discourses (*sutta*) are to be illustrated by both sets: those beginning with that which pertains to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and those beginning with that which pertains to seeing (*dassanabhāgiya*); this is the intended meaning.

The passage beginning with "In which sutta" and so forth is a demonstration of the manner of pointing out [the classification]. Therein, "pertaining to defilement" (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) means accompanied by a portion of defilement;
the sense is that it illuminates the meaning of defilement. This same method applies to the remaining [terms] as well.
Having thus shown the correlation of the mundane triad with the four terms beginning with "pertaining to defilement," by this—
Since the correlation of the remaining suttas and the remaining terms can be easily understood through this method, those have not been cited here;
rather, in order to show the transcendence of the *saṃkilesabhāgiya* (corruption-partaking) and other types [of suttas], it is said: “The *vāsanābhāgiya* sutta,” and so forth.

In that regard, although both the *saṃkilesabhāgiya* sutta and the *vāsanābhāgiya* sutta are indeed mundane (*lokiya*), nevertheless, just as with supramundane (*lokuttara*) suttas, [the same principle applies] to mundane suttas.
In order to show the meaning that "a discourse dealing with purification serves for the transcendence of a discourse dealing with defilement," it is said:
"A discourse dealing with purification is for the destruction of a discourse dealing with defilement.
Herein, "for the destruction" (*nigghātāya*) means for the abandoning. And it should be understood that by the word "discourse" (*sutta*), the meaning of the discourse is intended. And because...

Just as the plane of development (bhāvanābhūmi) is to be attained by transcending the plane of seeing (dassanabhūmi) regarding defiled states (saṃkilesadhamma), it is like purified states (vodānadhamma);
therefore it is said: "The discourse pertaining to development is for the relinquishing of the discourse pertaining to seeing.
Furthermore, when the qualities of one beyond training (asekkhadhamma) have arisen, there is no longer any function of path-development (maggabhāvanā). As for jhāna-development...

It is solely for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life; therefore it is said: "The discourse pertaining to the Asekhas is for the relinquishing of the discourse pertaining to development; the discourse pertaining to the Asekhas is for the sake of dwelling in happiness in this very life.

Now, in order to show [the relationship] by means of the triple categories themselves, the words beginning with "supramundane" (lokuttara) are stated. Regarding the terms "one-seed" (ekabījī) and so forth: he who, having become a stream-enterer, produces only one more individual existence and then reaches Arahantship, is called a "one-seed. As it has been said:

“And what kind of person is a ‘one-seed’ (ekabījī)? Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment.
Having produced only one more human existence, he makes an end of suffering. This is called a person who is a ‘one-seed.’”
But he who, having wandered and transmigrated through two or three families, makes an end of suffering, is called *kolaṅkolo* (one who goes from family to family).

As it is said: “And what kind of person is *kolaṅkolo*? Here, a certain person is one who has reached the third... [or] the final destination. Having wandered and transmigrated through two or three families, he makes an end of suffering.

This is called a person who is *kolaṅkolo*. In this context, “families” refers to states of existence (*bhava*). “Two or three” is merely a conventional expression here; even one who wanders up to the sixth existence is indeed *kolaṅkolo*.
But he who, having transmigrated through seven existences, makes an end of suffering, is called "one for whom there are seven births at most. As it is said:
"And what kind of person is one for whom there are seven births at most? Here, a certain person... [omitted] ...is his final destination.
Having wandered and transmigrated among gods and humans for seven times, he makes an end of suffering. This is called the person..."
"Seven times at most.
But what determines this classification for them? Some say it is "determined by past causes";
some say "the first path"; some say "the three higher paths"; and some say "the insight associated with the three paths."

In that regard, if one asserts that "the prior cause determines [the result]," it follows that while the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the first path has been established, the three subsequent paths would have arisen without such a decisive support.
If one asserts that "the first path determines [the result]," it follows that the three subsequent paths would be rendered purposeless.
If one asserts that "the three subsequent paths determine [the result]," then [it follows that] while the first path has not yet arisen...
Thus one would fall into the position that the three higher paths have already arisen. However, the doctrine that insight (vipassanā) determines [the result] is logical.
For if the insight for the three higher paths is powerful, one is called an "ekabījī" (one-seeded). If it is weaker than that, one is a "kolaṃkolo" (one who goes from family to family).
If it is weaker than that, one is a "sattakkhattuparamo" (one who has seven births at most). And in this context, he who [is a sattakkhattuparamo] among humans alone...
One who attains Arahantship after wandering through saṃsāra [seven times], and one who attains Arahantship after wandering only among the devas seven times—these are not intended here.
However, one who attains Arahantship by wandering through saṃsāra in a mixed manner, sometimes among the devas and sometimes among humans, is intended here.
Therefore, this term "one for whom there are seven births at most" (sattakkhattuparama) refers to him.
This should be understood by way of one whose inclination is toward the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭajjhāsaya*) mixed with the eight stages of realization.
For one whose inclination is toward the cycle, having purified the six celestial worlds from the very beginning and established himself in Akaniṭṭha, will attain final Nibbāna there.
Among them, he who makes faith his primary faculty and realizes the path of stream-entry is a *saddhānusārī* (faith-follower) at the moment of the path.

...is the name [of one liberated by faith]. At the moment of the fruit, however, having become one liberated by faith, he is classified as an "ekabījī" (one-seeder) and so forth, according to the method already described.
But he who, making wisdom his primary focus, realizes the path of stream-entry, is called a "dhammānusārī" (follower by Dhamma) at the moment of the path.
At the moment of the fruit, however, having become a "diṭṭhippatto" (one who has attained vision), he is classified as an "ekabījī" and so forth. And this [applies] to the eight...
This was stated by way of those who have not yet attained the liberations. However, one who has attained them is called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī) at the moment of the fruition.

In that context, regarding the three types of stream-enterers known as "liberated by faith," "attained to view," and "body-witness," they are subsumed under the three beginning with the "one-seeder" (ekabījī), and it is said:
"It is to be demonstrated by five persons: the one-seeder... [and so on]... the follower by Dhamma. Thus, there are five.

"By twelve persons" means: the one standing on the path of the once-returner (sakadāgāmimaggaṭṭha), the once-returner (sakadāgāmī), the one standing on the path of the non-returner (anāgāmimaggaṭṭha), the non-returner generally (anāgāmī without distinction), the five types beginning with the one who attains nibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyi), and the three—namely, the one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta), the one attained to vision (diṭṭhippatta), and the body-witness (kāyasakkhi)—making eight when distinguished;
thus, there are twelve. For among them, whoever [remains] in the Aviha heaven and so forth, at various points up to the midpoint of their lifespan...

One who attains parinibbāna without reaching [the midpoint of the lifespan] is one who attains parinibbāna in the interval (*antarāparinibbāyī*). However, one who reaches *arahantship* after having passed the middle of the lifespan is one who attains parinibbāna upon arrival (*upahaccaparinibbāyī*).

Likewise, one who, having been reborn in the Aviha heaven or others, realizes *arahantship* without volitional effort (*asaṅkhāra*) and with little exertion, is one who attains parinibbāna without volitional effort (*asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī*).
But one who [reaches it] with volitional effort (*sasaṅkhāra*) and with exertion...
He attains arahantship; this one is "one who attains parinibbāna with exertion. He has an upward stream of rebirth toward the higher Brahma-worlds, thus he is "one who goes upstream" (*uddhaṃsota*).
He goes to Akaniṭṭha by way of rebirth-linking, thus he is "one who goes to Akaniṭṭha" (*akaniṭṭhagāmī*).
In that regard, there is one who goes upstream and goes to Akaniṭṭha, there is one who goes upstream but does not go to Akaniṭṭha, and there is one who... [does not go upstream].
"One who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm" and "one who neither goes upstream nor to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

In this context, one who has attained the fruit of non-returning here, is reborn in the Aviha realm or others, and having remained there for the full span of that life, is reborn successively higher until reaching the Akaniṭṭha realm—this is called "one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm. However, one who is reborn in the Aviha realm or others and remains right there...

One who, without attaining final Nibbāna and without reaching the Akaniṭṭha realm, attains final Nibbāna in progressively higher Brahmā worlds, is called an "Upstreamer" (uddhaṃsota) who does not go to Akaniṭṭha.
One who, having passed away from here, is reborn specifically in Akaniṭṭha, is called an "Upstreamer" who goes to Akaniṭṭha.
However, one who is reborn in any one of the four [heavens] beginning with Aviha and attains final Nibbāna right there—[is neither of these two].
This person is called neither "one who goes upstream" nor "one who goes to Akaniṭṭha. Those liberated by faith and so forth are exactly as classified in what has been stated above.
Regarding the phrase "by nine persons": here, an Arahant who has not attained the eight liberations is called "liberated by wisdom" (paññāvimutta).

However, one who has attained them is [called] "liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta) by virtue of the liberation consisting in suppression and the liberation consisting in eradication, from what is designated as the body of form and the body of name respectively.

Because he is liberated from both parts, he is called "one liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*). Regarding the term "one who has reached the peak simultaneously" (*samasīsī*), there are three kinds of such persons:

one who reaches the peak simultaneously in terms of posture (*iriyāpatha*), one who reaches the peak simultaneously in terms of illness (*roga*), and one who reaches the peak simultaneously in terms of life (*jīvita*).

Among these, the one who [reaches the peak simultaneously] in postures such as standing is one who, having been endowed with whichever posture he was in when he began insight meditation (*vipassanā*)...
One who exerts effort and, having attained Arahantship in that very posture, passes away into Parinibbāna, is called one for whom the posture is the head (iriyāpathasamasīsī).

Furthermore, one who, having fallen ill, establishes insight while still within the illness, attains Arahantship, and passes away into Parinibbāna through that very illness, is called one for whom the illness is the head (rogasamasīsī). Craving is the head of obstacles; it is the head of bondage.
Pride has conceit as its head; views have misapprehension as their head; agitation has distraction as its head; defilements have ignorance as their head;
resolve has faith as its head; exertion has energy as its head; establishment has mindfulness as its head; non-distraction has concentration as its head;
seeing has wisdom as its head; occurrence has the life-faculty as its head; the range has liberation as its head; and formations have cessation as their head.
Among the thirteen heads [of phenomena], the path of arahantship exhausts ignorance, which is the head of the defilements;

the death-consciousness exhausts the life-faculty, which is the head of the process of existence. In this regard, the consciousness that exhausts ignorance is not able to exhaust the life-faculty, and the consciousness that exhausts the life-faculty is not able to exhaust ignorance. There is another [consciousness] that exhausts ignorance...

The mind is one thing, and the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) is another that reaches its exhaustion. One for whom these two heads reach exhaustion simultaneously is called "one whose head is level with life" (jīvitasamasīsī). But how is this simultaneous?
By way of equality of the occasion (vāra). For at whichever occasion the emergence from the path occurs—whether it be the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga)—[the two reach their end together].
There are five kinds of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa): five in the path of once-returning, five in the path of non-returning, and four in the path of arahantship.

Having established himself in these nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge, when he descends into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and attains final Nibbāna, by this twelfth equality, even this "equality of the two ends" (ubhayasīsapariyādāna) is indeed equal.
Therefore, this person is called "one whose end of life is equal to his end of the hair-tuft" (jīvitasamasīsī).

This [specific type] alone is intended here. Thus, the three—emptiness-liberated and so forth—namely, the faith-liberated, the wisdom-liberated, the both-ways-liberated, and the one who has attained the summit;
these seven disciples who are Arahants, together with the Paccekabuddha and the Sammasambuddha:
by means of these nine persons, the discourse pertaining to the state of one beyond training (asekkha-bhāgiya) is to be demonstrated.
*Rāgacarito* means one whose conduct (*carita*) is accompanied by lust; thus he is a *rāgacarito*. Alternatively, one who has acted or proceeded with lust is a *rāgacarito*;

the meaning is that his underlying tendency (*ajjhāsaya*) is lust, or that lust predominates in him. This same method applies to the remaining terms as well. *Rāgamukhe ṭhito* means standing in the state of being overwhelmed by lust (*rāgapariyuṭṭhāna*);
the meaning is that his lust is currently active. The same method applies to the other phrases too.
“Discourse pertaining to purification by habituation” (*vāsanābhāgiya-sutta*): this refers to a mundane discourse (*lokiya*) based on sentient beings (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*) that pertains to habituation.
For a discourse based on sentient beings that pertains to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) is demonstrated by persons of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*).

In that context, having applied the two terms “mundane” and “based on sentient beings” as recurring [to all subsequent categories], it is stated as “pertaining to habituation. “By those possessing virtue” (*sīlavantehi*) means by those possessing virtue and so forth.
"By persons. "Natural virtue," and so forth: those who are endowed with these are the persons (*puggala*). By mentioning them, there is a characterization of persons.
Alternatively, this method is shown by stating, "it should be demonstrated by means of those possessing virtue," following which "natural virtue," and so forth, is given;

thus it should be understood that the teaching is based on phenomena (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*) by way of natural virtue and so on, while it is based on beings (*sattādhiṭṭhāna*) by way of those possessing natural virtue and so on.

This has been stated. That mention of only the five types, beginning with natural virtue (*pakatisīla*), is merely illustrative, since the giving of merit, rejoicing in merit, hearing the Dhamma, teaching the Dhamma, and the rectification of views are also possible here.
Or rather, it is said "five" for the purpose of showing that these [other factors] too are included within this very category.
Therein, "natural virtue" refers to the virtue of abstinence acquired by nature. "Clarity of mind" refers to faith in the fruit of karma and faith in the Triple Gem.
“Knowledge (ñāṇa) should be demonstrated by means of wisdom (paññā)” means that in whatever sutta wisdom is mentioned, that sutta should be demonstrated as knowledge.

To show that it is not only by way of synonyms for wisdom, but also by way of synonyms such as the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya), that wherever wisdom is mentioned, that sutta should be demonstrated as knowledge, the words beginning with “by the faculty of wisdom” are stated. Its meaning is as follows:
— This has already been stated below. Regarding the phrase "or whatever else," etc.: "or whatever else" refers to any other designation for wisdom (*paññā*).
The meaning is that all such [designations] wherever they appear in a discourse (*sutta*) should be pointed out as "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*).
By "internal and external" is meant those discourses in which the internal sense-bases (*āyatana*) and the external sense-bases are mentioned.
That sutta should be demonstrated by those bases as "knowledge" and "the knowable.
Wisdom (paññā), being itself an object, is stated separately from the "knowable";

for wisdom is sometimes spoken of as being in the state of the knowable in a sutta, since it is the object of another instance of knowledge. "Whatever has become an object" means whatever has become the domain of knowledge.
"Form and so forth. By the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "whether internal or external," it includes the coarse and so on.

"All that, by way of the conditioned and the unconditioned": all of that should be demonstrated as knowable (*ñeyya*) according to its occurrence, both by way of its state as conditioned and its state as unconditioned.
For it is called the "Sutta on the Knowable" (*ñeyyasutta*) because of the knowable phenomena (*ñeyyadhamma*).

Or whatever particular statement the Blessed One speaks—referring to two [types of] suttas among the worldly, supramundane, and so forth—among those, he speaks and demonstrates a particular statement as the teaching of one [sutta] alone.
All that, exactly as it has been demonstrated, should be retained; just as all the suttas among the worldly and others... if...
Whether by way of one factor or by way of both, it should be understood exactly as it has been demonstrated;
the meaning is that each [factor] should be shown as being predominant. It is said:

"The cause is twofold: that which is karma accompanied by defilements is the cause of fruition, but not the other. Thus, it is stated that only karma together with defilements is the cause of fruition, and not otherwise.
"And those defilements. Regarding the phrase "the origin is the defilements": here, by the term "origin," those factors belonging to the side of origination are expressed.

And by the term "defilements," the meaning is those who possess defilements, that is, those who are defiled. "Whatever is seen" means whatever is seen. "In their respective planes" refers to the plane of ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) and so forth.
"In accordance with what is allowable and what conforms to what is allowable" means both by what is allowable (*kappiya*) and by what conforms to what is allowable (*kappiyānuloma*).

In this regard, what is allowable (*kappiya*) is stated explicitly in the text (*pāḷi*), while what conforms to the allowable (*kappiyānuloma*) is shown by way of inference through the Great Authorities (*mahāpadesa*).
"By the reason for which it was prohibited" means that whatever was prohibited by the Blessed One must be demonstrated by that very reason;
for the Blessed One prohibited only those things that invariably lead to states such as lust (*sarāga*). That [should be identified].
It should be demonstrated by way of being a cause for leading toward passion (*sarāga*) and so forth. "Of the Dhamma" means of the unconditioned Dhamma (*asaṅkhata-dhamma*).
"Of the noble Dhammas" means of the Dhammas consisting of the paths and fruits (*magga-phala*). The rest is easily understood.

And here, just as there is a manifold classification of the *paṭṭhāna* (conditional relations) from the mutual conjunction of the sections dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and so forth, [so too is it here].
In this way, even through the combination of worldly beings as the basis and so forth, many varieties of the *Paṭṭhāna* (Conditional Relations) are possible.

However, it should be understood that in the Pāḷi, both [categories] are presented by way of showing a single portion, for they can indeed be determined by a wise person through this method (*naya*). And just as with the sections dealing with defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and so forth, and the worldly (*lokiya*) and so forth—
This classification of the *Paṭṭhāna* is obtained in many ways according to the various types of combinations taken individually;

likewise, this method is certainly obtainable as appropriate for both combined together. For indeed, among the mundane discourses (*lokiya-sutta*), some pertain to defilement (*saṃkilesabhāgiya*) and some pertain to purification (*vāsanābhāgiya*).
Similarly, among the supramundane discourses (*lokuttara-sutta*), some pertain to penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*).
"Something pertaining to the state of one beyond training (asekkha). The same method applies to the remaining [categories] as well.

Thus, having added the twenty-eightfold *paṭṭhāna* to the sixteenfold *paṭṭhāna*, and having added the sixteenfold *paṭṭhāna* to the twenty-eightfold *paṭṭhāna*, the classification of the *paṭṭhāna* occurs according to its possibility through the appropriate divisions such as the dyads and triads.
It is to be understood by means of the textual passages found within the three Piṭakas. However,

since it would result in excessive prolixity and an overly burdensome commentary on the Nettippakaraṇa if each of those various textual passages were selected as examples and explained in detail for this meaning,
and since a wise person is capable of understanding this meaning through this method, [it is not done].
Therefore, we have not elaborated upon it. For this very reason, in the Pāḷi, the analysis of the *Paṭṭhāna* by way of mutual conjunction is shown only partially, and not exhaustively.
The commentary on the section on the *Sāsana-paṭṭhāna* is concluded.
The Concluding Statement:
And to this extent—
regarding the Hāras, the Nayas, and the Paṭṭhāna— there has been a thoroughly purified determination.
Analyzing the commentary on the meaning of the ninefold teaching,
the wise and masterful Great Elder Mahākaccāyana taught this *Nettippakaraṇa*, which is profound and subtle.
While residing in the monastery of the Great King Dhammāsoka,
in the city called Nāga, a place for entering the True Dhamma,
I have composed this commentary on its meaning for the sake of its long endurance.
Fully elucidating the meaning of the illustrative suttas and all their characteristics, this work— with its systematic analysis—
is completed from the recitation section of the twenty-seven canonical texts.
Thus, by compiling this, through the power of whatever merit I have attained,
having plunged into the teaching of the Lord of the World with purified practice of virtue and the rest—
May all embodied beings partake of the essence of liberation.
May the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One endure for a long time in the world,
and may all living beings always maintain reverence for it.
"May the rain fall properly in due season,
and may the Lord of the World, the King, who delights in the True Dhamma, govern the world by means of the Dhamma alone.
Thus was it composed by the teacher Dhammapāla, a resident of the Badaratittha Monastery.
The commentary on the meaning of the *Nettippakaraṇa* is completed.
The *Nettippakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā* is finished.
